content: Mikhail Bulgakov’s The Master and Margarita presents the story of Christ’s Passion curiously interwoven with a modern love-story, and with the adventures in twentieth-century Moscow of a mysterious stranger and his obstreperous retinue. By general consent one of the most important and original works of fiction to have emerged from the Soviet Union, it has been, since its posthumous publication in 1966-7, the subject of immense interest and debate. Dr Barratt’s book, the first comprehensive study of Bulgakov’s novel in English, begins with an account of its evolution and its reception inside and outside Russia. In the second part, the author puts forward, against the background of other critical approaches, his own interpretation of the key questions: the problem of the stranger’s identity, the meaning of the biblical narrative, and the place of The Master and Margarita in the European tradition. Andrew Barratt is Senior Lecturer in Russian, Otago University, New Zealand.

ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS Working on this book has taught me above all how much liter- ary criticism is a co-operative venture, and I take pleasure in recording my thanks to those who have given me their help. Colin Wright, Ellendea Proffer, and Donald Fiene were most generous in providing materials and in sharing the results of their scholarship. Julie Curtis read an early manuscript in which I first set out some of the ideas developed in the present study, making a number of useful suggestions for improve- ment. Carol Avins read a substantial part of the final manus- cript with a careful eye, and offered sound judgement and advice. My greatest indebtedness is to Lesley Milne, who has read everything I have written on Bulgakov, and whose patient guidance has been immensely valuable. Turning closer to home, I wish to thank Eric Herd for advice on mat- ters Faustian, and Albert Moore for sharing his expertise on religious subjects. Janet Gootjes dealt efficiently and cheer- fully with the drudgery that is the lot of research assistants; and Elizabeth Carruthers was the very model of a perfect sec- retary. To the staff of the University of Otago Library I am grateful for their promptness in supplying the many materials I requested from overseas. The University of Otago granted me a period of study leave during which the bulk of the back- ground work for this study was carried out. I would also like to record my gratitude to my colleagues, Peter Stupples, the late Jim Harvie, and Tom Gott for taking on the extra duties which resulted from my absence, and to the many students who have listened without complaint to my lectures on The Master and Margarita over the years. Their interest and enthu- siasm for the novel have been the source of lasting inspiration. Finally, to my wife Barbara I extend my deepest gratitude for her constant support and encouragement.

NOTE ON TRANSLITERATION AND TRANSLATION The system of transliteration used in this study is basically the one recommended by the Slavonic and East European Review, although in the main text I have made the usual concessions to common usuage (e.g. -sky for -skiy; Gogol for Gogol’). In rendering the proper names encountered in Bulgakov’s novel, I have chosen to transliterate, rather than translate. Thus I refer to Ivan Bezdomny (not ‘Homeless’), and to Mark Krysoboy (not ‘Rat-Killer’). Where Bulgakov has employed standard biblical names, I employ the forms found in the King James version (hence, Pilate, Judas, Behemoth, etc.); the non-standard forms, to which the author dedicated such attention, I have transliterated (hence, Ieshua, Yershalaim, Bar-rabban, etc.). Note, however, that I have preferred the forms Meigel and Aphranius (rather than Maygel, Afrany), and that I refer to the chapters containing the New Testament narrative as the ‘Jerusalem story’. All translations from the Russian are my own, unless otherwise indicated.

INTRODUCTION To produce a book about a book is to incur a debt of expla- nation somewhat larger than that which normally attends the writing of literary criticism. Yet, in the case of The Master and Margarita at least, it is not difficult to justify what might on the face of it seem a rather extravagant venture. Since its first appearance nearly twenty years ago, Bulgakov’s novel has been universally acknowledged as one of the few truly great masterpieces of modern Russian fiction. Although it was spared the sort of celebrity in the Western world which attached to the publication of Solzhenitsyn’s Cancer Ward or Pasternak’s Doctor Zhivago, its reputation as a ‘modern classic’ is now firmly enough established for it to be included in the teaching programme of almost every college and university offering courses in modern Russian literature. More significantly, the fact that The Master and Margarita (again in contrast to Cancer Ward and Doctor Zhivago) has actually been published within the Soviet Union has meant that, unlike them, it has been able to take its rightful place as a major landmark in the official cultural history of that country. These factors aside, there is another, more weighty, reason for submitting Bulgakov’s novel to the sort of detailed exam- ination envisaged here. The fact is that The Master and Mar- garita is a most complex and difficult book; it belongs to that group of literary works which seem not merely to invite, but actually to demand the attention of the professional critic. Where Cancer Ward, or even Doctor Zhivago—to remain with our original comparison—may be fairly readily compre- hended on a surface level, Bulgakov’s novel has repeatedly been found, even by experienced and well-informed readers, to be as perplexing as it is entertaining, offering so many clues to understanding that it inevitably thwarts any initial attempt to unravel its meaning. As Edmund Wilson has remarked of Joyce’s Ulysses, so we may say with equal cer- tainty of The Master and Margarita that it is doubtful whether

2 Introduction any human memory is capable, on a first reading, of meeting its demands. ' Like other modern novels which throw down a defiant chal- lenge to make sense of them, The Master and Margarita has not been failed by brave souls willing to enter unto the breach. Indeed, the prediction made in 1967 by Michael Glenny, author of one of the novel’s English translations, that “volumes and volumes of criticism and exegesis will be written on it in years to come’ has been realized perhaps more quickly than he might have anticipated.” Even within a few years of the novel’s publication, scores of articles had appeared offering a great variety of answers to the question on everybody’s lips: what is it all about? Since that time, The Master and Margarita has continued to support a thriving critical industry which shows no sign of exhaustion. It was, in fact, the very volume of the secondary literature generated by The Master and Margarita which first convinced me that a study of the present sort might prove useful. I still remember very well the difficulties I experienced when teaching the novel for the first time. Having read the text carefully (or at least what I believed then to be carefully), I turned to the available critical material for guid- ance and illumination only to find myself in a position not unlike that of Tolstoy’s Pierre, who, at the time of his ill- starred association with the Freemasons, felt astonishment at ‘the infinite variety of human minds, which ensures that no truth is perceived identically by two people’. Subsequent study has served only to confirm my initial suspicion that it would be well-nigh impossible to unearth any statement about the novel’s meaning that has not been contradicted by at least one other commentator. This is not to say that Bulgakov has been poorly served by his critics. Nevertheless, I believe that for the reader coming to the novel for the first time, the secondary literature is liable to represent a barrier by no means less formidable than the text of the book itself. Introduction 3 bulk: if one wanted to read everything that has been written on The Master and Margarita one would need considerable reserves of time, not to mention fortitude. Almost inevitably, there is also a great deal of duplication, especially among those studies written during the early 1970s. By far the great- est source of difficulty, however, is the one to which I have already referred—the seemingly uncontrollable proliferation of alternative interpretations. It is not that these divergences of opinion are in themselves a matter for concern; on the con- trary, they are a natural, and even desirable consequence of critical engagement with a novel as baffling as Bulgakov’s. Yet for those coming to the novel for the first time it is no easy matter to find a way through this ever-growing body of litera- ture, and to identify the particular critical issues to be addressed. It is for these new readers of The Master and Margarita that the present study has been written. The main material of the book is divided into two sections. In Part I, I set out to pro- vide certain basic information about the novel—its reception, the evolution of the text, its published versions, and so on— and also to consider a number of critical approaches which have commonly been applied to the novel over the years. The five chapters of Part II constitute a personal reading of The Master and Margarita, dealing in turn with the ‘shape’ of the Moscow plot; Bulgakov’s version of the Passion narrative; the story of the Master and Margarita; the connection with Goethe’s Faust; and Bulgakov’s last-minute addition—the Epilogue. Although no particular methodology has been adopted in the interpretative chapters, their organization has been deter- mined above all by a conscious desire to reproduce, as far as possible, the experience of grappling with the peculiar difficul- ties that Bulgakov’s novel presents to the reader. I have attempted, in particular, to keep in mind at all times the vast difference between what it means to read the novel and to re-read it. This distinction is important for a discussion of any fictional work, but in the case of The Master and Margarita it is crucially so. For like many ‘playful’ modern texts, this is a novel which sets its readers a distinct hermeneutic task. As we read this book we are confronted by a number of puzzles

4 Introduction which permit no easy solution, making us constantly aware of our limited understanding. But we are, at the same time, invited to transcend this unenlightened condition by engaging in a ceaseless activity of questioning and re-evaluation. The very difficulty of the novel thus turns out to be its central theme and the aim of interpretation becomes less a matter of extracting some ‘philosophy’ from it than an attempt to focus on the nature of understanding itself. It may be true, as one critic has recently suggested, that the main ideas of The Master and Margarita can be boiled down to a few key statements (‘Manuscripts don’t burn’, ‘Jesus existed’, “Everything will turn out right. That’s what the world is built on’);+ yet this must be considered only the beginning, not the end of inter- pretation in the sense intended here. In putting forward an account of the novel’s meaning which is necessarily a personal one, I have nevertheless kept in mind the need to situate this endeavour against the background of existing critical opinion. This I have done by summarizing representative arguments, and by taking particular account of those readings which differ from my own. As a result, I have been more than usually explicit not only about specific points of disagreement, but also about the critical assumptions which inform the many competing interpretations and approaches. As for my own assumptions, I shall endeavour to make these as clear as possible in the course of the analysis itself. But it will be as well to explain from the outset that my reading of the novel conforms to critical orthodoxy in one basic respect. From my remarks in the previous paragraph, it will be obvious that I view The Master and Margarita, quite unorigi- nally, as a roman-zagadka—a ‘puzzle-novel’. To adopt this pos- ition is to imply that the job of the critic is to seek a perspective from which the enigma may be dispelled. This type of venture has come under intense fire in these post-struc- turalist days, and the only defence that can be offered is, of necessity, a circular appeal to the novel’s generic status. As Laura Weeks put it in a recent article, ‘the text so obviously + A. C. Wright, ‘Mikhail Bulgakov’s Developing World View’, Canadian-American Slavic Studies, xv (Nos. 2—3,1981), p.16r.

Introduction 2 demands a resolution. Riddles, after all, are meant to be solved.”® These explanations and caveats recorded, it remains only to mention some of the special problems which beset the study of Bulgakov. The difficulties stem, in the first place, from the paucity of the documentary material available for inspection. By this I mean not so much to complain of the practical diffi- culty of gaining access to Soviet archives (which seems des- tined to remain a perennial hindrance to Western scholars), but rather to indicate the simple absence of many of the items which would be of immense potential usefulness.” In some cases, these deficiencies are directly attributable to a natural reticence on Bulgakov’s part. In common with his usual prac- tice, for example, he seems to have left no record of his author- ial intention regarding The Master and Margarita. Nor do we have much in the way of authenticated comments by Bulgakov on the work of other writers, especially of his con- temporaries. Besides providing invaluable information about his literary attitudes, such comments would also help to fill the more basic need for precise knowledge of his reading habits. This latter problem is all the more acute as both of the personal libraries accumulated by Bulgakov—the one left behind in Kiev in 1919, and the larger one which remained in his Moscow apartment after his death—have been almost entirely lost.’ Anyone who has consulted the burgeoning liter- ature which has grown up around the subject of the possible sources for The Master and Margarita will testify to the confu- sion and controversy that have been the fruits of this partial knowledge.” 9 L. The partial des- truction by Bulgakov himself of the notebooks containing the first version of The Master and Margarita, and the total destruc- tion, again by the writer’s own hand, of his diaries for the years 1926-9 represent a serious handicap to our knowledge and understanding of this crucial period in his life.? Equally regrettable is the apparent disappearance of at least some of the many materials gathered by P. S. Although a substantial number of memoirs have appeared over the last few years, including those of the writer’s second wife,'* these must be reckoned a meagre compensation for what has been lost. The consequences for any serious study of the writer are obvious. Although the assiduous efforts of a number of scho- lars have made it possible to construct a fairly detailed and reliable chronicle of Bulgakov’s life and work, the possibilities for a proper biography seem as remote as ever.'? Without a precise record of the day-to-day working of his mind and, more particularly, without more intimate knowledge of his intellectual pursuits, it seems unlikely that we will ever pen- etrate the core of his enigmatic personality. Bulgakova, and the writer’s own letters—would make the task of the biographer more feasible at least, it is far from sure that this would furnish enough material to form a comprehensive picture of Bulgakov’s emotional and intellectual development. It has to be accepted, therefore, that we must endeavour to elucidate the meaning of The Master and Margarita without havy- ing in our possession many of the necessary safeguards against the immoderate speculation to which even the most respected of the novel’s critics have at times been prone. And this is not to mention what must inevitably be accounted the most serious difficulty of all—the absence of a truly authoritative canonical text with which to work. This is a subject to which we will return in detail in Chapter 2. These are not the only problems confronting the student of Bulgakov. Even more harmful, in some respects, is the preva- lence, both within the Soviet Union and more especially in the West, of what might be termed a ‘Bulgakov cult’. The very circumstances under which The Master and Margarita came to be written and then rescued ‘from the desk drawer’ in which it had lain hidden for a quarter of a century have been sufficient in themselves to make Bulgakov yet another candidate— alongside Mandelstam, Babel, Akhmatova, Pasternak and so many others—for canonization as a martyr in the cause of free art. This is a natural, and necessary antidote to the alternat- ing campaigns of vitriolic criticism and hostile silence to which these writers were subjected during (and after) their own lifetime. Yet, as Clarence Brown wisely reminds us in a short essay on Mandelstam, ‘a cult disadvantages no one so much as its own object.’'* The greatest danger is that what begins perhaps as an honourable desire to ignore the writer’s warts devolves almost imperceptibly into the production of homiletics and even hagiography. When Vladimir Lakshin, to take an extreme example, writes that ‘Bulgakov bore the afflictions of his difficult literary path without martyrdom and without laceration’,'® he is promoting a romantic image of the '4 Clarence Brown, ‘On reading Mandel’stam’, in: O. One senses that it was in obedience to a similar impulse that Yury Lyubimoy, the director of the controversial Moscow stage version of The Master and Margarita chose to have the actors parade before the audience at the end of the perfor- mance bearing large photographic portraits of Bulgakov.'® Under prevailing conditions such reverential attitudes are likely to remain very firmly in place, yet we should not allow ourselves to be diverted from what they hide. On the basis of what we know for certain, it would not be difficult to compose a thoroughly uncharitable sketch of Bulgakov as an unrepen- tant bourgeois; a cultural snob; an individual at times patho- logically sensitive to criticism and with an unhealthy desire for fame and fortune; and a paranoid depressive reduced to writ- ing wish-fulfilment fantasies in which his enemies are routed. I would certainly not want to write such an iconoclastic piece myself—even to suggest that it could be written is probably enough to bring the wrath of many of the writer’s admirers upon my head. But this is my point, and if there is a lesson here, it is that the student of Soviet literature—perhaps more than the student of any other literature—must always guard against the lures of mythology, especially when that myth- ology has itself arisen as a counter-response to the myths officially promoted within the Soviet Union. THE NOVEL AND ITS RECEPTION Up until the winter of 1966, the literary journal Moskva led a quiet and generally undistinguished existence. A metropolitan monthly with a reputation for political conservatism, it occu- pied the broad middle ground between Novy mir—the nerve- centre of liberal sentiment since the 1950s—and such sentinels of orthodoxy as Oktyabr’ and Znamya. Even though it had not entirely avoided controversy (it had, in fact, come under strong fire from the establishment in 1957 for printing some stories by Konstantin Simonov)' its main claim to fame had resided in its policy of publishing writers whose works had been suppressed during the Stalin era, such as Bunin and Mandelstam. However, the publication, in the November issue for 1966, of the first part of The Master and Margarita was an event in the journal’s history of far greater magnitude than anything that had gone before. Within only hours of its appearance, the entire printing of 150,000 copies had been sold, and, together with the January 1967 issue (in which the second part of the novel was duly published) it became one of the most sought-after literary items in the Soviet Union.” No work since Solzhenitsyn’s then four-year-old One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich had created such an immediate sensation. In one important respect, the publication of The Master and Margarita was not quite the bombshell that Solzhenitsyn’s tale had been. The work of an author hitherto unknown to the Soviet reading public, One Day had come very much from out of the blue. Bulgakov’s novel, on the other hand, was the natu- ral—although none the less spectacular—climax of a process of posthumous rehabilitation that had been in train for more than a decade. 12 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives Bulgakov’s name, like those of many of his contemporaries, had first begun to be mentioned again in the years immedi- ately following the death of Stalin. In due course, his works too began to resurface, and, by the end of the fifties, several of his plays had been revived with outstanding success. But it was not until the sixties that his works started to find their way into print again. A long-awaited volume of his drama appeared in 1962,° as did a previously unpublished fictiona- lized biography of Moliére.* The following years saw a steady flow of publications: stories from the early cycle Notes of a Young Doctor;> Theatrical Romance, an unfinished satirical novel based on the author’s experiences at the Moscow Art Theatre;° an expanded edition of the plays;’ and, finally, a selection of prose works, including Bulgakov’s first novel, The White Guard.® With the appearance of each of these works the author’s reputation and following grew steadily. But it was only with the release of The Master and Margarita that the true discovery of the writer got under way. Only now could his career be viewed in its proper perspective. Hitherto, Bulgakov had been noted primarily for his contribution to the Soviet theatre; now it was as the author of this magnificent last novel that he registered his principal claim to greatness. Given the peculiar conditions of Soviet social and cultural life, The Master and Margarita was tailor-made for a succés de scandale. Here was a novel written during the dark era of the great purges, a novel whose very existence had for many years been known only to a trusted circle of the writer’s family and friends, a novel which, moreover, had more recently become the subject of increasingly exciting rumour and speculation. Yet who could possibly have anticipated its startling artistic novelty or the devastating power of its satire of so many aspects of Soviet life, not to mention the presence—almost unthinkable in a Soviet novel—of the historical Jesus as one of the central characters? The Novel and its Reception 13 of the author’s literary imagination been displayed in such measure. But this was not all. Perhaps even more importantly, The Master and Margarita struck a live nerve in the contempor- ary Russian audience in a way that none of Bulgakov’s earlier works could possibly have done. For this novel touched directly on the collective experience of guilt and introspection about the Stalin period which has even yet to be exorcised from the Russian mind. ‘Manuscripts don’t burn!’: the now famous words from the novel instantly became a proverb and a slogan. Simultaneously, they embodied a pledge of the indestructibility of art, and—for a short time, at least— revived hopes, both at home and abroad, that the process of ‘de-Stalinization’ was not completely at an end. ETE VOm LR NGAT CONE In retrospect, it is evident that The Master and Margarita appeared at a crucial moment in recent Soviet history. By 1966 the prospects for literature, as indeed for political life as a whole, did not look at all promising. The second Thaw of 1962 (the year of One Day and Yevtushenko’s poem “The Heirs of Stalin’) had given way, like the original Thaw of 1956, to a period of renewed vigilance. As early as 1963, political com- mentators in the West were already drawing attention to the signs of growing intolerance towards liberalization in the arts. With the ousting of Khrushchev the following year, things grew perceptibly worse, and the arrest, in 1965, of two writers, Andrey Sinyavsky and Yuliy Daniel, for publishing their works outside the Soviet Union was immediately interpreted as a declaration of purpose by the country’s new leaders. Although Solzhenitsyn probably overstates the case when he speaks of this as part of a planned ‘abrupt return to Stali- nism’,? there can be no doubt that this event signalled the beginning of a new and critical period for the Soviet intelli- gentsia. The trial and sentence of Sinyavsky and Daniel in 1966, the public hounding of Solzhenitsyn himself, the increasing political and ideological pressure on Novy mir— 9 A. Solzhenitsyn, The Oak and the Calf, tr. Harry Willetts (London, 1980), p.98.

14 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives these now notorious manifestations of the new order were an unmistakable indication that times had changed. That Bulgakov’s novel should have been published when it was seems, in this light, to be a curious anomaly. Why should a work so strikingly unorthodox both in form and content have been allowed to appear at a time when militant con- servatism was so obviously the order of the day? This is a point to which I will return at the end of the chapter. Of greater immediate importance, however, is the fact that, whatever the reasons for its publication, The Master and Mar- garita became a rallying point for the liberals and the site of one of the last pitched battles in their running war with the conservatives, a war which had been going on, at varying levels of intensity, for more than a decade. The controversy which flared up around The Master and Margarita took the form of two separate exchanges. The first was a debate between Igor Vinogradov and Lyudmila Skor- ino, which appeared under the rubric ‘Works which are the source of argument’ in the June 1968 number of Voprosy litera- tury.'° The second began in the same month with the publi- cation, in Novy mir, of a long article by Vladimir Lakshin, entitled ‘On Bulgakov’s novel The Master and Margarita’.'' Despite its seemingly innocent title, this was a provocative statement of liberal sentiment which, in turn, drew an angry response, in the December of the same year, by M. Gus, a well-known champion of official attitudes.'* The same month witnessed both a rejoinder from Lakshin,'? and, more signifi- cantly, another article, which—although apparently indepen- dent of the Lakshin—Gus polemic—effectively put an end to this, as to all further fighting between the two groups. The Novel and its Reception 15 Before considering the substance of these articles, we should note two odd features of their timing. The most intriguing thing is that this critical engagement took place no less than eighteen months after the initial publication of Bulgakov’s novel in Moskva. Indeed, before June 1968—with the excep- tion of the brief commentaries which had accompanied the original publication—only a small handful of articles had mentioned the novel at all.'® When one considers the immense interest generated by The Master and Margarita, this amounts to an almost deafening silence. That the silence should, more- over, have been broken simultaneously by a number of articles in prominent literary journals invites the suspicion that this was something more than a mere coincidence. It seems reasonable to suppose that the debate, like the silence which preceded it, was orchestrated ‘from above’. The peremptory manner in which the debate was terminated at the end of the year adds further weight to this supposition. The Debate Begins The participants in the Voprosy literatury debate were both seasoned campaigners. Vinogradov, a member of the editorial board of Novy mir, was one of the best-known of the younger generation of Soviet critics, while his opponent, Skorino, was a staunch neo-Stalinist who had displayed her colours at an earlier stage of the campaign against liberalism. It was she, in fact, who had written an attack, back in 1954, on Vladimir Pomerantsev’s famous article ‘On Sincerity in Literature’, one of the first major landmarks in the post-Stalin Thaw.'° The discussion was opened by Skorino. Viewed from the outside and from the distance of something like fifteen years, her article makes for disturbing reading. Its title, ‘Faces with- out Carnival Masks’, with its ominous echo of the phrase ‘unmasking of enemies’ (a euphemism employed to legitimate many of the worst excesses of the Stalin régime), was in itselfa reliable pointer to her critical position. In Skorino’s opinion, Bulgakov’s novel was a work alien to the spirit of Soviet litera- ture, and this is the unspoken thesis towards which her argu- '5 See, in particular, O. From the very outset, the author finds it difficult to restrain her indignation. ‘The role of the fantastic in The Master and Margarita’, she states, ‘is nothing less than to demonstrate [...] the utter instability, the irrationality [ ... |] of the real world.’'? From the standpoint of one raised on the tenets of a materialist philosophy this alone is a matter of serious concern. But this is not the worst of it. Even more heinous, in the critic’s eyes, is the fact that the very logic of the novel seems actually to demand that we accept the ‘reality’ of all the supernatural occurrences which result from the arrival of Woland and his crew in the Soviet capital. It is with espe- cial annoyance, therefore, that Skorino records the painful fate of the ‘business-like, practical’ Berlioz and Bezdomny, who, she says, are so ‘cruelly punished’ for their refusal to accept that the supernatural is a ‘fact’ of life no less real than their more customary experiences. '® Skorino’s discussion leads to the obvious conclusion that Bulgakov’s use of the fantastic in the novel is designed to undermine, even to ridicule, the ‘certainties’ of the materialist world-view. But rather than commit herself to so bald a state- ment of ideological heresy, the critic returns to her original position, stating that ‘in Mikhail Bulgakov’s novel, the fantas- tic serves to assert the impossibility of penetrating the chaos of life, or of discovering the laws which govern it’.'9 In other words, she adds—now unleashing one of the most powerful weapons in her verbal armoury—Bulgakov is advancing a philosophy of ‘passivity’. ‘Passivity’ is the key word also in the account of the Jerusa- lem narrative which follows. It must be emphasized straight away that Skorino’s line of reasoning here is unconvincing in the extreme, yet it is no less important for that. The basic con- flict of the four biblical chapters, she maintains, is between ‘men of action’, like Pilate, Matthew and Mark Krysoboy (sic!), on the one hand, and Ieshua, a man who, by contrast, embodies the ‘passive’ principle. The Novel and its Reception 17 gests that an insidious polemic is at work in the novel: in his idealized portrait of Ieshua, and his negative (sometimes even satirical) treatment of the other characters, so the argument runs, Bulgakov is attempting to persuade us that all action is pointless. ‘Ieshua’s homily of inaction, [the italics are Skori- no’s] his humanism of self-denial and all-forgiveness are placed higher than any action’.’? But Ieshua is not the only character to display such passi- vity. So too, according to Skorino, does the Master. And it is to the subject of his passivity that the third section of the article is dedicated. Noting the circumstances under which the Master came to write his novel in the cosy seclusion of his basement apartment, the critic concludes that Bulgakov is implicitly defending the notion of the artist’s ‘passive’ with- drawal from society as a positive ideal. This, in turn, provides her with the opportunity to restate one of the central prin- ciples of orthodox opinion—that true socialist art can never be pursued in isolation from ‘social demands’.”' In conclusion, Skorino turns her attention away from the Master to consider his ‘secret wife’, Margarita. She begins by asking the question which will surely have occurred to more than one of her readers: how are we to reconcile Bulgakov’s obvious approval of a heroine who is purposeful action incar- nate with what Skorino has identified as the author’s overall defence of ‘passivity’? Skorino dodges this problem with all the skill of an experienced debater. Margarita is indeed, she readily admits, an active character, and it is this very capacity for action which both guarantees the rescue of the Master and secures his eventual ‘reward’. But—and here according to Skorino is the rub—this activity is purchased at too high a price, for Margarita is only able to achieve what she does because of her willingness to “compromise with Evil’.** Even here, therefore, the critic manages to argue that Bulgakov is pursuing the same philosophical point, only from a different angle: when action is not shown to be pointless, it is shown to be the product of collaboration with the powers of darkness. It would be mislead- ing, however, to suggest that his article was conceived simply, or even primarily, as a response to Skorino. In the article itself he makes it clear that his opponent’s piece came into his hands only when his own work was at a relatively late stage. This is important because, although he does make a number of substantial (and, of course, pointed) references to Skorino’s opinions, for the most part Vinogradov develops his argument without directly challenging her views. In certain instances (the account of Ieshua, for example) one assumes that this dis- regard was prompted by the feeling that Skorino’s interpret- ation was so self-evidently misguided as to require no comment at all. But there are other occasions where one senses that this was not the case, and that Vinogradov shrank from a head-on conflict out of wariness. His opening dis- cussion of the fantastic is a case in point. We have just seen that Skorino had objected to Bulgakov’s treatment of the fantastic on broadly ideological grounds, detecting in this aspect of the novel a direct challenge to the materialist philosophy upon which Marxism-Leninism is founded. In his own comments on this topic, however, Vino- gradov avoids this philosophical question altogether. Although he is intent on defending Bulgakov’s use of the fan- tastic, he does so on purely Jiterary grounds, praising the author in particular for his innovative approach to motifs drawn from traditional demonology. This, he says, taking up one of the most characteristic slogans of the liberal camp, is the mark of ‘real art’.*S But this is no more an answer to Skori- no’s objection than the later assertion that his opponent’s critique of Bulgakov implies the automatic rejection of Gogol, Rabelais, Hoffman, and in effect any writer who has recourse to the fantastic as a literary device.*+ Vinogradov’s tactic makes for entertaining reading, but this does not alter the fact that, on this subject at least, he has swept the real issue under the carpet. Nor, as we shall see, was he the only one of the liberals to do so. Vinogradov’s discussion of the fantastic is of less immediate *S Vinogradov, p.45. *t Thid. 48.

The Novel and its Reception 19 significance, however, than those sections of his article where he deals with the Jerusalem plot and Woland’s role in the novel. As these are both subjects to which we will return at greater length in later chapters, a brief summary of Vinogra- dov’s position will suffice here. In his approach to the Jerusa- lem story, Vinogradov disregards altogether the question of ‘passivity’, choosing instead to focus his attention on the more vital issue of the moral dilemma which confronts Pilate: whether to follow the promptings of his conscience and spare leshua, or to bow before the various pressures imposed upon him by his duties as an officer of the Roman Empire. For Vinogradov (as for all the liberal critics) this moral issue was the central theme of the novel. It was in his subsequent dis- cussion of Woland, however, that the critic finally displayed his polemical venom. Obviously sensing that he was on the most solid ground, Vinogradov struck firmly at the weakest point of Skorino’s flimsy thesis by questioning her simplistic assumption that Woland can be taken to represent a conven- tional evil force. His subsequent analysis, which includes some interesting remarks on the subject of the Master’s final ‘reward’, is both penetrating and persuasive, and it effectively reduces Skorino’s argument about Margarita’s ‘acceptance of evil’ to ashes. The final word in the Voprosy literatury debate went, in accordance with the usual convention, to Skorino. Her ‘Reply to an Opponent’ did little more, however, than defend her original position. Vinogradov, she suggested, had been taken in by Bulgakov’s romantic depiction of evil, and hence had unwittingly re-enacted the folly of the Master and Margarita in the novel itself.7> As for Vinogradov’s discussion of Pilate, Skorino somewhat testily reminded her opponent that ‘per- sonal morality’ can never be allowed to supplant ‘civic duty’ as the basis for ethical behaviour in a socialist society.”° The Debate Continues If the exchange between Skorino and Vinogradov ensured that the battle lines were clearly drawn, it was with the entry 25 L. 20 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives into the arena of Lakshin—the undisputed ‘star’ of the Novy mir camp and béte noire of the Soviet literary establishment— that the fighting began in earnest. In his recently published memoirs, Solzhenitsyn (his general antipathy towards Lak- shin notwithstanding) has provided the following assessment of the man and his work: ‘Lakshin follows closely in the foot- steps of the nineteenth-century Russian critics. Like theirs, his articles usually contain no aesthetic analysis as such; they consist of social analysis, they elicit the hidden implications of the theme, they round out the moral portraits of the charac- ters (all of which is very useful and necessary for the unculti- vated Soviet reader).’*” Lakshin’s study of The Master and Margarita (to which, it must be added, Solzhenitsyn took par- ticular exception)’* is a paradigm of his critical practice, a monument to Soviet liberalism sixties’ style and, even now, one of the most interesting and perceptive general accounts of Bulgakov’s novel. In essence, Lakshin’s article adheres to the general line established by Vinogradov. (The two critics must, in fact, have been working simultaneously, and they may well have had access to each other’s work prior to publication.) Like his colleague, Lakshin dwells at length on Pilate’s moral dilemma as a conflict between personal conscience and political expe- diency. And, again like Vinogradov, he denies that Woland can be viewed simply as an emblematic representation of evil. Yet, from the very opening words (a defiant reiteration of the slogan ‘Manuscripts don’t burn’), the reader is in no doubt that this is a very different kind of article. Where Vinogradov works for the most part by allusion and understatement, Lak- shin—true to the spirit of Novy mir—speaks forcefully and directly, making explicit what is merely implicit in Vinogra- dov’s article: namely, that The Master and Margarita is above all a novel about the evils of Stalin’s Russia. Especially note- worthy in this respect is the lengthy section in which Lakshin deals with a subject overlooked by both Skorino and Vinogra- dov—Bulgakov’s satire of contemporary life. Concentrating in particular on the series of mysterious disappearances from *7 Solzhenitsyn, p.232. 8 Ibid. 238.

The Novel and its Reception 21 various Moscow apartments and institutions, he parades his political stance in an open reference to the purges: ‘A veritable host of domestic miracles and mystic everyday phenomena are detected by Bulgakov’s ironic eye in those aspects of reality, quite worthy of satire, which are linked with the mistrust, fear and suspicion, and other psychological consequences of the violations of legality which are registered in our memory of 1937.° Similarly, the Master’s anxiety, which causes him both to destroy his manuscript and to seek refuge in Dr Stra- vinsky’s clinic, is also explained by Lakshin as a characteristic feature of an age in which fear and cowardice had become the norm.3° The de-Stalinizing thrust of Lakshin’s discussion is equally evident in his remarks on the characters of Ieshua and the Master, both of whom he recommends to the reader as examples of persecuted genius. The following words on Ieshua neatly encapsulate the critic’s interpretation of both charac- ters: “The image of Ieshua in Bulgakov’s novel is the embodi- ment of free spiritual activity in general. The poet-prophet, scorned, insulted, persecuted, misunderstood, beaten with stones—this is an age-old theme of poetry ...’.°' As for Woland, Lakshin simply takes Skorino’s argument and turns it on its head. Unlike Vinogradov, he is not content merely to speak against the uncritical identification of Woland with evil. Instead, he puts forward the idea that, as the punishment of the Muscovites by Woland is, in almost every case, fully deserved, Woland himself (paradoxical though it might seem) is to be understood as the ‘punishing sword in the hands of justice, if not a voluntary servant of good’.%* This emphasis on justice, like the defence of free artistic activity, was one of the major preoccupations of Soviet liberal intellectuals, and it resurfaces at the end of Lakshin’s article, where the author states that the broad purpose of Bulgakov’s novel is to inspire ‘faith in the law of justice, of correct judgement, and of the inevitable retribution of evil’.%% *9 Lakshin, ‘Roman... ’, p.290. 3° [bid. 305. 3" [bid. 300. 3° Tbid. 295. 33 [bid. 307.

22 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives In the context of 1968, Lakshin’s article was fighting talk, yet there are clear signs that it was something of a rearguard action. Outspoken though it was, it has only to be compared with the same author’s earlier review of The Life of Monsieur de Moliére3+ if one wishes to appreciate how the changing political climate was forcing the liberals on to the defensive. In the earlier review, Lakshin had openly suggested that the plight of Moliére was to be interpreted as an allegory of the fate of the Soviet writer under Stalin. In his article on The Master and Margarita, however, he is a good deal more circumspect. Thus, while he pushes the liberal line further than anyone else was prepared to do, he obviously felt the need to make certain con- cessions to conservative opinion. One such concession—and this was something that particularly irked Solzhenitsyn*°— was the fleeting reference at the end of the piece to Bulgakov’s political short-sightedness.3° But this does not alter the fact that Lakshin’s article represented a bold resurgence of liberal opinion. As such, it was more or less bound to draw some sort of response from the conservatives. In the event, and perhaps a little surprisingly, it was not until the very end of the year that the ultra-conservative Zna- mya printed a reply to Lakshin by M. Gus with the provoca- tive title “Do manuscripts burn?’. In style and approach, Gus’s article exemplifies the very worst aspects of neo-Stali- nist literary criticism. Where Skorino had at least made an effort to adhere to the principle of reasoned argument, Gus begins by absolving himself of any such responsibility. Instead of advancing an alternative interpretation to that of his oppo- nent, he indulges for the most part in the standard polemical practice of label-mongering. Lakshin, he says, employing the euphemistic style so often affected by critics of the conserva- tive camp, had simply used Bulgakov’s novel as a means of advancing ‘certain currently fashionable literary-theoretical and philosophical conceptions’.*’ This was the preliminary to a more direct attack against Lakshin for attempting to advance what Gus describes as a defence of ‘non-conformism’. 44-V. The Novel and its Reception 23 Having exposed the ideological subversiveness of Lakshin’s position in broad terms, Gus proceeds to take issue with a number of specific points contained in his opponent’s article. The Novy mir critic is guilty, he maintains, of discussing mor- ality in the abstract, without relating moral issues to the ideol- ogy of the CPSU.3" The entire account of Pilate as a craven individual who allows. evil to be perpetuated despite the promptings of his better nature is dismissed out of hand as a mere figment of Lakshin’s imagination.?9 Most ominous of all, however, was Gus’s suggestion that the critical campaign against Bulgakov in the 1920s (the details of which can be found in Chapter 3 below) could not have been entirely with- out foundation—a most unsubtle reminder that militant con- formism was anything but a spent force, and a threat to the liberals which would certainly not have been lost on Lakshin. Lakshin himself lost no time in rebutting Gus’s argument. His response, which appeared in the December issue of Novy mir, 1s primarily of interest for its withering sarcasm. Here Lakshin exercised all his polemical skills to the full, most par- ticularly when he reproached Gus for not having read his Lenin carefully enough! To rub salt into the wound, he also included in his reply a passage from one of the Bolshevik leader’s last articles which spoke of individual conscience in a way which suited perfectly his argument about Pilate.*° The Termination of the Debate The argument between Lakshin and Gus is of interest not only for what it tells us about the reception of The Master and Margarita in Bulgakov’s native land, but also because it has turned out to be one of the last major examples of open dissen- sion between literary journals of markedly different political directions. Since the late sixties, in fact, Soviet journals have been characterized by a greater degree of homogeneity; such frank disagreement over the socio-political interpretation of literary works has become very much a thing of the past. By its title, its length, and its prominent position in the jour- nal, Motyashov’s article immediately signalled that it was a statement of ‘official’ policy. Written in the form of an over- view of recent literary trends, it began with a definition of the artistic responsibility confronting the Soviet writer. As is to be expected, what Motyashov had to say on this subject was not new; indeed, the critic was content merely to repeat a number of well-tried platitudes. He reminded his readers that the Soviet writer has a moral duty before his country, his party and humanity to produce works which are ‘good’ and ‘necess- ary’, works, that is, which ‘confirm for us the historical justice of the Revolution, help in liberating us from the evil of the past, teach us to love people, life, and summon us to struggle and victory’.t' This was the standard against which certain recent works were then tested. The first was Fyodor Abra- mov’s “Iwo Winters and Three Summers’, which Motyashov defended from the criticism that had been levelled against it from a number of quarters. For the purposes of contrast, he then turned to the work of Andrey Bitov, a writer who, despite the ‘nobility of his subjectively understood aims’, was in danger, the critic warned, of going down a ‘blind alley’.*? As his third example, Motyashov chose to examine the criti- cal response to The Master and Margarita. His opening com- ments left little doubt where his sympathies lay. ‘Why is it’, he complained, ‘that in certain of our critical works a respectful and solicitous attitude towards talent is understood as [entail- ing] an inevitable justification, even an apology of all its aspects and attributes?’ To illustrate his point, he cited Lak- shin’s famous article on Solzhenitsyn’s One Day.** The refer- ence to this article rather than to the same critic’s more recent +" Motyashoy, p.5. oe Moyeel, tit eS) Woytel, PY, “"V. 26 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives It will be plain from the above account that the significance of Motyashov’s article resided less in the opinions which it contained (and which differed in no substantial way from those expressed by Skorino and Gus) than in the manner ofits expression. Motyashov was speaking here in the calm, assured tone of an adjudicator, and not as a participant in the debate. As a statement of ‘official’ opinion, his article was decidedly anti-liberal in orientation, and its purpose was transparently to indicate that, in the eyes of those who control Soviet literary policy, the debate surrounding The Master and Margarita had run its course. The first (and in many respects the most excit- ing) period of the novel’s critical history was at an end. With the publication of Motyashov’s article it was also evi- dent that the writing was on the wall for the liberals. In the years that followed, Khrushchev’s heirs busied themselves most visibly with the task of putting the lid on ‘de-Staliniza- tion’. Tvardovsky was soon ousted from his position as editor- in-chief of Novy mir—an important symbolic victory for the conservatives and a major turning point in recent Soviet intel- lectual history. Liberal opinion, although far from dead, was forced either to seek an outlet in the samizdat network or else to accept that, under the new conditions, it would need to develop a more muted form of expression, returning to the ‘Aesopian’ language traditionally favoured by the radical Russian critics of the nineteenth century. To comprehend what the latter course meant in practice, one has to look no further than Lakshin’s later article “The Lessons of Bul- gakov’.°° Published, significantly enough, in the obscure jour- nal Pamir, it articulated a liberalism, which—although unrepentant—was so emasculated as to be hardly worthy of the name. But if honours in the larger political battle have gone (for the time being at least) to the conservatives, the victory in the smaller battle over Bulgakov’s novel has belonged to the liber- als. Despite the considerable pressure exerted against The Master and Margarita by the conservatives, no one, not even the ultra-orthodox Gus, was prepared openly to challenge the wis- °° V. The Novel and its Reception 27 dom of publishing the novel in the first place. Since then a full (and apparently uncensored) version of the novel has been released.°' Besides its importance as a notable success for the liberals, this is also the only instance I can recall in recent times of a controversial literary work appearing in a fuller form within the Soviet Union than abroad. Its republication in 1980, and again in .1984 (in relatively large editions of 100,000) suggests that the novel’s right to ‘citizenship’ as a legitimate Soviet novel has been established beyond question. Nevertheless, a large amount of territory still remains to be won. Since 1967, no further controversial works by Bulgakov have been published in the USSR. Most notably, the earlier satirical pieces, The Fatal Eggs and The Heart of a Dog, as well as such plays as Adam and Eve, Crimson Island, and Zoyka’s Apartment (for which Vera Smirnova had made a strong plea in the 1960s)°? have remained firmly under wraps. And the fact that certain volumes have long been promised (for example, a selection of memoirs, and an edition of The Master and Margar- ita in the scholarly Literaturnyye pamyatniki series),°? yet still show no signs of making their appearance must be taken as an indication that the liberals are not having things all their own way. This is most evident in the case of the anti-liberal critics. Read literally as attempts to account for the ‘meaning’ of the novel in Hirsch’s sense, the articles of Skorino and Gus will inevitably strike the non-Soviet reader at least as examples of misinterpretation of the most gross and perverse kind. Read as responses to the novel’s ‘significance’, on the other hand, they are perfectly understandable. By def- lating the image of the Master and by deflecting attention away from the moral cowardice of Pilate, both critics revealed that their primary purpose was to take the wind from the sails of the liberals and to thwart the ‘de-Stalinizing’ trends that they represented. Skorino and Gus destroy their credibility because the demand that they deal both with the ‘meaning’ and the ‘sig- nificance’ of The Master and Margarita resulted in a conflict so fundamental that it cannot be mistaken: in order to make their political point, they violate the integrity of the text by ignoring the many details which render their readings questionable. With Vinogradov and Lakshin, however, it is a different mat- ter, for in their work such a conflict is not so readily apparent. Judged simply as efforts to elucidate what the novel is about, their articles are extremely convincing and infinitely superior to those of Skorino and Gus. Yet it is precisely because their work is so persuasive that we must remind ourselves that they too—no less than their opponents—were participants in a pol- itical dispute, and that their work also was both the product and the vehicle of attitudes which threaten to distort the meaning of the book.5° The point is obvious, yet it has to be emphasized because the work of both critics (especially Lak- 55 KE. The Novel and its Reception 29 shin) has had a substantial influence on the development of Bulgakov criticism outside the USSR. That the Soviet liberal readings of The Master and Margarita have had such an impact on non-Soviet critics is hardly sur- prising. Not only were these articles truly path-finding works; they also articulated political views which alone would have assured them a sympathetic hearing in the West. In effect, Vinogradov and Lakshin were preaching to the converted. As we shall see in a moment, the initial reactions to Bulgakov’s novel outside the Soviet Union had already adumbrated the broad lines of enquiry subsequently explored in detail by the liberals. For these reasons, therefore, it is imperative to con- sider some of the limitations inherent in the liberal responses to the novel, limitations which have been carried over into much later writing on the novel. In essence, the Soviet liberal interpretations of The Master and Margarita are distinguished by two features. In the first place, they promote a view of the Master as a romantic seeker after truth, an independent spirit, an artist of genius unjustly persecuted in an age of officially sanctioned philistinism. Secondly, they offer an account of the biblical narrative which concentrates more or less exclusively on the ethical dilemma of Pilate. That both these features bear directly on crucial aspects of life in Stalin’s Russia is a point that requires little elaboration. The story of the Master, as related by the liberal critics, tells of the fate of the novel’s creator and also, by exten- sion, of an entire generation of creative artists whose system- atic annihilation has left one of the deepest scars on the collective Russian conscience. The story of Pilate, on the other hand, is shown to dramatize the existential predicament which results in the triumph of tyranny. When Vinogradov wrote of Pilate that ‘no circumstances can exculpate a man when he commits evil or even evades combat with it’,°? no Soviet reader could have mistaken the implication that he was speaking not so much of ancient Jerusalem, but of a period in Soviet history only recently past. It would be absurd to deny the validity of these arguments, yet both lines of investigation are at least as remarkable for 57 Vinogradov, p.73.

30 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives what they overlook as for what they examine. The Master, for example, is much more than a mere victim of the times. Bul- gakov’s portrait of his hero is considerably more ambivalent than either Lakshin or Vinogradov is prepared to concede. If his persecution by the Latunskys and the Arimans of this world is bound to evince sympathy, his abject condition as we observe him within the walls of Stravinsky’s clinic is presented in a manner which demands that we adopt a more critical attitude towards him. Although Lakshin is prepared at least to acknowledge the Master’s personal failings, he is no more willing than the other liberal critics to explore the implications of those failings for a portrait of the artist which is ultimately more important in terms of metaphysics than of politics. By dwelling upon the persecution of the Master rather than his weaknesses, and by emphasizing his achievements as a writer rather than exploring his deficiencies, the liberal critics provided an account of Bulgakov’s hero which was both nar- row and one-sided.>® Their discussion of the Jerusalem narra- tive, on the other hand, is deficient in a different way. Here it is not so much that they ignore the complexity of Bulgakov’s treatment of character and theme, but rather that their con- centration on the figure of the procurator means that the greater part of the biblical story passes without comment. Of the four chapters devoted to the ancient narrative, only the first concerns Pilate’s moral dilemma. The remainder— especially the story of Matthew in Chapter 16—seems some- how irrelevant to this theme, which is presumably why it hardly rates a mention in the liberal readings of the novel. These objections will provide the basis for my own dis- cussion later in this study (see Chapters 6 and 7). There is, however, a further limitation inherent in the liberal position which should be mentioned here, and it concerns the larger issue of the novel’s overall philosophy. The reader may have noticed that when Vinogradov and Lakshin speak of Pilate’s celebrated act of ‘cowardice’, they do so in a manner which admits no compromise. In Vinogradov’s comments on the ** Makarovskaya and Zhuk (pp.176; 172 f.) provide an extreme example of this tendency, claiming that “The Master is conceived by Bulgakov as an ideal person- ality’ and stating further that ‘he [i.e. the Master] is beautiful in the purity of his faith in goodness.’

The Novel and its Reception 31 culpability of those who evade combat with evil, as in Lak- shin’s suggestion that Woland might be seen as the bearer of the ‘punishing sword [ .. . ] of justice’, one detects an Old Testament moral absolutism which is far more appropriate to a discussion of Solzhenitsyn than it is to an account of Bulgak- ov’s view of the world. Notions of absolute guilt and retribu- tion sit most uneasily with the bare narrative facts of a novel in which those characters who fail the moral test—Pilate most obviously, and also the Master—are ultimately spared the con- sequences of the law of retribution. Lakshin himself indicates that an alternative principle, the principle of mercy, has an important place in the novel, yet he does not adequately con- sider the degree to which this principle contradicts and even supplants the absolutism he had earlier discerned in Bulgak- ov’s depiction of Pilate. As Lesley Milne has written, the opposition between retributive justice and redemptive justice lies at the heart of The Master and Margarita.°° Yet this was a problem which Lakshin and Vinogradov, by virtue of their political stance, were unable to place in a proper perspective. The ‘de-Stalinization’ movement of which they were part was from the outset characterized by an inflexible attitude towards the evils of Stalinism which was singularly ill-attuned to the kind of morality at work in Bulgakov’s novel. When he identi- fied the purpose of The Master and Margarita in terms of the faith it inspired in the ‘inevitable retribution of evil’, Lakshin was speaking for himself, but not necessarily for Bulgakov. There is a final shortcoming of the liberal position to which I have already alluded, and it relates to the problem raised by Skorino regarding Bulgakov’s use of the fantastic. In her orig- inal article, as we saw, Skorino had objected to the narrative logic of The Master and Margarita, which seduces the reader into accepting the ‘reality’ of the supernatural. Although the critic did not develop her argument fully, the basis of her objection was transparent enough. By positing a world in which such events as the performance at the Variety Club and Satan’s Ball are as ‘real’ as the day-to-day activities of ordinary Soviet citizens, Bulgakov was in effect proposing a metaphysical 9 Lesley Milne, The Master and Margarita. A Comedy of Victory (Birmingham, 1977), p-27.

The implications of Skorino’s remarks were obviously too serious simply to be ignored by the liberals. Like Vinogradov before him, Lakshin also made a particular point of stressing that Bulgakov’s use of the fantastic was to be understood purely as a literary convention. Now, it is obvious why the liberals should have adopted such a strategy, but we must be quite clear about what they have done. Because of their determination that Bulgakov’s novel should not become a ritual sacrifice at the shrine of a neo-Stalinist revival, they were forced into a position where they had to deny, or at least to suppress, what a great many readers would consider to be the most important aspect of the book—its metaphysical dimension. These comments point towards a question to which greater attention will be accorded in a later chapter: precisely what sort of novel is The Master and Margarita? Is it to be read pri- marily for its socio-political significance, or does its real mean- ing reside elsewhere? The Soviet liberal critics—for a variety of reasons—decided in favour of the former option, and their decision contributed in an important way to the shape of Bul- gakov criticism in the West. In Chapter 3, we will examine a number of critical approaches adopted by Western scholars, each of which relates in some way to the Soviet liberal response, and which together constitute a recognizable ‘first phase’ of interpretation with a firm socio-political orientation. Within the USSR, however, the critical endeavour took a dif- ferent turn. Since 1968, the debate over The Master and Margar- ita has been muted, and now that Bulgakovedeniye has at last established itself as a bona fide branch of literary scholarship, political polemic has given way to the careful accumulation of knowledge, open disagreement being reserved mostly for mat- ters of a strictly academic nature. For the most part, they took the form of short book reviews and contained little more than the usual synopsis of contents together with a few snap judgements. Collectively, however, they display two general features which are worthy of comment. First (and most obvious) is the broad political unanimity of opinion. The prime significance of Bul- gakov’s novel as an indictment of Stalin’s Russia was recog- nized and emphasized by reviewers everywhere. The satirical scenes were recounted with delighted approval; in the minds of many they were accounted the finest part of the book. Equally prominent was the recognition of the Master’s plight as a case-study of the suffering Soviet artist. As for the biblical narrative, here too it was the political implication which immediately came to the fore. The reviewer for the London Times who recommended the Pilate story as a moral allegory of the Stalin era which ‘conveys the message that absolute power can only corrupt’*4 was voicing an opinion which, with variations of emphasis and expression, can be found in dozens of other newspaper and magazine articles of the day. But where the reviewers were agreed on the novel’s signifi- cance as a political statement, they differed quite markedly in their assessment of its success as an aesthetic or philosophical whole. (Interestingly enough, the aesthetic problem had not figured at all in the Soviet debates.) Whether they were talk- ing of structure or ideas, one question was uppermost in the minds of many reviewers: does the novel cohere? Here, for example, is Michael Glenny on the subject of the novel’s philosophy: ‘As a philosophical disquisition in a fictional vehicle it is extraordinarily stimulating, yet it leaves the sense that there is still something missing: there is the feeling that Bulgakov just failed to place the keystone on his philosophical construct’.°> When it came to the unique construction of the novel—the combination of contemporary satire, supernatural fantasy and historical narrative—opinion was often even more severe. But this is not to say that they have nothing to tell us. It is significant that the two main concerns of the novel’s Western reviewers correspond precisely to the main trends in early scholarly studies of The Master and Mar- garita. But it is perhaps even more important to acknowledge that what these book reviews lack in profundity, they necess- arily gain in freshness and spontaneity. The product (one imagines) of a single reading, many of them manage to cap- ture the experience of the text in a way that the scholarly critic, trained to scour literary works many times before putting pen to paper, often fails to do. Thus, while we need not necessarily accept the conclusion of a considerable number of reviewers that The Master and Margarita does not cohere as an aesthetic unit or as a philosophical statement, we would do well to attend to the instinct which prompted so many experienced readers to express such an opinion. Most illuminating in this connection—all the more so as it reflects the experience of almost every reader of the novel that I have spoken to—is the statement by Stanley Reynolds that ‘the second half of the book is disappointing. The statement by the reviewer for Time magazine that ‘its publication for the first time in Russia is part of a literary rebellion that is sweeping through Russian letters’,’° has proved, in the light of subsequent developments, to be a rather grotesque instance of wishful thinking. To enter briefly into the realm of speculation, it may be sug- gested that four factors (at least) contributed in some measure to the decision to publish. Firstly, there is what some com- mentators have dubbed the ‘safety-valve’ mentality.’' The year 1967 was, as we saw, one of considerable tension both at home and abroad, in which the draconian measures applied against Sinyavsky and Daniel had played no small part. The release of The Master and Margarita, therefore, could have been intended as a diversionary tactic, a gesture towards liberaliza- tion which had the purpose of relieving some of the pressure which had built up against party and state. Oe tN Few periods in modern history have known so thorough a repression of artistic activity as the years when Stalin ruled in the Soviet Union. The story of this dark age has often been told, and the individual fates of its most prominent victims are so well known as to require no further comment here. Bulgak- ov’s experience, although more fortunate than that of many of his contemporaries, was extremely painful, and The Master and Margarita deserves attention, if for no other reason, as a defiant riposte to an age in which such literary works had been declared a harmful irrelevancy. Moreover, the story of its composition constitutes a moving testimony to the power of mind over physical circumstances. Bulgakov’s work on his last novel spanned a period coincid- ing almost exactly with the first twelve years of Stalin’s rule. Begun probably sometime in 1928, it went through many manuscript versions before acquiring the form in which it was secretly preserved by the novelist’s widow after his premature death in 1940. For Bulgakov, these were years of almost unre- lieved anxiety. One of the more prominent victims of the new spirit of militancy which came to the fore in the late twenties, he maintained a precarious existence thereafter. The press- ures which weighed upon the writer during his last decade were, however, less overtly political than financial, physical and emotional. Even after he had survived the worst period of official harassment and secured (almost miraculously) a limited source of income from his literary endeavours, he had to cope with the stress of a marriage breakdown. On top of all this there was the perpetual strain of living in a condition of what Solzhenitsyn has described in a different context as ‘literary schizophrenia’.' Throughout the thirties, Bulgakov lived an extraordinary double life as a writer. Visibly, his time ' Solzhenitsyn, p.128.

40 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives was divided between the largely onerous tasks of writing and adaptation for the Moscow Art Theatre and a number of other theatrical enterprises, and the composition of original works intended for publication or performance (which, with very few exceptions, they were denied). In the meantime, hidden from the gaze of all but a trusted circle of intimate friends, he worked, at first intermittently, then with ever greater dedi- cation, on the novel which he knew could only be a posthu- mous bequest to Russian literature. The sheer volume of all this work, not to mention the immense frustration connected with Bulgakov’s official life as a writer, would have been suf- ficient to tax even a healthy person. But, throughout these years, Bulgakov’s health was never good. Constantly afflicted by minor ailments, he was also subject to nervous disorders which manifested themselves in forms ranging from insomnia to agoraphobia. Even worse, by the late thirties Bulgakov became aware that he had developed symptoms of the sclero- sis of the kidneys which had killed his father at a similar age. His last two years witnessed an inexorable physical decline as the illness took its fatal course. If the eventual publication of The Master and Margarita in the Soviet Union seems increasingly astonishing with the years, the fact that it ever came to be written at all must be deemed nothing short of a miracle. A tremendous victory of the human spirit, it is a tribute both to the indomitable will of its creator, and to the patient dedication of his widow, Yelena Ser- geyevna, who, by seeing the novel through to the printed page, fulfilled a promise made at her husband’s deathbed.’ TPES EV OM UE TONS Oa eEer a NtO Ns als In an account of the Bulgakov archive which seems destined to remain the most important single source of information about the writer’s unpublished works, Marietta Chudakova provides the following list of holdings relating to The Master and Margarita: “lwenty notebooks containing successive handwritten redactions, two notebooks of [background] materials, three typed texts of the novel (two of which reflect * Chudakova, ‘Arkhiv ...’, p.141.

Markov recalls that the writer told him during the rehearsals of Days of the Turbins (i.e. 1926) that ‘he had long been tormented by the enigma of the New Testa- ment tragedy.’® Katayev is more specific, speaking of 1923 or 1924 as the year in which the novel first began to take shape in Bulgakov’s mind (OR, p.106), a supposition which is sup- ported by certain circumstantial evidence. As Chudakova points out in the same place, the years mentioned by Katayev saw a large output of anti-religious works devoted to the sub- ject of Jesus and Christianity. Proof that Bulgakov’s interest had been aroused by this phenomenon is supplied by the feuil- leton ‘Moscow in the twenties’. First published in May 1924, this journalistic piece contains the following humorous pas- sage: ‘In the year of Our Lord . . . (in the room next door a Komsomo] voice is heard: “‘He never existed!!’’)’.9 Two further items of a similarly circumstantial nature deserve mention here. The first is the fairly recent discovery of a close similarity (even down to details of wording) between Berlioz’s comments on Bezdomny’s poem in the first chapter of The Master and Margarita and a review by Sergey Gorodetsky of S. The review appeared in the December 1923 number of the journal Krasnaya niva, although it may have been read some time later by Bulgakov.'® Equally intriguing is the probable influence of another obscure work of the period, A. V. Chayanov’s novella Venediktov.'' Published, like Chev- kin’s play, in 1922, this work was illustrated by Natal’ya Ushakova, who gave Bulgakov a copy of the book when the two became well acquainted, either towards the end of 1924 or in 1925. These scattered pieces of information raise questions to which no definitive answer is likely to be provided. While it seems reasonable to suppose that by the mid-twenties Bul- gakov had already been attracted to the story of the passion, and that his imagination had been fired by the possibility of weaving a story around the adventures of the devil in the Rus- sian capital, we can say nothing of when, or how, these two themes became combined to form the basis upon which all versions of The Master and Margarita were to be founded. Nor can we be sure that the novel for which Bulgakovw’s father was to provide the ‘starting point’ had any connection (at least in 1926) with these historical and supernatural themes. Despite the signs of his relatively early interest in the sub- jects which were to surface later in the first redactions of The Master and Margarita, it is unlikely that Bulgakov had any immediate thoughts of putting pen to paper. The publication, in 1925, of the satirical collection Diaboliad, and the partial serialization in the same year of his first novel, The White Guard, finally ensured the writer’s emergence from the fringe of Russian literary life. But the difficulties surrounding the publication of the novel (which was destined never to appear in full within the Soviet Union during the author’s lifetime) may well have discouraged thoughts of another lengthy nove- listic venture. Other circumstances also conspired to turn his attention from fiction at this time. In response to a suggestion that he convert The White Guard into a play, Bulgakov wrote Days of the Turbins, a work which secured him both fame and (relative) fortune, and marked the beginning of a brief, but spectacular, period of success in the Soviet theatre. The immensely popular (and highly controversial) first play was followed by the satires Zoyka’s Apartment and Crimson Island, which drew similarly large audiences. But Bulgakov’s successes proved also to be his undoing, for Proffer, Bulgakov, p.255.

The Text 45 the very plays which had made his name brought him to the attention of the so-called ‘proletarian’ critics.'3 Bulgakov had, in fact, been singled out for censure as early as September 1925, when Leopold Averbakh, one of the most formidable exponents of proletarian criticism, had written a scathing review of the Diaboliad collection for Pravda.'* As Bulgakov’s fame as a playwright grew, so this spark developed into the fire of an all-out campaign of vilification and slander. Now identified, alongside Zamyatin and Pilnyak, as a writer alien to the ideals and aspirations of Soviet society, his position became increasingly precarious. The turning point came early in 1929, when Bulgakov’s new play, Flight was banned even before its planned premiére could take place. Within a few months, Zoyka’s Apartment, Crimson Island and Days of the Tur- bins were also removed from the repertoire by official order. This was an immense blow to the writer. Deprived almost overnight of the means to what had proved a most satisfactory livelihood, and labelled an enemy of the people at a time when such ‘enemies’ were already receiving summary justice, Bul- gakov was plunged into a state of acute uncertainty.'° Such, then, were the immediate circumstances under which the first two redactions of The Master and Margarita came to be written. Completed no later than May, 1929, work (on Redac- tion 1 at least) must have been begun during the previous year, if not earlier (TI, p.219). Our knowledge of these materials (as of all the manuscripts of the novel) comes from the work of Chudakova, but in this case, the critic is owed a special debt of gratitude. The first two redactions are con- tained in two notebooks which were later partially destroyed by the author during a bout of depression. Through a combi- nation of careful comparison, intelligent hypothesis and sheer patience, Chudakova has managed to ‘reconstruct’ these vital early variants and to provide a fairly reliable picture of their contents (OR, pp.g3-106).
