46 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives The fifteen chapters of Redaction 1 tell a story which, in its broad outline, will be quite familiar to the reader of the pub- lished text. As in the final version, the novel opens in the park at Patriarchs’ Ponds, where an editor and a poet (the future Berlioz and Bezdomny) have their discussion of the poet’s work about Jesus interrupted by the appearance of a myster- ious stranger, who proceeds to offer a highly unorthodox account of the passion story. The sequel also adheres to a recognizable pattern. The editor is gruesomely run over by a tram, thus fulfilling the stranger’s enigmatic prediction of his death; the poet attempts to warn his fellow writers of the devi- lish presence in Moscow but is packed off to a psychiatric cli- nic; we are introduced to the staff of the Variety Theatre, where the supernatural visitor puts on a demonstration of black magic; and in the aftermath of the performance various individuals are involved in embarrassing scenes involving counterfeit money. The manuscript breaks off at a point where two members of the theatre staff (the future Rimsky and Vare- nukha) seek permission to go abroad. Several basic features of the novel are already evident in this first variant. Crucial here, as throughout the text’s evolu- tion, is the opposition of two worlds, Moscow and Yershalaim, and of two figures, Woland and Ieshua. (Chudakova records that in one of the notebooks containing preparatory materials for the novel several pages are divided into columns, headed ‘Christ? and “The Devil’ (A, p.64).) Each of the narrative worlds has its own themes and its own stylistic manner. As Chudakova again reports, the Moscow scenes are reminiscent of the feuilletons and satirical short prose of Bulgakov’s early career, while the New Testament story is much closer to the serious tone found in The White Guard and an important early story, The Red Crown’ (A, p.80). Nevertheless, there are many ways in which this earliest text differs from the final novel. ‘The picaresque form of the Moscow narrative allowed Bulgakov to experiment with many scenes which had no place in later variants. Thus, the fourth chapter, which deals with the increasingly unlikely rumours surrounding the death of the editor, was subsequently recast completely; and a hilar- ious sequence involving the poet’s escape from the asylum, his attempt to steal the editor’s body, and a grotesque finale as

The Text 47 poet, corpse and hearse end up in the Moscow river, failed to survive the process of revision. More significant, however, are those differences which point to a later shift of conception. Woland, for example, first makes his appearance in this redac- tion all alone. The performance at the Variety Theatre is also a solo effort (A, p.6g). Only towards the end of the first redac- tion is there a reference to the retinue which is to play such a prominent part in the later versions (A, p.77). As yet, the New Testament narrative is shorter than in subsequent variants, although it does include a number of scenes which were later omitted. Moreover, its motivation is quite uncomplicated. Contained within a single chapter (the second), and entitled on various occasions “The Gospel of Woland’ and “The Gospel according to the D[{evil]’, it took the form of an eyewitness account by a very chatty Woland (TI, pp.220-1). The style of the Moscow chapters was also very colloquial, the story being rendered through the consciousness of a highly personal nar- rator constantly apologizing for his deficiencies as an author (A, p.66). The most fascinating part of Redaction 1, however, is its eleventh chapter. Probably entitled “Such is Erudition’, it comprises the unfinished biography of a character unknown in any later versions of the novel and not mentioned elsewhere in the manuscript. His name is Fesya, and the chapter tells of his development from a talented youth with a particular flair for foreign languages to his career as a professor of history and beyond. Fesya’s curriculum vitae provides precise details of an undergraduate paper on the subject of causation, of the themes of his various dissertations, and of his special interest in medieval history—including demonology (OR, pp.10o-1). Other particulars are similarly suggestive. We are told, for example, that Fesya had spent two years in Italy as a teen- ager, and that he enunciates Russian poorly (A, pp. 70, 71). But it is the political dimension of Fesya’s story which pro- vides the most significant clue to Bulgakov’s conception. Fesya was evidently the victim of the changed circumstances of Russian life in the post-revolutionary years. A history pro- fessor before 1917, he lost his university position after the Soviet takeover and became a schoolteacher. What is more, he was also the object of a scurrilous attack in a newspaper,

48 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives which claimed that he had mistreated the peasants on his estate before the Revolution (A, p.71). It would be unwise to overindulge in speculation about Fesya’s role in Bulgakov’s original conception for the novel. The fact that the hero is a scholar will remind us of the author’s earlier promise to Popov of a novel inspired by his father, who was, like Fesya, a historian by training. The details of Fesya’s career and of his intellectual interests, how- ever, bear no obvious resemblance to those of Afanasy Bul- gakov; Chudakova suggests that the novelist’s friend, Boris Yarkho, was the most likely prototype (OR, p.1o1). But when the same critic concludes that Fesya’s potential significance, although great, remains unclear, she errs on the side of (understandable) caution (A, p.77). Despite this disclaimer, Fesya’s story is self-evidently a case of political persecution and, as such, it has a polemical thrust which can be found in many of Bulgakov’s works written both before and after Redaction 1 (see, in particular, his treatment of the ‘misun- derstood scientist’ theme in The Fatal Eggs, Adam and Eve and Bliss). No less obvious is the autobiographical significance of the hero’s experience at the hands of the press. The removal of Fesya and the subsequent introduction of the Master as a central character in the Moscow chapters is, beyond any doubt, the most important single change in the evolution of The Master and Margarita. Nevertheless, there is a kinship between these two characters which suggests a poss- ible continuity of conception. The hero of the first redaction, no less than the hero of the final novel, is an outsider, a man of rare intellectual ability spurned by a society which has no place for such people. The connection between them is further signalled in the final text by a small but telling detail, which seems actually to describe the development of Bulgakov’s ideas: the Master, it transpires, like Fesya, is proficient in many languages, and had worked as a historian before taking on the new occupation of writing fiction. There is no way of knowing whether the novel was actually completed in this first redaction (TI, p. 226). Bulgakov was already reading from the novel to his friends in 1929 and pre- pared one of its chapters for separate publication (OR, pp.9g3, 102). But even ifno more than fifteen chapters were written at

The Text 49 this time, the conception evidently extended further. The pre- paratory materials for the first redaction suggest that the eventual Satan’s Ball scene was already in the author’s mind (A, p.73). The second redaction, unfortunately, sheds no light on this matter. Following a procedure which was to become customary during his work on the novel, Bulgakov returned in Redaction 2 to the beginning. He reworked the original Chapters 1, 2, 3 and 5, discarded Chapter 4, and wrote a con- clusion to Chapter 7 (unfinished in Redaction 1)—the story of the future Bosoy (A, p.78). The most interesting feature of this redaction was the development of the New Testament story. Although still all in one piece, this section was enlarged by almost thirty pages, the main additions being the introduction of the disciple Matthew and the story of Judas’s assassination (OR, p.103). There was also a discernible shift towards a more literary style and a less subjective mode of narration in this chapter (A, p.79). What was the novel called in 1929? The notebooks provide evidence of Bulgakov’s quest for a title: The Black Magician, W/oland] on Tour, and The Son of W[... ] were all eventually discarded in favour of The Engineer’s Hoof (TI, p.225). Despite the signs of uncertainty, each title evidently refers in some way to Woland, indicating his central importance in the original conception.'® Throughout these early years of work on the manuscript, Bulgakov was always to speak of this as his ‘novel about the devil’. As for the name of this ‘devil’, the manus- cripts show that Woland was chosen in preference to other alternatives. Antesser, Veliar and Azazello were apparently all possibilities, along with other well-known demonic names. Bulgakov’s notes also attest to his interest in the many differ- ent conceptions of the devil in various epochs and societies (A, p.77). The eventual choice of Woland—one of the devil’s less celebrated pseudonyms—has been seen by Chudakova as the sign of a trend which becomes more prominent in the later redactions, where many of the features identifyng Woland with traditional conceptions of the devil are removed (A, p-74). Even at this early stage, then, it would seem that Woland’s identity was intended to be something of a mystery. '© In the first redaction, Woland masquerades as an engineer.

50 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives The Crisis (1929-1932) Bulgakov abandoned his ‘novel about the devil’ in the spring of 1929. It was two full years before he resumed work on the project, and then only briefly; a further eighteen months were to elapse before he began again in earnest. No period in the writer’s life was more difficult than these three and a half years, and they left an indelible mark on the novel whose composition they interrupted. Bulgakov himself described 1929 as the ‘year of catas- trophe’ (A, p.81). And so it was. As we have seen, the year had begun with the banning of his plays. No longer the suc- cessful playwright, Bulgakov was soon to be on the breadline again; at a stroke of the censor’s pen he had been returned to the grind of his early Moscow days. But this was not the worst of it. Even though his career had been destroyed, the press campaign which had been mounted against the writer by the proletarian critics showed no sign of abating. On the contrary, Bulgakov’s enemies seemed bent upon adding insult to injury by dancing publicly on the grave of his recent career.'’ It is not surprising, therefore, that the strain at last began to tell upon the writer. His second wife describes in her memoirs how Bulgakov became increasingly suspicious and irritable at this time. He also began to sleep badly and developed a ner- vous tic.'® Not all of Bulgakov’s problems were professional, however. In the February of that catastrophic year he had first met Yelena Sergeyevna Shilovskaya (née Nyurenburg), the wife of a senior army officer (A, p.81). Bulgakov was immedi- ately attracted by this woman who not only shared his passion for the theatre but also proved to be a great admirer of his talent as a writer. Their attachment gradually increased over the next two years, by which time it was clear that both mar- riages were threatened. The pressures on Bulgakov’s professional and personal life encouraged him to take drastic action. In July 1929, he drafted a letter to several prominent Bolsheviks, including Stalin, in which he complained of his recent treatment by the '7 See, for example, I. Nusinov, ‘Put’ M. Bulgakova’, Pechat' i revolyutsiya, No.4 (1929), pp-40-53. '® Belozerskaya, p.113.

The Text 51 proletarian critics and requested permission to be ‘exiled’ together with his wife.'? It seems unlikely that any letter was actually sent at this time, but on 3 September a briefer and more businesslike letter containing the same request was dis- patched to Yenukidze, Secretary of the Central Executive Committee.*? Bulgakov also wrote to Gorky, whose influence with the Soviet government he hoped would aid his cause. But these efforts were in vain. No reply was forthcoming from the government, a circumstance which served only to increase the writer’s already serious unease. In a later letter to Gorky he referred pointedly to his ‘boundless fatigue’.*' Yet, despite his nervous exhaustion (or perhaps even because of it) Bulgakov continued to write. Leaving his novel about the devil to one side, he worked first on the draft of a new comedy, Bliss. Then, in September he began the highly autobiographical To a Secret Friend, a work which, like the first part of the eventual Theatri- cal Romance, told of his rise to prominence as a playwright.?? October saw the beginning of another play, a drama about Moliere, first known under the title A Cabal of Hypocrites. The play was finished, but Bulgakov’s attempts to have it staged met with the inevitable rebuff. In the middle of March, 1930, he learned that it had been vetoed ‘from above’. This new setback should hardly have been any surprise to a writer who had ample evidence already of official disfavour towards him. But for Bulgakov it proved the last straw. In a now famous fit of despair he put the manuscripts of several works—including the notebooks containing the novel about the devil—into the stove in his apartment. Yelena Sergeyevna has stated that this act took place on 28 March, the same day that Bulgakov wrote his (now equally celebrated) letter to the Soviet government (TI, p.219). The actual text of this letter has not been preserved, but we are fortunate to have at our disposal the extensive drafts of it, which develop in greater detail the writer’s thoughts of the previous July. Bulgakov stressed that he would be incapable of writing a ‘loyal’ play to suit the authorities, and defended his right to inveigh against censorship as he had done in the play Crimson Island. It is not clear, however, pre- cisely what request the writer made of the government. The drafts show him asking both for permission to emigrate and for the possibility to work in a consultative capacity in the Soviet theatre.’ The rest has become legend. On 18 April, the Bulgakovs received a personal telephone call from Stalin him- self. The writer was apparently offered the choice between the two alternatives mentioned above. On learning of the writer’s preference to remain in the USSR, Stalin immediately ensured that doors were opened. Within a short time, Bul- gakov was engaged as a consultant both to the Moscow Art Theatre and to the Theatre of Working Youth (TRAM).*# There was a further bonus; the press campaign against Bul- gakov suddenly ceased. By the standards of the time, Bulgakov had been most for- tunate, and his lucky star continued to shine throughout the grim purge years. His new position was, however, a decidedly mixed blessing. Although he was assured at least a modest income and spared the prospect of further official harassment, he had returned to the sort of frustrations from which he had only managed to escape in the mid twenties. His new duties for the two theatres (especially TRAM) involved Bulgakov in drudgery no less tedious than the journalistic work he had been obliged to undertake when first he arrived in Moscow. Nineteen thirty turned out, in fact, to be the writer’s most bar- ren year. Only one work, a scenario for a film of Gogol’s Dead Souls, was completed. To make matters worse, Bulgakov’s relationship with Yelena Sergeyevna had reached the point of crisis. But these moves offered no real solution to the writer’s problems and in May he sought a more drastic remedy. At the end of the month, he wrote another let- ter to Stalin in which he described the inhibiting effect of his theatre commitments upon his creative work and asked to be allowed to spend three months abroad later in the year.”° Sta- lin’s reaction to this letter is not known, but permission was not forthcoming. In the event, Bulgakov never was to leave his native land. Nevertheless, the remainder of the year witnessed his partial adjustment to the new circumstances. In July and August, he succeeded in writing a new play, Adam and Eve. Although of modest literary calibre, this dramatic piece was an important symbolic gesture, for it treated a controversial theme (war and pacifism) from a defiantly unorthodox pos- ition. There was never any real possibility of it being staged, and even though Bulgakov went through the motions of approaching various theatres, he did not seem too dishear- tened when the inevitable veto on its production was issued. In any case, his spirits received a boost when he heard towards the end of the year that the ban on his Moliére play had now been lifted.*? And then, in January 1932 came the most exciting news of all: Days of the Turbins was to be revived. The play’s ‘second premiére’ took place the following month. By 1932, then, the signs were more auspicious. But the main problem still remained unsolved. Adam and Eve notwith- standing, Bulgakov was still unable to concentrate properly on his own writing. It is most significant that he had tried dur- ing 1931 to make a fresh start on his ‘novel about the devil’ only to abandon the manuscripts almost as soon as he had begun. The cause of the block, to be sure, was partly the press- ure of other commitments, yet a letter to P. S. Popov of 20 April 1932 suggests a more deep-seated malaise. ‘I can write nothing about anything’, he complained in one of a series of anguished letters, ‘until I unravel the knot in my soul’ (A, p.103). 54 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives Towards the end of the summer Bulgakov and Yelena Ser- geyevna met again after a separation of eighteen months. Now convinced of their commitment to each other, they made the break from their respective families and were married on 4 October. It was only with this, his second, remarriage that Bulgakov felt able at last to settle down. Things were not going to be easy for either of them. Overwork and ill-health were to dog Bulgakov throughout their married life. But Yelena Sergeyevna succeeded in what was the most important thing: she returned Bulgakov to his vocation as a writer. Her presence made itself felt immediately. No sooner were the couple married than Bulgakov began to work again in earnest on the novel eventually to be known as The Master and Margar- ita (A, p.105). And with the return to composition came a new departure: Ieshua and Woland were now to be joined by a hero and heroine whose story was closely modelled on the recent experience of the author and his third wife. Towards a Full Version (Variants 2A, 2B, 3, 3A) Although Bulgakov’s attempts to resume work on his novel in 1931 proved abortive, the drafts which Chudakova has dated to this year (Redactions 2A, 2B) contain signs, albeit tantalizing, of the important new development in its concep- tion. Both redactions consist of a version of one complete chapter (the eventual Chapter 5, “There was an Affair at the Griboyedov’) together with fragments relating to later parts of the novel. Despite the addition to the Griboyedov chapter of a scene involving the poet Ryukhin and his envy of Pushkin, it is the fragments which constitute the main interest in each case. In Redaction 2A there are notes concerning the show at the Variety Theatre and, most fascinating of all, a phrase contain- ing the name Margarita (TI, p.229). This new character also figures in Redaction 2B, where there are preliminary sketches for what will become key scenes in the novel’s eventual dénouement. Here we find the outline of a chapter to be called ‘Woland’s Flight’ in which Margarita and an unnamed male companion are to play an important part; the first mention of Behemoth’s memorable whistle; and the enigmatic phrase “There you will meet Schubert and light mornings’, which is evidently the earliest passage to deal with the all-important

The Text 55 matter of the Master’s ‘reward’ (TI, p.229). Also preserved in this redaction is a new variation of the titlke—The Consultant with the Hoof(T1, p.231). But if, as Chudakova suggests, the broad shape of the final novel was already clear to the author as early as 1931, his personal circumstances at that time were evidently quite unconducive to the sort of sustained effort necessary to bring this expanded conception to fruition. Even when work began again seriously late the following year, it was to take almost four years before anything like a full ver- sion of the novel would be completed. Between autumn 1932 and summer 1936, Bulgakov worked, with a number of substantial breaks enforced by the pressure of his other commitments, on the manuscripts which make up the first full text of the novel. From 30 September 1933, the author began the practice of dating the successive entries in his notebooks, thereby enabling an accurate chron- icle of his progress (TI, p.233). From Chudakova’s descrip- tion of this period, it is possible to distinguish three main phases of composition. The first, which ended on 16 November 1933, saw the production of ‘three and a half fat notebooks’ containing seventeen chapters, some of which are represented only by a brief outline or a heading (TI, p.233). During the second phase, which lasted from 30 December 1933 until October 1934, work progressed much more irregu- larly. Although further chapters were written, the novel devolves into fragments after Chapter 19 (TI, p.237), which Chudakova interprets as a sign of Bulgakov’s desire to ‘fix as quickly as possible at least the general contours of a whole which was already clear to him’ (A, p.109). Between July and October a new notebook, with the heading ‘Conclusion’, developed these fragments into a fuller narrative. Taken together, these two phases of work resulted in Redaction 3. Then, between late autumn 1934 and summer 1936, Bulgakov made ‘extensive additions to the third redaction and [rewrote] individual chapters’ (TI, p.241). The product of this third period of composition is referred to here as Redaction 3A. The early chapters of Redaction 3, written in 1933, cover ground already familiar from previous versions of the novel. Woland arrives in Moscow; he encounters the editor and the poet; the editor meets his death in a hideous accident; and

56 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives chaos descends on the literary and theatrical worlds of the Soviet capital. Although there are certain new scenes here— Chudakova provides an extract from Chapter 7, a hilarious scene in which a children’s writer named Karaulina displays hyperbolic rage at being excluded from the list of those to be supplied with new housing (TI, pp.233—4)— these are inciden- tal to the overall conception. Throughout the writing of the novel, many such passages appeared and disappeared without leaving any obvious mark. Of much greater significance, how- ever, are the outlines (dated 6 October, 1933) of Chapters 10 and 11. The latter was entitled “The Gospel according to Woland. Chapter 1’. This indicates a double change. Most obvious is the shift of position; previously, the Jerusalem nar- rative had been introduced much closer to the beginning, in the second chapter. Although this compositional experiment was subsequently abandoned (in all later redactions, the pas- sion story begins, as before, in Chapter 2), the attendant decision to divide this part of the novel into separate chapters was retained, and carried through to the final text. Of equal significance was the inclusion, in Chapter 10, of an important new scene involving the future Bezdomny: ‘Ivanushka comes to in the clinic and asks for the Gospels in the evening’ (TI, pp.234—-5). In the event, he gets more than he bargained for; instead of reading the bible, the poet meets Woland again, from whom he hears the ‘true’ story of Pilate and Ieshua. This scene was soon to be remodelled, yet even in this form it reveals the growing importance of the poet in the novel’s design. But by far the most striking feature of Redaction 3 is the introduction, in Chapters 12 to 16, of a new story line concern- ing the ‘secret lovers’, Faust and Margarita (A, p.108). Bul- gakov’s new hero bears the name of Goethe’s character, it should be stressed, only in one of the chapter outlines; else- where he is referred to simply as ‘the poet’. While there is no reason to doubt Chudakova’s contention that Bulgakov never seriously intended using the name Faust in the novel proper, the fact that he immediately associated this love story with the Goethean prototype is clearly a matter of enormous signifi- cance. Most significant of all, however, is the designation of this ‘Faustian’ hero as the author of a novel about Pontius

The Text 57 Pilate (A, p.10g). But, as yet (October 1933), there is no evi- dence that Bulgakov fully appreciated the potential opened up by what eventually turned out to be one of his most brilliant strokes of invention. The basic story line concerning the two lovers was devel- oped during the following year. Already there is no mistaking the shape of things to come. The reader is told how the lovers came to be disunited; Margarita comes into contact with the supernatural; she is transformed into a witch and flies off to a sabbath. The latter scene, which apparently differs from the final “Satan’s Grand Ball’ due to a profusion of what Chudak- ova describes as ‘Rabelaisian details’, nevertheless performs the same broad function in the plot. As a reward for her ser- vices at the sabbath, Margarita secures the return of her lover (TI, p.236). The events related in the notebook entitled ‘Con- clusion’ are also recognizable. After their reunion, the lovers are poisoned and fly off with Woland and his retinue as Mos- cow is consumed by an apocalyptic fire. Their flight is inter- rupted by a scene in which they witness both the suffering of Pilate in the supernatural realm, and his release as he is finally forgiven for his act of cowardice. There follows a brief, incom- plete passage dealing with the poet’s own ‘reward’; here, for the first time, he is referred to as the Master (TI, p.238). Even though Chudakova describes Redaction 3 as the first full version of the novel, it was obviously not properly finished in 1934. All the major features of the final text are either pres- ent or clearly adumbrated, yet many of the finer details remained to be settled. The final sections, in particular, were still only roughly sketched in, and certain earlier chapters had not yet been written out in full. It could well be that these parts of the novel were not completely clear in the author’s mind at this time. All that is known for certain is that the per- ennial burden of overwork had by now so severely taxed his strength that sustained work on the manuscript had become increasingly arduous. In an attempt to relieve the pressure, the writer and his wife applied for permission to travel abroad, but their plans were again thwarted by officialdom. In June 1934 Bulgakov once more resorted to the desperate measure of writing personally to Stalin. He received no reply. By this time his nervous ailments were such that he undertook a course of

58 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives electrolysis treatment, which failed to bring any lasting ben- efit. An entry in Yelena Sergeyevna’s diary for 13 October refers to a variety of symptoms ranging from agoraphobia to a fear of being left alone and suggests that they were contem- plating the use of hypnosis as a possible remedy (A, p.115). As usual, however, the crisis passed, although there was no les- sening of Bulgakov’s workload. Indeed, 1935 was one of his busiest years. In the autumn he had two plays in rehearsal (Moliére and Ivan Vasil'evich) and a third (The Last Days (Push- kin)) had elicited interest from both the Moscow Art Theatre and the Vakhtangov Theatre (A, p.120). Under these difficult conditions, work on the novel was bound to proceed slowly. Yet proceed it did. By the summer of 1936, Redaction 3A, comprising additions and revisions to Redaction 3, had been completed. In this version, the role of the Master was expanded considerably. Most importantly, it is now he, not Woland, who meets the poet Ivanushka during his moment of re-evaluation in the clinic (A, p.112). And in Chapter 37, “The Last Flight’, written on 6 July 1936, the theme of the Master’s ultimate fate is worked out in greater detail than before (A, pp.124-6). (For the particulars of Bul- gakov’s evolving conception of this crucial episode, see Chapter 8 below.) Even so, Bulgakov evidently still did not consider the novel finished. The notebook containing Chapter 37 concludes with a new list of chapters and some notes which show that he was still reading sources concerning the New Testament story (A, p.124). As for the title, these years saw numerous possibilities: The Great Chancellor; Satan; I’m here too; The Hat with a Feather; The Black Theologian; He has appeared; The Foreigner’s Horseshoe; The Coming; The Black Magician—all these alternatives feature in the notebooks (TI, p.233). Towards a Final Text (Redactions 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) Having brought the draft of his novel to the point of near completion, Bulgakov soon embarked upon the task of revision. Between summer 1936 and autumn 1937 he pro- duced two further redactions, both of which were abandoned at a relatively early stage. The first of these (Redaction 4) extended only as far as part way through Chapter 5; the second (Redaction 5), which bore the title The Prince of Dark-

The Text 59 ness, comprised thirteen chapters, again starting from the beginning (A, p.128). Chudakova tells us very little about these two versions of the novel, leaving the impression that they are to be considered ‘false starts’ before work began on Redaction 6, the second complete version of the novel, towards the end of 1937. Bulgakov’s inability to settle to the job of revising his novel at this time is immediately comprehensible once one surveys the events of his life. Nineteen thirty six was, in fact, a turning point in his career. The year began full of promise, with the premiére of his play Moliére. After something like three hundred rehearsals and numerous revisions, it opened on 15 February to an enthusiastic audience.’® But, just as Bulgakov seemed to have achieved acceptance as a bona fide Soviet dra- matist once more, the play was subjected to damning criticism on the pages of Pravda. The review appeared on g March and the play was immediately withdrawn from the repertory. On 13 May there came another blow: the comedy Ivan Vasil’evich was cancelled at the stage of dress rehearsal.*? The impli- cations were obvious. Although Bulgakov was to retain his tenuous foothold in Soviet literary life, official favour was never going to manifest itself in the form of a total reprieve. What this meant in practical terms was that Bulgakov would be limited to the least satisfactory kind of literary endeavour as a source of income—the adaptation of classical works for the stage. Perhaps it was this dismal prospect that caused him at last to register his mounting frustration with the Moscow Art Theatre by resigning his position during work on a Shak- espeare project. He left the theatre on 15 September to take up the position of librettist with the Bolshoy company (A, p.122). One imagines that the work must have been, if anything, less congenial to him, but it had the signal advantage of sparing nim the anxiety with which his theatre endeavours had become synonymous. In effect, the decision may have been even more momentous, for, in retrospect, it suggests that Bul- gakov had recognized that from now on his only important literary efforts would be directed towards a private audience. “8 Wright, Mikhail Bulgakov, p.191. *9 Proffer, Bulgakov, p.409.

60 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives The traumatic events of 1936 interfered with Bulgakov’s work on his novel in more ways than one. On 16 November he began to write another long work, Theatrical Romance. The idea for this novel had been in the writer’s mind since at least 1929, when he had composed a version known as To a Secret Friend. A first chapter of the new work had been dictated as early as May 1934 (A, p.114). Now, in the wake of his severence from the Moscow Art Theatre, he wrote this merciless satire based, quite transparently, on his own ten years of experience. It was, as at least one critic has suggested, an unmistakable case of art as therapy for the artist.°° Theatrical Romance was never finished, however. In the autumn of 1937, Bulgakov decided to direct his efforts towards the completion of The Master and Margarita (A, p.124). Although constantly occupied with vari- ous libretti, he now devoted his spare time almost exclusively to the production of a sixth redaction of the novel. The result of some nine months’ concentrated work, Redac- tion 6 expands still further the material of the preceding ver- sions. As before, it is the story of the Master which accounts for much of this growth. This shift of emphasis is reflected in a new title: now, at last, the novel is known as The Master and Margarita (A, p.128). Chudakova also records other important decisions which suggest a substantial movement towards the text as we know it. The style of the Moscow narrative now departs from the chatty skaz of the early versions in favour ofa manner less personal and more literary, although still highly playful (A, p.129). And the Jerusalem story, originally con- ceived simply as the ‘Gospel according to Woland’, acquires its curious triple motivation. A combination of Woland’s nar- rative, Bezdomny’s dream, and the Master’s novel, it takes on a new complexity as a tale somehow independent of its tellers (A, p.130). The all-important epigraph from Goethe’s Faust is also added for the first time, appearing here in the original German (A, p.131). But, if these were all signs that Bul- gakov’s conception was now hardening, there is at least one instance which shows that his ideas had not fully crystallized. The version of the Master’s ‘reward’ in this redaction differs SO ibideainar

The Text 61 both from what went before and from what was to come (A pp.130-1). No sooner was this new manuscript completed than Bul- gakov set about the job of transforming it into a typescript. Armed both with Redaction 6 and with two other notebooks containing revisions, he dictated what amounts to a new ver- sion of the novel between the end of May and the end of June 1938. A letter from the writer to his wife dated June 13 pro- vides a vivid impression both of the immense effort and of the creative intensity involved as the typescript was taking shape: ‘The twenty-first chapter is being dictated. I’m buried beneath this novel. I’ve rethought everything, everything is now Clear to me’ (A, p.132). It is difficult to know quite what to make of this last remark. Most probably, Bulgakov is guilty of an excusable hyperbole. Certainly, Chudakova provides nothing which would support the idea of any major ‘rethink- ing’ at this stage, although she does refer to a further develop- ment in the depiction of the Master: now he is presented as a man who is both mentally ill and aware of his illness (TI, p.249). Without inspecting the manuscripts at first hand, it is clearly impossible to assess either the extent or the signifi- cance of the changes made. It would appear most likely, how- ever, that Bulgakov had not so much ‘rethought’ his novel in the summer of 1938, but rather that he had become more con- scious of where his earlier ideas had led him. The labour of producing the first typescript (and seventh redaction) of The Master and Margarita left Bulgakov physically and mentally exhausted. Leaving Moscow and the novel behind him, the writer devoted the remainder of the summer to projects more likely to add to his income. But by 19 Sep- tember he was already back to the typescript, which he began to submit to extensive revision and correction (A, p.135). At first this work proceeded slowly. As usual, there were other demands on Bulgakov’s time, and his health, which was never good, began to deteriorate more seriously. It is not known pre- cisely when the writer first diagnosed the symptoms of the her- editary sclerosis of the kidneys which was to cause his premature death, although, as a medical man, he must have identified the signs well before the dramatic worsening of his condition in August 1939. >)

62 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives But there is evidence to suggest a quite different reason for Bulgakov’s slow progress with the revisions. Before he could proceed further it seems that he felt the need to try the novel out on an audience. The novel was eventually read to a small group of friends in four sittings between 26 April and 14 May 1939.3’ The importance of these readings can be gauged not only from the memoirs of Vilenkin, who was a member of this privileged audience, but also from Bulgakov’s notebooks, which attest to a number of significant additions made at this very time. Chudakova records that the latter date was especially important, this being the day that the Epilogue (the last lengthy addition to the novel) was completed. To the same date she also assigns the introduction of two brief, but crucial, phrases. Now, instead of a ‘messenger in black’, it is Matthew who brings the news of the Master’s fate in the famous words: ‘He has not earned light, he has earned peace’. And Woland is given the equally memorable judgement on the Master’s novel, which, we now learn, is ‘unfortunately, not finished’ (A, p.135). The story of the last eight months of Bulgakov’s life is domi- nated by his struggle to complete the revision of the novel. Afflicted by all manner of painful symptoms, he worked on into the new year of 1940. Chudakova has recorded Yelena Sergeyevna’s account of the writer’s last engagement with the novel: ‘In 1940 he had made more additions to the first part; I read them to him. But when we passed on to the second part and I began to read about Berlioz’s funeral, he was about to begin the corrections, but then said: “All right. That will be enough, perhaps”. He did not ask me to read again’ (A p-140). The great value of Chudakova’s work is that it shows how much The Master and Margarita was a tale that grew in the tell- ing. The novel as we know it is the result of a collision between two very different stories, between an original, and extremely ‘literary’, conception involving the visit of the devil to Moscow complete with unorthodox gospel, and a deeply personal story > 3" V. Vilenkin, “O Mikhaile Afanas’eviche Bulgakove’, Vospominaniya s kommentar- iyami (Moscow, 1982), p.392.

The Text 63 based on the events which interrupted that first project.” It is the mark of Bulgakov’s genius that the product of what can only be described as a historical accident is a novel in which the heterogeneous materials converge and interpenetrate to achieve the impression of effortless unity. What Chudakova’s research reveals is that this effortlessness is indeed an illusion and that few novels can have cost their author greater effort. Finally, it also confirms what many readers have suspected— that the novel is, properly speaking, unfinished. Although the final redaction is complete in the narrow formal sense, the evi- dence is that, but for the writer’s premature death, it would certainly have undergone further revision.23 It would be pointless to speculate on the possible nature of these revisions, yet we can be fairly certain that Part II (which most people feel instinctively to be the weaker) would have been altered substantially. It is not only that Part II was never reworked in the final redaction, but also that this part of the novel had passed through fewer versions to reach this form, Bulgakov’s practice having been regularly to abandon an unfinished ver- sion only to begin again from Chapter 1. The message for the critic 1s obvious. While we can only do our best to interpret the text that we have, the indeterminacy of its second part ensures that whatever we say about it must inevitably remain rather tentative and provisional. As it stands, The Master and Margarita ends up leaving many of the questions which it poses both unanswered and unanswerable. ues ENG ESRD BexiUeAi PE RSS| PB Gyn Tl Vi When one surveys the full range of the writing projects upon which Bulgakov was engaged during the twelve years of his work on The Master and Margarita, the fact that the novel remained unfinished becomes far less remarkable than that it was ever written at all. Almost without exception, these works were exactly what they sound like—uncongenial chores undertaken with the sole pur- pose of keeping the bailiffs from the door. Although always competent and workmanlike, they occupy only a peripheral place in the writer’s euvre and shed very little light on his real preoccupations during these all-important years. But not all of his other writing ventures were of this sort. Up until 1936 at least, Bulgakov still retained the hope of reviving his fortunes as a dramatist, to which end he wrote a number of original plays. These plays, together with a few unfinished prose pieces, not only represent a substantial achievement in their own right, but also provide a sort of running commentary upon the novel as it was taking shape. The interconnection of The Master and Margarita with other works written concurrently is a large and interesting subject which has yet to receive the careful, detailed treatment it deserves. All that can be offered here is a highly selective over- view. Again, the facts can be easily gleaned from a tabular summary (see Table 2). Of particular interest in the present context are those original works written during the eventful hiatus between the abandonment of the first two redactions of The Master and Margarita and the commencement of the third, all of which contain elements which appear, in retrospect, to point the way forward to the new material yet to be incorpor- ated within the scheme of the novel. Most prominent in this respect are the interrelated themes of the artist and of the per- secuted genius, later to be combined in the story of the Mas- ter. Bulgakov’s treatment of these themes in such works as A Cabal of Hypocrites (Moliére), and Adam and Eve will be con- sidered in the chapter which follows. For the present I shall limit the discussion to those points which provide support for Chudakova’s suggestion that the author was already experi- menting in his other literary works with aspects of story and character soon to be transferred to the novel (A, p.g7). THE RUSSIAN TEXTS ‘A knowledge of the true text is the basis of all criticism’; thus, W. W. Greg, writing some fifty years ago, formulated the guiding principle for literary scholarship.37 The conduct of literary life in the Soviet Union has, however, been notor- iously unconducive to the achievement of this ideal condition. When works are denied publication and circulate in clan- destine copies, when officially published works are first sub- jected to the rigours of political censorship, when the archives containing the relevant manuscript materials are not open to outside scrutiny, there will always be doubt regarding the reliability of the texts with which we work. These problems are illustrated by the story of the publication of The Master and Margarita. It is ironic that, having lain in the desk drawer for more than a quarter of a century, Bulgakov’s novel appeared in no less than three different Russian versions within six years of its original publication. The first was the text which featured on the pages of the journal Moskva and which was reproduced in Paris later in 1969.3° Even as the novel was making its belated appearance, however, it became widely known that this text had been quite heavily ‘edited’. Very soon, the excised pas- sages made their way abroad, where they were published first as a supplement to the existing versions,*? before being incor- porated within the Possev edition, which was considered for some time to represent the novel in its entirety.*° But the issue 3° See Chapter 6, below. 37 W. Although not itself without certain textological dubiety, this version, which has now been reprinted several times, is the fullest available and has gained general, if some- what guarded acceptance as the ‘canonical’ text of the novel. Even though it was very rapidly superseded, the Moskva version retains more than the simple historical interest of being the first printed text of the novel, for it also provides one of the best examples we have of recent Soviet censorship at work. The facts are easily established. Analysis of the Possev text (in which the passages omitted by the Moskva editors are conveniently italicized) yields the following statistics. Part I of the novel suffered twenty cuts, which affected seven of the eighteen chapters, accounting for some 58g lines, or about 6.5 per cent of text. The corresponding figures for Part II are 135 cuts, affecting all chapters, and amounting to 1,646 lines, or just over 20 per cent of text. Immediately apparent, of course, is the imbalance in the distribution of the cuts between the two parts of the novel, an imbalance which is all the more striking when one considers that just two lengthy excisions account for 80 per cent of the total lines removed from the entire first part. How 1s this disparity to be explained? One answer would be to suggest that Part II contains more material of a politically sensitive nature than Part I. But, although this may be so, the difference would surely not be so pronounced as the bare figures imply. What is more, it can easily be demonstrated that many of the excisions from Part II do not readily admit of a political explanation. Indeed, many critics have expressed their perplexity regarding the rationale governing a large number of these cuts.*' It is possible, therefore, that the expla- nation lies less in the nature of the text itself than in the fact of its serial publication. It could well be that the Moskva editors felt the need for more rigorous censorship after the first part of the novel had produced such a huge and rapturous response from the Russian reading public. Many of the editorial intrusions in Part IT do seem to display an arbitrariness born * See, for example, H. Muchnic, ‘The Master and Margarita’, Russian Writers (New York, 1971), p.307.

The Text 69 perhaps of a desire that they simply be seen as a mark of extra vigilance. But perhaps politics was not the only factor involved here. Given the less ‘finished’ nature of Part II, many of the editorial decisions may have been prompted by nothing more sinister than the wish to rid the novel of superfluous details. Nor should we discount Yanovskaya’s suggestion that the principal criterion in this exercise was the need to save space.*? These other considerations notwithstanding, there can be no doubt that a good number of the editorial cuts in the Moskva text were politically motivated. Both of the lengthy omissions from Part I, for example, yield readily to this type of explanation. The story, in Chapter 7, of the series of myster- ious disappearances from apartment number 50 (pp.491-3) must have been considered too direct an allusion to one of the most distressing aspects of life in Stalin’s Russia. The reten- tion of Nikanor Ivanovich’s dream, which makes up the bulk of Chapter 15 (pp.577-87) would presumably also have been expected to reopen the same collective wound in its evocation of the grotesque theatricality of the various ‘trials’ and ‘exposures’ associated with the purge years. Many of the shorter cuts display a similar logic. Margarita’s fears for the Master and her suspicion that he may have been exiled (pp.637-8), together with her assumption, later in the same Chapter 19, that Azazello is a police agent about to make an arrest (p.641), must have been found to speak rather too openly of the uncertainty and paranoia that ruled in Moscow in the 1930s. Similarly revealing is the omission of a number of references in Chapters 23 and 24 to the considerable physical suffering experienced by the Master whilst under interrog- ation by the security agencies.*9 While the omissions mentioned above refer rather pointedly to the past, there are others where the danger may have resided rather in their continued relevance to Soviet life in the 1960s.44 The numerous satirical references to the security 4? It is also easy to imagine the line of thought which might have provoked the removal of the poet Ryukhin’s con- fession (‘I don’t believe in anything I write!’ (p.489)) and of the Master’s complaint about critics whom he suspects of writing ‘something other than what they want to say’ (p.561). Korov’ev’s later comment, ‘Remove the document and you remove the man’ (p.706), while fortunately not so widely applicable to life in the post-Stalin era, nevertheless has an aphoristic force which would have made it the more danger- ous for being so immediately memorable. The Moscow story was not the only part of The Master and Margarita to have been scrutinized for political implications. The Jerusalem narrative also attracted the attention of the censor. The section which suffered most in this respect was that part of Chapter 26 which contains the conversations of Pilate with Aphranius. That these particular passages were so heavily reduced in the Moskva text suggests a fear of their potential for generating an allegorical reading. Pilate’s ambi- valent and unorthodox dealings with his ‘secret policeman’ could hardly fail to evoke the spectre of Stalin, who used the internal security agencies in much the same way, the most notorious example being the assassination of Kirov. (For further details on the possible allegorical dimension of the Jer- usalem story, see Chapter 3 below.) However, of all the omissions from the ancient narrative, critics have attributed the greatest significance to the fate of the several references to the sin of ‘cowardice’. Of the four occasions on which this crucial notion is invoked (pp.721, 735, 745, 796), the first and the third were removed; the other two escaped unscathed. To suggest, as one critic has done on the evidence of one of these omissions, that the entire sense of the novel has thereby been lost in the Moskva version is certainly to overstate the case.t? But these cuts speak nevertheless for an editorial desire to impair the most potent political dimen- sion of the Pilate story. One is only left to ponder the reason for removing just two of the comments about cowardice. But, whatever the intention of those responsible for the publication of the novel, the surviving references to Pilate’s cowardice were more than sufficient for the liberal critics to isolate this con- cept as a synonym for the moral dilemma which confronted all those in positions of power during the Stalin era. Other omissions from the Moskva text display a logic of a somewhat different type. There are, for example, a number of occasions on which details are removed which might encour- age the reader to hunt out real-life prototypes for the fictional characters. Thus, the titles of Ryukhin’s poems mentioned in Chapter 6 (p.484) did not appear in the journal publication, nor did Woland’s later explanation to Margarita of the back- ground of Baron Meigel (p.690). Rather more baffling is the removal of an entire series of references connecting Margarita with ‘Queen Margot’ in Chapters 21 and 22.4° The cuts are consistent, yet the workings of the editors’ minds on this occasion remain mysterious. The omission of many of the comments referring to the nakedness of Margarita and Natasha during their supernatural adventures, on the other hand, has been taken by many to indicate a puritanical streak in the controllers of Soviet literature.*”? Similarly revealing is the tendency to abbreviate those passages in Chapter 21 cele- brating Margarita’s primitive joy as she wrecks the apartment of the critic Latunsky. Many of the omissions from the des- cription of events at Satan’s Ball suggest the same intention to reduce the emphasis on the bizarre and antisocial. Neverthe- less, there are still many cuts which resist convincing explana- tion. Why, for example, exclude from Chapter 24 Behemoth’s ridiculous tale of his nineteen days in the desert and the later scene of his ineffectual shooting competition with Azazello? (pp.693, 695-6). There is ample evidence that some of the cuts inflicted on the novel in its first publication were designed to thwart certain political readings. But if this was the aim, it was inevitably doomed to failure. As we saw in the previous chapter, there was no shortage of talented critics in the USSR for whom even a mutilated text of The Master and Margarita represented the most devastating critique of the Sta- lin era since Solzhenitsyn. The only way such a reaction could have been prevented, one imagines, would have been not to publish the novel at all. The issue of The Master and Margarita in the 1973 Romany volume somewhat unexpectedly opened a new chapter in the history of Bulgakov’s text. The long-awaited publication of the novel (the first to appear officially in the Soviet Union since the Moskva edition) offered its readers rather more than they had probably bargained for, as it represented a version even more full than any that had appeared before, including Possev.*9 Not only were the censorship cuts which had marred the Moskva version reinstated almost in full,°° this text also included passages unknown from any previous version. It may reasonably safely be assumed that the very few occasions on which the Romany text omits short passages con- tained in Possev are also the product of a similar desire to reconstruct as accurately as possible a text which accorded with Bulgakov’s final intentions. Bulgakova (it is essential to distinguish these from cor- rections made by her under the author’s dictation or simul- taneously with his correction of one of the other copies), bringing the typescript into line with the text she supposed to represent the authentic will of the author’ (A, p.31). The reader of Viktor Petelin’s memoirs is likely to be even more sceptical, for that writer recounts how the chief editor of Romany told him that certain textual problems which arose during the preparation of the book were solved by appeal to Ye. 74 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives were disregarded on the ground that they distorted the author's own style. It would be fruitless even to attempt to pursue this discussion any further, but it is clear that the problems of establishing a truly reliable text for The Master and Margarita are immense, and one would be naive in imagining that these problems would be solved simply by publishing all the relevant materials, helpful though this would be. Given the facts—an unfinished manus- cript, authorial revisions scattered amongst various typescripts and notebooks, and later editorial work by the author’s widow— itseems most likely that no single ‘authentic’ version of the novel will ever be produced. For the present, at least, the Romany text will have to be accepted as the best available. Although far from unimpeachable, it is apparently free from censorship cuts, and if it errs in any direction, it is perhaps the case that it includes too much, rather than too little. (On this point, see the dis- cussion of the novel’s final words in Chapter 8 below.) The implication for interpretation of the novel is self-evident: given the uncertainty surrounding the text (particularly its second part), it would be unwise to insist too rigidly on any reading which relies very heavily on fine points of linguistic detail. PHREEPAPPROACHES The purpose of this chapter is to explore three approaches to The Master and Margarita which were particularly prominent in the early years of the novel’s critical history. Although they differ markedly in their focus, all three have contributed read- ings of the novel which are unmistakably political in orien- tation. A PORTRAIT OF THE ARTIST? Such is the nature of intellectual life in the USSR that few readers of Lakshin’s influential Novy mir article would have required his guidance in order to discover in Bulgakov’s depiction of the Master a ‘concealed self-portrait’ of the author.’ In fact, the salient details of Bulgakov’s career (like those of many others who suffered repression during the Stalin years) were so well known by the time the novel appeared that one might wonder only at the tentativeness of Lakshin’s state- ment. The explanation is, of course, political; in the volatile atmosphere of the late 1960s it was inadvisable to dwell too insistently upon a powerful ‘de-Stalinizing’ tendency which would have been self-evident in any case to the intelligent Soviet reader. Outside the Soviet Union it was a different story. Free of the constraints which hampered the efforts of their Soviet counterparts, and addressing an audience for whom the relevant information would have been less familiar, critics and reviewers seized upon the novel’s autobiographical element, elucidating its significance as a case-study in literary politics under Stalin. That a knowledge of Bulgakov’s life adds an important dimension to an understanding of The Master and Margarita is a ' Lakshin, ‘Roman .. . ’, p.302.

78 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives point which requires little elaboration. As we saw in the pre- vious chapter, the correspondence between the fictional experiences of the Master and the actual events of Bulgakov’s life is quite pronounced. The Master suffers at the hands of Ariman and Latunsky in much the same way that Bulgakov had done by courtesy of the RAPP critics;* the Master’s manuscript shares the same fiery fate as the first drafts of the novel which was eventually to tell of its burning; and the account of the relationship between the Master and his ‘secret wife’ Margarita inevitably invites comparison with the author’s liaison with Yelena Sergeyevna. Smaller details simply reinforce the identity between the character and his creator: for example, it appears that Bulgakov was particu- larly fond of wearing a skull cap like the one which adorns the Master’s head. If the overlap between fact and fiction on the pages of The Master and Margarita is clearly too important to ignore, it must nevertheless be recognized that this has been the source of enduring misconceptions about the novel. The problem derives from an inclination on the part of many early com- mentators to allow a moral assessment of the facts of Bulgak- ov’s life to interfere with an aesthetic engagement with the text. An extreme example is furnished by the following extract, in which the real and the fictional have become totally conflated: “She [i.e. Margarita] destroys the apartment of the scoundrel Latunsky who tried in every way possible to ruin the Master and delayed the publication of his novel by twenty-five years’ (my italics).+ Although such flagrant confusions of life and literature are rare, many critics have fallen no less com- pletely into the same sort of error. Hence the tendency— almost universal in the early days and still prevalent today— to view the Master, like his creator, as an archetypal victim of Stalinist literary politics. Three Approaches 79 of the Master as a case of social injustice. Indeed, Bulgakov actually enhances the force of his novel as a polemical self-por- trait by including in his hero’s tragic tale harrowing details which have no precise counterpart in his own real-life experi- ence. Bulgakov did not himself take refuge in a psychiatric hospital after burning the manuscript of his novel. Nor did he disappear from the face of Moscow for three months, a hiatus in the Master’s biography which Western commentators were quick to interpret as a veiled allusion to a period of internment and interrogation by the security police. In short, the Master suffers considerably more in the novel than Bulgakov did in life. But this only makes it the more imperative to weigh the political significance of these details against other elements in the Master’s portraiture which pull in a different direction. The Master is a victim of his times, but he is not only that; the mistake is to see the part as the whole. In order better to appreciate the competing impulses which helped to shape Bulgakow’s ‘self-portrait’ in The Master and Margarita, it will be useful to examine one of the most import- ant documents relating to this period in the author’s life—the letter he wrote to Stalin in May 1931. Here is a part of it: Since the end of 1930 I have been suffering from a serious form of neurasthenia with attacks of fear and heartfelt depression. I have a number of projects in mind, but lack the physical strength and the conditions necessary to carry them out. The cause of my illness is perfectly clear: in the broad field of Russian literature in the USSR I was the sole literary wolf. I was advised to dye my coat a different colour. This was stupid advice. Whether dyed or with its coat clipped short, the wolf will never look like a poodle. They treated me like a wolf. For several years I was subject to the laws of the literary hunt, cornered in a fenced yard. I feel no anger, but I am very tired. After all, even a hunted animal can become tired. The animal announced that he was no longer a wolf, no longer a writer. He fell silent. And that, Ict us say plainly, is faintheartedness.° Like other letters written by Bulgakov during these troubled years, this one makes for painful reading. Despite the dis- 5 Note, however, the response of Viktor Petelin (‘Geroi Bulgakova’, p.241), who states that this has ‘no significance at all’. ® Milne, ‘K biografii .. . ’, p.155.

80 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives claimer, it is an understandably angry response to the despic- able treatment handed out to him by the members of the new literary establishment. What makes this passage of particular interest, however, is the tension within it between the contra- dictory attitudes of self-pity and self-criticism, each of which is the more striking due to its hyperbolic form of expression. How could Bulgakov refer to himself as the only ‘literary wolf’ when the cases of Zamyatin, Pilnyak and Mandelstam (to mentioned only the most celebrated) were fresh in the minds of all who were concerned for the fate of Russian literature? But, by the same token, he is surely too hard on himself by far when he speaks of his recent behaviour as a renunciation of his profession. Although the overstatement in the letter to Stalin may be dismissed as the temporary product of Bulgakov’s distress, the underlying ambivalence was a more permanent psychological condition. This state of mind may be traced back to his very earliest autobiographical fragments, ‘Notes on the Cuffs’, in which the author presents himself first as the valiant defender of nineteenth-century Russian culture against the barbarism generated by the October Revolution, then as a man cringing in his bed, fearful of a ring at the doorbell in the middle of the night.’ From the very beginning, it would seem, Bulgakov was caught between a belief in his sacred calling as a writer in Soviet Russia and an awareness of his temperamental inade- quacy for the task which he felt history had imposed upon him. The agonizing experiences of 1929 and 1930 only exacer- bated his awareness of a problem which had pursued him throughout his literary life. Projecting the Self: From Fesya to the Master The contradictory impulses which eventually fused in the portrait of the Master will become more evident if we consider briefly some of the other heroes created by Bulgakov during these turbulent years. The first of these is Fesya, the enigmatic figure who appeared in the earliest version of The Master and Margarita. Chudakova’s description of Fesya indicates that he was conceived as an outsider, a man of talent and potential ’ Bulgakov, Rannjaja neizdannaja proza, pp.15 f.

Three Approaches 81 denied the possibility of a creative intellectual life due to the conditions created by the Soviet régime. It is easy to detect in Fesya a projective image of Bulgakov’s self-pity, especially as he is the first of three characters who collectively fit the stereo- type of the ‘persecuted genius’. The second work to feature such a hero was the first variant of Bliss, a play which possibly dates back to 1929, and is again known to us only through the account furnished by Chudakova. Reyn, the scientist-hero of this manuscript differs markedly from the character of the same name in the later version of the same play. Chudakova speaks of this earlier figure as ‘a man of inner firmness, coun- tervailing the time [in which he lives]’, adding that in this first draft ‘Reyn’s persecution and tiredness were emphasized.”® The third representative of the archetype is the only one avail- able for direct inspection—Yefrosimov, the hero of Adam and Eve. A scientist like Reyn, Yefrosimov is portrayed as a bril- liant, unworldly man cast adrift in a world dominated by aggressive, philistine values. This play is probably the most outspokenly ideological of all Bulgakov’s works, and it turns on the contrast between the appealing humanism of the gifted man, and the singularly unattractive political commitment of Adam and Daragan, men who represent the new Soviet era. The kinship between the Master and these earlier examples of persecuted genius is unmistakable. Yefrosimov, in particu- lar, shares several features in common with the hero of the novel. Innocents at large in a hostile environment, both men display their unworldliness in the same act of absent-minded- ness: neither can remember the name of his former wife. Each character also becomes involved in an extra-marital relation- ship. In leaving her legal husband Adam to serve the eccentric Yefrosimov, Eve realizes an ambition which is thwarted, in Margarita’s case, by circumstance and her own indecision. No less important is the dénouement of the play, in which Yefrosi- mov and Eve are rewarded with the promise of ‘peace’, a motif which clearly foreshadows the conclusion of The Master and Margarita.° 8 Chudakova, ‘Arkhiv .. .’, pp.112 f. a 9 The ending of the first variant of Bliss was apparently very similar, see ibid., p-113.

82 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives These observations have to be set against the connection between the Master and a very different Bulgakov hero—the Moliére of his play A Cabal of Hypocrites. Written in 1929 and 1930, and subsequently staged under the title Moliere in 1936, this play charts the final stages in the life and career of the great French dramatist. Here, as in his later unorthodox bio- graphy of the playwright, The Life of Monsieur de Moliere, Bul- gakov was concerned with a simple question: how was it that Moliére, a writer whose plays expressed ideas and attitudes thoroughly inimical to France’s ruling élite (especially the church) managed not only to have these plays staged, but even to get royal approval for them? The secret of his success, in Bulgakov’s interpretation, lay in the dramatist’s willingness to compromise his beliefs and even to stoop to hypocrisy. His Moliére is a pragmatist of the sort who believe that the end justifies the means. But the methods he 1s obliged to employ in the pursuit of his objectives make him a less than sympathetic type. The worst of it, however, is that no real benefit accrues from these tactics in the long run. Moliére’s enemies (the ‘cabal’ of the play’s title) ultimately prove more expert in the ways of deceit, spreading malicious rumours which result in the withdrawal of royal patronage from the playwright’s theatre and the imposition of a total ban on his play Le Tar- tuffe. Moliére dies a sad and defeated man, reduced by his cruel experiences to cynicism and world-weariness. As history, A Cabal of Hypocrites is highly unreliable. ‘Essen- tially fiction based on certain details from Moliére’s life’, com- ments A. C. Wright, the play shows ‘comparatively minor concern for their accuracy or chronology’.'® Behind this cava- lier attitude towards historical fact the same critic has dis- cerned a transparently autobiographical purpose, suggesting that the ‘cabal’ has its counterpart in the RAPP critics, while the banning of Le Tartuffe corresponds to the fate of Days of the Turbins. But the personal importance of A Cabal of Hypocrites is not confined to the theme of the artist’s persecution. Invidious though Moliére’s position is, Bulgakov is at pains to empha- size the Frenchman’s personal failings, dwelling in par- © Wright, Bulgakov, p.186. In an interview at the time, Bulgakov confessed that he had written a ‘romantic drama, not a historical chronicle’ (Ye. Zemskaya, ‘Materialy k tvorcheskoy biografii Mikhaila Bulgakova’, Voprosy literatury, No. 11 (1984), p.199).

Three Approaches 83 ticular upon his growing fear and suspicion as his enemies prepare for the kill. As a result, the play represents something other than an angry statement about the harassment of the writer; it appears rather that the story of Moliére provided Bulgakov with a vehicle for the expression of his feelings about his own recent act of ‘faintheartedness’. In this portrayal, therefore, Moliére’s experience is truly tragic, as it stems from a personal insufficiency which prevents him from recognizing and responding properly to the lofty calling of the artist. A similar conception may be detected in the portrait of the Master in The Master and Margarita. A victim, like the French dramatist, of cruel political circumstances, he is reduced to a condition of despair by the acknowledgement of his own fail- ure of will in burning the manuscript of his novel. The deep affinity between the two heroes is suggested in particular by a detail which is carried over from the play into the novel. As Wright again has indicated, the Moliére of the final act of A Cabal of Hypocrites, where he appears dressed in nightcap, underwear and dressing gown, bears an uncanny resemblance to the figure of the Master when first we see him at Stra- vinsky’s clinic.'' On each occasion, we are invited to witness the spectacle of a writer weighed down by a sense of his inade- quacy. In the words of Yanovskaya, both characters display a Jeli ‘most paradoxical combination of strength and weakness’. Projecting the Self: From ‘The Red Crown’ to Pontius Pilate Although discussion of the autobiographical element in The Master and Margarita has tended for obvious reasons to focus on the story of the eponymous hero, this is not the only part of the novel which may be illuminated by this kind of approach. From the examples cited in the previous section, it may be seen that the autobiographical impulse is represented in Bul- gakov’s euvre in two distinct modes—a ‘literal’ mode, in which the author’s real-life experience is transposed largely unmodi- fied into the work of fiction or drama, and a ‘metaphorical’ mode, whereby identifiable personal themes find repeated expression in stories which have no ostensible connection with ' Wright, Mikhail Bulgakov, p.196. '* Yanovskaya, p.197.

84 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives the writer’s own life. In Bulgakov’s early work (‘Notes on the Cuffs’, Notes of a Young Doctor, and The White Guard would be typical examples) the ‘literal’ mode is predominant. From the mid 1920s onward, however, it was the ‘metaphorical’ mode which assumed the greater importance, being particularly evi- dent in such plays as Flight, Adam and Eve, and A Cabal of Hypocrites. The Master and Margarita has the distinction amongst Bulgakov’s works of being the only work in which both these autobiographical modes are present, the ‘literal’ mode in the figure of the Master, and the ‘metaphorical’ in the character of the fifth procurator of Judaea, Pontius Pilate.'? The nature of the link between Pilate and Bulgakov is sig- nalled in the extract from the letter to Stalin quoted above, where the writer had referred with undisguised scorn to his act of ‘faintheartedness’. The reader of The Master and Margarita could hardly fail to detect in this statement an echo of the cel- ebrated words about the ‘cowardice’ of which Pilate is guilty. Yet Pilate is only one of a series of characters created by Bul- gakov to be afflicted by this particular failing, the roots of which reach deep into the writer’s psyche. The immense per- sonal significance of this theme may be gathered from a letter written to Popov in the spring of 1932, in which Bulgakov con- fessed to the ‘five fatal mistakes’ of his life: But nothing can be done about that now; you can’t turn back the clock. I only really curse those two attacks of timidity which came upon me as unexpectedly as a fainting fit, causing me to commit two of the five mistakes. I do have a justification for this: the timidity was fortuitous, the product of weariness. I grew tired during the years of my writing career. But the justification brings me no consolation.'+ Even though Bulgakov supplied no further clues regarding the two attacks of ‘timidity’ over which he still experienced remorse, we can be reasonably certain that one of them was the ‘faintheartedness’ described in the letter to Stalin. As for the other, the evidence points back to a short but important early work, “The Red Crown’. Published in 1922 under the thinnest of fictional disguises, 'S Chudakova’s work is invaluable for those wishing to explore this topic in greater detail. ‘4 Chudakova, ‘Arkhiv . . .’, p.102.

Three Approaches 85 “The Red Crown’ deals with Bulgakov’s traumatic journey to the south of Russia during the Civil War in search of his brother Nikolay. The first-person narrator (and it is here that the fiction most obviously resides) is a psychiatric patient whose derangement has resulted from his failure to intercede on behalf of a Bolshevik sympathizer, standing by as this man was brutally executed by a White general. Whether Bulgakov personally witnessed an event precisely like the one described in the story must remain an open question, but there can be no mistaking the fact that the theme of execution (and the guilt which it inspires) becomes a common refrain in later works. In the words of one critic, “The Red Crown’ provides ‘a key to Bulgakov’s symbolic system’.'® Certainly, there is a straight line of development from this story to the play Flight, in which Khludov has been driven to the point of mental ill- ness due to his direct responsibility for a similar hanging.'° In the light of these earlier works, it is not difficult to understand why Bulgakov should have been attracted to the story of Pilate and the crucifixion or why, when it came to the actual compo- sition of the biblical narrative, he should have drawn upon a number of motifs previously employed in these and other writ- ings. It is clear, then, that The Master and Margarita is a novel more profoundly personal than it might first appear. A combi- nation of the ‘metaphorical’ and ‘literal’ autobiographical modes, it may be viewed as an attempt by the author to exor- cise two ghosts. Nowhere in Bulgakov’s work is the therapeu- tic urge more evident; it is here perhaps that we come closest to comprehending the source of that power which drove the writer to pursue his final literary project despite the most for- midable obstacles. In the story of Pilate he confronted the theme of cowardice, moral capitulation and guilt which was the abiding obsession of his adult years. In the story of the Master he addressed the latest (and probably most traumatic) manifestation of that moral failing in his own life, the ‘faint- *S Proffer, Bulgakov, p.140. '© Yanovskaya (p.185) comments on Khludov as follows: “Somewhere at the root of this character were tragic impressions of the Civil War. I think these were direct, personal impressions.’

86 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives heartedness’ which resulted in what he saw as the betrayal of his profession as a Russian writer. We have moved a long way from the point with which this chapter began. There I drew attention to the critical blindness that has been the product of a biographical approach to The Master and Margarita which deals only in the correspondences between the facts of Bulgakov’s life and the fictional experi- ences of the Master. But if the novel is viewed instead as the site at which a number of autobiographical themes and modes converge, it is possible both to transcend these limitations and to gain a real insight into the nature of Bulgakov’s conception. The benefits of adopting this broader view of the novel’s auto- biographical base are several. In the first place, it offers a cor- rective to those narrow political interpretations which have presented the Master only as a victim of the times, and the story of Pilate’s moral capitulation primarily as a metaphor of the moral sickness afflicting Stalin’s Russia. The recognition of the twin autobiographical impulse also sheds light on the structure of The Master and Margarita as a ‘double novel’. The novel’s two heroes, the Master and Pilate, although so differ- ent in their character, status and experience, are nevertheless bound together at the deepest level by a common sense of guilt over an act of ‘faintheartedness’. The Master burns his novel; Pilate condemns an innocent man to death. It is here, I believe, that we must seek the explanation of one of the novel’s most basic features—the intimate connection between the fate of the Master and the fate of Pilate in the supernatural finale. Most importantly of all, however, the double focus of the autobiographical theme offered Bulgakov a unique advantage, of which, it appears, he became fully aware only in the actual course of writing the novel. By investing the theme of ‘cowar- dice’ so firmly in the tale of Pilate, the author enabled himself to release the story of the Master from the confessional urge which was its immediate inspiration. Michael Glenny was right, therefore, when he played down the ultimate signifi- cance of the autobiographical element in the Master’s portrai- ture.'’ Although the hero’s story begins, in the retrospective narration of Chapter 13, as a relatively transparent reflection '7 Glenny, p.1t.
