SATIRE If there is one feature of The Master and Margarita which impresses the reader on a first encounter with the novel, it is the vast entertainment offered by its satirical treatment of life in the Soviet Union. This was an aspect of Bulgakov’s accom- plishment which received universal praise from the reviewers, including those whose overall impression of the novel was less than enthusiastic. Full of wit and comic invention, the satiri- cal scenes are not only memorable, they are also the most immediately accessible part of the book, even for those who have little knowledge, either direct or indirect, of life in the USSR. For the reader who does have such knowledge, The Master and Margarita offers that unique pleasure which derives from the recognition of the familiar in a comic guise, be it the soft drinks stand in the park at Patriarchs’ Ponds with its sole offering of warm apricot soda, or the difficulty experienced by Behemoth as he attempts to gain entrance to the privileged realm of the restaurant at the Griboyedov Club. It is a rare conversation between Soviet readers of the novel which does not include the shared reminiscence of at least one of Bulgak- ov’s satirical thrusts. Some of these—like Sokov’s description of his stale sandwiches as being of ‘second-category freshness’ (p.622)—have become virtually proverbial. Bulgakov developed his skills as a satirist during the heyday of Soviet satire—the early and middle 1920s. Both in the short feuilletons he wrote for the periodical press, and in such longer works as The Fatal Eggs and The Heart of a Dog, he more than proved his mastery of the genre. It was upon this earlier experience that he drew in full measure when he came to write The Master and Margarita. In many cases, the targets of the satire are identical with those found in the feuilletons he wrote for the journal Nakanune. The severe housing crisis with its attendant corruption and graft; the naive faith in social pro-

Specific scenes in the novel may even be traced back to indi- vidual feuilletons. The performance of Pushkin’s The Covetous Knight during Nikanor Ivanovich’s dream in Chapter 15 1s a recognizable reprise of a section in “The Golden City’ which described a piece of agitprop drama designed to encourage the conservation of forests.'® Similarly, the critique of the Gri- boyedovites for their utterly bourgeois values recalls another sketch of 1923, ‘Forty times Forty’, in which the Nepmen had been berated for the same failings.'° The fact that so many of the satirical scenes in The Master and Margarita have their roots in Bulgakov’s very earliest pub- lished writings indicates the need to counter the common opinion that this part of the novel is to be understood primar- ily as a satire of life in Stalin’s Russia. But such overt satirical references to the Stalin period are the exception, rather than the rule. The greater part of the satire is far more universal in scope, exposing such general human foibles as greed, deceit and vanity in situations which have no real political significance. The main orien- tation of the novel’s satirical element is neatly summed up in Woland’s often-quoted question during the black magic per- formance: ‘Tell me, my dear Fagot [...] do you find the population of Moscow significantly changed?’ (p.537). The words are, of course, ideologically charged, but the question is not directed specifically against Stalin’s Russia; it is rather that Woland seeks to undermine the faith of those who would have us believe in the perfectibility of humanity in a post-revol- utionary society. There was no shortage of people talking in such terms in the early years of Soviet rule. Bulgakov’s satire in The Master and Margarita is most sus- tained in those episodes which deal with the life of Moscow’s literary community. Here too, the author drew upon themes which had long been present in his writing. In such early pieces as ‘Notes on the Cuffs’, ‘What are we to do?’ and ‘Chamberlain Pushkin’, we find the same mocking view of the new literary formations and their ideological attitudes as that which informs the later novel. More specifically, the atheistic poet Ivan Bezdomny has a forebear in Rusakov, an episodic character in The White Guard. But although Bulgakov’s dislike of the ‘proletarian’ movement, his antipathy towards Futur- ism, and his distrust of the growing regimentation of artistic life remained constant, his literary satire in The Master and Margarita has a topicality which identifies it very much as a product of its particular time. The specific objects of Bulgakov’s literary satire are readily identifiable. The MASSOLIT organization of which the unfortunate Berlioz is the head has its real-life counterpart in the proletarian group RAPP. The Griboyedov Club is the ‘House of Writers’, a centre for writers and journalists which was set up in the 1920s, and still boasts a fine restaurant.** 22 Klaus Mebnert, The Russians and their Favorite Books (Stanford, 1983), pp.61 f.

Indeed, there are other allusions to the Futurist poet which seem to run counter to any satirical intention. Once again, it is Gasparov who has pointed out that when the Master is heard to mutter some- thing about ‘slanting rain’ (p.559), he is quoting from the last line of Mayakovsky’s ‘Going Home! (On the Atlantic)’. In its original version, the final quatrain of this poem reads: I want to be understood by my native land, But I will not be understood—so what? Through my native land I will pass at an angle Like the passing of the slanting rain.°' The purpose of this hidden quotation is most puzzling when viewed against the context of the earlier Mayakovskian motifs. There is no satire here; it appears rather that Bulgakov is using Mayakovsky’s phrase as a means of evoking the Mas- ter’s own predicament. This suggests a deeply ambivalent attitude to the Futurist poet, who is both implicated via the satire in the activities of the literary estabishment, yet indirectly identified, like the Master who speaks his words, as a victim of incomprehension by his contemporaries. The discussion so far has been concerned with the scope and the objects of Bulgakov’s satire in The Master and Margar- ita. In an important sense, however, this is to avoid the central issue, namely, what is the satire doing here? In order to answer this question, we must examine both the nature of Bulgakov’s satire and its distribution on the pages of the novel. The first matter may be addressed with reference to the comments on Bulgakov’s satirical themes contained in Vladimir Lakshin’s introduction to the 1966 edition of the author’s works. Writing of The Master and Margarita, Lakshin mentioned both the speci- fic critique of contemporary literary life, and the general 3" Tbid. 206.

Three Approaches 93 exposé of ‘proprietorial and predatory bourgeois attitudes, and cowardly time-serving’.3* What is of interest here is not so much the substance of Lakshin’s comment as its tone. Even when allowance has been made for the clichés, this is a very angry piece of writing, and it is the anger which seems s0 little in accordance with the tenor of Bulgakov’s satirical manner in his last novel. Lakshin speaks of the satire as if it were born of the desire to instruct and reform, having as its end (in Dry- den’s famous phrase) the ‘amendment of vices by correc- tion’.*3 The basic feature of such satire has been identified by one recent critic as a tendency to exploit the ‘reader’s expec- tations of retribution’.** Now, Bulgakov was certainly not immune to the lure of this kind of writing—witness The Fatal Eggs and The Heart of a Dog—but the satirical quality of The Master and Margarita is of another order altogether. One senses no real indignation here, only a tolerance which invites us simply to laugh at human foibles. The question of retribution has already been broached in this study, and it will figure prominently in the interpretative chapters of Part II. It is appropriate, therefore, to emphasize here that Bulgakov does more than merely eschew the retribu- tive impulse of ‘angry’ satire; in effect, he confounds that impulse by laying bare the manner of its operation. There is no need to demonstrate that the satirical scenes of The Master and Margarita abound in examples of punishment; if anything, there is a veritable superabundance of acts of retribution against the sinful. From the metaphorical exposure of Bosoy to the literal exposure of Moscow’s female citizens in the aftermath of the black magic performance, all manner of human weaknesses are subject to instant and dramatic chasti- sement. As a result, the ‘reader’s expectations of retribution’ are not so much fulfilled as over-fulfilled. And with that satia- tion comes a growing sense of distrust and resistance to the appetite which was its cause. As the cases of punishment mul- tiply, the reader becomes increasingly aware of the sheer banality of most of the ‘sins’ revealed in satirical scenes which 3? Lakshin, ‘O proze M. The most significant element in this disruptive strategy has been identified by Makarovskaya and Zhuk, who raise the crucial question: is there any real or lasting punishment of vice in the novel?3> Surveying the information provided in the Epilogue, the two critics conclude that the acts of summary justice are neither real nor lasting. This observation is of supreme importance, for it identifies a radical challenge to the novel’s satirical scheme; in a few brief paragraphs the Epilo- gue effectively annuls the retributive momentum of the earlier scenes. The shift is marked by one of Bulgakov’s most sub- versive gestures. As the Master and Margarita prepare to leave their basement apartment, Azazello exclaims: ‘And now fire. Fire, with which everything began and with which we will bring everything to an end!’ (p.787). The apocalyptic promise could hardly be more explicit, but it is all the more remark- able for not being fulfilled: Moscow is not destroyed, Woland’s visit is gradually forgotten, and life goes on as before. From this new vantage point the earlier scenes of exposure and punishment appear in an entirely new light, not as satire of the reformist kind at all, but as that sort of satire which is associated with carnival. Such writing has no correc- tive tendency; in the words of Mikhail Bakhtin, its especial appeal resides in the celebration of a ‘temporary liberation from the prevailing truth and from the established order’ .3° Can The Master and Margarita be read, then, as a satirical novel? The answer is that it can, and it has. But, as Patricia Blake put it back in 1967, to do so is rather like reading Crime and Punishment as a detective story.*’ Most critics nowadays would agree that this sort of approach will yield a most impo- verished understanding of Bulgakov’s novel. What has been suggested here, however, is something more than this—that the author’s handling of the satire can be viewed as part of a broader narrative scheme designed deliberately to disorien- tate the reader. This diversionary purpose may be dis- cerned not only in the Epilogue, but also in the very distribution of the satire in the novel. When Edward Ericson writes that Bulgakov’s satire is ‘intermittent’, he is insuffi- ciently precise.*? The important thing is that the satirical scenes are especially prominent in Part 1, where they are invariably associated with the antics of Woland and his entourage. In Part II, however, the satire is conspicuous by its virtual absence. When it does eventually recur—in the scenes where Korov’ev and Behemoth visit the foreign currency shop and the Griboyedov Club, for example—these episodes seem quite irrelevant to the main action of the novel. After one has read of Margarita’s magical adventures, of Satan’s Ball, and the Master’s novel, the satire of everyday life takes on a lesser significance. What had first seemed central appears in retros- pect to be peripheral. This is a point to which I shall return in a different connection in Chapter 5 below. 96 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives The possibility of reading Bulgakov’s novel as an allegory was raised even by its first reviewers. To begin with, this type of interpretation was reserved almost exclusively for the Jeru- salem story, and the main argument extended no further than the line advanced by the Soviet liberal critics, namely, that Pilate’s act of cowardice should be understood as a cryptic statement about the moral condition of many of those who lived under Stalin. ‘Pilate stands for all time-servers in Bul- gakov’s Russia, who longed for Good, and yet betrayed it by failing to oppose Evil,’ wrote one commentator.” ‘Pilate con- demns an innocent man to death,’ added another. ‘How many such innocent people were destroyed in the Soviet Union!’* Quite soon, however, Bulgakov’s commentators began to sup- plement this kind of reading by drawing attention to the alle- gorical significance of seemingly innocent details. A common example is provided by the two five-branched candelabra which burn in the temple at Yershalaim. The remarkable form of these candelabra, it has often been suggested, alludes to the five-pointed stars which adorn the Kremlin wall and other public buildings in the USSR. The ‘cryptographic’ tendency has also led to more detailed and imaginative suggestions. D. G. B. Piper has detected in the story of Judas’s assassination a precise parallel to the mur- der of Kirov, which is widely believed to have been committed by the Soviet security police on Stalin’s secret instructions.** Elena Mahlow, who has devoted an entire book to an allegori- cal interpretation of The Master and Margarita, extends the approach further still. Starting from the same basic premiss— that the fate of Ieshua is to be understood as an allusion to ‘the betrayal and execution of man which takes place in Soviet Russia of the Stalinist period’*3—she proceeds to decipher the details of the Jerusalem story in more abstract terms. Although some of the points raised above have not been challenged, the efforts of those who have tried to build these details into a coherent allegorical framework have been treated with extreme caution, if not outright scepticism. (Mahlow’s work, it should be added, has been generally acknowledged as an example of careful textual scrutiny being harnessed to a thoroughly misguided purpose.) At its worst, this kind of interpretation appears wilfully arbitrary, both in its selection of material for analysis and in its attribution of allegorical meaning. What reason have we to believe, for example, that ‘Stravinsky’s psychiatric clinic represents a forced labour camp’, as one critic has claimed?°° Even the less outlandish proposals are open to serious question on a number of grounds. Most obvious is the danger of anachro- nism. Piper’s suggestion that the assassination of Judas alludes to the murder of Kirov, for example, could only be entertained seriously if it were known that this episode was added after December 1934. If one works from Angus Fletcher’s definition of allegory as an ‘aesthetic surface which implies an authoritative, thematic, ‘“‘correct”’ reading’,>® then Bulgakov’s novel clearly fails to fit the bill. Rather than enabling the sort of ‘authoritative’ reading that Fletcher requires, it has given rise to a considerable number of competing allegorical interpretations. If cryptography really was Bulgakov’s purpose, the critical reception of his novel would suggest that he was singularly incompetent at the task. There is, however, one final problem and this is the most intractable. Soviet critics have (for obvious reasons) resisted from the outset the allegorical interpretations suggested by their foreign counterparts. Altshuler referred to these readings as ‘naive’,°? and later critics have also been steadfast in coun- tering the claims of those they scathingly dub ‘Sovietolo- gists’.°° In their view, the allegorical dimension of the novel resides only in the minds of the critics who have put it there. But can we be so sure that Bulgakov intended no allegorical meaning to his work? We know that Russian readers and writers have always been especially attuned to this sort of writing, and at the very time that Bulgakov was beginning work on The Master and Margarita, Boris Pilnyak’s Tale of the Unextinguished Moon provided controversial evidence that the mode was far from dead. Even if Bulgakov had not been inspired originally to write in an allegorical manner, it seems impossible that he could have remained insensitive to the possibilities for allegorical readings of his novel which the events of the 1930s would have opened up. Although this could have been the product more of chance than design, the potential for allegorical readings could be seen as an example of what Gabriel Josipovici has called ‘indirection’, a desire deliberately to tantalize the reader by leaving false signs which lead to understanding only when the trickery has been exposed. ‘The overt direction of the pointing finger’, writes Josipovici, “helps alert us to the silent unseen object away from which the finger points.’°' According to this view, the allegorical dimension, like the satirical element in the novel, would emerge as part of a process whereby Bul- gakov frustrates initial understanding by overdetermining the novel’s meaning. Thus allegory, like satire, would prove ulti- mately to be a distraction, encouraging a type of reading which is inevitably self-defeating. These last remarks suggest that the importance of the approaches to The Master and Margarita as satire and allegory lies not so much in their specific findings as in the larger prob- lems which they raise. By forcing us to ask what kind of novel we are dealing with, they make us realize that the difficulty of Bulgakov’s novel is above all a product of its generic instab- ility. Instability is the key word here. It is not simply the case that The Master and Margarita comprises a diverse mixture of styles, as has been indicated by the many writers who have suggested the connection between Bulgakov’s literary practice and the tradition of Menippean Satire.°? To speak only of diversity is to underrate the subversive vigour of this most playful of novels. Our first experience of the novel, to be sure, is centrifugal rather than centripetal. 4 SR UCU RE Critical discussion of the structure of The Master and Margarita has from the outset been inextricably bound up with questions of genre. It is easy to see why this should have been so, for the presence within Bulgakov’s novel of several disparate story lines is intimately connected with problems of narrative mode. This is not just a case of multiple plots (as in a conventional realist novel like Anna Karenina, where various stories co-exist within a single, stable narrative world), but what one early critic described as a ‘pluralism of planes’, a puzzling combi- nation of apparently incompatible fictional subjects and styles.’ The observation, although an obvious one, is most important, because it identifies the broad purpose of many of the early structural analyses of the novel. Starting from the same position, many writers attempted to define the different ‘planes’ by number and type. The results were striking in their homogeneity; despite inevitable disagreements and variations of terminology, there was a marked consensus of opinion. The ‘triple-plane’ theory, although it continues to command a strong following, is open to a number of serious objections. Is it true, for example, that there are only three ‘planes’? The ‘triple-plane’ theory has recently been exposed to a more fundamental attack from writers who have challenged the assumption that the ‘planes’ can be so simply identified in terms of a complete overlap between story, narrative voice and genre. A DOUBLE NOVEL For Taranovski-Johnson, as for many earlier commentators,’ The Master and Margarita is above all a ‘double novel’, in which the division between the two main narrative lines—the story _of Teshua and Pilate,.and the story of Woland’s coming to ~Moscow—overshadows _ and subsumes all other features of “structure. In her view, the style of these chapters is best described as a mixture, in which the constituent components are present in varying degrees at different points in the novel.'* The great value of this approach is that it enables a precise description of the changes of emphasis in the style of the Moscow narrative without falling into the sort of oversimplification inherent in the ‘multiple-plane’ position. The model is amenable to further refinement and could serve as the basis for the detailed stylistic analysis that the novel so richly deserves. As the pres- ent study is not the place to conduct such an analysis, I merely hope, in the remainder of this section, to give an idea of some of the issues that it would raise. The main problem for the reader of the Moscow narrative is to decide just who is telling the story. Identification of the nar- rating voice (or voices) is of paramount importance in the interpretation of any fictional work, and it involves a number of related issues. How much does the narrator know? Is the narrator partial or impartial? Is he presented in a personal manner, even as a character in his own right, or is the story told simply by a disembodied voice? Let us consider the open- ing chapter of The Master and Margarita with these questions in mind. Here is how it begins: ‘One spring day, at the hour of an extraordinarily hot sunset, two citizens appeared in Patriarchs’ Ponds in Moscow’ (p.423). This is expository prose of the most unremarkable kind. The third-person narration is neutral and objective; we are listening to the undramatized ‘authorial’ voice which is the stock-in-trade of the nineteenth-century realist novel. The remainder of the first paragraph continues in like manner, the neutrality of the description being only slightly coloured by the reference to Berlioz’s ‘respectable’ hat and spectacles of ‘supernatural dimensions’. The impression of impartial narration is disrupted far more seriously, however, at the beginning of the second paragraph, where a distinctly personal element intrudes for the first time. ™ Ibid. 277.

Structure 107 The characters are introduced by name: ‘The first was none other than Mikhail Aleksandrovich Berlioz, chairman of the board of one of the most important Moscow literary organiz- ations [ .. . |’. The unmistakable partiality of the ‘none other than’ is reinforced in the fourth paragraph, at which juncture the style acquires a more relaxed, colloquial feel: ‘Oh, yes, we must point out the first odd thing about that dreadful May evening [...]’ (p.423). From here on, the narration, although still predominantly composed of objective report, is characterized by regular interpolations of the subjective voice. In short, then, the beginning of the Moscow narrative is rendered in a manner which combines elements of ‘objective’ narration and personal narration that are, strictly speaking, incompatible. The combination is especially disturbing because Bulgakov seems deliberately to alert our attention to the logical problems that it poses. Most noteworthy in this respect 1s the way in which the incursions of the personal voice are often accompanied by a shift in the time perspective. The opening episode is presented overall as a dramatic scene, cre- ating the illusion (common enough in realist fiction) that the events—although they belong to the past—are being narrated as they actually occur. But the personal voice undermines this illusion by insisting that we are reading a retrospective report. Indeed, such comments as the following are a constant refrain: ‘This speech, it was discovered later [... ]’ (p.425); ‘Later, when, to be frank, it was already too Inte [ides eat. |e (p.426). The paradox generated by the combination of personal and impersonal narration is most palpable, however, in a passage which focuses attention on the immensely privileged position occupied by the personal voice. The passage in question fol- lows the details of the eyewitness accounts of Woland supplied during the later investigations, at which point the narrator identifies himself as the possessor of information inaccessible to the ordinary citizens of Moscow: ‘It has to be admitted that not one of these reports was any use at all’ (p.426). The mere presence here of the personal voice is sufficient to raise the problem which informs the entire Moscow narrative. In effect, the fusion of a highly personal manner with the communica- tion of knowledge which is (in the novel’s own terms) ‘super-

108 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives human’ affirms the logical impossibility of the tale itself; as we read of these extraordinary events, we must surely wonder just how the personal narrator (or, indeed, any personal narrator) could have gained access to the truth. In addition to this epistemological paradox, the Moscow chapters are further complicated by the problem of ambiguity. We have already seen that the ‘personal’ narrator makes no pretence at impartiality. On a number of occasions, the dra- matic presentation of the debate between the Moscow literati and their unusual interlocutor is accompanied by a commen- tary apparently sympathetic to the point of view of the editor and the poet: ‘Bezdomny made an angry, hurried reply to the question which was admittedly far from clear’ (p.430); ‘enquired Berlioz with quite natural irony (p.432). The sense of identity between the narrating voice and the two characters is enhanced by the constant references to Woland as ‘the stranger’ and ‘the foreigner’, and at times the narration appears even to adopt the type of expression favoured by the literary men: ‘ “‘Forgive me’’, said Berlioz after a pause, look- ing at the nonsense-mongering foreigner |... ]’ (p.433). But although the marks of sympathy are everywhere to be found, one cannot be certain what they signify. When the unfortu- nate editor is introduced as ‘none other than Mikhail Aleksan- drovich Berlioz’, we might wonder whether the phrase implies real or only mock respect. In the other instances too (as in the later satirical scenes) the narrator’s true position remains veiled. Although most readers assume a sarcastic intention, this is in the end only an assumption: by defying the conclusive attribution of a narratorial ‘attitude’, Bulgakov confers upon the Moscow plot a teasing openness which remains one of its principal sources of pleasure. But ambiguity and narrative playfulness are not restricted to the scenes involving members of the literary establishment or the population of Moscow at large. Despite the suggestions of many critics to the contrary, the story of the Master and Margarita is not itself without moments of ambivalence. The mistake is to allow the undeniable seriousness of the story element (the Master’s persecution, Margarita’s grief, and so on) to interfere with a proper receptiveness to the capricious- ness of the narration. Most obvious (even notorious) in this

Structure 109 respect is the passage which opens the second part of the novel: ‘Follow me, reader! Who told you that there is no real, true love in the world? Tear out the liar’s vile tongue! Follow me, reader, and only me, and I will show you such a love!’ (p.632). The unexpected intrusion of this highly mannered style, to which Taranovski-Johnson refers as the ‘rhetorical first-person’,'> creates very real difficulties. Although this type of diction has been encountered before—the account of the culinary delights on offer at the Griboyedov Club had ended with the admonition ‘But you are being distracted, reader! Follow me!’(p.474)—the apparent arbitrariness of this stylis- tic connection only intensifies the effect of puzzlement. What is more, each passage is itself deeply ambivalent. On both occasions the reader is being exposed to serious instruction. We cannot doubt that we are supposed to abhor the veniality of the Griboyedovites, and to cherish the story of ‘true love’ which is about to unfold. Yet the crudity of the rhetoric, a sty- lization of the didactic novella,'t thwarts so simple a moral engagement with the text. One recent student has even taken the stylistic mannerism as a signal of parodic intent. The story of the Master and Margarita can, in fact, be shown to com- prise a number of stock motifs of the romance which have been subjected to parodic reversal. In the person of Margar- ita, Bulgakov presents us with a modern version of the beauti- ful lady trapped in a loveless marriage to a powerful man. Her situation at the beginning of Chapter 19 is analogous to that of the damsel who ‘waits for the return of her knight by the mir- ror in her husband’s castle’.'° But, of course, the husband is no tyrant, the ‘castle’ no impregnable fortress, and (most sub- versively of all) it is the woman who will be called upon to res- cue her knight in distress! For if these two main story lines are seen, for all their differences, as two varieties of an essentially similar narrative playfulness, this allows the supernatural finale of Part II to emerge in clear contrast. It is only in those chapters, which deal with events beyond the realm of normal time and space (especially Chapters 29 to 32), that one can distinguish a stable, consist- ent and unambiguous narrative voice. Narrative, then, becomes a pointer to metaphysics: the account of activities in ‘this’ world, and their dénouement in the world which lies beyond involve us in quite different types of reading experi- ence. To conclude: The Master and Margarita is a novel comprising two discrete narrative strands—the one a fluid, diverse struc- ture concerning Woland’s visit to Moscow and its conse- quences, the other a comparatively simple, unified tale about ancient Jerusalem. But although they are so dissimilar in both construction and style, there is one most important respect in which these two narratives are alike. In the discussion of the opening chapter, we saw how the combination of an unmis- takably personal voice with a superhuman omniscience results in a text which is, in a strict logical sense, an impossibility. Curiously enough, the Jerusalem story creates a similar para- dox. Here, by contrast to the Moscow plot, the source of the narrative is explicitly given: this is Woland’s tale, an eyewit- ness account, as he himself explains to the incredulous Mos- cow literary men (p.460). Yet the emphatic motivation of the story only serves to highlight its lack of verisimilitude: this ‘personal’ (and supposedly oral) narration displays no mark whatsoever of personality or of spoken delivery. The full impact of the paradox is experienced only later, however, when it transpires that the subsequent sections of this tale, even though they are rendered in the same impersonal literary manner, derive from ‘personal’ sources other than Woland, Chapter 16 being Ivan Bezdomny’s dream, and Chapters 25 and 26 parts of the Master’s novel. The implications of this curious triple narration will be explored further in Chapter 6 below. For the present, it will suffice to note the manner in which both parts of this ‘double novel’ call to mind the ulti- mate mystery of their own being.

Wright’s analysis yields a master story involving an identi- cal cast of roles—the persecuted protagonist (Ieshua, the Master); the persecuting antagonist (Pilate, Latunsky); the informer (Iuda, Aloisy Mogarych); and the disciple (Matthew, Ivan Bezdomny). The scheme is an attractive one, and it sheds light on a number of key issues, especially the theme of the disciple. But it is the very attractiveness of the approach which should put us on our guard. Like all such pat- terns, this one proves on inspection to be rather too neat. It is, in both senses of the word, only a partial account of the com- plex interrelationship between the two plots. Notable in the first place for the exclusion of several important characters (where do Woland and Margarita fit into this scheme?), it also ignores other connections (such as those between the Master and Pilate, or Margarita and Bezdomny) which imply the possibility of alternative matrices. The latter objection forms the substance of an important article by Edythe Haber, who put forward a timely critique of the monistic endeavour. All that these critics had succeeded in doing, in her view, was to offer so many competing versions of the novel’s ‘master plot’ as to invalidate their basic assumption. The purpose of struc- tural analysis, the same writer argued, should not be to attri- bute primacy to any particular pattern of parallels, but rather to elucidate the plurality of such patterns in the novel.?° In the wake of Haber’s challenge to the ‘monistic’ accounts of the novel’s structure, the ‘pluralistic’ position was taken up and developed independently by two critics. As a result, the monistic search for order gives way to a pluralistic celebration of chaos, and the Jerusalem narrative is displaced from its pre-eminent position as a mythopoeic centrepiece which confers meaning on the Moscow narrative. Gasparov treats the novel purely as an aesthetic object, as the site of a prodigious interplay of echoes and allusions which operate not only between the novel’s two plots, but also within the individual story lines. Gasparov’s approach to structure finds a counterpart in the work of Milne. Where Gasparov uses the phrase ‘motif struc- ture’, Milne talks of ‘figurative likenesses’ between different parts of the novel (a term borrowed from Auerbach’s notion of the figura). The advantage of this type of thinking, she explains, is that a ‘figurative likeness’ need not imply a com- plete overlap, for it “can rest upon one point of concordance only, thereby relieving the comparison of any rigidity; the characters and incidents lose none of their unique individu- alive The work of Gasparov and Milne has succeeded in breaking the ‘monistic’ zmpasse identified by Haber. But, although they have demonstrated that the structure of The Master and Mar- garita is a more complex affair than many of their predecessors were prepared to allow, it must be recognized that pluralism also is not without its drawbacks. The release of artificial con- straints, while absolutely necessary, has opened up the path of excess, and the search for ‘motifs’ or “figurative likenesses’ always threatens to devolve into pyrotechnic displays of impressionism and ingenuity. Gasparov’s work illustrates the point. Many of his suggestions—such as his detection of the theme of ‘accursed money’ (in the form of Iuda’s thirty pieces of silver, and the Muscovites’ false roubles and dollars)—are quite unexceptionable.*? But others stretch credulity beyond its limits. Even if one accepts the critic’s basic premise that the most serious subject may find its reflection in the most trivial episodes, it is difficult to agree with his contention that the 28 Milne, The Master and Margarita, p.5. 79 Gasparov, pp.229 f.

Is there a middle way between the extremes of monism and pluralism? In a later section, I shall suggest that there is, and that the ‘monistic’ position may be rescued by looking else- where than to the surface manifestations of story and charac- ter for the essential connection between the two plots. First, however, we should explore further the question of ‘motifs’. FIGURES IN THE CARPET We have seen that Bulgakov’s penchant for repeated motifs was recognized even by the very earliest commentators on The Master and Margarita. Here again it was the work of Lakshin that provided the lead. In his detailed study of the novel, Lak- shin drew particular attention to the numerous references to the sun and the moon which are scattered throughout both the Moscow and Jerusalem stories. Referring to the heavenly bodies as the ‘two silent witnesses’ to events ancient and modern, he suggested that they perform a vital commentative function.?’ The critic explained this function in terms of a sim- ple opposition, the sun being the customary symbol of life, joy and genuine light, and the moon representing the more sinis- _ter world of shadows and enigmas.** Lakshin’s observations immediately passed into common currency, finding their way into the mainstream of Western scholarship through the work of Proffer.3 It was here, however, that Lakshin’s line of inter- pretation (which had been endorsed by Proffer) came under challenge. Once more, the dissonant voice belonged to Haber, who began by pointing out that the sun never really seems to be a life-affirming force in the novel, its oppressive heat being *° Thid. 200. 3 Lakshin, ‘Roman . . . ’, p.288. 2 elibic: 33 Proffer, “The Master and Margarita’, pp.40q ff.

Yet it is, in several respects, atypical of the novel’s ‘motif structure’. Remarkable first of all for its pervasiveness, it is a purely ‘internal’ motif, the meaning of which may be fixed without reference to any extratextual sources. More important still is the immense thematic significance of a binary opposition which bears directly on the metaphysical vision of the entire novel. The majority of the motifs belong to a different category altogether. Devoid of symbolic meaning, they are perhaps best described as allusive refrains which draw upon a wide range of literary, mythical and religious texts to create an intricate network of interconnections, an aesthetic pattern which teases and delights the imagination by its associative fecundity. A great deal of effort has been invested in the elucidation of Bulgakov’s allusive refrains over recent years, and it would be futile to attempt even to summarize the enormous literature which has grown up around this subject. The following dis- cussion, therefore, will deal (albeit selectively) with just one topic—Bulgakov’s choice of names—the aim being no more than to indicate the perspectives opened up by this kind of study. The notebooks to The Master and Margarita attest to the care

Structure 119 with which the author approached the naming of his charac- ters, many of whom (even the most minor) underwent several changes of appellation before a final version was decided upon. The end result is a dazzling display of comic invention and ingenious allusion which loses nothing in comparison with the art of such accomplished practitioners as Fonvizin, Gogol, Dostoyevsky and Saltykov-Shchedrin. Like his great predecessors, Bulgakov. took a particular pleasure in exploit- ing the potential of Russian for creating meaningful names. Thus, amongst the habitués of the Griboyedov Club, we dis- cover a Dvubratsky (‘two brothers’), a Nepremenova (< nepre- menno: “without fail’), and a Shpichkin (< shpik: ‘secret agent’) (pp.474, 477). The noms-de-plume Bogokhulsky (‘God- abuser’) and Sladky (‘Sweet’, cf. Maksim Gorky, ‘Maksim the Bitter’) are obviously included for parodic purposes, whilst in Adelfina Buzdyak Bulgakov achieves one of his finest exotic effects, combining the idea ofa dolphin (del'fm) with an echo of the colloquial verb duzit’ (‘to kick up a row’) (p.477). These flights of fancy, although numerous, play no real part in the novel’s allusive network. Other names, however, were clearly chosen for their evocative potential. That one of the Master’s principal adversaries should be called Ariman, for example, is grimly appropriate. The name, as T. R. N. Edwards explains, has a demonic connotation: ‘Ariman is Ahriman, Angra Mainyu, “negative thought’, the demon of darkness and falsehood in Persian mythology’.3° The presence of dark forces amongst the artistic fraternity is also suggested by the name of Styopa Likhodeyev (‘evil-doer’). Like the nar- rator’s anguished summary of the recreational activities of the Griboyedov Club members (‘In a word—hell.’—p.477) these names point up one of Bulgakov’s less subtle ironies: the suggestion being that the everyday life of Moscow is at root more ‘diabolical’ than the behaviour of the ‘devils’ who invade the Soviet capital. The name of Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy, on the other hand, is interesting for its evocation of a New Testa- ment passage. In Acts 6:5, a certain Nicanor is amongst the seven chosen by the church at Jerusalem to administer alms. 38 T. R.N. Edwards, Three Russian Writers and the Irrational (Cambridge, 1982), Pp. 159.

120 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives The irony is again unmistakable: it is difficult to imagine an individual less worthy than Bulgakov’s money-grubbing Nik- anor Ivanovich to bear the name of his philanthropic prede- cessor. The greatest source of interest for most commentators has been the presence within The Master and Margarita of a number of famous names. It is here that the richest contributions to the ‘leitmotif structure’ are to be discovered. Take the Gri- boyedov Club itself, for example. Why should Bulgakov have chosen to attach the name of the author of The Misfortune of Being Clever to an institution which in reality was known as Hertsen House? The implausibility of the explanation offered within the novel itself merely intensifies the mystery: “The building was called ‘“‘Griboyedov House” because it had apparently once been owned by the aunt of the writer, Alek- sandr Sergeyevich Griboyedov’ (p.471). Edwards has dis- cerned in this passage a ‘pleasing irony’, which he attributes to the ‘implicit application of the title of Griboedov’s play to an organisation of writers who in his view are excessively con- cerned with the intellect at the expense of the spirit’.39 The suggestion is persuasive, yet there is perhaps more to the Gri- boyedov motif than this. It is surely no coincidence, for example, that the Sof’ya Pavlovna who reluctantly admits Korov’ev and Behemoth to the restaurant in Chapter 28 shares her Christian name and patronymic with the heroine of The Misfortune of Being Clever. Nor should it be forgotten that Griboyedov was the author of a ‘Fragment from Goethe’, a version of the Vorspiel auf dem Theater from Faust, the very work which provides the epigraph for The Master and Margarita. It may well be, therefore, that the significance of the allusion does not reside in ironic commentary at all, but rather in the sheer playfulness which enables the creation of unsuspected connections between seemingly discrete themes and episodes. This conclusion finds support in Bulgakov’s use of composers’ surnames. Bulgakov’s passion for music is legendary. Musical enter- tainment featured prominently in the life of his family, and as 39 bid. 155.

This knowledge served him well at the beginning of his literary career; during his sojourn in Vladik- avkaz Bulgakov supplemented a meagre income by introduc- ing concert performances with short talks about composers and their works.*° In his last novel he put his erudition to an altogether more sophisticated purpose, creating a pattern of musical associations _which continues to fascinate his readers.*' The first of Bulgakov’s musical references in the novel is the name Berlioz, which the editor, Mikhail Aleksan- drovich, shares with the famous French composer. Given the proximity of the novel’s epigraph to Misha Berlioz’s first appearance, it is perhaps the Faust connection which will be immediately the most obvious, for the composer had made his own contribution to this theme with La Damnation de Faust. However, as several writers have pointed out, the associations with his most famous work, Symphonie fantastique, are rather more suggestive. Not only does the symphony end with a witches’ sabbath (thereby evoking ‘Satan’s Ball’), its fourth movement is also of significance, as this is a dream sequence which culminates in the vision of execution by guillotine (hence prefiguring the gruesome decapitation of the editor).** The two motifs are later conjoined in the chapter ‘Satan’s Grand Ball’, when Berlioz’s severed head is brought in on a platter. The other composers’ names in The Master and Margarita present a greater challenge to the literary detective. A search through the original compositions of Rimsky-Korsakov, for example, yields no obvious connection which would explain the present of Rimsky in the novel. But the Russian composer is also well known for his work as an orchestrator, in which field his most notable success was with Mussorgsky’s Night on Bald Mountain. A different feature of Bulgakov’s allusive practice in The Master and Margarita is illustrated by a number of references to Pushkin. Of these one of the most prominent is the moment during the dream of Nikanor Ivanovich when the dreamer witnesses a performance of Pushkin’s short drama, The Cove- tous Knight: Until his dream Nikanor Ivanovich had known nothing at all about the works of the poet Pushkin, even though he knew the name well enough and would be heard several times a day to make comments like: ‘So Pushkin’s going to pay the rent then, is he?’, or ‘And was it Pushkin who unscrewed the light bulb on the staircase?’, or ‘Who’s going to buy the fuel oil—Pushkin?’ (p.583) Bulgakov’s point is transparent enough. Nikanor Ivanovich’s experience provides an extreme (although humorous) example of the trivialization to which the great Russian poet has become subject in the modern world. In the house manager’s idiolect, the name Pushkin has been stripped of all real significance: for his purposes, the name of any famous person would serve equally well. But this is not the only way in which Pushkin’s achievement is belittled in this scene. The performance of The Covetous Knight is indicative of another type of trivialization. The edifying spectacle which Nikanor Ivano- ‘ vich is obliged to witness in his dream is an obvious case of the misappropriation of art for narrow propagandistic aims. In this case, however, Bulgakov pursues a recognizably polemi- cal purpose in confronting the pseudo-poet Ryukhin with a reminder of the true poetic achievement of Pushkin. In order fully to appreciate these references, and other, more indirect allusions,*’ it is necessary to look outside The Master and Margarita. ‘The clue is provided by the line Ryukhin quotes from Pushkin’s ‘A Winter Evening’, for it is this same poem which features in Bulgakov’s play about Pushkin, The Last Days. As its title suggests, The Last Days focuses on the web of intrigue surrounding the notorious duel in which the great poet lost his life. In his treatment of this subject, Bul- gakov adhered to the line established in contemporary Soviet historical writing, emphasizing Pushkin’s fate as the victim of Nikolayevan politics. But, although derivative in its historical interpretation, the play was highly original in its dramatic presentation of the central character. Apart from a brief moment when the mortally wounded poet is borne across the stage on a stretcher, Pushkin never appears on stage, nor does he utter a word. Structure 125 and a writer from the speeches and attitudes of others is clear and unambiguous. Whether he is writing scurrilous epigrams or deliberately offending against the rules of court etiquette, Bulgakov’s Pushkin is a man of fierce independence and defiant incorruptibility. This is why he is hounded to his death. In The Master and Margarita, as in The Last Days, Pushkin’s incorporeal presence marks him out as an ideal figure whose significance is experienced specifically in terms of his absence. Taken together, the play and the novel acquire the status of a private myth, in which the death of Pushkin represents the moment of Russia’s fall from grace, while the pitiful condition of modern Moscow (in which the poet’s memory inspires only grotesque trivialization) appears an inescapable feature of the post-lapsarian state. It is most appropriate, therefore, that the final stage of the Master’s story should be accompanied by a Pushkinian allusion. The title of Chapter 30, ‘It’s time! It’s time!’, echoes the opening line of the famous late poem ‘It’s time, my friend, it’s time; my heart desires peace’. The crucial word here is ‘peace’ (pokoy), for it is ‘peace’ that the Master is promised by Matthew in one of the novel’s most enigmatic sentences—‘He has not earned light, he has earned peace’ (p.776). This is a Subject which will be considered in detail in cussion by noting here that the Master’s ultimate destiny can be understood in terms of a release from the fallen condition through the achievement of a ‘peace’ which implies a sort of identity with Pushkin, the progenitor of true art. This discussion of Bulgakov’s use of motifs might easily be extended, especially as this type of study has become so popu- lar over recent years. The consequence of this intense critical endeavour has been a greatly enhanced awareness both of the complexity of the novel’s aesthetic patterning and of its immense centrifugal force. Such is the range of associative thinking unleashed by the novel that other, more ‘normal’ reading strategies are at least partially suspended, if not more severely impaired. Even on a first reading, an appreciation of the mysterious interconnections at work in the text tends to obscure the details of plot and character which are the con- ventional guides to interpretation. This suggests that the

126 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives motifs function perhaps more as a diversion than as a ‘key’ to understanding. While some refrains (notably, the sun and moon, Pushkin) may perform a commentative role, the ‘motif structure’ as a whole is probably best viewed as an intricate, yet ultimately meaningless, mechanism, a game for the eru- dite and the imaginative. But the word ‘diversion’ suggests more than just a game, and this is why it was chosen to des- cribe Bulgakov’s practice. It is difficult to resist the suspicion when reading some recent studies that the allusiveness of the novel has induced a_ hypersensitivity to ‘motifs’ which threatens to devolve into an infinite regress of arcane specula- tion.*® One can only wonder whether this too is not the pro- duct of deliberate ‘indirection’ on the author’s part, and yet another of the tricks he likes to play on his readers. ENCOUNTERS WITH STRANGERS The study of ‘figurative likenesses’ and other motifs has had the positive benefit of exposing the simplifications entailed in those approaches to structure which I have termed ‘monistic’. But, although it must be accepted that most of the parallels of character, plot and event are far less neat than earlier accounts of the novel have suggested, the basic notion of ‘parallel worlds’ nevertheless resists the deconstructive forces identified in the pluralistic readings. The deliberate construc- tion of the ‘double novel’, together with the unmistakable overlap between the time-scale of the two plots, ensures that this perception is not seriously damaged. More than this, however, I shall suggest in the remainder of this chapter that there 7s one major parallel between the two stories which is not open to the criticisms canvassed above, and which will serve as the starting point for the consciously ‘monistic’ interpret- ation contained in Part II of this study. Nowhere in The Master and Margarita are the correspon- dences between the two plots so numerous as in the first three chapters. The basic similarities of setting and weather (both stories begin on a stifling spring day) are reinforced by a number of smaller details. The cries of the water-vendors in Jerusalem (p.450) will remind us of the poorly stocked drinks stand at which Berlioz and Bezdomny buy warm apricot soda in the vain hope of slaking their thirst (p.424). Each city also has its characteristic flora and fauna. The linden trees of Mos- cow have a counterpart in Jerusalem’s cypresses; and the swallow which darts under the colonnade of Pilate’s palace (pp-444, 449) is recalled by the presence of the humble spar- row which flies out of the tree in the park at Patriarchs’ Ponds (p.461). The details of setting point towards the essential similarity between the two dramatic scenes which are acted out in the opening chapters. In Moscow, as in Jerusalem, an outsider (Woland, Ieshua) confronts a representative of the status quo (Berlioz, Pilate) who has the support of a helper (Bezdomny, the centurion Mark).49 The affinity betweeen the two situ- ations is again emphasized by parallels. Both Berlioz and Pilate experience immediate unease on encountering the out- sider, Berlioz’s ‘unfounded [ .. . | fear’ (p.424) being anala- gous to Pilate’s ‘inexplicable anguish’ (p.452). During the ensuing debates, each man also reveals an unshakable ration- alism, which is expressed in their refusal to countenance the possibility of the supernatural. When the ‘foreign professor’ displays his knowledge of the exact content of the conversation between Berlioz and Bezdomny, the editor can only conclude: ‘The devil, he heard everything’ (p.434). Similarly, when Ieshua divines the nature of Pilate’s malady, the procurator resorts to a ‘natural’ explanation of this curious phenomenon: the prisoner, he decides, must be a ‘great physician’ (p.442). His concern to attribute a profession to his captive mimics the willingness of Berlioz and Bezdomny to believe that Woland is a historian (p.435). 49 See Milne, The Master and Margarita, pp.5 ff.

128 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives The common role of Woland and Ieshua as outsider figures is also reflected in a number of correspondences. In the course of their respective interrogations, both men are asked about their marital status (neither has a wife) (pp.448, 460), and about their linguistic expertise (Woland describes himself as a ‘polyglot’, while leshua knows Greek in addition to Aramaic) (pp.434, 438). Equally striking is the fact that the odd behav- iour of each man gives rise in the minds of their interlocutors to the thought that they might be dealing with the insane. After Woland has uttered his obscure prediction of Berlioz’s death, Bezdomny is moved to ask bluntly: ‘You haven’t ever been in a hospital for the mentally ill by any chance, have you, citizen?’ (p.433). In Chapter 2, when the procurator confronts Ieshua with the accusation that he incited the people of Jeru- salem to destroy the Temple, the prisoner replies: ‘I have never urged anyone to do such things. Do I look like a half- wit?’ (p.443). Although Pilate accepts Ieshua’s claim to sanity, it is nevertheless on the grounds of diminished respon- sibility that he later hopes to have him spared legal punish- ment (p.445). But the most important bond between Woland and leshua resides in their mutual determination to challenge the faith by which their interlocutors live. As Milne has indi- cated, both debates touch at one point on the same basic phi- losophical issue: Woland challenges Berlioz’s certainty that man controls his own destiny (p.430); in a similar vein, Ieshua later questions Pilate’s conviction that his is the power of life or death over his subjects (p.443).°° Detailed discussion of the two stories will be reserved for a later occasion. Yet we may conclude here that the parallel between Woland and Ieshua is not only the first, but also the primary link between the novel’s two plots; it is the ‘figure’ which comprehends all the others (even including the connec- tion between Ieshua and the Master). The entry of these two ‘mysterious strangers’ dramatizes the same existential theme: in each case, we witness a collision between the representa- tives of two separate spheres of being, between those who are identified with this world (be it modern Moscow or ancient Jerusalem) and an individual whose mysterious arrival ges- 5° Ibid. 5 f.

Structure 129 tures towards another, unsuspected, higher world. There are, of course, many important differences in the surface manifes- tations of these two collisions, just as there are obvious dissi- milarities between the protagonists. Woland’s deviousness is the antithesis of Ieshua’s innocence; and the latter’s utter helplessness in the face of worldly power is in complete con- trast to Woland’s easy mastery of the earthly adversaries whom he encounters. But, for all that, the central issue is the same: how do the representatives of ‘this’ world respond to the advent of the ‘stranger’? The question is, above all, one of understanding, and in Part II I shall attempt to show how the stories of Pilate and the Master—although they are again so remarkably dissimilar in form—may be comprehended as variations on this fundamental theme. Pilate and the Master are both ‘worldly’ characters, yet they are extraordinary indi- viduals whose superiority over their fellows is reflected in the profound suffering they are obliged to endure. But for each man this suffering is the prelude to, even the pledge of, a new wisdom, which is synonymous with an understanding of the true purpose of the ‘stranger’ whom they had encountered in life. There is, in conclusion, one further aspect of my argument which should be anticipated here. The theme of understand- ing, which is connected with the figures of Woland and Ieshua, is a problem not only within the text, but also of the text. By this I mean that the position of the ‘worldly’ charac- ters with regard to the ‘strangers’ may be seen as a metaphor of our own situation as readers of The Master and Margarita. Just as the unexpected appearance of Woland and Ieshua in the worlds of Moscow and Jerusalem entails a fundamental challenge to the received ideas of those societies, so their unex- pected appearance in this novel defies our own conventional expectations no less completely. In the latter case, appearance is very much the watchword, for it is in the apparent identity of the two ‘strangers’ with two of the central figures in Christian thought—the devil and Jesus—that the whole difficulty lies. The enigmatic connection between Woland and leshua is, therefore, assured an immense shock value, because it cuts across a long and hallowed tradition of thought which places such figures on opposite sides of the providential order. For

130 Text, Context, Critical Perspectives the reader, then—no less than for the characters within the fiction—the path to truth lies along the line of greatest resis- tance. The first step is also the hardest, for it involves the abandonment of traditional notions that are as old as Chris- tian civilization.

It must, however, be acknowledged that, notwithstanding the validity of the preceding discussion, this kind of approach is open to serious objection as a comprehensive interpretative strategy. The search for patterns of parallels and oppositions, repetitions and echoes is an endeavour which, of necessity, runs counter to the act of reading, thereby inviting a percep- tion of the novel as a spatial object, rather than as a dynamic experience. As a result, interest in other, less static, features of structure will tend to be discouraged. There are, in fact, two aspects of the novel’s construction which have manifestly failed to attract due critical attention. The first is the division of the text into two parts; the second is the status of the Jerusa- lem narrative as an embedded story within the Moscow plot. The purpose of the present chapter is to retrieve these elements of the novel from the neglect which they have suf- fered, and I shall begin by insisting that it is to the Moscow plot, as the ‘frame’ narrative of The Master and Margarita, that we should look first for the source of meaning and coherence. What is the Moscow plot about? In the broadest terms, the story of Woland’s visit to the Soviet capital concerns the prob- lem of human understanding. To be more precise, it provides an example of what Terence Cave has termed a ‘recognition’ plot. The distinguishing feature of such plots, Cave tells us, is that they entail ‘a change from ignorance (agnoia) to knowledge (gnosis)’. As an illustration, and in order to elaborate upon his definition, he cites the case of Oedipus Rex, in which ‘Oedipus does not simply discover a truth of which he was previously unaware, but is the victim of a progressive unfolding, the truth being present in a disguised form from the outset.’' These ' Terence Cave, ‘Recognition and the Reader’, Comparative Criticism. WHO ART THOU THEN? A QUESTION AND TWO WRONG ANSWERS ‘Who art thou then?’: the famous question from Goethe’s Faust which stands as the epigraph to The Master and Margarita immediately alerts us to a problem which will recur with dis- turbing regularity in the course of the Moscow story. Just who, exactly, is Woland? This is the question that exercises the curiosity of Berlioz and Bezdomny when first they encounter the mysterious stranger in the park at Patriarchs’ Ponds. Their speculation on this subject follows a predictable course; from an initial certainty that he must be a foreigner of some description, they progress to the eventual conclusion that their strange interlocutor must be a ‘Russian emigré’ who has come to the Soviet capital on an espionage mission (p.433). But, before they can even begin to take the action demanded of them as loyal citizens, the hapless pair are dis- armed by the stranger himself, who belatedly explains that he is a specialist in black magic who has been invited to Moscow in order to decipher some old manuscripts. Such are the bare bones. Where, however, does the reader stand with regard to all this? Not with Berlioz and Bezdomny; that much is obvious. Bulgakov ensures from the outset that there is an ironic distance between the reader and his ‘heroes’. The narrative tone, which hovers disconcertingly between gentle mockery of Berlioz and Bezdomny and an assumed sympathy with their point of view, guarantees that we will look upon them with a condescending smile. Far more import- ant is the fact that the ‘explanation’ offered by Woland is, in reality, no explanation at all. Even if we accept that the ‘pro- fessor’ is an official guest of the Soviet government (which is a

Who the Devil? .. . 135 considerable concession in itself), there are still many things about him which remain quite mystifying. How exactly did he make his way into the park? How could he have had a break- fast-time conversation with Kant? And what about his ability to read the minds of others? In short, the ‘rational’ explana- tion provided by Woland, and so gratefully received by Ber- lioz and Bezdomny, simply will not do for us at all. There is, however, a further reason for the reader to experi- ence a comfortable sense of superiority over the editor and the poet. We watch their antics with detached amusement not only because we perceive their credulity as a mark of their unwillingness to allow even the possibility of the supernatural into their world, but also because we have a strong suspicion, if not an absolute conviction, that, unlike them, we actually know who Woland really is. Bulgakov leaves some fairly obvious clues. To begin with, there is the epigraph from Goethe’s Faust, which prepares us for the intrusion of the supernatural even before we read a word of the novel proper. What is more, anyone at all well acquainted with Goethe’s work will read Bulgakov’s opening chapter with a certain sense of familiarity, for it corresponds closely to the scene in Auerbach’s cellar in Faust 1. The dramatic situation is strik- ingly similar. In Faust, the drinkers, unaware of the true iden- tity of Mephistopheles and his companion, take the two to be travelling scholars, although they notice (as do Berlioz and Bez- domny in the case of Woland) that one of them has a lame foot. The highpoint of Goethe’s scene comes when Mephisto- pheles, unimpressed by the range of wines on offer at Auer- bach’s hostelry, magically supplies each drinker with the wine of his choice. In the same way, Woland is able to provide Bez- domny with the precise brand of cigarette that the latter names as his preference (p.431). Both scenes also end in a comparable manner. When the drinkers at Auerbach’s finally realize that something is amiss, three of their number advance on Mephistopheles to kill him, only to find that he will evade them by miraculous means. Similarly, in Chapter 4, after Ber- lioz has met with his bizarre death, Bezdomny’s frantic efforts to apprehend Woland and the cat are thwarted by the super- natural powers possessed by his quarries. It goes without saying that the degree to which one will

136 Interpretation appreciate the nuances of the opening chapter will depend entirely upon how well one knows Goethe’s Faust. But it would take a most unsophisticated reader to experience any real dif- ficulty in recognizing Woland’s diabolical pedigree. What is more, one needs no knowledge of Goethe at all to savour the irony that the word ‘devil’ is perpetually on the lips of Bulgak- ov’s characters, an irony which culminates in the sublimely comic moment when Berlioz and Bezdomny deny the devil’s existence in conversation with the ‘devil’ himself. Bulgakov has clearly taken great pains to establish, from the very beginning of The Master and Margarita, a connection between his novel and Goethe’s Faust which invites us to identify Woland as a Mephistophelian figure. This conclusion is confirmed by other evidence. The name Woland itself (of which we learn only later) recalls ‘Junker Voland’, which is mentioned in Faust as one of the devil’s pseudonyms.* The poodle emblem on the ‘professor’s’ cane also gives the game away. And, later still, there are other scenes in the novel—the performance at the Variety Theatre, and Satan’s Ball—which correspond to parts of Goethe’s work (the Emperor’s court scene from Faust 2, and the Classical Walpurgisnacht scene from Faust 1, respectively). The opening chapter, therefore, simultaneously dramatizes the theme of the Moscow plot (the problem of identifying Woland) and presents us with two alternative solutions, of which one (that entertained by Berlioz and Bezdomny) is clearly inferior to the other, which we, as readers, are invited to infer from the narrative. The editor and the poet are unable to recognize Woland because the common-sense, materialistic view of the world to which they are committed automatically excludes any possibility of a supernatural explanation of their odd experiences. ‘Berlioz’s life’, the narrator tells us, some- what superfluously, ‘had taken shape in a way that had made him unaccustomed to unusual phenomena’ (p.424). The reader, on the other hand, is permitted to transcend this nar- row viewpoint, to perceive its insufficiencies, and to adopt a * Goethe, Faust, line 4025. This opposition is fundamental and absolute, and hence- forth I shall refer to these two viewpoints (borrowing my terms from Hans Jonas)? as the ‘mundane’ and the ‘extra- mundane’, respectively. In a novel otherwise so full of ambi- guity and paradox, on this point at least the reader can relax in the certainty that he has a solid foundation for understand- ing which will not be challenged or undermined. The mun- dane viewpoint is consistently exposed to ridicule right through to the Epilogue, where the narrator says, with his ton- gue very firmly in his cheek: “Time and again we must do jus- tice to the investigating commission. Everything possible was done not only to apprehend the criminals, but also to explain all that they had done. And, indeed, all this was explained, and the explanations cannot be accepted as anything other than sensible and irrefutable’ (p.803). Nowhere is Bulgakov’s mockery more obvious, and the novel ends, as it began, with an invitation to laugh at the pitiful inadequacy of those who would like to sweep the supernatural under the carpet of a materialistic philosophy. But what of the alternative ‘solution’ to the problem of recognition? That Berlioz and Bezdomny fail utterly in their attempt to discover Woland’s identity is quite evident. Does it necessarily follow, however, that the reader succeeds in pene- trating the mystery? The answer is both yes and no. We should note that Bulgakov’s narrative strategy encourages us to do two things at once: the first is to comprehend the insufh- ciencies of the mundane viewpoint; the second is to assume that Woland is a Mephistophelian figure. Because these two operations are performed simultaneously, there is a very real likelihood that the reader will conclude that these two pos- itions are equally valid. But this is manifestly not the case. While there can be no doubt that Berlioz and Bezdomny are quite wrong when they take Woland to be a ‘foreign pro- fessor’, this does not mean that the reader is automatically correct in assuming that Woland is a Mephistophelian figure. 3 Hans Jonas, The Gnostic Religion. In other words, the ‘recognition’ of Woland as Mephisto- pheles is necessarily true only in so far as it identifies him as a super- natural being. In retrospect, it becomes clear that, although we have been per- mitted to take a quantum leap of understanding, we have also been seduced into making a fundamental error. The problem of establishing Woland’s identity is rather more intractable than first we are led to believe. When Taranovski-Johnson suggests that, by recognizing who Woland is in Chapter 1, the reader passes the ‘test’ of understanding, she misses the cru- cial point.> We ‘pass the test’ only in the sense that we per- ceive the defectiveness of the mundane vision; by identifying Woland with ‘Mephistopheles’, however, we fail almost as completely as Berlioz and Bezdomny to appreciate the real reason for his coming. ‘Recognition’ of this sort is not synony- mous with understanding; on the contrary, it even constitutes a barrier to the achievement of real knowledge. FORM AND FUNCTION: CRITICAL DISCUSSIONS OF WOLAND The abandonment of the Mephistophelian hypothesis is dou- bly discomforting, for it involves both the acceptance that we have fallen victim to Bulgakov’s narrative sleight of hand, and the experience of ambiguity and puzzlement instead of our previous (albeit misplaced) certainty. Yet the process of re- evaluation is more radical even than this. By so thoroughly confusing the issue of Woland’s pedigree, Bulgakov raises doubts not simply about the identity of his devil, but about a method of enquiry which rests upon the supposition that ‘rec- ognition’ is a matter of tracing Woland’s ancestry in the liter- ary and extra-literary tradition of demonology. With this shift of perspective, the discussion of Woland takes on a new com- plexion—and complexity. There is no denying that Woland resembles the devil (he resembles any number of devils, to be ‘4 Vilenkin, p.394.

Wiss, MUI RCRA INIUOUN) Oye Isis, PI Gwre TWO PATHS TO UNDERSTANDING From the above remarks it should be plain that the problem of recognizing Woland is best approached as a dynamic process, a ‘progressive unfolding’, to return to the words of Terence Cave, and that the two parts of the novel are designed to induce, in turn, the states of agnoia and gnosis. The precise nature of the relationship between the two parts of the novel will be better understood if we first look in more detail at the structure of Part I. The most obvious structural feature of Part I is that, after Chapter 5, the story divides neatly into two separate strands, the one (Chapters 7, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18) dealing with the further adventures of Woland and his companions in Moscow, and the other (Chapters 6, 8, 11, 13, 16) with Bezdomny’s experiences in the smaller world of Stravinsky’s clinic. The bifurcation is maintained throughout Part I and it is very care- fully balanced, the focus shifting regularly from the one narra- tive level to the other. The effect—on a first reading at least—is disconcerting: the two stories develop virtually independently and it is most difficult, as a consequence, to determine the nar- rative logic which has led to their combination. Each story pro- gresses under its own momentum and within its own ‘world’. It is not just that the stories each have their own distinct setting; the opposition extends to many other facets of the narrative. Where the supernatural, for example, plays a prominent part in the ‘Woland in Moscow’ story, it is excluded from the story of Bezdomny in the clinic. Where the Woland story is packed with incident, the Bezdomny story is more concerned with psy- chology than action. Where the Woland story is often hilar- iously funny, the Bezdomny story is almost entirely serious.

146 Interpretation There is, however, a more fundamental difference beween the two stories, which stems from the position in which each separate story stands in relation to the narrative which pre- cedes the bifurcation of the plot. The first five chapters are, in a broad sense, similar to the opening of many mystery novels. Bulgakov’s technique could be used as a text-book case: first, establish a dramatic scene which will appeal to the reader’s imagination and demand further elucidation, then proceed to unravel the mystery slowly throughout the remainder of the narrative. Chapters 1 to 5 of The Master and Margarita fulfil the first demand admirably: Woland arrives in Moscow (where from?); he has an odd conversation with Berlioz and Bezdomny (why them?); he tells them the story of Christ’s confrontation with Pilate in a highly unorthodox version (again, why?); then he disappears from the scene after the violent death of Berlioz. All of these events are clearly designed to arouse one of our basest literary instincts—sheer curiosity to know what on earth Woland is up to. Of the two story lines which follow, however, it is only the ‘Woland in Moscow’ narrative which seems likely, on the face of it, to provide the information necessary to satisfy our curiosity on this all-important point. By comparison, the Bezdomny story will, of necessity, strike one as somehow irrelevant to the main purpose—fascinating and absorbing, to be sure, yet something of a distraction, even a hindrance to unravelling the mystery. This, at least, is how I would suggest that it appears on a first acquaintance with the novel. Appearances, however, are often deceptive, and in The Master and Margarita they are almost invariably so. I shall argue below that the Woland story, which initially promises so much, ultimately fails to provide anything in the way of real understanding, and that, conversely, it is the Bezdomny story alone which turns out to be the true path to enlighten- ment. WOLAND’S ADVENTURES IN MOSCOW: A CUL-DE-SAC H. G. Wells once described the art of writing fantasy in terms of two basic formulae, the first involving ‘one decisive miracle

Who the Devil? ... 147 established early in the reader’s belief and domesticated’, and the second comprising a series of subsequent scenes depicting the ‘impingement of the marvel on ordinary human affairs’.?? The Master and Margarita—or at least those parts of the novel with which we are concerned here—conforms exactly to the Wellsian pattern. Chapters 1 to 5 establish the ‘one decisive miracle’ of Woland’s coming; the remainder of the Moscow scenes in Part I fulfil the second function. The reader’s intel- lectual position throughout these later episodes is one of com- fortable superiority; we watch the behaviour of the citizens of Moscow with the detached amusement guaranteed by the privilege of greater knowledge. In this respect, each successive scene merely reenacts the opposition of mundane and extra- mundane awareness established in the opening chapter. As a consequence, the reader’s mind is free to concentrate on the more pressing matter of finding out what Woland has come to Moscow for. The task, at first, is simple enough. As the story unfolds, so the strange logic governing Woland’s activities is laid bare. Woland meets Berlioz; Berlioz dies; Woland takes over Berlioz’s apartment and disposes of his flat-mate; from this base, Woland organizes the extraordinary black magic show at the Variety Theatre. And his purpose? Once again, perfectly understandable: Woland has come to test the citi- zens of Moscow, to expose their petty vices and to punish them accordingly. ‘Have these citizens changed inwardly?’ (p.538)—Woland’s question to Korov’ev (omitted from the Moskva publication) puts the object of his endeavour beyond any doubt. This ‘explanation’ of Woland’s endeavour has a seductive appeal which has proved well-nigh irresistible. Bulgakov, it seems, has laid on a grand entertainment in which Woland appears to conform to the stereotype of the devil who tempts and punishes, thereby permitting the reader to rejoice as all manner of petty offenders meet their nemesis. This, as we have seen, was the view of Lakshin; it is also an opinion which is expressed, either explicitly or implicitly in any number of reviews and critical articles. Here is what Hoisington has had 22 Cited in W. R. Irwin, The Game of the Impossible: A Rhetoric of Fantasy (Urbana, Illinois, 1976), p.36.

Do the Moscow scenes of Part I impart a sense of moral order and purpose quite so absolute as this? Surely not. There are, admittedly, many cases of ‘well-deserved punishment’. The fate of the money-grubbing Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy, for example, is totally satisfying in this way. This is justice of the most primitive sort, and Bulgakov ensures that it will be savoured to the full by having Woland say: ‘I have taken a dis- like to this Nikanor Ivanovich. He is a rogue and a swindler. Can you not do something to prevent him coming again?’ (p.516). The exposure of Sempleyarov’s marital infidelities during the display of ‘black magic’ invites an equally mali- cious pleasure. Nor must we forget the suffering of the general Moscow public as their ‘magic’ money is transformed into worthless scraps of paper and their fashionable clothes embar- rassingly vanish into thin air. A similar sort of crude justice is at work in later scenes, as, for example, when Berlioz’s uncle, Poplavsky, is sent packing after trying to establish his claim to his nephew’s apartment, or when Sokov, the individual who serves at the buffet in the Variety Theatre, attempts to trick Woland into taking pity on him in his ‘financial ruin’. It will be noticed, however, that most of these cases of ‘well- deserved punishment’ are concentrated in that part of the nar- rative which covers the preparations for the show at the Variety Theatre and the performance itself. This alone should give us cause for thought: is this not, perhaps, another of Bul- gakov’s ‘snares’?
