Just as our initial identification of Woland as ‘Mephistopheles’ proved subsequently to be misleading, so also the sense of certainty about his purpose conveyed by the Variety Theatre episodes is undermined in the account of their aftermath. The most obvious sign that all is not as it first seemed is the fact that once the Variety Theatre show is over, the ‘rationale’ of the Moscow scenes is exhausted. If Woland’s purpose was simply to test and punish the citizens of Moscow, why does he stay on after the Variety Theatre show? But there is more to it than this. While the events leading up to the show had all made some sort of sense, what happens afterwards (especially in Chapters 14, 17, and 18) appears doubly superfluous, for the events which take place after the show seem, if anything, to work against the broad moral purpose which so many critics have discerned in the preceding scenes. Consider the experi- ence of Rimsky in Chapter 14. In contrast to the gay, carnival mood of the ‘black magic’ show, this is gothic horror pure and simple: the supernatural green corpse-like figure at the win- dow and the fortuitous salvation ‘by cock-crow’ take us into another realm. There is no laughter here, nor can there be any question of ‘well-deserved punishment’. The same obtains for the experience of Dr Kuzmin in Chapter 18. Why, one wonders, should Woland’s associates terrorize perfectly inno- cent citizens if the exposure of vice is their principal mission? The case of Kuzmin, in particular, makes it difficult to accept the assertion by one critic, who wrote of Woland that ‘neither he nor his suite cause any evil for the sake of evil.’*° The other activities of Woland’s cohorts give rise to similar doubts. This is, however, only one of the means by which the author ensures that our response to Woland will become increasingly complex as the story pro- gresses. Of these, the two most prominent involve decapitation. The first is that of Berlioz, which is des- cribed in Chapter 3. Berlioz’s bizarre death, it will be remem- bered, is the event which provides the final proof (if such were needed) that Woland really does possess supernatural powers. To this extent, therefore, it contributes to the reader’s sense of intellectual superiority over the unfortunate editor. In addition, as I have already suggested, the scene contains a strong element of ‘poetic justice’: by challenging Woland as he did, Berlioz seemed almost to invite calamity upon himself. Together, these considerations forge a powerful distancing device which ensures that we observe Berlioz’s death dispas- sionately, if not with a certain cruel satisfaction. But, as he leads up to the description of the accident, Bulgakov suddenly changes his narrative stance; the humorous tone of mock respect for his hero gives way to a passage of greater gravity, which concludes as follows: Berlioz did not cry out, but all around him the whole street shrieked in despairing female voices. The tram driver slammed on the electric brake, the tram dipped its nose towards the ground, after which it immediately lurched forward, the glass flying from its windows with a clatter and a tinkle. In Berlioz’s brain someone cried out despair- ingly, ‘Surely not? ...’. Once more, and for a final time, the moon flashed, but it was already flying to pieces. Then everything went dark. The tram passed over Berlioz and a round, dark object was tossed on to the cobbled slope by the railings of the avenue in Patriarchs’ Ponds. Rolling down that slope, it bounced along the cobbles of Bronnaya Street. It was the severed head of Berlioz. (p.463) This passage achieves a striking effect due to the mixture of perspectives contained within it. Berlioz’s death is presented both as a physical fact and as a subjective experience, hence emphasizing its gruesome concreteness at the same time as *7 See, however, Proffer, “The Master and Margarita’, p.399.

Who the Devil? ... 153 ‘I promise!’ wheezed the head. ‘For God’s sake, stop tormenting him!’—a woman’s voice from one of the boxes suddenly echoed above the clamour. The magician turned his face in the direction of the voice. ‘Forgive him! Forgive him!’—at first individual and predomi- nantly female voices rang out, then they merged into a chorus with the men. (p.541) This scene recalls the previous one both in its hideous central event, and in the repetition of certain details—the screams of the women, and the key word ‘despairing’. But it is as a dra- matic re-enactment of the contradictory urges at work in the earlier scene that this extract is most significant. In much the same way as the reader had been previously, the audience here is caught between the intellectual urge to see ‘punish- ment’ effected and horrified compassion at the sight of the suf- fering which is the inevitable result of the retributive impulse. In addition to all this, the story of Bengalsky’s decapitation is clearly designed to convey a moral point. The entire episode is only too obviously a piece of provocation on the part of Woland’s ‘assistants’, the cry for retribution against Ben- galsky being deliberately engineered by the devious Fagot in order to test the audience and teach them a lesson. This edu- cative purpose is particularly prominent in the continuation of the passage quoted above: ‘What do you command, messire?’ Fagot asked the masked man. ‘Well now,’ the latter responded pensively, ‘they are only people like any others. They love money, but then they always have... Mankind loves money, whatever it is made from: leather, paper, bronze or gold. They are frivolous... but still... mercy does sometimes beat in their hearts [.. . ]’ (p.541) In the immediate context, this brief moral fable seems irrel- evant to the main business of the ‘black magic’ show. As before, Bulgakov takes care not to disturb the narrative flow for too long, and the grotesque is experienced only as a fleeting deviation from the predominantly comic norm. When the novel is re-read, however, it takes on a new meaning entirely, for the contrast which it dramatizes—between the urge for retribution and the urge for mercy—touches on what sub- sequently proves to be a central problem. In this connection,

154 Interpretation it should be stressed that Bulgakov invests the contrast here with a particular mythic power by identifying the compassion- ate urge specifically as a feminine attribute, which, in this scene, finally comes to dominate over the masculine element in the audience. This is a point to which we will return in Chapter 7, where the role of the novel’s principal female character, Margarita, will be examined. But the full force of the fable will only be appreciated if it is realized that the les- son which it contains applies as much to ourselves, as readers, as it does to the audience at the Variety Theatre. The need to supplant the retributive mentality by another way of thinking is something that has to be done if Bulgakov’s novel is to make real sense. Like the audience at the theatre, we are in danger of being duped into adopting an attitude which threatens to compromise our humanity. The two decapitation scenes provide early examples of a narrative device employed regularly in The Master and Margar- ita. They have a double function. By their apparent incon- gruousness, they disrupt the surface ‘logic’ of the narrative, thereby threatening to expose the ‘snare’. But, by pointing the reader towards a truer understanding of Woland’s purpose, they also fulfil a positive role. For this reason, I propose to call these, and other such cases, ‘corrective leads’. As Part I moves towards its conclusion, then, our sense of confidence about Woland and his mission is eroded. The ‘moral order’ which seems to govern the performance at the Variety Theatre cedes to disorder, uncertainty and fear. But, apart from these implicit clues, Bulgakov also includes, in the very last chapter of Part I, two brief passages which are more or less explicit instructions that it'is necessary to reinterpret what has gone before. The first is the enigmatic telephone con- versation which Sokov hears as he waits to make his com- plaint to Woland. Woland is talking to Baron Meigel, whom he invites to a function to be held at midnight that same day (p.620). This is the first reference to the forthcoming ‘Satan’s Ball’ and, even though it offers no precise indication of what is to follow, it is evidence enough that Woland has more on his mind than the Variety Theatre show. Indeed, Woland himself openly says as much when, a few minutes later, he makes the following admission to Sokov: ‘My dear fellow! I will let you in

Who the Devil? ... 155 on a secret. I am not really an artiste. All I wanted was to observe the Muscovites en masse, and this was most con- veniently done in a theatre. So my suite here (he nodded in the direction of the cat) organized the seance, while I just sat and watched the Muscovites’ (p.624). Woland is really only telling us what we should have seen for ourselves all along; namely, that in almost all these extra- ordinary happenings (with the most notable exception of Bengalsky’s decapitation) he has been conspicuous by his non-involvement, and in many cases. even by his physical absence. Far from being the sole end of his coming to Moscow, the Variety Theatre show is, on his own admission, essentially peripheral to his main purpose. In effect, he is telling us that this entire sequence of events has been nothing less than an elaborate red herring, and that if we wish properly to under- stand the reason for his presence in Moscow, we will need to adopt a new perspective. It is precisely such a new perspective that Bulgakov promises as he brings Part I to an end: ‘What other strange events occurred that night in Moscow we do not know and, of course, we will not enquire, especially as the time has come for us to pass on to the second part of this true narration. Follow me, reader!’ (p.631). By drawing attention at this point to the formal division of his novel into two parts, Bulgakov explicitly indicates that this division involves a radi- cal break. When he takes up the Moscow story again at the beginning of Part II, the disjunction could hardly be more obvious; the Variety Theatre débacle and its aftermath are now completely forgotten as we plunge into the story of Mar- garita and her ‘true, faithful, eternal love’ (p.632). We may conclude this section by returning to a question raised earlier—the experience of ‘disappointment’ to which a number of reviewers confessed on reading the second part of The Master and Margarita. As we saw in Chapter 2, this response may be explained simply as the unintentional result of the circumstances of the novel’s composition, and, in par- ticular, of Bulgakov’s failure to revise and polish the second half of the book. What I am suggesting here, however, is something quite different. Even when due allowance has been made for these external factors, the ‘disappointment’ of Part II demands attention first of all as the product of a deliberate

156 Interpretation strategy designed by Bulgakov to mislead and disorientate the reader. The structure of The Master and Margarita proves, therefore, to be a dynamic affair, by means of which expectations are both aroused and frustrated, thereby obliging the reader to adapt to a constantly shifting horizon. Like many modern writers, Bulgakov makes a particular point of exploiting the tension between reading and re-reading. By the time we have reached the end of Part II, we find that our original response to the two plot lines in Part I has been reversed. On a second reading, the story of Woland and his cohorts in Moscow, which had originally seemed so important, recedes from view, while the story of Bezdomny emerges in a new light, as the narrative line which truly prepares us for the events and experiences of Part IT. FROM RECOGNITION TO UNDERSTANDING: IVAN BEZDOMNY So far we have considered a variety of answers to the question ‘Who is Woland?’ ‘Taking them in order, they may be sum- marized as follows: (1) Woland is a foreign professor; (2) Woland is ‘Mephistopheles’; (3) Woland is the devil; (4) Woland is the agent of punishment. These statements are not mutually exclusive: the latter three, in particular, are likely to form a single act of ‘recognition’. As solutions to the problem of Woland’s identity, none is fully satisfactory, although they are obviously unsatisfactory in different ways. As we have seen, it is essential to distinguish between the first statement, which implies that a ‘common-sense’ solution is possible, and the other three, which assume Woland’s supernatural origin. But despite their superiority over the ‘foreign professor’ theory, none of the three latter propositions stands up to close scrutiny: any attempt to comprehend Woland’s activities in terms of conventional demonology must ultimately founder on a number of paradoxes. ‘Recognition’, where this involves the simple attachment of ready-made labels, does not imply proper understanding; it is at best only a transitional stage on the path to enlightenment. This is where the poet Ivan Bez- domny comes in.

Who the Devil?... 157 The importance of Bezdomny has been stressed in many critical studies of The Master and Margarita. Despite consider- able divergences of opinion, both on points of detail and on matters of overall interpretation, there has been little dis- agreement over the general nature of his development. Bar- bara Kejna-Sharratt formulates the majority view nicely when she talks of the poet’s ‘trials and tribulations’ in terms of a ‘pil- grim’s progress’ of sorts.*9 In the course of the novel, so this argument runs, Bezdomny undergoes a crisis of faith and a conversion: he begins as the ‘disciple’ of Berlioz, but ends as the ‘disciple’ of the Master. This is a most fruitful line of inves- tigation, and it raises some important issues to which we must return later. For the moment, however, I propose that we view Bezdomny’s development from a slightly different angle, and that his movement from the larger world of Moscow to the confines of Stravinsky’s clinic be seen first of all as a metaphor of the reader’s own progress towards understanding Woland. On his first appearance in the novel, Bezdomny is immedi- ately identified as Berlioz’s protégé. He listens respectfully as the editor explains to him the defects of his poem about Christ, and he accepts his judgement without question. Dur- ing the ensuing debate between Berlioz and Woland, the poet loyally echoes the opinions of his master, albeit with a crude extremism that even Berlioz himself finds embarrassing. In short, he is an ignoramus whose main concern is to mouth unthinkingly the dominant creed of his society. But why, it might be asked, does Bezdomny not share the fate of his men- tor? His response to Woland, after all, differs in no obvious way from that of Berlioz. However, Bezdomny is dis- tinguished from his colleague by something which seems at first of trifling significance, but which proves ultimately to contain the promise of deliverance. He is the author of a poem about Christ. Bezdomny’s poem, we are led to believe (and there is nothing in the novel to suggest otherwise) is a hack work, typi- cal of the literature of ‘social command’, written to order by numerous authors in the twenties and thirties. By virtue of its subject alone it seems to demand comparison with the Mas- 9 Kejna-Sharratt, ‘The Tale of Two Cities . . . ’, p.334.

158 Interpretation ter’s novel, and it has become something of a critical common- place to emphasize the differences between the two works, in terms both of their literary accomplishment and the circum- stances of their composition. Unlike Bezdomny’s poem, it has been argued, the Master’s novel commands our respect as an authentic work of literature, the product of free artistic endeavour. But, true though this is, there is one crucial simi- larity between the two works which this argument ignores. The first (and almost the only) thing we learn about Bez- domny’s poem is that, despite the author’s atheistic intention, it is a work in which, no less than in the Master’s novel, the figure of Jesus emerges as a real creature of flesh and blood. Their differences of talent and temperament notwithstanding, both Bezdomny and the Master are inexplicably drawn to the story of Jesus the man, and this is what singles them out from their fellows. It is a mark of their spiritual vitality, which, in Bezdomny’s case, has survived even the conscious effort on his part to extinguish it. Bezdomny’s attitude to Woland passes Tee three dis- cernible phases. The first has already been discussed and requires no further comment. With the violent death of Ber- lioz, Bezdomny is shocked out of his initial complacent accept- ance of the ‘foreign professor’ theory. His vain pursuit of Woland and the cat suffices to convince him that he is dealing with no mere mortals. And it is this new knowledge that inspires him to set about warning his fellow Muscovites with- out delay of the danger to which they are exposed. But, although he is convinced of Woland’s malevolent purpose and of his supernatural origin, Bezdomny is unable to say pre- cisely who it was he encountered in the park. He is an extraordinary and mysterious individual, one hundred per cent of the way. But that is precisely what makes it so interest- ing! The man was acquainted with Pontius Pilate—what could be more interesting than that? Bezdomny gives up any idea of trying to expose Woland’s ‘devilish’ nature not because he has realized the futility of any such endeavour, but because he now com- prehends that Woland’s real importance resides not in his dia- bolical antics at all, but in the fact that he has brought to the world the story of Ieshua and Pilate. This is a moment of truth not only for Bezdomny, but also, I would suggest, for the 3! The identity of the voice is suggested in Mahlow, p.99.

160 Interpretation reader as well. For who would not be prepared to admit that, in the excitement of observing the escapades of Woland and his cohorts in Moscow, he had lost sight of what Bezdomny now reminds us—that this ‘devil’ is also a new evangelist? Bezdomny has passed into higher state of consciousness, and he takes us with him. His new understanding is rewarded in two ways: he is permitted to dream the continuation of Woland’s story about Pilate, and he meets the Master, who— unlike Berlioz, Rimsky, Likhodeyev and all the rest—is to be the central figure in the drama of Woland’s coming. We need consider Bezdomny no more for the present. After Chapter 17 he disappears from view, resurfacing briefly only at the very end of the novel. This is as it should be, for his job is essentially complete; he has guided the reader towards the truth. Like Bezdomny, we too must learn to strip away the veneer of diabolical trickery in order to perceive what Woland’s visitation really signifies. But this is not the only reason that Bezdomny’s transformation demands attention. His experience is also crucial in another way, for it rehearses a drama which is to be re-enacted, with new variations, in the second part of the novel, by Bulgakov’s hero and heroine. Just like the erstwhile poet, the Master and Margarita are, in their own turn, obliged by circumstances to confront the fact of Woland’s presence in Moscow. And, like Bezdomny again, they both progress from an initial, false understanding of Woland and his mission, to a truer knowledge which comes only as a result of their personal dealings with him. The parallel is perhaps more readily apparent in the case of Margarita than it is in the Master’s instance, but it is to the Master that I shall turn first. THE MASTER Although the Master has been the subject of extensive critical discussion, it is curious to note how little consideration has been accorded to the manner in which his character develops in the course of the novel. The oversight may be attributed to the approach adopted in so many studies. As we saw in Chapter 3, it has been traditional (especially amongst West- ern scholars) to view the Master as a fictional projection of

Who the Devil? .. . 161 Bulgakov’s experience at the hands of the Soviet literary establishment. There is no need to go into these biographical matters again here, but it should be acknowledged that such an approach to The Master and Margarita will almost inevitably ignore the dynamic element in Bulgakov’s portrayal of the Master. This is because all of the narrative information rel- evant to this kind of discussion belongs to the Master’s past, rather than to his present experience in the novel. The fre- quent and sometimes lengthy commentaries on the circum- stances surrounding the composition of the Master’s novel, his romance with Margarita, the treachery of Aloisy Mogarych, his retreat to Stravinsky’s asylum, and so on, have tended to overlook the fact that, important though all this background material may be, this is not what engages the reader dramati- cally. All this information is conveyed by means of a flash- back, when the Master tells his own story to Bezdomny in Chapter 13, and, as is usual when such a strategy is employed, the account inevitably lacks immediacy. This may well have been a narrative inconvenience enforced upon Bulgakov by the form of his novel, yet the effect is to distinguish clearly between the Master’s past, of which we learn in Part I, and his present, which is the subject of Part II. In his case, as in all others, the division between past and present is marked by the moment of Woland’s arrival, and dramatic interest is gener- ated by the impact of Woland’s coming upon both his fate and his understanding. The Master’s dealings with Woland comprise three distinct phases: (1) he discovers from Bezdomny that Woland has arrived in Moscow; (2) he meets Woland in person after Mar- garita has secured his return from Stravinsky’s clinic; (3) after his death, he rides with Woland and his entourage to his final retreat. Each phase marks an important moment in the Mas- ter’s evolution towards understanding, and the problem of recognition features prominently throughout. The first instance is in Chapter 13. On this occasion Bezdomny tells the Master of the extraordinary adventures which had resulted in his being committed to the asylum. Sensing that he is in the presence of a man of superior learning, the poet concludes his account by asking the Master to explain who it was that he encountered at Patriarchs’ Ponds. After a brief hesitation, the

162 Interpretation Master obliges him with an answer: ‘Yesterday, at Patriarchs’ Ponds, you met up with Satan’ (p.551). On a first reading of the novel these words will not necessarily strike us forcibly; in all likelihood, they will simply confirm our own preconceptions regarding Woland’s identity. Yet there is something about the Master’s behaviour here which should give us pause for doubt, if only momentarily. Is he not a little too ready to indulge in self-congratulation for his superior knowledge? Certainly, he makes no effort to disguise his satis- faction that his understanding surpasses that of Berlioz. And towards Bezdomny himself his manner is condescending in the extreme. There can be no mistaking the patronizing note in his question: ‘Forgive me, perhaps you haven’t heard even the opera Faust?’ (p.551). This i is a magnificently ironic pas- sage. By mentioning Faust, the Master does not display his wisdom at all; it is rather that he unwittingly exposes his con- ceit. What makes the irony so particularly disarming, how- ever, is that it is so cunningly disguised. For the conceit which it lays bare is one which the reader has been encour- aged to share. Only when we ourselves have discarded the ‘Mephistophelian’ hypothesis can we see the Master’s frailty for what it is. The Master’s conviction that Woland is Satan inevitably conditions his entire,response to Bezdomny’s tale. Bezdomny, it should be noted, tells the Master two things about Woland: that he narrated the story of Pilate and Ieshua; and that he predicted the gruesome death of Berlioz. Although he is struck by the extraordinary congruence between Woland’s story and his own artistic intuition (“Oh, just as I guessed! I guessed it all!’—p.550), the Master does not ponder the deeper impli- cations of this mystery, which is quickly displaced in his thoughts by the news of Berlioz’s death. This latter disclosure awakens the Master’s desire for vengeance against those other members of the literary establishment whom he holds respon- sible for his present distress: ‘Only one thing do I regret: that it couldn’t have been the critic Latunsky or the writer Mstis- lav Lavrovich instead of this Berlioz’ (p.550). The Master’s feelings are only human, but they are a mark of his inferior wisdom; the urge for retribution renders him unresponsive to the greater revelation of which Bezdomny is the unconscious

When the Master and Woland finally meet face to face, in Chapter 24, the problem of recognition is immediately raised by Woland himself. ‘Do you know with whom you are now speaking?’, he asks the Master (p.702). Although the Master replies that he does, it is evident from his subsequent behav- iour that he is still unapprised of Woland’s true purpose. The latter, for his part, tries valiantly to open the Master’s eyes. He feigns surprise when the Master informs him of the subject of his novel (“That’s astonishing! And you could find no other theme?’—p.703). This is a transparent attempt to remind the Master of what he had overlooked previously—that he, Woland, is also the ‘author’ of the same story of the passion. To the same end, he restores the manuscript from the ashes of the stove, and he insists that the novel is unfinished, promis- ing enigmatically that it will bring the Master some new sur- prises (p.709). But these efforts are to no avail; the Master doggedly resists the lesson that Woland strives to teach. The restoration of the novel brings him no satisfaction, serving only as a reminder of the personal suffering he has endured for its sake, while the prospect of further composition revives his heartfelt loathing for the entire endeavour. The Master’s physical existence thus draws to its close without him realizing what Woland has come to do. Even after he has been returned, together with Margarita, to the cosy basement apartment, he remains prey to utter cynicism and world-weariness. While Margarita spends the night re- reading parts of the novel, the Master himself finds oblivion in sleep—a scene which furnishes final, dramatic evidence of his unenlightened condition. It is only after his death that a new awareness finally dawns. The very same Master who, only seconds before his death, had suspected only treachery in the administration of poison, is heard to exclaim: ‘now I under- stand everything’ (p.786).3* What is it that the Master under- stands? Quite typically, Bulgakov never tells us; the reader is left to infer the nature of the Master’s new wisdom from his 32 The Master’s enlightenment was even more prominent in earlier versions of the novel. MARGARITA When Margarita encounters Azazello in the first chapter of Part II, it is immediately evident that she is being tested in precisely the same way that Berlioz and Bezdomny were at the beginning of Part I. There are, in fact, a number of parallels between the two opening chapters. In each case, the dramatic confrontation between the ordinary Moscow citizen and the supernatural visitor takes place in a park setting, and the ensuing conversation follows a similar pattern. Like Berlioz and Bezdomny, Margarita is both disturbed and offended by the strange behaviour of an interlocutor who possesses bizarre and inexplicable powers. Azazello displays the ability to read minds, and when he later quotes from the Master’s novel, he again reveals his extra-mundane origin and also briefly re-enacts Woland’s role as unorthodox evangelist. In her response to these unusual experiences, Margarita demon- strates that, initially, she stands no higher than Berlioz or Bez- domny. Just as they had done before, so she too works through a series of ‘rational’ explanations for what has occurred: Aza- zello must be a secret policeman who has come to arrest her; her maid, Natasha, must have shown him the few fragments of the Master’s novel to have escaped the flames; he must be a pimp attempting to procure her services for a rich foreigner. As Margarita considers each of these hypotheses, the reader is made privy to her thoughts, which are no less uncharitable than those entertained earlier by the two literary men. And the final mark of her unenlightened condition is that (again like Berlioz and Bezdomny) she expresses her exasperation with Azazello by taking the devil’s name in vain: ‘You should have come straight out with this at the start rather than talk- ing the devil knows what sort of nonsense about a severed head’ (p.641).

Who the Devil? ... 165 Margarita differs, however, from Berlioz and Bezdomny in one crucial respect: she is willing to abandon her common- sense notions about her supernatural companion. But this does not weigh particularly strongly in her favour, as her ability to transcend the mundane condition is not the product of any real wisdom on her part; it is simply that her desper- ation to be reunited with the Master is such that she will agree, quite literally, to anything. Bulgakov’s refusal to idea- lize his heroine’s initial understanding is reflected in sub- sequent passages, where he again insists on the real source of her boldness. Thus, during her magical flight, we read that ‘the hope that she would succeed there in achieving the return of her happiness made her fearless’ (p.663). And again, as she listens to Korov’ev’s instructions prior to the ball, we are told that ‘the hope of happiness made her head spin’ (p.667). Whatever else we might think of her, Margarita’s understand- ing goes no further than her own narrow ambitions, at least not to begin with. The unspoken condition of Margarita’s suitability for Aza- zello’s mysterious mission is her acceptance of the literal fact that she is in contact with the supernatural. Once she casts off the habit of mundane thinking (and this is only after Azazello has adopted some fairly desperate tactics, it should be added) she has passed the first stage in the quest for understanding. But, as always, what is achieved has to be weighed against what has yet to be learned. Margarita’s desire to be reunited with her lover, Bulgakov tells us in a typically ironic passage, was such that she was ‘soglasna idti k chyortu na kulichkv’ (p.644). The Russian (which is perhaps best rendered by as ‘she was prepared to go to hell and back’) implies a journey to the devil, and Margarita’s subsequent adventures are enough to con- vince her that it is upon precisely such a journey that she has embarked. But, in her case, no less than for Bezdomny and the Master, the discovery of Woland’s ‘devilishness’ is only a transitionary state, and her subsequent experiences in Part II demand attention as a test of her ability to discern the truth about Woland’s identity which has been obstructed by her initial act of ‘recognition’. As it was for Bezdomny and the Master, the test is again signalled by an explicit request that Woland be identified. When Margarita arrives at apartment

Margarita confirms this statement, and in so doing unwitt- ingly proves herself unworthy of Korov’ev’s compliment. Like the Master before her—and, of course, with equal, if not greater, justification—she has seen no further than Woland’s diabolical trappings. When the ball begins, therefore, she is in for a shock, for the witches’ sabbath in which she had been expecting to participate turns out to be something very differ- ent altogether. This is not the place to consider the proceedings at Satan’s Ball in any detail, although we may note that this is the scene in which the disjunction between Woland’s demonic form and his real function is fully exposed for the first time. As we shall see in Chapter 7, it is here too that Margarita attains true wis- dom, a wisdom which comes, as it does on every occasion, with the realization that, for all his ‘devilishness’, Woland is no ordinary devil. DPE DE GCE PACrOIN SSE xeP OSE Let us return finally to the question with which we began: Who is Woland? Clearly, there can be no simple answer. Indeed, the entire novel—or at least those parts of it which concern events in Moscow—dramatizes the problem of recog- nition in all its complexity, involving characters and reader alike in a process of discovery which disturbs and disorien- tates by inviting false assumptions before insisting on a funda- mental re-evaluation. But do we ever learn Woland’s real identity? We do, if only in a rather negative sense. By the end of the novel, we can at least say who Woland isn’t: he isn’t a foreign professor; he isn’t a conventional devil; he isn’t a sim- ple avenger figure. To say who Woland actually is, however, remains a problem of far greater difficulty, and in the final chapter of the novel proper Bulgakov adopts what can only be described as a deliberate tactic of mystification to ensure our continued puzzlement over this vital issue. Who the Devil? ... RTE WHO IS WOLAND? Let us imagine ourselves, finally, in the position of one of those original ‘readers’ of The Master and Margarita. Bulgakov has just brought his reading to a conclusion and, like Yelena Ser- geyevna and Fayko, we have in our hands a piece of paper on which to write down an answer to the author’s question about Woland. What are we to write? One thing is obvious: a state- ment of the type ‘Woland is the devil’ or ‘Woland is Mephisto- pheles’ will not suffice, for this is no ordinary question. It is, in fact, a riddle—or, to be more precise, the riddle which is the novel itself. We do not solve the problem of Woland’s identity simply by naming him, and even if we do decide ultimately to continue referring to him as ‘the devil’, we must do so in the clear knowledge that this does not imply any real kinship with traditional devil figures. Rather than attempt to trace Woland’s demonological pedigree, then, we should turn our attention in the opposite direction and look carefully at the very things which place him outside traditional demonology, namely, his telling of the story of Ieshua and Pilate, and his function as saviour to the Master and Margarita. Woland’s twin roles of unorthodox evangelist and agent of deliverance cannot be accounted for by reference to any con- ventional notion of the diabolical, yet they can be accommo- dated within another tradition: that of the Gnostic religion.*? Woland’s activities in The Master and Margarita fit him per- fectly for the title of ‘gnostic messenger’. The Messenger—also known as the Alien—is, according to Gnostic teaching, the supernatural being who comes to earth periodically bearing a message which, if properly deciphered, promises the possi- bility of divine illumination. Perhaps the most important feature of the Messenger, however, is that he will be recog- nized only by a very small number of people (or ‘pneu- matics’), in whom the divine spark has not been totally extinguished by the conditions of earthly existence. Hans Jonas provides the following account of the ways in which the Messenger may be received when he enters the cosmic realm: ‘The name “‘the alien’ indicates the kinds of reception he 43 On the links between The Master and Margarita and Gnosticism, see II]’in, p.78; Krugovoy, op. cit.

¥72 Interpretation finds down here: the welcoming exultation of those who feel themselves alien and exiled here [ . . . |, the shocked surprise of the cosmic powers who do not comprehend what is happen- ing in their midst [ . . . ]; finally, the hostile bonding together of the sons of the house against the intruder’.** This passage provides a gloss on the Moscow narrative of quite uncanny precision. If Berlioz and (initially) Bezdomny may be taken to represent the aggressiveness of the ‘sons of the house’, the vast majority of Moscow citizens belong to that lesser category of ‘cosmic powers’ who exist in a state of docile incomprehension. The Master, Margarita and Bezdomny (after his initial resistance) make up the privileged third group for whom alone initiation into the lost secret of divine wisdom is possible. While they do not welcome the Messenger with the ‘exultation’ of which Jonas speaks, their stories tell of a gra- dual awakening to the truth about Woland’s mission and, by extension, about their own superior potential. Thus, my own piece of paper would read as follows: despite his superficial diabolical features, Woland is not the devil but a gnostic messenger. This solution is doubly attractive, for it both captures the paradox contained in the novel’s Faustian epigraph and returns us to the bifurcation of the plot in Part I, a formal division which may now be seen to mirror the dis- junction between Woland’s apparent purpose and his true mission. At this point I shall bring the first part of the interpretation to a close. Having established Woland’s role as a messenger figure, we are in a position to examine the nature of the mess- age he brings to Moscow. We shall see in the following chapters that the message is presented in two ways. The first (and most obvious) is the Jerusalem narrative which com- prises the central core of The Master and Margarita. Of no less importance, however, is the ‘message’ conveyed indirectly by Woland to the Master and Margarita in the process of ensur- ing their salvation and reward. + Jonas, p.76.

COWARDICE AND OTHER SINS Page for page, no part of The Master and Margarita has stimu- lated so much critical discussion and scholarly enterprise as the version of the passion story which forms the novel within the larger novel about Woland’s coming to Moscow. After surveying the literature which has grown up around this sub- ject, it may even come as some surprise to note that, quantita- tively speaking, the four Jerusalem chapters account for a mere sixth of the Romany text. This seeming imbalance may be explained first of all by the relative ease with which the Jeru- salem narrative can be understood, even on a first reading. In marked contrast to the Moscow chapters, with their perplex- ing strategies and shifting perspectives, this is a story which appears to emulate the coherence and lucidity of the great Russian novels of the nineteenth century. What is more, where the Moscow chapters often seem slight and even some- what repetitive (consider, for example, the series of escapades involving the ordinary citizens of Moscow), the Jerusalem plot is taut and condensed. But it is obvious that extrinsic factors have also played a major part in the process of critical selec- tion. Most significant in this respect has been the powerful impulse, initiated by the Soviet liberal critics and continued outside the USSR, to exploit the potential of the Jerusalem chapters for a political reading of the novel (see Chapter 3, above). Even if this tendency had not been present, the fact remains that by offering a fictional portrait of the figure who stands at the heart of the Christian religion, Bulgakov auto- matically ‘loads’ this part of the novel. The story of Ieshua Ha-Notsri is bound to impinge most powerfully on the con- sciousness of those for whom Christianity remains a dominant influence (or, as in the case of the novel’s Soviet readers, a dominant counter-influence) in the cultural, ethical and intel- lectual life of their society. Taken together, these factors both explain and, to a large

174 Interpretation extent, justify the immense interest generated by the Jerusa- lem chapters in The Master and Margarita. Yet they have also led to overstatement and selectivity. Boris Nartsissov displays the first of these failings when he claims that, contrary to appearances, it is the Moscow story which plays a ‘subser- vient’ role to the Jerusalem story.’ Although most critics would probably shrink from such an extreme statement, many have proceeded from the same implicit premiss in discussing the novel, presenting the Jerusalem plot as a sort of matrix for the Moscow narrative which is its frame. Makarovskaya and Zhuk write that the ‘digression into the lofty realm of history permits the writer to achieve a fuller and more trenchant sat- irical portrait of contemporary “‘spiritual”’ time-servers, pre- pared in the name of a falsely understood “order” to sweep the Master from their path without even having read a single word of his novel’.* Even more prevalent—and correspond- ingly more serious in its consequences for an interpretation of the novel—has been the inclination to concentrate on the pre- dicament of Pilate, particularly as it is presented in Chapter 2, to the virtual exclusion of other important aspects of the ancient story. As a counterbalance to these trends, it is necessary to repeat two basic points. Firstly, the Jerusalem narrative, no matter how great its overall importance, remains strictly sub- servient to the Moscow story in narrative terms. The initial part of the present chapter will explore the nature of that ‘subservient’ relationship in an attempt to tease out some of its implications for what may best be described as the meta- physics of the novel. The second matter to be stressed is that the story of Pilate’s moral capitulation, even though it pro- vides the initial stimulus for the Jerusalem narrative, has to be viewed as part of a larger story involving Aphranius and Matthew. As we shall see, to admit this is also to admit that, for all its seeming simplicity, the Jerusalem story is far more complex and ambiguous than one might first be prepared to believe. Cowardice and other Sins 175 THE JERUSALEM NARRATIVE: EPISTEMOLOGICAL STATUS It has already been seen that the decision to include within the pages of The Master and Margarita an unorthodox version of the trial and crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth was fundamental to Bulgakov’s initial conception of the novel. The lengthy chapter entitled “The.Gospel according to the Devil’ figured prominently in the first known redaction and contained material subsequently expanded and divided amongst the four chapters of the final text. As the original chapter title itself suggests, the source of the narrative in this early variant was Woland, and the entire piece was cast in the form of an eyewitness account.? In the course of Bulgakov’s further work on the novel this material underwent a number of major changes, yet in two fundamental respects it remained unal- tered from start to finish. Although finally split up into four chapters, it retained its status as an ostensibly autonomous narrative, which was both continuous and complete. Also unchanged was the particular insistence that this version of the ancient events be taken as a true and unassailable account of what actually happened. But this is not to say that the changes to the passion story were inconsiderable. From Chudakova’s description of the creative evolution of the novel it emerges that Bulgakov’s revision of the Jerusalem chapters involved not only the expansion mentioned above, but also a certain number of excisions, some of which will be considered later. But such changes, no matter how numerous, are ultimately of far less consequence than a single fundamental shift in the motivation of the entire Jerusalem segment. The narrative, which first took shape as an account by Woland of what he had witnessed two millennia ago, is presented in the later redactions as ema- nating from no less than three separate sources. While Chapter 2 remains, as it was originally, ‘Woland’s’ tale, Chapter 16 takes the form of a dream vision experienced by Ivan Bezdomny as he lies in Stravinsky’s clinic, and Chapters 25 and 26 turn out to be parts of the Master’s novel, once 5) 3 Chudakova, ‘Opyt rekonstruktsii . . . ’, p.g6.

With this major new decision came a change of language: instead of Woland’s chatty, idiosyncratic style, the narrative was rendered in a more uniform, ‘neutral’ literary style devoid of personal features. This change is marked in the final text by the detail which accompanies the beginning of Woland’s tale: ‘ ““No proof is necessary either’’, the professor answered, and he began to speak softly, at which point his accent disappeared for some reason, “‘It’s all simple: in a white cape™.. ~~ {p.435): This single alteration brought an exciting new dimension to the Jerusalem story. For what was initially quite unremark- able—namely, the unity and continuity of this narrative sequence—now becomes both fascinating and mysterious. How is this curious concordance between Woland’s tale, Bez- domny’s dream and the Master’s novel to be explained? The answer is, in fact, quite simple, and it has been formulated many times. Donald Fanger’s version has the advantage of being both one of the earliest and one of the neatest: ‘To return now to the question of the Master’s novel: by merging it with Woland’s account and Ivan’s dream, Bulgakov seems to be suggesting that truth subsists, timeless and intact, avail- able to men with sufficient intuition and freedom from con- ventional perception.’* This is a crucial insight. The Jerusalem story, as Fanger shows, has a double importance. As Woland’s message to a fallen world, it has the value of a historical truth untainted by subjective evaluation and immune from the influence of myth. But once the identity between this message, Bezdomny’s dream and (in particular) the Master’s novel is revealed, this same story becomes also the mark of superior understanding mysteriously available to a select few. But although Fanger succeeds admirably in identifying the dual aspect of the Jerusalem story, the particular context in which he was making his remarks caused him to reverse their order of priority. When we read the novel, it is as Woland’s message to the Muscovites that the ancient narrative first assumes significance. And, even though we will be intrigued * Donald Fanger, ‘Rehabilitated Experimentalist’, Nation, 22 Jan. 1968, p.118.

ELST ORY NVI RS US Lob 'G END: BULGAKOV’S CHALLENGE TO THE GOSPELS Generically speaking, the Jerusalem story may be defined as a historical novel, a mode of writing which is distinguished by the fact that it automatically invokes a body of knowledge which lies beyond the narrative details supplied by the text itself. As a result, the reading of such works involves an act of comparison, in which the newly given is weighed against the previously known. Of course, not all historical novels exploit this circumstance to the full. The vast majority (the ‘historical romances’ which fill book-stands around the world) tend actually to suppress this potential activity either by concen- trating very little upon the depiction of known historical events and personages, or else by drawing upon a subject about which the reader will be assumed to have little prior knowledge. Conversely, it is virtually axiomatic that the better known the historical subject the more prominent is this oper- ation likely to be. Stories of Jesus constitute an extreme, even a unique case, for here the act of comparison is necessarily much more clearly defined than is ordinarily so, as the nove- listic account will be set against the evidence of the single text upon which we ordinarily draw for our knowledge of the his- torical events—the New Testament. Thus, no sooner is the name of Pilate mentioned at the beginning of Woland’s tale than an entire series of expectations is set in motion, and the

178 Interpretation remainder of the narrative is read with at least half a mind to establishing the degree of divergence from the scriptural version. Even on a most cursory reading, it is apparent that Bulgak- ov’s version of events differs markedly from the New Testa- ment stories. Behind these differences it is possible to detect both an historical and a polemical purpose. On the one hand, the author is evidently concerned, as many historians have been, simply to derive a credible and logical sequence of events from the notoriously confusing and _ inconsistent materials of the gospels. Bulgakov’s particular solution to these problems will be considered in more detail below. It 1s, however, the polemical factor which is immediately the more obvious, and it is to this that we must attend first. Bulgakov alters the gospels not simply to make them appear historically credible, but also (and more subversively) to challenge the very validity of these sacred writings. Bulgakov’s determination to distinguish his version of events in ancient Jerusalem from that found in the biblical sources is signalled first of all by a series of devices of defami- liarization. For the most part these involve proper names, the most notable being the replacement of the biblical Jesus (‘Iisus’ in Russian) by ‘Ieshua’, which, as Milne explains, is a ‘phonetic rendering of the Aramaic’.° The same procedure (although linguistically less precise) results in the use of ‘Yer- shalaim’ (cf. Ancient Hebrew ‘Erushalaim’) for the more familiar Jerusalem. The purpose in both cases is unmistakably to divest people, places and events of their conventional bibli- cal connotations. A similar effect is achieved by naming the site of the execution ‘Bald Mountain’ rather than Golgotha, and by using the descriptive phrase ‘hanging on posts’ instead of the highly emotive ‘crucifixion’.° Considered in isolation, these changes are rather innocuous and their importance is perhaps more symbolic than real. Far more profoundly disturbing to conventional notions, however, are those occasions on which Bulgakov actually departs from > Milne, The Master and Margarita, p.7. ® Originally, Bulgakov had not been so concerned with defamiliarization. Ieshua first bears the name Jesus, and Golgotha also appears in the first version of the novel. (Chudakova, ‘Arkhiv . . . ’, p.67; ‘Opyt rekonstruktsii . . . ’, p.g7).

It will suffice here to identify four basic types of difference between Bulgakov’s narrative and the gospel stories, provid- ing just a few examples of each. To the first type, which is also the most explicit, belong the cases where well-known epi- sodes from the bible are specifically denied. Thus, Ieshua’s hands are tied, rather than nailed to the wooden framework on which he meets his death; Ieshua himself personally dis- credits the story of his entry into Jerusalem on an ass; and the ‘filthy rags’ (p.596) which were once the clothes of the con- demned men are left to rot on the hillside by executioners who cast no lot for the privilege of owning them (cf. Matthew 27:35; Mark 15:24; Luke 23:24; John 19:23). Equally unset- tling (and more numerous still) are those places where elements of the canonical text undergo transformation. Bulgak- ov’s Judas, for example, is not a disloyal disciple, but simply an unprincipled young man prepared to stoop to any action in return for some easy money. And Gethsemane, tradition- ally associated with Jesus’s agony and betrayal, here takes on a new significance by means of an ironic reversal which makes it the site of Judas’s assassination. Bulgakov’s inventions offend against the gospels in much the same way. The account of Ieshua’s betrayal and arrest, provided by report in Chapter 2 (pp.446-7), is particularly noteworthy in this respect as it displaces two of the best-known New Testament stories—the Gethsemane episode and the Last Supper. Finally, there are the numerous omissions which characterize the Jerusalem chapters. Thus we find no counterpart here of so prominent an episode as the infamous crowning with thorns. Even more startling is the absence of all the disciples except Matthew, while the implicit removal of the resurrec- tion as a future possibility deprives Bulgakov’s story of the supernatural dénouement which is crucial to the Christian version. But Bulgakov’s challenge to the gospels is not restricted purely to matters of fact. Perhaps more shocking (and not only to the orthodox Christian) is his portrayal of Ileshua. Chapter 2 opens in a manner which can be construed only as a calcu- lated provocation on the part of the author. It begins quite

180 Interpretation tamely with a description of Pilate in the palace of Herod the Great. Although some of the details will be novel (Pilate’s hatred of the smell of roses, his dreaded ‘hemicrania’), as will the name Yershalaim for the Judaean provincial centre, this is a passage which provides the pleasure—unique to historical or certain documentary works—of seeing the familiar ren- dered in concrete, dramatic form. But with the arrival of the ‘accused from Galilee’, this comfortable sense of familiarity is rudely disrupted. The confrontation between Pilate and Ies- hua immediately provokes a dramatic and memorable scene. Even before the interrogation gets under way, the procurator deems it necessary to have Ieshua beaten for addressing him as ‘good man’ instead of using the official title ‘Hegemon’. Of itself this is of little real consequence for Ieshua’s image; the gospels, after all, contain several references to similar cases of physical violence against the person of Jesus. But the gospel writers always confine themselves on such occasions to a terse report (e.g. John 19:1, “Then Pilate therefore took Jesus and scourged him’), a literary device which achieves an effect of vital importance: by this means they convey the cruelty and injustice without in any way detracting from the humanity and dignity of the victim. Bulgakov, however, chooses to use his dramatist’s eye to fill in the physical details. Here is the description of Ieshua’s beating at the hands of the massive Mark Krysoboy: “The centurion’s movement was careless and easy, but the bound man instantly crashed to the ground as though his legs had been knocked out from under him. He gasped for breath, the colour drained from his face and his eyes took on a crazed look’ (p.437). The details emphasize precisely what is glossed over in the New Testament narra- tives—the physical vulnerability of Ieshua and the sheer indignity of this violent abuse of his person. Bulgakov’s hero, unlike the Jesus of the gospels, is thus immediately stripped of any superhuman aura. Bulgakov’s iconoclastic purpose is further revealed in the sequel to the passage just quoted. After striking Ieshua, Mark Krysoboy utters a threat of further violence: ‘A Roman procurator is to be called ‘Hegemon’. Other words should not be used. Stand to attention. Do you understand me or shall I hit you again?’

Don’t beat me.’ (p.438) This scene is troublesome not just because Ieshua displays an all too human fear of violation. More seriously, his readiness to comply with the centurion’s instructions appears to be nothing less than a moral capitulation. Subsequently it becomes clear that Ieshua’s use of the term ‘good man’ is a central article of his faith and teaching. But the reader has no time to recover from this initial shock before the interrogation itself throws up a series of radical changes of the sort men- tioned above. The prisoner’s name is not the expected Jesus, but Ieshua Ha-Notsri (Pilate’s name, we should note, had deliberately not been subject to defamiliarization); he is twenty-seven, which is some six years younger than the age conventionally ascribed to Jesus at the time of his trial; he was born in Gamala, not Bethlehem; and he is the son not of Joseph the carpenter but of an unknown father who was possi- bly a Syrian (p.437) 7 The disturbing impact of these details is compounded by the comic effect of Ieshua’s inappropriate response to Pilate’s question about his name, which Pilate assumes to be a deliberate pretence of stupidity (p.438). Only the habit of Christian reverence would prevent us from agree- ing with the procurator at this point. Bulgakov’s portrayal of Ieshua concludes in the same man- ner as it began. The account of his execution contains a series of details which counteract the grandeur of the corresponding part of the gospel stories. From the flies which swarm greedily over Ieshua’s face, armpits and groin, to the coarse words he utters with the ‘hoarse voice of a brigand’ (p.597), everything in this scene is designed to puncture the image of Jesus pro- moted by Christian mythology and iconology. This point demands to be stressed because, although it has often been made, the intensity of Bulgakov’s heterodoxy has equally often been underestimated, especially by those who would claim The Master and Margarita as a Christian novel. The potential historical con- sequence of Matthew’s endeavour is sensed by Ieshua him- self: “ “they have all made a muddle of what I said. I’m beginning to fear that this muddle is going to continue for a very long time. And it’s all because he notes down wrongly what I say” ’ (p.439). The ‘muddle’ to which Ieshua alludes is, of course, nothing less than the Christian religion as we know it! At a later point in the narrative we are given a brief insight into the genesis of one small yet significant part of the immense ‘muddle’. During his final conversation with Aphra- nius, Pilate voices his suspicion that the story could easily get around in Yershalaim that Judas had committed suicide, to which Aphranius responds, ‘That may be so, Procurator’ (p.740). As with all exchanges between these artful men, there is more here than meets the eye. In their usual indirect and ambiguous way they have uttered, respectively, an instruction and a promise. The implication is that the famous lines of Matthew 27:5 (‘And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself’) are the product of a rumour deliberately circulated at Pilate’s request in order to hide the truth from the world. In brief, the challenge to the New Testament stories con- tained in the Jerusalem narrative is such as to render utterly superfluous Woland’s explanation to Berlioz and Bezdomny that ‘nothing of what is written in the gospels actually ever took place’ (p.459). His own account, by contrast, is accorded the status of absolute historical truth, which it >-:hieves both by supplying the ‘actual’ facts and by revealing how the great ‘muddle’ of the Christian canon emerged through a combi- nation of evangelistic incompetence and procuratorial schem- ing. The opposition of historical truth and Christian legend is reinforced by one of the novel’s finest (and most worrying) ironies: the Master’s novel, which contains the ‘true’ record of events in ancient Jerusalem is destroyed by its creator in the precise manner that Ieshua had recommended to Matthew as a means of ridding the world of his inauthentic notes. The ‘muddle’, it seems, is destined to last longer even than Ieshua could have possibly feared.

184 Interpretation AGAINST THE ATHEISTS Important though it is as a challenge to conventional religious attitudes, Woland’s ‘gospel’ is not only directed against Chris- tian orthodoxy. This iconoclastic tale was initially inspired, it must be remembered, not by the desire to convince his lis- teners, Berlioz and Bezdomny, of the historical unreliability of the gospels (of which they were never in any doubt in the first place), but rather to demonstrate to them the mistakenness of their belief that there had never been.a real Jesus. “You must bear in mind that Jesus did exist, Woland announces as he embarks upon his story (p.435). In adopting so radical a stance on the matter of Jesus’s histor- icity, Woland’s interlocutors (more particularly Berlioz, who is very much the spokesman here) identify themselves as typical representatives of the militant atheism which dominated ideo- logical life in Russia in the early years of Soviet rule. A special place in the anti-religious propaganda generated by this atheis- tic movement was occupied by the works of the so-called ‘myth- ological school’. The most famous advocates of this position, Arthur Drews and John Robertson, argued passionately for the proposition that every detail in the gospels could be identified as a transformation of myths which pre-dated Christianity. On this ground, the very historical existence of Jesus was called into question.'° Berlioz’s speeches in Chapter 1, therefore, merely provide further evidence of his political and ideological ortho- doxy.'' As a result, Woland’s ‘gospel’ comes to occupy a rather curious middle ground in the religious debate of the post-revol- utionary period. It is a provocation which would have been guaranteed to offend equally against the tenets of officially approved atheism and the orthodox Christian attitudes which still flourished both inside and outside the Soviet Union. In the Moscow chapters the ‘snare’ is so cunningly laid as to render its detection possible only after the exercise of con- siderable mental effort. But in the inserted narrative the ‘snare’ is no sooner set (‘Jesus did exist’) than it is exposed. Within a page, the reader is fully alerted to the difference between that Jesus and this leshua; the name tells it all. The intellectual problem (‘Who is Woland?’, ‘Did Jesus exist?’) surrenders to the same pattern of solution, but in the case of the Jerusalem story, the method of narration ensures that the path to wisdom is short and straight. The absolute simplicity of the exposition does nothing, however, to alleviate the shock value of a narrative device which both invites and denies our usual ways of thinking about Jesus. In fact, it may well be that the very ease with which we are ena- bled to progress beyond the second position serves only to heighten the enormity of the shift of consciousness demanded of the reader. To abandon one’s conception of Woland as the devil is one thing; to cast aside the Jesus of Christianity is another matter altogether. But one point should not be over- looked: once again, the rhetoric of the novel has forged a mys- terious bond between Woland and Ieshua. BULGAKOV'S QUEST OF THE HISTORICAL JESUS The immense (and dual) polemical force of the Jerusalem nar- rative is, without doubt, its most striking feature. But, in tell- ing the story the way he does, Bulgakov does not only pursue a polemical point. No less importantly, he approaches his chosen subject with the temperament, and something of the rigour, of a historian. An examination of this aspect of his work will serve as a useful preliminary to the literary inter- pretation which will occupy the remainder of this chapter. The Jerusalem segments of The Master and Margarita purport to offer a truly miraculous solution to a question which has fascinated historians at least since the dawning of the age of reason: to what extent can the stories of Jesus contained in the

Cowardice and other Sins 187 New Testament be credited as a true and accurate record of the actual events they are supposed to describe? This ‘quest of the historical Jesus’ (to borrow the title of Albert Schweitzer’s classic exposition) has occupied the minds of many thousands of scholars of every political and religious persuasion, and it has produced the most various solutions imaginable. At the extremities stand those who represent the two groups men- tioned in the previous section (both of whom were prominent in post-revolutionary Russia): the ultra-conservative Chris- tians, for whom no alternative to the New Testament stories is acceptable; and the so-called ‘myth’ critics, who endeavoured, as we have seen, to relegate the entire gospel canon to the realm of fantasy. Between these uncompromising positions one finds the large majority, who have sought to apply accepted criteria of historical validation to this most difficult set of sources. It is to this intellectual tradition that Bulgak- ov’s ‘novel within a novel’ may truly be said to belong. By choosing to concentrate on the story of the trial and execution of Jesus, Bulgakov addressed himself to that part of the New Testament which, while it is generally accepted to be the least assailable in terms of its factuality, is also the most complex due to the multiple paradoxes and inconsistencies which characterize the gospels at this point.'? In order to pre- pare himself for the daunting task of transforming this very difficult material into a narrative which would be at once psy- chologically and historically convincing Bulgakov undertook a considerable amount of background research. Although the precise extent of his reading is not known, we do have enough information to establish the broad outline. Chudakova, as usual, is the source of the most tangible evidence on this sub- ject. From her description of Bulgakov’s personal library it emerges that the writer possessed a number of works put out by the Moscow ‘Atheist’ publishing house, the most notable volumes being those of Drews and Robertson, together with a similarly provocative study by Barbus and the stenographic record of a subsequent debate between Lunacharsky and Metropolitan Al. It will be suggested below that the sources were employed by the author in three ways: to provide concrete details relating to the life, customs and physical conditions in first-century Jerusalem; to furnish interpretations of charac- ters and events; and to offer solutions to the logical and his- torical problems created by the gospel narratives. Perhaps the most obvious difficulty confronting the would- be author of a fictional work about Jesus is the paucity of that sort of detail necessary to create a purely physical impression of the world of ancient Jerusalem. THE GOSPEL PROBLEM: BULGAKOV’S PSEUDO- HISTORICAL SOLUTION From the above account it can be seen how Bulgakov’s con- ception of a human drama involving an honourable, yet cow- ardly Pilate, a pacific and idealistic Jesus, and a defective disciple may have been moulded by his reading of the christo- logical literature available in his day. Such were the para- meters within which Bulgakov worked as he set out to construct a logical and convincing narrative of the trial and execution of Ieshua. In this endeavour he faced two different, though related, sets of problems. The first concerned the psy- chology of Pilate, a matter in which the gospels are notor- iously weak. Cowardice and other Sins 193 from convincing in this respect.?9 Bulgakov had to find a way, therefore, to motivate Pilate’s change of heart towards Ieshua and to explain why, once his imagination had been stirred by this extraordinary man, he nevertheless felt obliged to put him to death. This last point raises the second set of problems, which are of a purely historical nature. How many trials did Jesus undergo? What was the nature of each of these trials and what was the legal relationship between them? What charges were brought against Jesus? What was the jurisdiction of the Sanhedrin court? How and why was Barabbas pardoned? In attempting to resolve these difficulties, Bulgakov obviously drew upon his own resources of psychological intui- tion and historical imagination. But the nature of his overall conception meant that his solution had to appear to be histori- cal, rather than novelistic. The degree to which the Jerusalem chapters will convince the reader that they are a ‘true’ account of events subsequently distorted in the gospel narratives will be in direct proportion to the persuasiveness of his reconstruc- tion of the New Testament material. The urge towards nove- listic invention had to be counterbalanced, therefore, by the deductive skill of the biblical historian. The ease with which Bulgakov treats this most intractable material speaks for his immense natural gift of historical insight, and his solution, while it is not historical in the proper sense of the word, is an intellectual feat far too easily underestimated. Bulgakov was aided in his task of historical reconstruction by the efforts of others who had travelled the same path. Far- rar, for example, offers a detailed account of Jesus’s trials and their interrelationship.*° But the main influence in this area, as Zerkalov suggests, was David Strauss’s massive Life of Jesus.t' The importance of Strauss’s work for the Russian writer lay not so much in the individual solutions he proposed to specific problems encountered in the gospels as in the general manner in which he conducted his investigation. For the historically minded reader the most impressive feature of these chapters is the deceptive facility with which Bulgakov supplies answers to all of the major puzzles. This aspect of the novel has been well analysed by Elbaum, whose main findings will be summarized here in order to sketch in what is also a vital background to the predicament of Pilate.?° Ieshua is brought before Pilate, we are given to assume, as part of a campaign to curb one of the sporadic outbreaks of political unrest which were a common feature of Judaean life. Like others arrested at the same time (Bar-rabban, Dysmas and Gestas), Ieshua is suspected of dissident activities, and it is Pilate’s task to ascertain the truth before deciding on the suitability of punishment. The interrogation is based on the charges contained in two parchment documents. The first prompts Pilate to make three accusations: that Ieshua incited the people to destroy the Temple (p.436); that he entered Yer- shalaim on an ass (an act tantamount to a declaration of being the Messiah) (p.443); and that he knew Dysmas, Gestas and Bar-rabban (and hence was a party to the Zealot cause) (p.444). Ieshua unequivocally denies each of these charges, on which ground Pilate—who is obviously convinced of the man’s political nalvety—concludes (as in Luke 23:4) by disco- vering ‘no crime’ in him. Fearing, however, that Ieshua’s idealistic notions might lead to further misunderstandings and disturbances, he decides to keep him out of harm’s way at his seaside residence. But the dramatic production of the second parchment gives Pilate cause to reconsider. In this new docu- ment there is a single charge concerning Ieshua’s comments on the subject of power, comments which had been drawn from him by the cunning Judas and witnessed by agents of the Sanhedrin hidden in Judas’ house. The allegation of lése- majesty is far more serious in Pilate’s eyes, and Ieshua’s sub- sequent failure adequately to rebut this charge puts the pro- curator in a position where to withhold punishment would be to arouse dangerous suspicions regarding his own loyalty to the paranoid Tiberius. Particularly important is the suc- cess with which Bulgakov demonstrates the operation of a legal system whose working the gospel writers surround with mystery. Right at the beginning we are told that Pilate’s role in the Ieshua case is to decide whether the death sentence passed on the prisoner by the Sanhedrin priests should be con- firmed. Further information regarding this two-tier system 1s conveyed in the conversation between Pilate and Caiaphas, on which occasion Bulgakov proposes a quite brilliant solution to one of the most awkward historical problems—the choice between Jesus and Barabbas as the recipient of the imperial pardon. The question is this: why, if there are four condemned men, do only two of them qualify for this privilege? The answer, Bulgakov suggests, is that, unlike Dysmas and Ges- tas, who were arrested and tried by the Roman authorities, Ieshua and Bar-rabban were brought to justice by the Jews. Bulgakov is similarly inspired when he deals with the related, and equally vexed, issue of the procedure by which the choice is made. By shifting the responsibility for the decision from the crowd of Jerusalem citizens to the Sanhedrin elders, and the place of its announcement from the public square to the inner sanctum of the Palace of Herod, Bulgakov achieves the seem- ingly impossible, retaining the substance of the gospel narra- tives, yet avoiding their incongruity. If much has been made here of Bulgakov’s historical researches, this is because of the important light that the author’s use of his sources sheds both upon his overall concep- tion of the Jerusalem chapters and upon his unique literary achievement in this section of the novel. It must be repeated, however, that Bulgakov’s solution to the problems he treats is ultimately only pseudo-historical. PRE JERUSALEM STORY: STRUCTURE, STYLE, POINT OF VIEW The four chapters of the Jerusalem story are divided into three segments which deal, respectively, with Ieshua’s interrogation and trial (Chapter 2), with his execution (Chapter 16), and with the assassination of Judas, which is its indirect conse- quence (Chapters 25 and 26). I begin with this bare summary because it enables us to appreciate two points which have all too often been overlooked—the tripartite structure of the ancient narrative, and the dispersal of its three parts within the larger novel which is their frame. This narrative organiz- ation achieves a curious double effect. While it ensures that each of the segments is read as a discrete unit, the very separ- ation of the three segments thrusts upon the reader the responsibility for combining them into a complete narrative. Not that this is a difficult matter. On the contrary, the three sections of the Jerusalem story display a straightforward lin- ear sequentiality which alone creates a powerful impression of unity. This same impression is reinforced by the eventual revelation that the three segments are, in fact, identical with the product of a single narrative act—the Master’s novel. In short, then, Bulgakov encourages the reader to seek out the unity of the Jerusalem narrative and does everything to facilitate that quest. But, as it was with the Moscow chapters, so it is here: it is precisely when things are made easy for us that we need to be most wary. True to the perverse logic of narrative ‘indirection’, Bulgakov invites us to discover unity 48 Zerkalov, pp.70 f. 49 Wright, Mikhail Bulgakov, pp.211-5.

198 Interpretation in the Jerusalem chapters, only to divert our attention from the remarkable disunity of this part of the novel. Imagine for a moment that the four chapters of the ancient story have been removed from the larger context of The Master and Margarita and issued under separate cover. The result would be a text which, although continuous in the purely temporal sense, is anything but a seamless fabric. So great are the shifts of focus, theme and character, in fact, that it is necessary to talk in terms of three largely separate stories, which deal, respect- ively, with Pilate’s act of cowardice (Chapter 2); Matthew’s agonized impotence (Chapter 16); and Aphranius’s ambigu- ous performance of his duty (Chapters 25 and 26). Each story has, in addition, its own distinctive mode of nar- ration. Chapter 2 might best be described as a tragic drama. The entire piece could, in fact, quite easily be transposed on to the stage. The psychological, philosophical and_ political dimensions of the fable are conveyed almost entirely by means of dialogue, the theatricality being enhanced by the simple sequential time structure and the number of references to the movements, gestures, facial expressions and vocal qualities of the protagonists. Chapter 16 is, by contrast, decidedly tragi- comic in tone, an effect which is achieved in part by a shift in the narrative method towards a reliance upon retrospective report. The choice of flashback as the means of telling the reader of Matthew’s vain attempt to spare Ieshua his suffering automatically denies this segment the gripping immediacy of the earlier chapter, creating an ironic perspective which ensures that we will respond to the account of his misfortunes with the condescension which comes with the benefit of hind- sight. The irony (even the black humour) of Chapter 16 is suc- ceeded, in Chapters 25 and 26, by a tale of unsettling ambiguity. Although here too narrative report predominates over dramatic presentation, there is no flashback, and the emphasis is very much upon externals. This section reads almost like a scenario for an adventure film of the detective variety, and, like such films, it relies for its effectiveness on carefully engineered suspense and uncertainty regarding the motives of the characters involved. The shifting tone and style of the Jerusalem narrative also help to disclose another aspect of its discontinuity, which is

Cowardice and other Sins 199 experienced as a progressive movement away from the fami- liar material of the biblical subtext. The story of Pilate, Ieshua and Caiaphas, however iconoclastic, relies heavily on the New Testament narratives for its choice of incident and dramatic conflict. But the two segments which follow display an increasing emancipation from the biblical material. Chapter 16 adheres to the broad outline supplied by the gospels, but draws on invented scenes for its substance, while the final seg- ment breaks completely from the known and predictable pat- tern of events. Although the main event (the death of Judas) and certain details (e.g. the thirty pieces of silver) remind us of the biblical subtext, these chapters immerse us in a world of subterfuge for which the gospel stories provide no prep- aration. To read the Jerusalem narrative, therefore, is to experience a gradual alienation from the hermeneutic paradigm supplied by prior knowledge of the New Testament. At the same time, it is to submit to a process of increasing separation from the personality of Ieshua. The narrative perspective employed in the three segments means that Ieshua’s role is progressively reduced: the active participant in the debates of Chapter 2 is only a passive presence in Chapter 16, while in Chapters 25 and 26 he is sensed even more indirectly as an absent influence. In this way, Bulgakov dramatizes for the reader the central theme of the Jerusalem chapters, which turns on the very difficulty of keeping Ieshua’s personal example truly present in the understanding and the behaviour of those who survive and follow him. Before looking at Bulgakov’s version of the passion story in detail, I wish to return briefly to my original point. The immense diversity of the Jerusalem narrative, its disjunctions of character, theme, and manner, are disturbing and obvious. Yet the overwhelming majority of critics have read this part of The Master and Margarita as if it presented no difficulties of this sort. Starting from the premiss that the ethical dilemma experienced by Pilate is central to the Jerusalem story (even to the novel as a whole in the opinion of some),°° most writers have proceeded as if the three sections of the narrative rep- °° Piper, p.140.
