Cowardice and other Sins 201 of the Pilate story as it is developed in this chapter. The trial of Ieshua involves the procurator in a test both of his ethical sense and of his spirit. Called upon in his capacity as judge to confront ‘an extreme existential situation [involving] the choice between loyalty and betrayal, personal conscience and political expediency, courage and moral cowardice’,>? he is also obliged, as a man, to experience the mysterious attraction of Ieshua’s ideas and his personality, to ponder the signifi- cance of his coming to the world. It is to this latter subject— the covert plot of Chapter 2—that the present discussion will be devoted. Even though his conception of Pilate derives in both its main aspects from the New Testament stories, Bulgakov obviously realized that if this dual conception was to be ren- dered in a convincing manner this would require considerable revision of the gospel materials. The ‘Markan hypothesis’, as we saw in the preceding section, demanded a particularly careful, logical account of the various constraints—legal, social and political—under which Pilate was obliged to oper- ate. Without this (and it is here, of course, that the gospels themselves are so critically deficient) the procurator’s decision to execute an innocent man will appear quite simply inexplic- able. The ‘Johannine hypothesis’ raises problems of a similar order, the principal difficulty again concerning the matter of psychological plausibility. How is the modern author to con- vince the reader of Pilate’s rapid change of heart towards the prisoner from Galilee? In order to appreciate the deftness with which Bulgakov solves this problem and the complex issues which this solution raises, we must examine closely the course of Pilate’s dealings with Ieshua. It has already been suggested (in Chapter 4 above) that the initial confrontation of Pilate and Ieshua may be described as a collision of two opposite principles—the worldly and the unworldly. As Roman procurator, Pilate is the quintessential representative of temporal power. Shrewd, calculating and utterly cynical, he could not be more different from Ieshua, who is quite unversed in matters of state, and whose main characteristics are an extreme naivety and idealism. We have %3° Milne, The Master and Margarita, p.14.

It is not only that Ieshua appears weak and vulner- able; his words and actions seem even to lend credence to the procurator’s opinion that he must be half-witted. This initial impression is reinforced on later occasions where Teshua’s dis- ingenuousness verges on the obtuse. Consider, for example, his inability to take Pilate’s quite unsubtle hints on the ‘cor- rect? way to respond to the charge contained in the fateful second parchment: ‘ “Did you ever say anything about the great Caesar? Answer! Did you?.. Or... didn’t... you?” Pilate placed somewhat greater emphasis on the word “didn’t” than is customary at a trial and his eyes conveyed to Ieshua an idea that he seemed to want to suggest to the pris- oner’ (p.446). But of course Ieshua is quite oblivious both to the danger with which he is threatened and to the import of Pilate’s promptings, and he answers with his usual openness. The fact that he is so unaware means, however, that his can- dour is rendered less than totally admirable. A man who says that he enjoys telling the truth can command absolute respect only when we are certain that he does so in full knowledge of the consequences of his honesty. Ieshua’s behaviour tends to evoke mere pathos, especially when it is viewed in the light of his belated understanding: ‘But you should set me free, hege- mon [... | I can see that they want me killed’ (p.448). On this evidence alone it is difficult not to sympathize with Pilate’s earlier inclination to dismiss the case against Ieshua on the grounds of diminished responsibility. The point deserves to be stressed, because our perception of Ieshua’s obvious limitations in the sphere of worldly affairs will appear later in a different light, as a pledge of a capacity of spirit beyond that of ordinary men. As in John’s gospel, Pilate and Ieshua face each other in Bulgakov’s novel not only as judge and accused in a political trial, but also as participants in an intellectual debate. The debate actually begins even before the interrogation proper gets under way—a reversal which points to the real priority that philosophical matters are to assume in the avowedly official proceedings. Quite unaccustomed to the formalities of dealing with Roman dignitaries, Ieshua commits a faux pas: he

Cowardice and other Sins 203 addresses Pilate not as ‘Hegemon’, but as ‘good man’, a blunder for which he receives a swift and violent rebuke at the practised hands of the centurion Mark Krysoboy. The point at issue is something far more important than mere etiquette, for Ieshua’s idiosyncratic form of address is the mark of one of the two main tenets of his faith—the belief that all people are good. Pilate’s response amounts to a counterdemonstration: by having Ieshua beaten he means to prove himself unworthy of the sobriquet bestowed indiscriminately by the wandering philosopher upon all whom he meets. In this single brutal act is distilled the procurator’s own certainty of the inherent evil of humanity. Pilate and Ieshua already appear in this first exchange as philosophical adversaries, the procurator’s cynical misanth- ropy matching the intensity of the prisoner’s unbounded trust in man’s propensity for goodness. It is inevitable, therefore, that the two should come into conflict again when Ieshua gives voice to his other sacred belief—his certainty in the com- ing of a new and better age to replace the present one. In a phrase which distinctly echoes the New Testament idea of the Kingdom of God, Ieshua first expounds this faith as he explains the metaphorical meaning of his words about the des- truction of the temple: ‘the temple of the old faith will tumble down and the new temple of truth will be created’ (p.441). Once more, Ieshua’s optimism meets with an equal and opposite reaction from the hypersensitive Pilate, who this time unleashes the withering force of his rhetoric in the phrase with which his name has become synonymous: ‘What is truth?’ (p.441). Such, then, is the substance of the philosophical debate between the Roman procurator and the Galilean prisoner; although they will clash again later, there will be nothing new in terms either of the issues raised or of the intellectual pos- itions occupied by the two men. Pilate and Ieshua end up, exactly as they began, representing two views of the world which are completely antithetical. Nevertheless, with the pro- curator’s famous words on truth the discussion takes an unex- pected turn which has the most important consequences for his eventual understanding of what has passed between him- self and the accused man. Up until this moment, Pilate has

204 Interpretation had the upper hand, not only in the crude political sense, but also in intellectual terms. Against his cogent objections, Ies- hua’s ideas appear to be precisely what the procurator takes them for—the utopian notions ofa naive idealist. By depriving Ieshua of the calm majesty of the gospel Jesus, Bulgakov also ensures that the sheer impracticability of his philosophical views is exposed to the harshest of lights. But, no sooner is this done, than the roles are suddenly reversed. Before he can even savour the devastating impact of his ‘What is truth?’, the ground is cut from under Pilate’s feet as Ieshua reveals a hith- erto unsuspected side of his nature. First of all, he displays a seemingly miraculous ability to read the procurator’s mind, divining the suicidal thoughts induced by the severe migraine with which he is afflicted. This uncanny power of diagnosis is complemented by Ieshua’s equally uncanny knack of success- fully predicting the abatement of the pain. And, as if this wer- en’t enough, Ieshua pushes home his advantage over Pilate by disclosing the spiritual ailment which 1s the source of the pro- curator’s malaise: ‘you are too introverted and you have utterly lost your faith in people’ (p.442). This passage has a shock value which is ensured by a number of factors. For the first (and, as it turns out, the only) time in their conversation Ieshua has wrested the initiative from Pilate: the prisoner passes his verdict on the judge. As the latter (like his scribe) is reduced to a condition of mute amazement, Ieshua speaks with a dignity and insight of which he could hitherto scarcely have been believed capable. Most important of all is the mystery surrounding his ability to div- ine the nature of Pilate’s malady, for this introduces the possi- bility of a supernatural dimension into the narrative, a possibility which is especially interesting due to the striking parallel, already noted in a different context, between Ieshua’s behaviour in this scene and that of Woland in Chapter 1. Just like Woland, Ieshua both displays extraordinary powers and defies the attempt by his interlocutor to explain them away by recourse to normal reasoning: he insists that he is not the ‘great physician’ that Pilate assumes him to be (p.442). We should not be misled either into thinking that Ieshua’s sub- sequent disclosure of the deductive method by which he dis- cerned Pilate’s thoughts of his dog necessarily supplies an

Cowardice and other Sins 205 adequate account of all his insights. This does not explain how he detected Pilate’s suicidal inclination, nor does it offer any clue regarding the source of his ability to predict the cessation of the procurator’s physical suffering. Even if this latter pre- diction is not regarded as being tantamount to a miraculous cure, the very prediction itself lies well beyond the sphere of normal phenomena. These points should be weighed against the tendency amongst critics to play down and even some- times to deny the presence of a supernatural element in the Jerusalem chapters.°# Ieshua preserves his advantage over Pilate in the sequel to this passage. Even though there is no supernatural element here, once again the connection between Ieshua and Woland is fully evident. The crucial exchange (an obvious reworking of John 19: 10-11) concerns the oath which Pilate demands of Ieshua as a pledge that he had not incited the people of Yer- shalaim to destroy the Great Temple: ‘What would you have me swear by?’ asked the unbound man with extreme animation. ‘By your life, perhaps,’ the procurator answered, ‘now is the very time to swear by it, for you must know that it hangs by a thread.’ ‘But surely you don’t believe that you have hung it so, hegemon?’ the prisoner asked. ‘If you do, you are mistaken.’ Pilate shuddered and replied through clenched teeth: ‘I can cut that thread.’ ‘Here too you are mistaken,’ the prisoner objected, smiling brightly and shielding his face from the sun with his hand. ‘You must surely admit that only he who has hung the thread is able to cut it?’ (p.443) As Woland had done with Berlioz, so Ieshua offers Pilate a timely reminder of the inevitable limitations of human power. And, even though he does not follow up this argument with any gruesome demonstration, Ieshua emerges from this debate the clear victor, sharing for once the calm superiority of Woland. Although it represents only a brief hiatus in the official pro- ceedings, which subsequently speed towards their inexorable 54 El'baum (p.44) puts this down to hypnotherapy.

206 Interpretation conclusion, this scene shocks Pilate into a new awareness which is revealed variously in the narrative which follows. Most obvious, of course, is the fact that Ieshua’s healing powers provide the procurator with an added incentive to pre- vent the threatened travesty of justice. Here is a man who might render a valuable medical service. But, beyond this bla- tant self-interest there are also signs of a fundamental change in his attitude to Ieshua’s ideas. The nature of this change may be perceived in the following passage, where the two men resume their discussion: ‘So Mark Krysoboy, the cold, stalwart executioner, and the people who, as I can see,’ the procurator pointed to Jeshua’s disfigured face, ‘have beaten you for your preaching, and the robbers Dysmas and Gestas, who along with their gang killed four soldiers and, finally that filthy traitor Judas—these are all good people?’ ‘Yes,’ answered the prisoner. ‘And the kingdom of truth will come?’ ‘It will come, hegemon,’ Ieshua answered with conviction. ‘It will never come!’ Pilate suddenly shouted in such a terrifying voice that Ieshua recoiled. (p.448) In purely intellectual terms, nothing has altered here. Ieshua remains committed to the two central tenets of his faith, while Pilate displays the same critical spirit as during their original argument. What zs different, however, is the emotional com- mitment with which the procurator pursues his philosophical point. Where he had previously preserved the appearance of cynical indifference, Pilate now argues with the passion and vigour of an Ivan Karamazov. The mode of argument employed here is, in fact, very similar to that used by Dos- toyevsky’s Ivan in the famous confrontation with his brother Alyosha in Book 5, Chapter 5 of The Brothers Karamazov, and the point at issue is also essentially the same. But the outcome of this collision of principles is quite different. Where Alyo- sha’s certainty in the goodness of the divine process is shaken by the catalogue of human vice thrown at him by his brother, Ieshua’s faith holds firm, a circumstance which causes Pilate to abandon rational argument in favour of a shrill emotional outburst. The procurator still does not accept Ieshua’s views, but it is now obvious that they matter to him immensely. This is the mark of his vitality of spirit.

Cowardice and other Sins 207 It is in Ieshua’s absence, however, that Pilate’s new sensibi- lity finally manifests itself in the form of an insight, which comes at the moment he repeats for the last time his insistence that Bar-rabban be pardoned. Here is the passage in question: Everything was lost; there was nothing more to talk about. Ha- Notsri was leaving for ever and there was no one to cure the procura- tor’s terrible, fierce pains; there was no remedy for them but death. But it was not this thought that struck Pilate now. It was the same inexplicable anguish (loska) that had visited him on the balcony which now permeated his entire being. He sought to explain it immediately, and the explanation was strange: the procurator sensed dimly that he had somehow not said everything he wanted to the condemned man and that perhaps he had not listened to every- thing properly either. (p.452) This is an experience of illumination as important for Pilate as that subsequently to visit Ivan Bezdomny in Dr Stravinsky’s clinic. Each case involves a leap of understanding which results in a new perception of an ‘unexpected visitor’ pos- sessed of extraordinary powers. Where Bezdomny will later abandon his conviction that Woland is a demonic force for destruction in favour of a view which recognizes his function as a ‘messenger’, Pilate here realizes that Ieshua’s real signifi- cance resides not in his healing powers, but in the idealistic faith which he has brought to the world. To complete the parallel, both Bezdomny and Pilate are rewarded for their new vision by the experience of a dream. But this is to run ahead. The first section of the Jerusalem narrative closes on a note of tragic irony: it transpires that the very procurator whose act of moral cowardice ensures Ies- hua’s physical annihilation is the one person to whom it is given to understand, however dimly, the true import of his coming. This dilemma is captured perfectly in the threat which Pilate directs against Caiaphas, but which is, in reality, self-reflexive. Conjuring up a near future in which Ieshua’s death will already be a reality, the procurator warns the high _ priest: ‘Then you will remember Bar-rabban who was spared — and you will regret that you sent to his death the philosopher with his sermon of peace’ (p.454). Pilate seems to speak almost as a proselyte on this occasion, yet it should not be thought that he has been converted to Ieshua’s faith. Although

208 Interpretation his words reveal a fuller understanding of Ieshua’s philos- ophy, the procurator’s new sensibility does not necessarily involve conversion at all, it consists rather in the realization that Ieshua’s idealism provides the necessary counterweight to the deadening force of his own cynicism, and that the ‘sermon of peace’ which Ieshua preaches offers an antidote to the ‘cruelty’ of which Pilate himself is the supreme representative. By a strange paradox, it is his very resistance to Ieshua’s ideas which seems to guarantee the procurator’s understanding. When the Jerusalem story resumes, we shall learn that the converse is also true, for Ieshua’s sole avowed disciple proves to have no proper understanding of the man whose faith he purports to follow. ‘The true and only disciple’ At no point in the Jerusalem story are the discontinuities mentioned above more apparent than in the transition from Chapter 2 to Chapter 16. It is almost as if we were reading a different novel. By resuming the account of Ieshua’s execution in the way he does, Bulgakov creates a double shock. The pro- curator, who was hitherto the central protagonist, is now inex- plicably absent, his place being filled by a new hero, the disciple Matthew Levi. What is more, this shift of focus is accompanied by a radical change in the narrative tone. Where Pilate’s encounter with Ieshua was treated with dignity and decorum, Matthew’s adventures are presented in a manner which can only be described as serio-comic. These obser- vations give rise to a question which has only too rarely been asked: why should Bulgakov have chosen to alter the focus and style of his narrative in this curious way? To answer, as one critic has done, that Matthew is introduced to provide an example of ‘uncompromising bravery’ against which the ‘moral capitulation’ of Pilate will stand out in starker relief is not sufficient.°° Matthew’s loyalty obviously does stand the test where Pilate’s courage falters, yet by dwelling on the dis- ciple’s single saving grace, such an explanation distorts a nar- rative whose evident purpose is, on the contrary, to emphasize 55 Skobelev, p.125.

Cowardice and other Sins 209 his manifold failings. Although we might agree that Matthew has to be viewed as a foil to the procurator, the juxtaposition of their characters demands to be described in different terms. Bulgakov’s portrait of Matthew Levi is one of unremitting disapproval. Even before he enters the story in person, his reputation is seriously undermined by Ieshua’s disavowal of the parchment on which the former publican has inscribed his imperfect record of his master’s sayings. As we have seen, the problem is that, as protoevangelist, Matthew’s zeal is unfortu- nately matched by his incompetence, a combination which, as Ieshua himself is only too aware, threatens the direst conse- quences for the proper preservation and propagation of his teaching. In Chapter 16 we are given to learn that, in his deeds no less than in his words, zeal and incompetence remain the hallmarks of Matthew’s character. The chronicle of the disciple’s half-baked plan to save Ieshua, of its bungled execution and his subsequent melodramatic despair makes for comedy of the blackest hue. Cowardice may be a terrible sin, but it is not the only human failing on display in the Jerusalem story. Considered in the abstract, Matthew’s attempt to spare leshua the indignity and the physical suffering of a Roman execution attests to a thoroughly honourable intention. Such is Matthew’s humane concern for his teacher that he gives no thought for his own welfare. But his scheme is laudable only in part, for Bulgakov makes it plain that the disciple’s motives are not entirely pure. Crucial in this respect is the moment when Matthew rehearses in his mind the speech that he will address to his master as he plunges the knife into his back: ‘Ieshua! I save you and depart together with you! I, Matthew, your true and only disciple!’ (p.593). The rhetoric is pure comic-strip melodrama, but what makes this more serious than laughable is Matthew’s evident desire for glory: his act of deliverance is also imagined as a piece of self-aggrandizement. Herein resides the unkindest of ironies: Matthew’s egoistic impulse reveals just how far he is from being a ‘true’ disciple of Ieshua. But this is not the only occasion on which Matthew proves unworthy of his calling. After the planned knife attack has ended in fiasco, the disciple calls upon God to perform by mir-

210 Interpretation aculous means the act which had proved beyond his own mor- tal powers. Although quite laughable in its childlike naivety, the request is a gross impiety, a sin which is compounded by Matthew’s later angry reaction when no divine intervention ensues: ‘I was mistaken!’, cried Levi, now completely hoarse. “You are the god of evil! Or have your eyes been clouded by the smoke from the temple censers and have your ears ceased to hear anything other than the trumpet sounds of the priests? You are not an omnipotent god. You are a black god. I curse you, god of robbers, their soul and their protector.’ (p.595) Matthew’s blasphemy smacks very much of Job’s conceit, yet Bulgakov’s hero is denied the tragic splendour which attaches to his Old Testament counterpart.°° The disciple’s petulant recantation, no less than his faith itself, is a thoroughly pitiful affair, and the entire scene slides into bathos. No sooner has Matthew challenged the divinity than he experiences a horr- ible doubt as storm clouds suddenly appear on the horizon: ‘Levi thought that he had been insanely hasty with his curses. Now God wouldn’t listen to him’ (p.596) By comparison with the subtle delineation of Pilate’s character, Bulgakov’s portrait of Matthew is a crude carica- ture. Where Chapter 2 combined a complex and convincing psychological study of political behaviour with a truly com- pelling philosophical dispute, Chapter 16 is a satirically trans- parent fable illustrating the distance which may separate the substance of faith from the behaviour of one who professes to practise it. The difference could hardly be more complete, and its effect is all the more disquieting as its purpose remains obscure. It is not until Chapters 25 and 26 that the total design becomes clear as procurator and disciple at last come face to face in a scene which brings the underlying drama of understanding to the surface. 5° Jovanovic suggests that this is an echo of Matthew 27:46 (“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?’), while Mahlow has detected a parallel with Ivan Karamazov (M. Cowardice and other Sins 211 ‘A very good and inquisitive man’ Of the main protagonists in the passion story, none has exerted a greater fascination over the minds of modern writers than Judas. Attracted in the first place by the awesome conse- quences of his legendary act of betrayal, writers of such vastly different backgrounds and temperaments as _ Leonid Andreyev, Nikos Kazantzakis and Robert Graves have applied their considerable imaginative powers to the task of explaining the motives which may have inspired him. Uncon- vinced by the biblical story of a man moved by pure greed to deliver his master into the hands of his enemies, each of the writers named has proposed a solution of far greater com- plexity and psychological insight. For Bulgakov’s purpose in The Master and Margarita, however, the story of Judas was of relatively slight importance. Although obviously aware of the difficulty surrounding Judas’s motivation, and presumably unimpressed by Farrar’s insistence upon avarice as his domi- nant drive,°’ Bulgakov opted for an alternative more radical and at the same time more conservative than those offered by the writers named above. The decision to remove Judas from the ranks of the disciples meant that he was able to retain the conventional motive by drawing the portrait of a man so lac- king in principle as to undertake any treachery for a suitable financial reward. But the result, inevitably, is a character of little interest. Indeed, Bulgakov’s Judas is hardly a character in the proper sense at all, for his importance resides almost exclusively in his passive function as a pawn in the games of others. Employed first by Caiaphas in order to trap Ieshua, he is used just as cynically by Pilate, in the finale of the Jerusalem story, to serve the procurator’s own political and psychologi- cal purposes. The tale of Judas’s assassination at the hands of Aphranius and his accomplices raises some of the most difficult issues connected with the Jerusalem story. Like Chapter 16, this section has an immediate alienating effect due to the sheer unfamiliarity of its subject matter. But the occurrences des- cribed in Chapters 25 and 26 are also disturbing in another 57 Farrar, pp.527 ff.

ON) Interpretation way. For here it is not only that the reader is supplied with an unexpected (and perhaps even unwanted) new dimension to the biblical story, but also that this narrative material is ren- dered in a manner as full of ambiguity and hidden impli- cations as the very best detective writing.°® The tragi-comic account of Matthew’s misadventures offered no scope for deductive reasoning; by contrast, the story of how Judas meets his violent death demands that this faculty should be exer- cised to the full. The immediate problem which faces the reader of Chapters 25 and 26 is to discover Pilate’s real intention regarding Judas. In the course of events, we learn that the title of Chapter 25 (‘How the Procurator tried to save Judas of Ker- ioth’) is a deliberate mystification which mimics Pilate’s own devious manner of making his wishes known. The alert reader will almost certainly suspect straightaway that the procura- tor’s apparent concern for Judas’s safety is a mere pretence, but it is only in retrospect that we can be absolutely certain that his ostensible effort to avert the threatened calamity is, in fact, a veiled instruction to Aphranius that he should take steps to ensure the contrary. Aphranius himself is obviously no stranger to his master’s ways, and he proves as adept in the practice of verbal subterfuge as he is in the art of interpreting the procurator’s cunning remarks. The scene in which he requests that Pilate ‘punish’ him for his ‘dereliction of duty’ in failing to prevent Judas’s murder is a magnificent piece of sus- tained dissimulation by both men. The facts, of course, tell a different story: Pilate’s ‘rebuke’ takes the form of a material reward for a job well done. Once his true intention is clear, Pilate’s motives in arrang- ing for Judas’s assassination are as readily understandable as his desire to maintain the facade of non-involvement. The most important part of his plan, it should be noted, is not the death of Judas itself, but the scandal which it enables—the anonymous return to Caiaphas of the blood money paid to Judas, together with an offensive note. Pilate can scarcely con- ceal his delight when he receives Aphranius’s report of the ® See Pope, op. cit. The present discussion follows part of Pope’s argument quite closely.

Cowardice and other Sins Os very real embarrassment suffered by his adversary as a result of this stratagem. The satisfaction he derives from this news is not only political, however; more importantly, his act of ven- geance also answers a deeper psychological need. By causing unpleasantness to the man whose intransigent behaviour deprived him of the possibility of having Ieshua spared at the eleventh hour, Pilate is patently seeking to evade his own sense of guilt over the matter. Nor is this all. The actual words chosen by the procurator to inform Aphranius of his plan speak of a deeper motive still. “My information’, the procura- tor had said on that occasion, ‘is that one of Ha-Notsri’s secret friends, incensed by the monstrous treachery of that money- changer, 1s arranging with his accomplices to kill him this very night and to throw back the money received for his treachery to the high priest with the note, “I return the accursed money!” ’ (p.723). The ‘secret friend’ who makes such an arrangement is, in reality, none other than Pilate himself, which suggests that the plan has the further psychological purpose of allowing the procurator to believe that his actions somehow prove his ‘loyalty’ to Ieshua. This is to say, then, that his scheme is doubly delusive. If Pilate’s motivation becomes transparent once his plan is executed, the part played in this furtive affair by Aphranius proves to be a greater puzzle. At first sight, we might even wonder if there is any puzzle here at all, for Aphranius appears to be nothing more than a willing functionary, whose sole concern is the efficient performance of assignments entrusted to him by the procurator. Yet, as several critics have noted, there is rather more to Aphranius than unthinking loyalty. Despite his unswerving dedication to duty (witness the assassination itself), there are signs that his attitude to Pilate is not just that of an unquestioning servant. The clue to his deeper feelings is contained in the report of Ieshua’s execution which he furnishes on his return to Yershalaim in Chapter 25. The simplest way to approach Aphranius’s report is to examine the series of questions and answers through which it is conveyed. The most important exchanges may be summar- ized as follows: (1) Pilate asks if drinks were administered to the condemned men prior to the execution, to which Aphra-

214 Interpretation nius answers that they were, but that Ieshua refused to take his; (2) On hearing this, the procurator wishes to know what Ieshua actually said on this occasion. Aphranius responds: ‘He said [ . . . ] that he was grateful and that he laid no blame for his life being taken away’; (3) Pilate is equally interested to learn if Ieshua preached anything during his execution, and hears the (now famous) words: ‘The only thing he said was that amongst human faults he considered cowardice one of the most important’; (4) In response to further questions, Aphra- nius attests to the general strangeness of Ieshua’s behaviour during these last hours, referring in particular to the ‘dis- mayed smile’ that was constantly on his face (p.721). How much trust can be placed in Aphranius’s account? In the procurator’s mind, at least, there is no room for doubt. Convinced of Aphranius’s loyalty and having no other source of information to draw on, he accepts this as a truthful, though painful, record of what transpired. For the reader, however, it is a different matter, because there are certain discrepancies between Aphranius’s version of events and the description of the execution in Chapter 16 which give rise to the suspicion that he is being less than totally honest. The greatest doubt surrounds Aphranius’s first statement concerning Ieshua’s refusal to accept the drink. In Chapter 16 we had been told quite specifically how, Ieshua had drunk greedily from the sponge that was offered to him (p.597). Is Aphranius lying to the procurator? This may well be our initial reaction, and a number of critics have levelled such an accusation against him.°? But this charge overlooks the crucial fact that two dif- ferent drinks are involved.®° Aphranius and Pilate are talking of a drink offered before the execution; Chapter 16 tells of a sponge of water gratefully accepted by Ieshua only minutes before his death. Yet it must still be wondered why Aphranius should have omitted to tell Pilate of the second drink, especially when he sees the obvious distress caused to the pro- curator by the story of Ieshua’s refusal: ‘ ‘““The madman!” Pilate said, grimacing for some reason. A vein began to throb beneath his left eye. ““To die from sunstroke! Why deny what °° See Mahlow, p.45; Utekhin, * “Master i Margarita”... ’, p.104. °° El’baum, p.81. Cowardice and other Sins 215 is prescribed by law?” ’ (p.721). It can only be assumed that Aphranius withholds the information because this distress is precisely what he wishes to cause. This would also explain his uncharacteristic (and rather stagey) display of ‘absent-min- dedness’ when he fails to make it clear at first that the prisoner who refused the drink was Ieshua (‘Forgive, me, hegemon! [ ...] Did I not say who it was? Ha-Notsri’—p.721). The delay, no less than the news itself, could not have been better designed to aggravate the procurator’s anxiety. Although Aphranius technically tells no lie in his report about the drink, his act of omission casts a shadow over the remainder of what he says. Did Ieshua actually behave in the manner that Aphranius claims? And, most importantly, did the condemned man really pronounce the words that are attri- buted to him? On these points, Chapter 16 offers no evidence to support an argument one way or the other, although the all- important statement about cowardice is later corroborated by a similar passage in Matthew’s parchment (p.745). While this does not constitute firm proof—Matthew’s notes themselves being far from unimpeachable—we may nevertheless assume that, as before, no actual falsification has taken place, even if only on the ground that a man as cunning as Aphranius would be unlikely to run the risk of exposure. Yet it would appear just as likely that his account of Ieshua’s speeches is as cruelly selective as his earlier statement about the drink. Ieshua’s words on cowardice could not be better chosen to exacerbate Pilate’s guilt, but the real question is whether this was Ies- hua’s own intention, or the result of careful ‘editing’ by his reporter. Of Aphranius’s relentless urge to cause the procura- tor the maximum suffering there can, at least, be no doubt. As one critic puts it, each of Aphranius’s statements is evidently designed ‘to punish the already guilt-ridden Pilate, who is clearly agonizing precisely over his own cowardice’.”' When Pilate tells Aphranius of his suspicion that Ieshua may have a number of undetected ‘admirers or followers’, it would appear, therefore, that he speaks more truly than he knows (p.721). As usual, the procurator is talking cryptically: he mentions these hypothetical admirers only in order to ePyPopesper2:

216 Interpretation broach the subject of Judas’s assassination. His choice of expression once again suggests a subconscious urge to prove his own admiration for Ieshua, but the irony is that in Aphra- nius he confronts a man whose behaviour points to the conclu- sion that such ‘secret followers’ do actually exist outside the procurator’s mind. All the evidence suggests that Aphranius must be leading a double life. His role in these two chapters is thoroughly ambiguous. Although he will carry out to the letter Pilate’s instruction regarding Judas, he has ensured, even before the plan is unveiled, that the procurator’s satisfaction will be poisoned. By aggravating the very guilt that the assas- sination was designed to allay, Aphranius thwarts Pilate’s delusive fantasy. He does so, we must imagine, in a malicious spirit, yet what he cannot realize is that his act also prepares Pilate indirectly for a moment of greater wisdom. Aphranius’s provocations ensure that Pilate comprehends the utter futility of the assassination even before it is carried out. Alone on the balcony, at the beginning of Chapter 26, the procurator experiences another wave of ‘anguish’ (toska): the procurator kept trying to understand the cause of his spiritual torment. And although he quickly realized what it was, he attempted to deceive himself. It was clear to him that this morning he had lost something which could not be returned, and that now he was trying to compensate for that loss by petty, insignificant and— most importantly—belated actions. (p.725) This is the minute of Pilate’s tragic gnosis. Self-deception is no sae possible, and the assassination plan is seen for what it ep of his cowardly act. (It is also a grotesque perversion of Ieshua’s own intention: compare Ieshua’s very real concern for his betrayer with Pilate’s obviously bogus desire to ‘save’ Judas—pp.447, 724.) But, as before, the inevitable pain which accompanies the experience of anguish is the guarantee of new understanding. On the first occasion, as we saw above, Pilate’s anguish led him to a better appreciation of Ieshua’s significance. Now he is rewarded in a different way—by the experience of a prophetic dream. To translate the Russian toska as ‘anguish’ is to approxi- mate only one part of its meaning. Along with ‘melancholy’

Cowardice and other Sins 217 and ‘depression’, the Oxford Russian Dictionary lists ‘ennui’, ‘yearning’ and ‘nostalgia’. It is this latter, transcendent aspect of Pilate’s anguish which finds an outlet in his dream. The dream itself is simply described. As he drifts into sleep, the procurator sees the moonbeam which extends towards his couch beneath the colonnade become transformed into a shin- ing path. Still in the company of his faithful dog, Pilate ascends this path with Ieshua. As they walk, the two men engage in a discussion ‘about something very complicated and important’ in which ‘neither was able to convince the other’ (p.734). The execution has never taken place, and the two men have all the time they need to continue their debate. Up to this point, the dream is experienced as a joyous release from the concerns which afflict the procurator’s waking mind. A transparent wish-fulfilment fantasy, it promises the dreamer a double benefit. Not only is Pilate miraculously relieved of the terrible burden of conscience, he is also permitted to remedy the particular dissatisfaction that he had experienced during his earlier bout of anguish (‘somehow he had not said every- thing he wanted to the condemned man and [... | he had not listened to everything properly either —p.452). But with the ensuing conversation the mood changes abruptly. In the dream, Ieshua repeats the words about cowardice, to which the procurator responds: ‘No, philosopher, I object: it is the most terrible fault’ (p.735). This is no wish fulfilment, and in the following sequence Pilate actually recapitulates the very trauma from which the first part of the dream had released him. Groaning and sobbing in his sleep, the procurator expresses his conviction that, were he to have the chance again, he would be perfectly prepared to sacrifice his career for the sake of the innocent Ieshua. The dream concludes, however, on a different note again. The debate breaks off, and Ieshua now stands in the procura- tor’s path, where he utters a prediction: ‘Now we shall always be together [ ... ] Whenever my name is mentioned, your name will be mentioned too! I, a foundling, the son of unknown parents, and you, the son of an astrologer-king and a miller’s daughter, the beautiful Pila’ (p.735). Remarkable first of all for its ambiguity—is this a threat or a promise?— Ieshua’s prediction also supports and amplifies Pilate’s earlier

218 Interpretation suspicion (experienced again during his earlier moment of anguish) that his meeting with Ieshua would bring him ‘immortality’ (p.452).°? But, as with all of the most significant passages in The Master and Margarita, the full meaning of Pilate’s dream is disclosed only later in the novel. It is not until Chapter 32, in fact, that we come to understand that the procurator’s vision is of a prophetic order. In this final chapter, Woland interrupts the flight to the final refuge in order to display to the Master and Margarita the lonely figure of Pilate languishing on a mountain top. This is one of the most important scenes in the entire novel and it will be con- sidered in more detail in the next chapter. For the present, we need only mention its conclusion. Moved by the sight of Pilate’s distress, Margarita secures his release. As a result of her intercession, the procurator is enabled, precisely as he was in his dream, to ascend the moonlight path with Ieshua | (p.798). What appeared initially to be a mere wish-fulfilment fantasy turns out in retrospect to rehearse a crucial moment of the novel’s dénouement, to which, in the words of one critic, it provides the ‘teleological key’.® In the immediate context of the Jerusalem story, Pilate’s dream is both a mark of his superior capability (such dreams are visited only upon the elect in Bulgakov’s novel) and a reminder of his earthly limitations. The brilliance of the trans- cendent vision is dimmed by the irksome presence of the dreamer’s guilt. And when Pilate awakens, the brief experi- ence of joy is lost in the flood of renewed despair. The gap between potentiality and actuality is conveyed with immense poignancy: the procurator’s consciousness of his historical tra- gedy constrains his perception of a higher reality in which such tragedies are annulled. The same tension is at work in the final tableau where Pilate, Ieshua’s ‘secret friend’, comes face to face with the wandering philosopher’s only self-con- fessed disciple, Matthew.
