Cowardice and other Sins 219 imagines, with mixed and somewhat unclear intentions. Despite the disciple’s evident hostility towards him, the pro- curator is moved by a determination to display his magnani- mity, which is manifested finally in the suggestion that Matthew take on the job of librarian at his Caesarea resi- dence. While this might be interpreted as yet another attempt by the procurator to salve his conscience, this is surely not his only motive. The offer- is made, it should be noted, immedi- ately after Pilate has briefly inspected Matthew’s infamous parchment, a circumstance which suggests that the offer should be seen as an attempt to ensure that Ieshua’s teaching be at least partially preserved, albeit in a form of dubious reliability. Better an imperfect record, Pilate would seem to be saying, than no record at all. For his part, Matthew again proves incapable of showing himself in anything but the worst possible light. Although his distrust of the procurator is only natural, the ‘unkind smile’ which ‘distorts’ his face (p.744) speaks for a profound unge- nerosity of spirit even before this is displayed in his proud ges- ture of rejecting Pilate’s offer. What damns Matthew here is not the rejection itself—this could, after all, suggest an honourable fastidiousness—but the manner in which he chooses to convey it. When asked to explain the reason for his refusal, the disciple tells Pilate: ‘because you would fear me. It wouldn’t be so easy for you to look me in the face now that you've killed him’ (p.745). Like Aphranius before him, Mat- thew seeks to aggravate the procurator’s suffering. But, unlike Aphranius, he pursues his vengeful purpose with a primitive crudity which enables Pilate to turn the tables on him and deliver a simple moral: ‘I know you consider yourself to be a disciple of Ieshua, but I must tell you that you have assimi- lated nothing of what he taught you. For, if you had, you ‘ would have certainly accepted something from me. You should bear in mind that, before he died, he said that he blamed no one [... ] You are cruel, but he was not cruel’ (p.745). Who better to recognize such cruelty than the ‘cruel fifth procurator of Judaea’? Bulgakov does not allow the procurator to emerge from this exchange entirely without stain, however. No sooner has he passed judgement on Matthew’s cruelty than he himself takes

220 Interpretation an equally unkind pleasure in dashing the disciple’s hope of wreaking vengeance against Judas. The pride with which the procurator reveals his own part in the assassination places him dangerously close to Matthew’s own level: he too is far from immune to the urge to prove himself the ‘true and only disciple’. As Altshuler astutely points out, none of the “disci- ples’ in The Master and Margarita is the equal of the power he pretends to serve.°* CONCLUSION: THE ABIDING ENIGMA Whenever the Master speaks of his ill-fated magnum opus he refers to it as his novel about Pontius Pilate. As a description of the Jerusalem narrative (with which, of course, the novel 1s identical) this is apt, yet imprecise. Apt because it captures the particular emphasis of a passion drama in which Jesus is more a Catalyst than a central protagonist, it is imprecise inas- much as it makes no mention of Matthew, whose story illumi- nates that of Pilate by offering a contrastive study in human inadequacy. In these two stories, Bulgakov demonstrates the twin function of Ieshua’s coming, which involves a test of courage and a test of understanding. In so doing, he also sug- gests the operation of a bleak dialectic. Each man fails one test but passes the other: deficient in courage, Pilate nevertheless displays a potential for understanding far in advance of Mat- thew, whose inability to comprehend Ieshua’s teaching is matched by a fearless loyalty that puts the procurator to shame. The prospect is doubly depressing. In the first place, the narrative perspective in Chapters 2 and 16 ensures that the reader will perceive each man’s weakness rather than his strength. The story of their meeting, on the other hand, reveals the impossibility of the two men combining their talents, the result of which is the most bitter irony of all: the man who allows Ieshua to be destroyed is eventually moved by the urge to immortalize his teaching, yet the man who has had the necessary exposure both to Ieshua’s personality and to his ideas will succeed in handing down to posterity only the most inaccurate and inadequate record. °+ Al’tshuler, p.6.

Cowardice and other Sins 221 But the Jerusalem story does not only tell of human frustra- tion, it also creates a feeling of frustration in the reader. Although it is totally satisfying in a formal sense, the narrative nevertheless leaves the impression that the most important part of the story has not been told. The source of this impres- sion is the increasingly indirect manner in which Ieshua is presented. As we become absorbed in the account of the unsuccessful attempts by Pilate and Matthew to prove them- selves worthy disciples, the personality of Ieshua himself becomes an ever more insubstantial and shadowy presence. The immense significance of his coming is in no way dimi- nished, yet the man and his ideas represent an abiding enigma. What can be said of Ieshua on the basis of what we learn from the Jerusalem narrative? Most obviously, he is the embo- diment of an absolute idealism which renders him absolutely vulnerable in the face of the evil manifested not only in the celebrated cowardice of Pilate, but also in the conniving malice of Caiaphas and the unprincipled duplicity of Judas. This, for Lakshin, is the tragic core of the passion story.°5 But what of Ieshua’s actual teaching? With his emphasis on the individual’s innate capacity for good and his rejection of all forms of power, he stands, as Milne has pointed out, in the main stream of philosophical anarchism.°° Such is Ieshua’s overt message, and it is all that we learn from his own lips. As a teaching about this world, it is clear and unequivocal. Rather more difficult to assess, however, are the sayings attributed to him by Aphranius and Matthew. Denied the stamp of complete authenticity, these sayings are also prob- lematical because they do not all have a discernible bearing on the drama which is ostensibly being enacted in these chapters. The most prominent of Ieshua’s reported com- ments is his statement on cowardice. Repeated in a slightly different form on no less than three separate occasions, this remark also commands attention by its unmistakable rele- vance to current events. But it is precisely because these words are so relevant that we must treat them with care. 65 Lakshin, ‘Roman... ’, p.298 f. 66 Milne, The Master and Margarita, p.8.

209 Interpretation Although due note has to be taken of Ieshua’s opinion that cowardice numbers amongst the greatest human weaknesses, it must also be acknowledged that the reason why this opinion is accorded so much weight is due to its strictly accidental func- tion as a comment on Pilate’s recent behaviour. This is, in fact, only a part of Ieshua’s message, and if we look again at each of the occasions on which cowardice is mentioned, we will find that this is not the sum of what Ieshua had to say. The first reference to Ieshua’s teaching on cowardice is con- tained in Aphranius’s report on the execution. In the same speech we also learn of the dying man’s insistence that he ‘laid no blame’ for his death. At the time, these words have little impact. Not only do they lack the aphoristic force of the state- ment about cowardice, their intended meaning is actually thwarted by Aphranius who uses them as another means of increasing the procurator’s sense of guilt. Little wonder, then, that Pilate, overawed by the terrible implication of the state- ment about cowardice, fails at first to appreciate the signifi- cance of Ieshua’s very real concern that he be relieved of the burden of conscience. Only when he talks later with Matthew does he finally interpret the statement properly, realizing that this immense capacity for forgiveness and compassion offers an antidote to the ‘cruelty’ displayed by Ieshua’s disciple, by Aphranius, and even by Pilate himself. This insight is as cru- cial as it is brief, yet its implications are neither explored nor developed. Pilate’s interview with Matthew also gives rise to what is perhaps the greatest mystery attaching to Ieshua’s ideas. Learning that the disciple’s parchment had been found on his person, the procurator takes the opportunity to inspect it. After some difficulty, he manages to decipher three passages: “There is no death .. . yesterday we ate sweet early figs’; ‘We shall see the clear river of the water of life... mankind will look at the sun through clear crystal’; ‘greatest sin... cowar- dice’ (pp.744-5). While the final statement on cowardice is the one which will again catch the eye, it is the first two extracts that create the real interest here. Quite different in emphasis from the now familiar aphorism, they also invoke an important biblical subtext—the book of Revelation (see, Revelation 21:4, ‘and there shall be no more death, neither

Cowardice and other Sins 203 sorrow nor crying’; Revelation 22:1, ‘And he showed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the lamb’). These words serve to remind us, therefore, of the important transcendent element in Ieshua’s teaching. Conveyed initially in his confident promise of the ‘kingdom of truth’, in Matthew’s jottings it acquires the force of an apocalyptic prophecy. Each mention of the moral instruction on cowardice is thus accompanied by the suggestion of an alternative principle, which is no less important, but somehow always receives less emphasis. Aphranius’s report tells also of Ieshua’s forgive- ness; Pilate’s dream also offers the possibility of release from guilt; Matthew’s parchment contains the promise of another kingdom not of this world. But, in the context of the Jerusalem narrative the potential liberation offered by the spirit of mercy and transcendence is completely overshadowed by the ‘cruel’ spirit of guilt and vengeance which holds the residents of Yer- shalaim in its grasp. In bringing this story to Moscow, there- fore, Woland has performed only the first part of his role as ‘messenger’. In defiance both of the atheists, who have attempted to suppress it altogether, and of the Christians, who have enshrined a perversion of the truth, he has restored the proper record. Yet the very form of that record ensures that the transcendent aspect of Ieshua’s teaching remains hidden. Woland’s subsequent task, therefore, is to reveal this hidden meaning. As in the gnostic tradition, what is hidden is a higher truth concerning the universal process of which this world is only a part, and this can neither be imparted directly nor appreciated fully even by the most blessed of mortals. With this in mind, we may turn to the story of Woland’s deal- ings with the Master and Margarita, for it is they who are to be the chosen objects of his secret instruction.

BN PEERY Hien NOtr AND THE-HEROINE To insist, as I have done, that the story of the Master and Margarita be discussed in terms of the ‘recognition’ plot is to recommend a fundamental shift in the emphasis of most criti- cal writing about Bulgakov’s hero and heroine. It has been customary for critics to commend the Master and Margarita to the reader for those positive characteristics which mark their superiority over the ordinary citizens of Moscow: the Master for his artistic achievement in writing his novel about Pilate; and Margarita for her feat of courage in bringing about her lover’s salvation. As for Woland, his part in this story is generally viewed in terms of the conventional deus ex machina, his purpose being to ensure that the hero and heroine receive their just deserts. But this is only the immediately visible sur- face. Although the reunion of the Master and Margarita and the granting of their final ‘reward’ are the events which bring the novel to its natural conclusion and provide it with a readily discernible moral perspective, contact with Woland involves hero and heroine alike in something other than the mere righting of wrongs. The ‘foreign professor’ does even- tually ensure that justice is done, but he also engages the two main characters in a test of understanding which reveals their insufhciencies and enables them to attain a new awareness both of themselves and of the human condition. I shall begin with Margarita, for it is she who is first (and most obviously) tested in this way. MARGARITA Margarita’s experiences in Chapter 19 are magical in more ways than one. On the morning of her fateful encounter with Azazello, we are told, she had awoken from her sleep in an unusual state of excitement. The cause of her elation is a

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 225 dream which had given rise to the conviction that ‘today at last something would happen’. The passage continues as fol- lows: ‘I believe,’ Margarita whispered triumphantly, ‘I believe! Something will happen! It cannot fail to happen, because why, really, should I have been sent lifelong torment? I admit that I have told lies and practised deceit, living a secret life hidden from people, but one cannot be punished so cruelly for that’ (pp.633-4). Initially, this seems little more than a piece of wishful thinking on Margarita’s part, especially as this hushed statement of faith is the direct pro- duct of her having deliberately ‘warmed and nurtured [the premonition] in her soul so that it would not desert her’ (p.633). In the event, however, such doubts will prove unfounded. Something does happen; Margarita meets Azazello and the path to salvation is opened up before her. It needs to be stressed from the outset that the source of Margarita’s faith in the providential order is ultimately mys- terious. The inspiration for her dream vision, as for the Mas- ter’s novel (the connection is a crucial one), defies rational explanation. Equally important, and again mysterious, are the words in which she expresses her faith. The phrases ‘life- long torment’, ‘cruelty’ and ‘punishment’, which at first sight seem only a rather melodramatic expression of Margarita’ s personal preoccupations, take on a new meaning entirely when we observe her behaviour at Satan’s Ball and in the final scene with Pilate in Chapter 32. The same is true of the actual dream vision which prompted her statement of belief. In the context of Chapter 19, the image of the desolate wooden hut occupied by the Master is disturbing and ambiguous. But when (again in Chapter 32) we eventually learn of the Mas- ter’s reward and of his ‘final refuge’, Margarita’s dream acquires significance as a dim prefiguration of the precise manner in which providence is to operate. Like Pilate’s dream in Chapter 26, this one proves, in retrospect, to be truly pro- phetic. At the beginning, however, Margarita’s instinct is far in advance of her understanding. Indeed, her first reaction on meeting Azazello is so obtuse that she almost lets the golden opportunity slip through her fingers. Quite extraordinarily, Margarita fails to perceive any connection between the pro-

226 Interpretation mise conveyed in her dream and the meeting with Azazello. Even though she is eventually moved to follow his instruc- tions, she does so, as we remarked in Chapter 5, more out of desperation than faith: she accepts Azazello’s proposal because she feels that she has nothing to lose, not out of any sense of certainty about the workings of a benign providential order. Edward Ericson is right, therefore, when he writes that Margarita enters into her ‘pact’? with Woland because ‘she knows intuitively that crucial truth which Woland later enun- ciates and which Bulgakov gives primacy by placing it in the novel’s epigraph.’' But what he fails to indicate is how deeply this intuition lies buried within her being. When she rises to the bait offered by Azazello, Margarita (to paraphrase the famous line from Eliot’s Murder in the Cathedral) does the right deed for the wrong reason. In her own mind, she is convinced that she has entered into some sort of alliance with the powers of darkness; in reality, she has already made contact with the agents of providence. Her subsequent experiences are designed to disencumber her of this misconception and to bring her initial intuition to the point of conscious under- standing. In short, she will come to realize who Woland is. But, as we saw in Chapter 5, the task of recognition is always fraught with difficulty. The perverse logic of the novel requires that the individual penetrate Woland’s demonic disguise while being bombarded with evidence which serves to per- petuate the deception. Margarita’s assumption that Woland is the devil, although mistaken, is quite natural, and when, in the following three chapters, she is caught up in a series of events involving magic cream and broomstick rides over the Russian countryside it is little wonder that she assumes that she is on her way to a witches’ sabbath. A proper understand- ing of her experiences will come neither easily nor quickly, but the adventures in which Margarita engages on her way to her destination are a subtle preparation for what is to come. Even as she engages in those activities conventionally associated with the black arts, she is being transformed so that she might ' Ericson, p.32.

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine ooF be able to carry out the greater task that awaits her. The first sign of this covert preparation is an episode which accompa- nies the initial exercise of her supernatural powers. Margarita the Witch No sooner does Margarita assume witch’s form than she sets out to wreak vengeance against the man she holds primar- ily responsible for the Master’s ruin—the critic Latunsky. In so doing, she acts in obedience not only with her own wishes but also with those of the Master himself. We have already seen that when the Master had first heard from Bezdomny of Woland’s escapades, he had immediately yielded to thoughts of retribution against his enemies (p.550). But circumstances prevent Margarita from exacting vengeance in quite the way that she and her lover might have hoped. Latunsky is not at home when she calls, and she has to content herself with the lesser, yet equally primitive, pleasure of wrecking his apart- ment. There is, however, another chance circumstance which proves even more important. As she prepares to leave the site of her vandalism, Margarita sees a small child through the window of one of the other apartments in the block. Frigh- tened by the noise of the flying glass, the child has woken up to find himself alone. Margarita is moved by the child’s plight, and she enters the apartment to comfort him. This is how the scene concludes: ‘But where are you, aunty?’ ‘I’m not anywhere,’ Margarita answered, ‘I’m in your dream.’ ‘I thought so,’ the boy said. ‘You lic down,’ Margarita ordered, ‘put your hand under your check, and I'll be in your dream.’ ‘Do that, please,’ the boy agreed, putting his hand under his cheek. ‘T’ll tell you a story,’ Margarita said, and she placed her hot hand on his cropped head. ‘Once upon a time there was this aunty. She had no children, and no happiness either. First she cried for a long time, and then she became wicked .. . ’ Margarita fell silent and took her hand away. The boy was asleep. (p.656) Like the prophetic dream before it, this brief exchange has a significance which can be appreciated fully only when the

228 Interpretation entire scheme of the novel has unfolded. This is, in fact, another of the novel’s ‘corrective leads’. As with the earlier examples of this device (the two beheading scenes discussed in Chapter 5), the exercise of compassion plays a crucial part in this brief interlude: Margarita’s urge for vengeance has given way to a display of mercy. But on this occasion the unexpected event also performs a predictive function. When the novel has run its course, we come to realize that, to use Margarita’s own words, the time for ‘wickedness’ (the Russian adjective zloy suggests the notions of anger, viciousness and malevolence) has, like the time of ‘crying’, passed away. In leaving Moscow, Margarita will also leave behind her worldly sorrows and the retributive mentality to which they gave rise. And there is more. When we read the final pages of the novel, we under- stand that her behaviour with the boy was, as it were, a rehearsal for her final apotheosis—her appearance in the dream vision which visits the suffering poet, Ivan Bezdomny, in the Epilogue. On a first reading, Margarita’s encounter with the child, like the other ‘corrective leads’, will tend to be quickly forgot- ten as we become absorbed in the description of her broom- stick ride over the vast expanses of the Russian countryside. This is the part of the narrative which corresponds most closely to the demonological tradition of the witches’ sabbath. The details of Margarita’s experience bear a marked similar- ity to the flight of Renata, the heroine of Valery Bryusov’s famous novel Fiery Angel. But where Renata’s magical journey is followed by her participation in a sabbath of the sort des- cribed in Orlov’s History and other studies of devilry, Margar- ita has something altogether different in store for her when she finally dismounts from her broomstick on the bank of the deserted river. It is typical of Bulgakov that he does not defy the antici- pation of a sabbath immediately. When Margarita first stands beside the river, she detects ‘some small moving figures’ and hears the faint sound of ‘nagging jolly music’, details which temporarily keep the prospect of a sabbath alive (p.660). Her subsequent plunge into the river may be read, therefore—like Bezdomny’s earlier dip in the less pure and refreshing waters of the Moscow River—as a symbolic event, a ‘baptism’, which

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 229 marks her passage into a new state of awareness. The transi- tion is marked by the final denial of the expectations gener- ated by the preceding narrative. After a curious interlude, during which she has a conversation with a fat man who is also bathing in the river, Margarita finally proceeds to the source of the music she had heard, only to find that it is pro- duced by a group of ‘fat-faced frogs’ and that the moving figures are those of dancing rusalki (water-nymphs) (p.662). The effect is striking. Despite the attendance of naked witches and a supernatural being with goat’s legs, these traditional figures have been removed from the dark world of medieval demonology and transplanted into the magical realm of the fairy tale. This is no sabbath; Bulgakov actually tells us now in so many words that it is a triumphal ‘reception’ (p.662). And, rather than being journey’s end, it turns out to be only the half-way point in the longer journey to Satan’s Grand Ball. The reversal is complete—and not only in a metaphori- cal sense—for the last leg of this magical excursion involves a return to the place from which Margarita had only so recently departed. The change in the mode of transport has a similar significance. The broomstick (appropriate only for a flight to a sabbath) is now abandoned in favour of a magnificent black limousine chauffeured by a crow. The point is made quite explicitly in Margarita’s words to Korov’ev on her arrival back in Moscow: ‘An amazingly strange evening [.. . | J had expected everything, only not this!’ (p.665). What Bulgakov is doing here—to use the term favoured by the Russian Forma- list critics—is ‘laying bare’ his technique: Margarita’s com- ment is, in effect, an instruction to the reader to cast off the comfortable, yet false, sense of certainty which attached to the expectation of a sabbath, and to be prepared to observe the events at the forthcoming ball without such preconceptions. The need for the reader to adopt a new perspective on events is further signalled by the interchange between Mar- garita and the fat man she encounters at the river. Naked, except for a top hat balanced on the back of his head, the lat- ter greets Margarita with unrestrained delight: ‘What’s this? Is it she whom I see? Why, it’s you, Claudine, undespondent widow!’ (p.661). The fat man is, of course, quite mistaken, and Margarita feels no compunction about telling him so in

230 Interpretation the most unladylike language. Their exchange concludes as follows: ‘Oh,’ he exclaimed quietly, and shuddered, ‘I humbly beg your par- don, radiant Queen Margot! I didn’t recognize you. The cognac’s to blame, damn it!’ The fat man dropped on one knee, removed his top hat with a flourish and made a bow, mumbling some nonsense in a mixture of Russian and French about the bloody wedding of his friend Gues- sard in Paris, about cognac, and how he was cast down by his sad mistake. (p.661) As it stands, this is one of Bulgakov’s more enigmatic scenes. It is puzzling in two ways, for neither the mistaken identifi- cation of Margarita as the widow Claudine nor the sub- sequent (and apparently correct) recognition that she is Queen Margot seems to make much sense. The matter is com- plicated still further when one remembers that, just a few pages earlier, Natasha had referred to her former mistress as ‘my French queen’ (p.658). There are, however, enough details here to uncover at least one part of this pattern of allusions, and Bulgakov makes things easier still in the follow- ing chapter by including further information. During the preparations for the ball, Korov’ev replies to Margarita’s enquiry about her ‘royal blood’ by telling her that she is the ‘great-great-great-great-granddaughter of a ‘certain French queen of the sixteenth century’ (p.668). The reference is to Marguerite de Valois (1553-1615), popularly known as ‘la reine Margot’, whose marriage to Henri de Navarre (later Henri IV) prompted the infamous St Bartholomew’s Day massacre.” Yet, as is so often the case in The Master and Mar- garita, the mere identification of the allusion explains rather less than we might wish, for it is not immediately clear pre- cisely where the connection between the historical Marguerite and the fictional Margarita may lie. The allusion remains opaque in this respect until Margarita’ s subsequent behaviour at the ball has been described. Only then can it be seen, as one critic has remarked, that the ‘courage and compassion’ dis- * Milne, The Master and Margarita, p.13. Yanovskaya (p.251) notes that Bulgakov looked up the details of Marguerite de Navarre in the Brockhaus—Efron encyclopedia.

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 231 played by Marguerite de Valois during the massacre prefi- gures Margarita’s achievement at Satan’s Ball.3 At Apartment No.50 The preparation of Margarita for the Grand Ball begins long before her final arrival in Moscow, involving her in a course of instruction which relies on hints and insinuations rather than direct enlightenment. Caught between her con- ventional demonological expectations and the contradictory evidence of her actual experiences, Margarita arrives at the mysteriously darkened apartment No.50 in a state of much greater uncertainty than when she had embarked on her magical journey. But although she now has less idea of what might await her in the immediate future, this very lack of con- fidence ensures that she will now have an openness and flex- ibility of mind which will enable her progress to higher wisdom. Margarita is greeted on her arrival at the apartment by Korov’ev, to whom has been entrusted the task of preparing the ‘queen’ both mentally and physically for her responsi- bilities as hostess at the ball. But although he proves both dili- gent and punctilious in the pursuit of his duty, Korov’ev is by no means as open with Margarita as he likes to pretend. His immediate disclaimer (‘We are the enemies of all innuendo and mystery —p.667) deserves to be treated with the utmost scepticism. For the fact is that his various instructions and explanations are anything but explicit. He does, it is true, tell Margarita that she has been called upon to take the part of Woland’s ‘queen’ at the ‘spring ball of the full moon, or the ball of the one hundred kings’ (p.667). And he goes on to pro- vide a number of invaluable details about the ball, telling Margarita both of the ‘executioners’ who will kiss her knee (p.665), and of the expected attendance of ‘persons, the capacity of whose power, in their own day, was extremely great’ (p.667). Yet, like the final physical preparations—the 3 As Milne (ibid.) points out, Bulgakov’s inspiration here may have been more literary than historical, the source being Dumas’s novel La Reine Margot. Dumas has always been immensely popular with the Russians. It is interesting to note that Mak- sim Gorky also alludes to Dumas’s heroine as an example of ideal femininity in My Universities.

232 Interpretation baths in blood and rose oil, and so on—this information pro- vides no substantial insight into the real nature of the ordeal that lies ahead. Nor does it offer a proper explanation of why Margarita has been chosen for this most arduous of assign- ments. The indeterminacy of Korov’ev’s remarks makes for only a part of the difficulty in this scene. Equally disturbing, in their own way, are the several distractions which divert Margari- ta’s attention away from the serious business at hand— Behemoth’s unavailing attempts to cheat Woland at chess; the cat’s later absurd explanation of his improbable appearance; the chess pieces which come miraculously to life in the manner of Lewis Carroll’s Looking Glass characters; and even Korov’ev’s own humorous, yet utterly irrelevant, story of the recent attempt by a Moscow citizen to obtain more commo- dious accommodation by unorthodox means. This is the same sort of exuberant mystification as had abounded in the Mos- cow episodes of Part I, and it plays the same diversionary role—hence, Woland’s recommendation to the cat that he ‘leave those cheap tricks for the Variety’ (p.670). But in the midst of all this innocent horseplay there is one episode, which, although it seems just as irrelevant, stands out by virtue of its incongruity. Significantly, it is the only episode in this chapter in which Woland himself plays a central part, and this is the demonstration of the magical properties of the unusual globe that stands on his bed. This globe permits the beholder to observe events as they occur at any place on earth. The particular scene that Margarita is given to observe is one of horrifying violence. It is wartime, and a small cottage is destroyed in an explosion which also kills the woman and the child who were its occupants. The description concludes with the following exchange: “That’s all,’ said Woland with a smile, ‘He was too young to have sinned. Abadonna’s work is impeccable.’ ‘I wouldn’t want to be on the opposite side to that Abadonna,’ said Margarita, ‘Whose side is he on?’ “The more I talk to you,’ Woland responded amiably, ‘the more I am convinced that you are very intelligent. I shall reassure you. He is impartial in the extreme and sympathizes equally with both of the warring sides.’ (p.675)

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 293 The ‘Abadonna’ to whom Woland refers is presumably the Abaddon of the Book of Revelation 9:11, the ‘angel of the bot- tomless pit’, yet the recognition of this allusion adds little, if anything, to a real appreciation of what Woland is up to here. But one thing, at least, is clear: the incident that Margarita witnesses provides a shocking example of the senseless suffer- ing of the innocent in time of war. The question remains, however, why Woland should have chosen such a scene to demonstrate the operation of his globe. And why, also, does he conduct this demonstration with such cruel cynicism? His choice of words (‘That is all’) and the smile with which he accompanies them show us a side of his character that we have not witnessed before. The most obvious explanation of this seemingly uncharacteristic behav- iour 1s that Woland is not so much expressing his true senti- ments as engaging in a provocation designed to draw Margarita out. ‘He is studying me,’ Margarita had thought when first she saw the globe (p.669). Again her intuition serves her more truly than she appreciates. Woland is indeed ‘studying’ Margarita, and his every move in this scene dis- plays his cruel determination to test her mettle. The demon- stration, together with the callous commentary, allows him to discover both the strength of Margarita’s compassion and her ability to face up even to the most horrifying displays of evil. Encouraged by her response to this first experiment, Woland proceeds with one further test: Margarita is introduced to the awesome figure of Abadonna in person, a challenge to which she again proves equal. Woland is evidently heartened both by Margarita’s display of courage, and by the fervour of her humane response, yet there is one aspect of his behaviour in this scene which requires further comment. Does Woland really imagine that he is offering ‘reassurance’ to Margarita when he tells her that Abadonna is ‘impartial in the extreme’? Once again, one sus- pects a provocation on his part, and this suspicion is rein- forced when Margarita receives her last instruction from Korov’ev. Here too ‘impartiality’ features prominently. ‘Amongst the guests there will be various sorts,’ Margarita is told, ‘but you must show no favour, Queen Margot, to any of them’ (p.677). This is a most important injunction, to which

234 Interpretation we will return in the discussion of the aftermath of the ball. For the present, it is sufficient to record the fact that Woland’s paradoxical behaviour immediately before the main proceed- ings renders this instruction problematical. If Margarita is really expected to show no favours at the ball, why does he present her beforehand with such a terrifying representative of impartiality as Abadonna? Satan’s Grand Ball It is difficult to overestimate the importance of Satan’s Ball, for it is an episode which has a crucial bearing both on the story of the Master and Margarita and on the overall philoso- phic design of the novel. The ball, the reader has been led to believe, is the real reason for Woland’s visitation, and we read this chapter, therefore, in the expectation that here at last we shall be given to understand his purpose. And so we are. But, as is always the case in his depiction of Woland, Bulgakov seems intent upon veiling his meaning at precisely those points in his narrative where it is being unveiled. The key to this paradox lies once again in the opposition of form and function: the scene in which Woland reveals his true mission is also the one in which he appears to be most recognizably ‘demonic’. There is no limit to Bulgakov’s playfulness when Woland is around. Satan’s Ball fulfils our ‘demonic’ expectations of Woland in several ways. First of all, there is the very title of the chapter, which remains one of the very few places in the ‘authorial’ narrative where Woland is actually named as Satan. This direct identification augments a statement from the previous chapter, when Margarita had first caught sight of Woland: ‘Her eyes were drawn to the bed, on which sat he whom only so recently poor Ivan had attempted to con- vince at Patriarchs’ that the devil did not exist. This very non-existent one was sitting on the bed’ (p.669). The same chapter had also been distinguished by a resurgence of the linguistic clichés referring to the devil. Korov’ev, for example, is recommended to us as ‘the magician, sorcerer, interpreter, or the devil knows who, in actual fact’ (p.665). But this latter detail should immediately make us wary, for such tricks of language are always associated with the false

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 235 identification of Woland (see, especially, Chapters 1 and 1Q). The events of the ball also rely heavily on traditional demo- nological motifs, of which the baths in blood, the Bacchana- lian revels, and the drinking of blood from skulls are only the most obvious examples. Certain details can be traced specifi- cally to the sources that Bulgakov is known to have consulted during his work on the novel. Chudakova has pointed out that the idea of having not just witches, but representatives of all ranks and classes present at the ball is related to a passage from the Brockhaus—Efron encyclopaedia which Bulgakov had copied into a notebook.* The exotic details, on the other hand—the orchestra of monkeys, the parrots, and so on— were probably inspired by the second chapter of Part IV of Orlov’s History. Entitled “‘Demonism in India’, this was based on the work of the Frenchman Bataille and provided a colour- ful account of devil worship in Calcutta and Ceylon. But it is the expectation that Satan’s Ball is to be a witches’ sabbath that remains the most prominent demonological element in this chapter. This, as we have seen, is what Mar- garita has been preparing herself for all along, and Bulgakov ensures that this preconception is kept alive by playing up the connection with Goethe’s Faust. During his conversation with Margarita prior to the ball, Woland had complained of his rheumatism, the onset of which he ascribes to an event on the Brocken Hills in 1571 (p.674). The date is probably a red her- ring, yet the location is a transparent allusion to the first of Goethe’s famous Walpurgisnacht scenes. It is no surprise, then, that a group of ‘Brocken idlers’ should number amongst the guests at the ball itself (p.686). The Faustian subtext is further invoked by the mention of the poodle pendant that Margarita has to wear throughout the proceedings. And, perhaps most significantly of all, Margarita’s expectation (in Chapter 24) of a favour from Woland in return for her services recalls the fol- lowing passage from Goethe: ‘Und kann ich dir was zu Gefal- len tun,/ So darfst du mirs nur auf Walpurgis sagen’ (lines 2589-90). | + Chudakova, ‘Arkhiv ...’, pp.72 f.

236 Interpretation In short, these Faustian motifs combine with the other tra- ditional details to create a strong impression that at Satan’s Ball we are likely to witness a witches’ sabbath of a standard type. But, no matter how powerful this impression may be, the actual events at the ball suggest that such notions must be abandoned entirely if their real meaning is to be penetrated. Despite the proliferation of demonological elements, it is diffh- cult, even on a first reading, to resist the conclusion that Satan’s Ball is concerned with something quite different from simple devil-worship. This same conclusion is suggested in other ways. Despite the emphasis on nakedness, there is no explicit mention here either of the sexual excesses or of the bestiality that are the most notorious features of witches’ sab- baths. And, even though the ball does conclude with a blood sacrifice, there is nothing in this to suggest a deliberate tra- vesty of Christian ritual. It is also quite evident that neither of the two main sequences that make up Satan’s Ball—the procession of the damned, and the execution of Berlioz and Baron Meigel— have any precise counterpart in the activities traditionally associated with sabbaths. They do, however, bear a striking resemblance to two extremely well-known elements of religious mythology. The procession of the damned recalls similar pas- sages in such religious works as the Revelation of St Peter, and more particularly, the most celebrated of all literary versions of this myth—the opening cantos of Dante’s Jnferno.° If Mar- garita is cast here in the role of Dante, then Korov’ev is her ‘Virgil’, introducing her to the damned and telling her their individual stories. The execution of Berlioz and Meigel, on the other hand, evokes another aspect of the same apocalyptic tra- dition—the last judgement of sinners. By embedding these religious motifs within a context which first suggests a most extreme form of anti-religious activity, Bulgakov achieves a reversal which is both radical and typical. The story of Frieda, it has also been suggested, bears a certain resemblance to the famous story of Francesca da Rimini (Prikhod’ko, p.53).

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 257 ‘demonic’ is only a mask for something which is, in essence, the very antithesis of diablery. Let us consider the events of the ball in more detail. The procession of the damned which passes before Margarita dur- ing the first part of the proceedings seems, on the face of it, to pose few problems of interpretation. Like its counterpart in Dante, this scene furnishes a catalogue of human sinfulness and illustrates its dire-consequences for the individual. Bul- gakov’s procession includes both notorious historical figures, like Caligula, Messalina and Malyuta Skuratov, and others less well known and even unnamed. Again following Dante’s example, Bulgakov chooses to tell some of the stories in detail. Margarita’s role in this scene also seems relatively uncompli- cated. She is required to confront not only the horror, but also the sheer banality of evil—the latter being exemplified in the account of the Moscow dressmaker who had holes drilled in the walls of her customers’ fitting-rooms to accommodate the interests of male voyeurs. Margarita is obliged to observe all this, we must remember, without showing any outward sign of complaint or favour. This, it seems, is the nature of her test, and she passes it only at the expense of considerable physical suffering. By the end of her ordeal, she experiences an almost unbearable pain in her knee, while the poodle pendant around her neck has grown heavier by the minute. Important though all this is, it is only one part of the story, and (notably) that part in which Woland himself plays no direct part. When he does eventually make his belated appearance at the ball, the mood changes dramatically. Both the procession of the damned and the drunken revelry which followed it are forgotten as the ‘host’ lays on a brief but edify- ing moral fable. The shift of perspective is marked by one small detail which again draws attention to the denial of our expectations: Woland enters dressed in the same shabby clothes that he had worn during the preparations. Woland’s dramatic demonstration comprises two distinct, yet related parts. The first concerns the unfortunate Berlioz. As Woland comes into the banquet chamber in the company of Azazello, Abadonna, and the rest, the severed head of Ber- lioz is brought in on a platter. This is the speech that Woland addresses to the head:

238 Interpretation ‘Everything has come true hasn’t it? [ . . . ] Your head has been cut off by a woman, the meeting didn’t take place, and I am living in your apartment. This is fact. And a fact is the most stubborn thing in the world. But now we are interested in what follows, not in facts that have already occurred. You were always an advocate of the theory that once the head is cut off the life of a human being ceases, that he is transformed into ashes and passes into non-being. I am pleased to inform you, in the presence of my guests—even though they serve to prove a very different theory—that your theory is both solid and witty. In any case, all theories are of the same worth. There is even one which maintains that to each will be given accord- ing to his faith. May that be so! You are passing into non-being, and I shall be glad to drink to being from the vessel into which you are transformed.’ (p.689) I have quoted this passage at length because it contains one of the statements which has often been taken to express a key point in the entire philosophy of The Master and Margarita—‘to each will be given according to his faith’. Is one correct in attributing such significance to these words? Certainly, this is one of the very few places in the novel where Woland—his habitual sarcasm notwithstanding—appears to speak plainly and without ambiguity. His actions seem similarly uncompli- cated. By despatching Berlioz into the state of ‘non-being’, he reminds us of the materialist conceit (of which the erstwhile editor is the foremost representative), and demonstrates the operation of a simple, though cruel, moral code. Berlioz’s hour of judgement is nigh, and he is now made finally to answer for his presumptuousness. ‘The second part of Woland’s demonstration is less clear immediately. This is due largely to the fact that his new ‘vic- tim’, Baron Meigel, has not been encountered previously in the story. Whether this was the product of design or necessity we will probably never know, although the reference to Mar- garita knowing the baron by sight (p.690) might suggest that Bulgakov was attempting to tie up what is one of the novel’s most glaring loose ends. Whatever the case, the meaning of this scene depends on the rather clumsy device of having Woland sketch in the salient details of Meigel’s background. The baron, we are informed, serves in the Entertainment Commission, where he has responsibility for acquainting

Enter the Hero... and the Heroine 239 foreign visitors with the sights of the Soviet capital, a euphem- istic description which is exposed by Woland’s subsequent explanation that Meigel is, in other words, ‘an informer and a spy’ (p.690). No sooner has this been said than Meigel, like Berlioz before him, receives his summary punishment. Together, these two deaths facilitate the final celebration sig- nalled by Woland’s toast to ‘being’: the blood shed as a result of Meigel’s execution’ fills the vessel provided by Berlioz’s skull. Bulgakov adds to the momentousness of these events by the inclusion of two typically theatrical gestures, both of which accompany the violent death of Meigel. The first is when Aba- donna removes his dark glasses, thus belatedly fulfilling Mar- garita’s earlier request (pp.675—6). Then, as he prepares to propose the toast, Woland is suddenly and miraculously transformed: “Then a metamorphosis occurred. The patched shirt and worn-out slippers disappeared. Woland appeared in a black chlamys with a steel sword at his hip’ (p.691). The transformation is extraordinarily impressive, all the more so when we subsequently perceive that it foreshadows his final metamorphosis during the flight to the Master’s ‘eternal refuge’. On a second reading, therefore, it can be appreciated that this is the first time that we see Woland, albeit briefly and imperfectly, in his ‘real’ form. Bulgakov’s choice of metamorphosis here, as elsewhere in the novel, as the central dramatic event is both a reminder of the ‘recognition’ plot at the heart of The Master and Marganta and a visual image which prompts the movement of the mind required of the reader. Once Woland is perceived in his new form (that is, without the kind of distortion imposed by the ‘demonological’ perspective) his ‘grand ball’ yields an allegor- ical meaning which is relatively uncomplicated. In Berlioz and Meigel Woland can be said to have shown us two categor- ies of men who stand doomed to perdition. Berlioz is des- patched into non-being for having embraced a world-view which takes as its premise the denial of a supernatural dimen- sion of existence; there can be no grace for those who will not admit even the possibility of the realm in which that grace is to be experienced. The fate of Meigel, on the other hand, pres- ents a terrible example to those who would pursue a course of

240 Interpretation consciously immoral behaviour. These two deaths point not simply to the existence of a transcendent order but also to its ultimate justice. According to this reading, Satan’s Ball belongs not to any ‘demonological’ tradition but to the apocalyptic tradition. Despite the superficial trappings, this is no witches’ sabbath; it is rather a version of the last judgement of sinners, in which the two principal elements—the scene of judgement, and the exposure of the sins of the damned—are simply reversed. True to the apocalyptic tradition, the notion of justice conveyed here is based firmly on the law of retribution. After the Ball It remains to be asked what significance all this has for Margarita. That Satan’s Ball is the occasion on which she, like the reader, is obliged to confront the discrepancy between her preconceived notions about Woland and his real nature has already been seen. But can we safely assume that the Woland who demonstrates the law of retribution at the end of Chapter 23 is the ‘real’ Woland? Many critics have made such an assumption, which has led directly to the conclusion that Woland’s behaviour at the ball represents an allegorical state- ment of one of the novel’s central philosophical propositions. But to do this is to remove the episode from the context in which it occurs. Viewed within that context—the testing of Margarita—Woland’s ‘demonstration’ takes on an entirely different significance. Apart from the charge of acontextuality, the argument men- tioned above lays itself open to several other important objec- tions. The actual form of words used by Woland during his ‘demonstration’ suggests the need for certain caution. Here, as on other occasions, Woland displays an almost legalistic pre- cision in his choice of expression. Crucial in this respect is his statement that ‘all theories are of the same worth. There is even one which maintains that to each will be given according to his faith’ (p.689). If one raises Woland’s ‘demonstration’ to the level of an absolute moral category—as some critics have done—one does so against Woland’s own insistence that the particular ‘theory’ which it illustrates, like any other, has only a relative value. Woland’s words, then, contain a sort of loop-

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 241 hole, opening up the possibility of a certain deviousness on his part, without providing immediate confirmation that such is his purpose. But this suspicion rapidly hardens into a convic- tion as the events following the ball are described in Chapter 24. These developments cast an entirely different light upon the ball as a whole and upon the meaning of Woland’s ‘dem- onstration’ in particular. In contrast to the portentousness of the ball, Chapter 24 marks a return to the colloquial style and seemingly incon- sequential narrative of Chapter 22. Once more we are treated to scenes of innocent horseplay and sheer nonsense, in which Behemoth features prominently, making up ludicrous stories about himself, and participating in that hilarious shooting competition with Azazello. Although self-evidently insignifi- cant in their own right, these distractions again have an important part to play in the proceedings. Precisely because they are distractions, they will tend to divert Margarita’s attention during what is, in fact, the third and final stage of her test. What, exactly, is the nature of the test to which Margarita is subjected in Chapter 24? To begin with, it is necessary to recognize the distinction made earlier between the overt and the covert levels of testing. The overt test is quite easily des- cribed. Margarita is deemed to have fulfilled her part of the bargain. She has played hostess at the ball as instructed, thereby deserving the expected reward. It turns out, however, that there is a further, unspoken condition of her agreement with Azazello, which is that she must not be the one to raise the matter of her reward with Woland. Margarita’s instinct is unerring, as always; even though no mention of the reward has been made, she prepares to leave the fateful apartment. It is this final gesture that prompts the expected dénouement. Woland calls Margarita back, admits quite openly ‘We were testing you’ (p.697), praises her for being too proud to beg, and finally asks her to name her request. What follows has often been the subject of discussion, but for the sake of clarity, the details need to be repeated. In reply to Woland’s inquiry, Margarita states her wish that Frieda, a guest at the ball whose story had moved her deeply, be spared further suffering: ‘I want them to stop giving Frieda the ker-

242 Interpretation chief she used to suffocate her child’ (p.698). That Margarita should make this request rather than ask for the return of the Master comes as a major surprise. After all, the desire to be reunited with her lover had been her sole reason for embark- ing on her adventure in the first place. Whereas the reader is merely surprised by this development (especially as the title of the chapter had promised the Master’s return), Woland is apparently also most displeased by it, remarking caustically that he will need to seal his quarters against the ‘mercy’ which threatens to find its way through the gaps like a draught (pp.698-g). But, his disapproval notwithstanding, Woland is incapable of preventing the request from being fulfilled. Acts of mercy, he explains, fall outside the jurisdiction of his ‘department’, for which reason also (and by a most fortunate chance for Margarita) it does not count as the wish to which she is entitled. Quite unexpectedly presented with a second opportunity of having a wish granted, Margarita wastes no time in asking for the return of the Master, which Woland immediately brings about. So much for the overt testing of Margarita and the apparent logic of the narrative in the opening section of Chapter 24. There are, however, a number of fundamental difficulties which suggest the need to look more carefully at this chain of events. The first concerns Margarita’s eligibility for her reward. Early in Chapter 24, Korov’ev takes great pains to indicate how splendidly Margarita had performed her duties at the ball, insisting on the good impression she had made upon all the guests (p.692). But in singing Margarita’s praises, Korov’evy omits to mention something far more serious—that Margarita had actually failed to fulfil the one specific instruction that had been given to her prior to the ball. She had been told that she should ‘show no favour’ in her behaviour towards any of Woland’s ‘guests’ (p.677). But show favour she did, albeit only once. When confronted by Frieda she proved incapable of maintaining the mask of impartiality, despite the efforts at the time of both Behemoth and Korov’ev himself to remind her of her ‘duty’ (p.684). There can be no doubt about it; according to the terms of her agreement, Mar- garita has failed, yet both Korov’ev and Woland overlook this fact. Why?

Enter the Hero. . . and the Heroine 243 Before attending directly to this question, let us consider another curious feature of the behaviour of Woland and his entourage in Chapter 24. As Azazello prepares to display his remarkable prowess as a marksman, he says boastfully: ‘It’s one thing to hit the critic Latunsky’s window with a hammer, and another thing altogether to hit him in the heart’ (p.694). The apparent casualness of this remark is a transparent deception, as also is Woland’s ‘innocent’ request that Margar- ita explain who this Latunsky might be. Once again, then, there is a puzzle. Why is Margarita being reminded of her recent attack on Latunsky’s apartment at such a seemingly inappropriate moment? By disturbing the surface logic of events, these two difficul- ties lead directly to the covert level of Margarita’s test. Let us take the second case first, for here the purpose of the test is most readily seen. By reminding Margarita of Latunsky, Woland and his assistants seek to rekindle the primitive desire to avenge the Master’s suffering which had found expression in her violent activities when first she had been transformed into a witch. Margarita’s reaction—both to the mention of Latunsky’s name and to the eager suggestion by Azazello and Behemoth that they complete the task of destruction in her stead—shows how far she has progressed. ‘ “‘No!”’ Margarita exclaimed, “‘No, I beg you, messire, that will not be necess- ary’ (p.695). She has risen above the narrow retributive urge, and this is evidently what Woland had wanted to find out. But what is the connection between ¢his test and the pro- ceedings at Satan’s Ball? Ostensibly there is none. If we accept that the main purpose of the ball was to test Margari- ta’s fortitude, then it is most difficult to explain why she should be subjected to this new trial. But what if the ball really had another purpose? At this point we may return to the residual difficulty surrounding Woland’s decision to overlook Margarita’s failure at the ball and to reward her regardless. There are two possibilities. Either Woland has, quite arbi- trarily and inexplicably, changed the terms of their agree- ment, or else the terms of their agreement were never what they had seemed to be in the first place. This would mean that the original condition (‘you must show no favour’) was a

244 Interpretation deliberate deception, intended to mask the true nature of the test to come. Of these two hypotheses, the latter recommends itself for a number of reasons. To begin with, it helps to explain Woland’s odd behaviour at the moment when Korov’ev gave Margarita the crucial instruction. As we saw in the discussion of Chapter 22, Woland simultaneously recommended an absolute impartiality while stimulating Margarita’s natural compassion. The paradox would be resolved, however, if one were to accept that the overt instruction that Margarita restrain her compassionate urge was, in reality, a covert instruction to do just the opposite. This would mean that, by showing favour to Frieda at the ball, Margarita would actually have passed the test. And it would also explain Woland’s insistence on rewarding her afterwards, despite her ostensible failure. When viewed from this perspective certain aspects of the ball acquire a new prominence. The fact that Frieda is so obviously out of place amongst the notorious evil-doers and conscienceless criminals who are presented to Margarita can also be seen as part of the covert test. By having Frieda appear in this company, it is as if she is being ‘smuggled past’ Margarita—hence also the desperate attempts by Behemoth and Korov’ev to distract her once it is clear that she has not fallen for the ruse. Equally interesting is Margarita’s response to the execution of Baron Meigel. The execution is an act of ugly and explicit violence and, as such, it is highly reminiscent of an earlier ‘execution’—the decapitation of Bengalsky in Chapter 12. Bengalsky’s ‘execution’, it will be remembered, had generated a tension between two opposite imperatives— the urge to punish, and disgust at the physical violence involved in the act of punishment. The same tension is present in the case of Meigel. In Chapter 24, the only thing that Margarita has to say of this ‘punishment’ is that she had been shocked and upset by it (p.693). Everything points once more to the remarkable sureness of Margarita’s instincts. Her every response speaks of her subli- minal awareness of the real test that she has to undergo: she ignores her explicit instructions and shows favour to Frieda at the ball; she sees Meigel’s death not as an example of just

Enter the Hero. . . and the Heroine 245 retribution but as an act of distressing violence; and, in refus- ing to endorse the further ‘punishment’ of Latunsky she impli- citly rejects vengeance as a principle for justice. The moment when she finally releases Frieda from her suffering is, there- fore, the supreme mark of her victory, the apotheosis of the spirit of compassion, which counters the force of Woland’s earlier ‘demonstration’ in kind. This final point raises a most important question about Woland. Does he want Margarita to succeed or fail? Inter- preted literally, his remarks to Margarita when she insists on the reprieve of Frieda would suggest the latter. Yet it is quite possible that his apparent disapproval of her mercy is only the last in a series of devious provocations. This matter need con- cern us no further for the present, however. Whether as adver- sary or ally, Woland’s role as the agent of Margarita’s higher destiny is beyond question. He has brought her to the point where she has at last rediscovered her ‘royal blood’, earning the release of the Master by the sheer strength of her moral example. It should be noted, in conclusion, that the interpretation of Margarita’s act of mercy presented here runs counter to the tendency of some critics to diminish the value of her sacrifice. Milne, for example, finds in this only a ‘dim figural reflection of Ieshua’s love for mankind’.° Haber makes a similar obser- vation when she writes, in a different context, that Margarita ‘substitute[s] a narrower love of one man for Ieshua’s all- embracing love’.’ The comparison with leshua is, of course, necessarily invidious, and to stress Margarita’s limitations in this way is to miss the real point. However far she may stand from the ideal represented by Ieshua, Margarita has neverthe- less taken a major step in the right direction. Her display of mercy towards Frieda demonstrates the full extent of the transformation she has undergone. Margarita performs her act of deliverance in the absolute conviction that, in so doing, she will automatically deprive herself of the one chance of her own personal happiness. It is an act of the purest altruism and, as such, the plainest evidence that she has now trans- © Milne, The Master and Margarita, p.12. 7 Haber, pp.4or f.

246 Interpretation cended her ‘narrower love of one man’ to at least approach the ideal embodied in Ieshua. Bulgakov himself seems to encour- age this view by means of a small, yet memorable detail. When Frieda was released from her suffering she fell to the ground and ‘spread herself cross-like before Margarita’ (p.700). In her dealings with Woland, Margarita has, then, passed through the various phases of understanding identified earlier in the discussion of the ‘recognition’ plot. In her story, the ‘mundane’, the ‘demonological’ and the ‘retributive’ explana- tions of Woland’s purpose mark the successive stages of her progress to true enlightenment, which comes when she herself becomes the medium through which Woland’s message is conveyed. By means of paradox and provocation Woland enables her to demonstrate the sublime principle of mercy which he, like Ieshua before him, brings as a gift to an imper- fect world. Once Margarita has enacted the drama of redemp- tion, the Master is retrieved from Stravinsky’s clinic and her main task is over. She now moves aside for the Master to occupy stage centre. THE MASTER The testing of Margarita, which dominates the opening sec- tions of Part II, is both complex and explicit. The testing of the Master is, by contrast, rather less explicit, although equally complex and important. His meeting with Woland involves him both in the drama of ‘recognition’ (as we saw in Chapter 5) and in a similar expansion of his wisdom. But before considering this process in detail, it is necessary to deal with the Master’s ‘prehistory’ and to review some of the more common views of his character and fate. Three ‘Romantic’ Views The tendency amongst both Western writers and the liberal critics within the Soviet Union to discern in the Master a por- trait of the ideal artist has been remarked upon more than once in this study. This trend has manifested itself in three dif- ferent views of the Master, each of which may be termed ‘romantic’ inasmuch as they dwell exclusively upon the posi- tive attributes of Bulgakov’s hero. The first of these, which we

Enter the Hero. . . and the Heroine 247 might call the ‘persecuted genius’ view, has already been treated at some length in Chapter 3 and requires no further elaboration here. The Master, so this argument runs, is the only authentic artist in a world where true artistic values have no place and where fame and fortune are guaranteed only to those who are prepared to place their talents, however meagre, at the service of the state. As for the real writer, all he can expect is calumny and vilification at the hands of the press, and duplicity from his erstwhile friends. The Master, in short, is presented as the innocent victim of a cruel and oppressive regime, a conclusion which makes this the most unashamedly political reading of his story. The other two ‘romantic’ conceptions of Bulgakov’s hero dwell, by contrast, not upon the conflict between the artist and society, but upon the nature of art itself, of which they offer different, and mutually exclusive, explanations. Both arguments take as their premise the postulate that the Mas- ter’s novel is, ipso facto, a work of true genius. What is at issue is the type of inspiration that produced it. One answer is that it is the work of a ‘sublime liar’.* This opinion, which informs a great many early discussions of the novel, has more recently found its fullest and most coherent expression in an article by W. J. Leatherbarrow.? The Master and Margarita, in Leather- barrow’s view, is above all an ‘eloquent plea for a return to quixotic romanticism’, this latter being defined as a ‘restless- ness born of dissatisfaction and a desire somehow to refashion the life that has caused the dissatisfaction’.'®° The two rep- resentatives of this ‘romantic dissatisfaction’, the same critic continues, are Ieshua and the Master, both of whom are ‘dedi- cated to the idea that reality should be other than it is’."’ The Master’s novel is viewed, accordingly, as the embodiment of his protest against the real world in which he finds himself, a blow in defence of the freedom of creative imagination. This objection finds oblique expression in the work of Gas- parov, a critic who has also promoted the idea of the Master as ‘inspired liar’, but who comes to a radically different con- clusion about Bulgakov’s purpose. In his opinion, therefore, the Master, by virtue of his very occupa- tion as a novelist, emerges as Ieshua’s ‘antagonist’.'* But Gas- parov’s argument, even though it works against the interpretation of the Master’s endeavour promoted by Leath- erbarrow and others, nevertheless founders against the same rock. For both critics equate the Master’s novel with Matthew Levi’s parchment, despite the strong evidence which points to the opposite conclusion. Although Ieshua objected to what Matthew had written, this was not because it was ‘literature’, but because it was a falsification of the facts. The prime virtue of the Master’s novel, by contrast, is that, even through the mists of twenty centuries, he has managed somehow to divine the very truth that Matthew, the contemporary witness, so obviously failed to record. The nature of the Master’s achieve- ment, conveyed in the final text by his exclamation ‘I guessed it all!’ (p.550), was actually spelled out in so many words in a passage from an earlier redaction which was subsequently deleted: ‘ “Listen to me, Master,” said Woland, “In your Tbidk 38: 't Gasparov, pp.244 f.

Everything was exactly as you have told it’’.’'5 From this it follows that the Master’s novel is emblematic of a different, though equally ‘romantic’ view of art. The true work of art, Bulgakov implies, is the product not of the free creative imagination, but of mysterious intuition. This is a fundamentally religious conception, and it accords, rather intriguingly, with the account of the creative individual pro- vided in the writings of C. G. Jung. ‘Jung looked upon himself, and other creative people’, writes Anthony Storr, ‘as being vessels through which superior or new insights were made manifest. This superior knowledge or wisdom Jung referred to at various times as the ‘“‘collective unconscious’? and as “God’’.’'° These comments are of particular interest not simply because they offer such an apt description of the Mas- ter’s inspiration, but also because Jung’s now notorious idea of the ‘collective unconscious’ might be seen to have found fic- tional expression in Bulgakov’s presentation of the Jerusalem narrative as a sort of primordial truth accessible to a number of individuals. This third ‘romantic’ view of the Master as the ‘vessel of superior knowledge’ nowadays enjoys the support, either implicit or explicit, of the majority of the novel’s commenta- tors. But although it provides the most satisfactory account of Bulgakov’s broad conception, it has, no less than the other ‘romantic’ readings, contributed to the sort of critical myopia mentioned above. At its most extreme, this inclination to idea- lize the Master has resulted in statements like the following: ‘Finally, everything about everyone in M. Bulgakov’s book is known to the man who has written the novel [i.e. the Master]: it is to him that both the individual heroes and their interrela- tionships are known and subservient.’'’ There is no need to demonstrate that this exaggerates the Master’s powers and misrepresents his achievement, but it should be noted that such extraordinary claims have been far more common than one might expect. 250 Interpretation there has often been a reluctance to examine the Master’s faults and weaknesses. The Master is not perfect; nor is his novel. It is to these imperfections that we must now turn our attention. Against the ‘Romantic’ View There is one aspect of Bulgakov’s literary sensibility which is at once the most typical, and yet perhaps the most difficult to grasp; this is his disarming ability to mock the very things he holds most dear. This ability is nowhere more evident in The Master and Margarita than in his depiction of the Master. In marked contrast to his critics, who have almost invariably adopted a tone of reverence and moral gravity when speaking of the Master, Bulgakov himself refuses to take his hero quite so seriously. This has not, of course, gone entirely unnoticed. Joan Delaney—who has done more than any critic to counter- act the tendency to idealize the Master—drew attention many years ago to certain features of his portrayal which contribute to his ‘slightly ridiculous aspect’.'® Yet it could be argued that the Master cuts a more risible figure even than Delaney is pre- pared to admit. From the moment he first appears in the novel, his image is constantly undermined in a variety of ways. At times, as in the following exchange, the mockery of the ‘authorial’ narrator is quite open: ‘You're... a writer?’, the poet asked with interest. His guest’s face darkened and he threatened Ivan with his fist before saying: ‘I am a master’. He became stern and took from his dressing gown pocket a black cap which was thoroughly filthy and had embroidered upon it in yel- low silk the letter ‘M’. He put on this cap and displayed himself to Ivan both in profile and full face, so as to demonstrate that he was a master. (pp.552—-3) Everything here, from the sheer pomposity of his diction and the crude theatricality of his gestures to the final non sequitur, makes the Master seem more comic than tragic. On a later occasion, the comedy even descends briefly to the level of '® Joan Delaney, ‘The Master and Margarita: The Reach exceeds the Grasp’, Slavic Review, xxxi (1972), p.93.

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 251 farce, when the Master, like Yefrosimov in the play Adam and Eve, proves unable to recall the name of his first wife (p.556). The Master’s account of his affair with Margarita is also the source of humour, although here the comedy is of a more indirect kind. It is not that the Master’s story is intrinsically funny—quite the contrary, in fact—it is simply that he tells it in a way that makes it inadvertently so, for his tale is replete with the sort of hackneyed clichés and melodramatic effects one associates with the very worst boulevard romances: Love sprang between us like a murderer springs out of the ground in an alley. (p.556) I struggled with myself like a madman. (p.562) I could pronounce only the word: ‘You... you..?’ (p.563) ‘I perish together with you.’ (p.564) The catalogue of the Master’s dubious literary skills in this scene could be extended without difficulty. It is appropriate to recall the suggestion, mentioned above in a different context, that the story of the Master and Margarita as recounted in Chapter 13 might be read as a parody. The initial portrait of the Master is most remarkable, there- fore, for its ambivalence. The brute facts of the Master’s experience are bound both to evince sympathy for him and to arouse indignation against those responsible for his destruc- tion as a man and a writer. Yet the narrative manner employed by Bulgakov works against a moral engagement of such crude simplicity, ‘de-romanticizing’ the Master and pro- moting a more detached assessment of his predicament. Perse- cuted genius the Master may be, but his feet are made of clay. The Master’s Failure of Will: The Writer and Society Despite his outbursts of anger against the critics Ariman and Latunsky and his false ally, Aloisy Mogarych, the Master who relates his story to Ivan Bezdomny is a man burdened above all by the consciousness of his own shortcomings. ‘I have no surname,’ he tells the former poet, ‘I have renounced it, just as I have renounced everything in life’ (p.553). The rhetoric is again inflated, yet there is no mistaking the trou- bled conscience that speaks to us here. And, later, when the Master describes the onset of his paranoia, the evident pain

252 Interpretation and shame which this memory causes him suggests that he looks upon his psychic disorder as the manifestation of a moral failure. Here, as in his final insistence on the incurabi- lity of his disease (p.566), one detects a sense of personal guilt no less absolute than that which afflicts Pontius Pilate. In the Master’s eyes at least, cowardice is undoubtedly the greatest of sins, and one which allows no possibility of remission. The cowardice for which the Master holds himself to blame is the burning of the manuscript of his novel, through which act he simultaneously capitulated to the forces of mediocrity and betrayed his calling as an artist. This twin theme is devel- oped by means ofa series of parallels between the story of the Master and the central characters of the Jerusalem story— Ieshua and Pilate. We saw in Chapter 4 that the connection between the Mas- ter and Ieshua has long been acknowledged. It has, in fact, been the subject of extensive discussion and (almost inevi- tably) of disagreement. The problem, as is commonly the case with narrative parallels, has been to decide whether the device is intended to indicate a similarity or to point up a contrast. Thus, while one early reviewer recommended the Master to his readers as ‘an obvious Christ-figure’,'? a later critic con- tended that ‘the Master has few things in common with the hopeful, naive Ha-Nozri.’*° Before considering this problem any further, let us examine the nature of the connections between the two men. Here we need only summarize the find- ings of Leatherbarrow, who has indicated five points of con- tact: Ieshua’s physical crucifixion corresponds to the Master’s metaphorical ‘crucifixion’ by the critics; the Master, like Ies- hua, dies during a storm; both men leave behind disciples (Matthew, Ivan Bezdomny); both are condemned due to the ‘cowardice’ of those who represent the status quo (Pilate, the ‘petty Pilates’ of Moscow); both are betrayed by an individual inspired by greed.*' It must be admitted that these parallels "9 Choice (July-August 1968), p.633. *° E, Profler, ‘On The Master and Margarita’, Russian Literature Triquarterly, vi (1973), p.564. *" Leatherbarrow, pp.32 f.
