Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 253 are not equally precise or convincing (the first and fourth, in particular, seem somewhat forced) but this does not detract seriously from the main argument. The links between the Master and ITeshua are unmistakable; it could even be argued that these are the most prominent of all the many interconnec- tions between the novel’s two major story lines. It is crucial to note, however, that the concordance between the story of the Master and the story of Ieshua lies only at the level of dramatic conflict. It does not extend to the character of the two protagonists. It is possible, therefore, to reconcile the two positions referred to above by suggesting that the parallel is intended both to indicate the most exacting require- ment of the Master—namely, that he must be prepared, in the defence of his art, to emulate the example of Ieshua—and to emphasize his failure to meet this demand. It is not only that the Master displays none of the disarmingly simple idealism promoted by Ieshua, he also lacks the courage to withstand his ordeal. The nature of the Master’s failure is fully exposed, however, by means of the connection with Pilate. The parallel, as was indicated earlier in a different context, is richly suggestive, for it invites us to view the Master’s behaviour in the same light as Pilate’s act of cowardice. Each man is, in fact, tested in a similar manner. Confronted—directly, in the case of Pilate, indirectly, in the case of the Master—by the person of Ieshua, they are placed in a situation which demands of them the strength of will to act in accordance with what their con- science dictates as the only right thing to do. Each is charged—the one literally, the other by means of his art— with the responsibility of preserving Ieshua’s life; yet neither man is equal to the task. Pilate, as we saw in the last chapter, bows before the demands of his temporal office and allows the execution of Ieshua to take place against his better judgement and his personal wishes. The Master fails no less completely. No sooner is he exposed to the danger of becoming, like Ieshua, the innocent victim of persecution, than he loses heart, burning the manuscript of his novel, and thereby renouncing his vocation as an artist. But, even though he fails, the Master, no less than Pilate before him, is at least potentially redeemed by the sense of

254 Interpretation guilt with which he is burdened as a result of his experience. His repeated insistence to Bezdomny that he ‘no longer has a surname’ (pp.553, 560) reveals the profound sorrow of a man who has accepted his own inadequacy and this counteracts the pomposity of his ‘I am a master’, which is now exposed as a piece of mock bravado. The knowledge of his present degra- dation easily outweighs whatever pride the Master may have in his past achievement. The Limits of Artistic Vision So far I have been concerned exclusively with the moral issues arising from the conflict between the Master and the Soviet establishment, political and literary. But, to return the distinction made in Chapter 5, it must be stressed that these issues relate to the Master’s past, rather than his present. No sooner does Woland appear on the scene than the Master’s story enters into a completely new phase. True to his role as a ‘messenger’ figure, Woland has come to turn the Master’s thoughts in a different direction. His purpose is to divert attention away from a moral failing which the Master himself acknowledges towards a new understanding of his novel and its significance. It is this part of the Master’s story that corre- sponds to the experience of Margarita considered in the first part of this chapter. ~ When Woland meets the Master face to face in Chapter 24, he comes straight to the point, displaying a dogged resolve to turn the conversation at every available opportunity to the one subject that the Master seeks so studiously to avoid—his novel about Ieshua and Pilate. The Master’s reaction is understandable; for him the novel is the source of painful memories which revive the sense of injury and guilt which have led him to his present lowly state. But if Woland dis- regards the Master’s attempts at evasion, we may imagine that he does so not out of insensitivity to his suffering, nor even less out of a desire to be cruel, but because he has some- thing important to tell him about his novel. What is Woland trying to tell the Master? As we saw in Chapter 5, he informs him of two things. First, he reminds the Master that his novel is not his unique creation (‘That’s asto- nishing! And you could find no other theme??—p.703). Then

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 255 he makes a promise: ‘Your novel will bring you some more surprises yet’ (p.709). It is typical of Woland that neither statement is fully explicit. As in his dealings with Margarita, Woland speaks in a manner which makes great demands on his listener, who is expected to infer his meaning. In the first case, this is easily done. What Woland is saying, in effect, is this: “You have written a novel about the crucifixion. This is an astonishing coincidence, because I just recently told exactly the same story to Ivan Bezdomny and Misha Berlioz in the park at Patriarchs’ Ponds. What could this coincidence mean?’ In other words, Woland is telling the Master—albeit somewhat cryptically—that the novel conveys a vision that is not uniquely his, that he is the ‘vessel’ of a mysterious revela- tion. Such, then, is the first part of Woland’s message, which coincides with the third of the ‘romantic’ views canvassed above. But Woland seeks to do more than simply alert the Master to this hitherto unperceived aspect of his achievement; hence, his second statement—the enigmatic promise of future surprises. We are obliged to wait, however, until after the Master’s ‘death’ before finding out what these surprises may be. (The timing, as we shall see, is most important.) Only in Chapter 32 is the suspense finally broken by Woland’s announcement that the Master’s novel has been read (the unnamed reader presumably being none other than Ieshua himself), and that ‘only one thing was said, that it is unfortu- nately not finished’ (p.796). Woland has certainly been true to his word, for this is a surprise indeed. Now we understand fully that Woland has come to open the Master’s eyes not only to his success, but also to his failure. His vision, although truly ‘astonishing’ as a retrieval of the lost truth about events in ancient Jerusalem, is nevertheless crucially deficient. No sooner has Woland told the Master that his novel is incomplete than he proceeds to demonstrate the nature of its insufficiency in a brief, but memorable scene.** ‘So I wanted to show you your hero,’ he continues, pointing to the lonely 22 The story of Pilate on the lonely mountain top is probably adapted from an item in the Brockhaus—Efron encyclopedia which tells of the legend that Pilate appears on Mt. Pilate near Lucerne every Good Friday and washes his hands (El’baum, p.83).

256 Interpretation figure of Pilate languishing on a narrow mountain ledge, ‘For almost two thousand years he has been sitting and sleeping on this ledge, but when the full moon comes, as you see, he is tor- mented with insomnia’ (p.796). Woland’s words are charged with hidden implications. The Pilate whose terrible fate the Master now sees is recommended to him specifically as his hero, the suggestion being that this mythic projection of eter- nal punishment is intimately connected with the portrayal of Pilate in the Master’s novel. Now that he is in the superna- tural realm, the Master is granted the power to see the deficiency of what he had created. More than this, he is ena- bled to put things right. It is Margarita, however, who plays the main part in the act which brings the story of Pilate to its proper conclusion. Profoundly disturbed by the sight of the procurator’s suffering, Margarita is moved by the same com- passion that she had displayed towards Frieda at Satan’s Ball. The connection with the earlier scene is crucial, and Woland himself explicitly draws attention to it: ‘Is this a repetition of the story with Frieda?’ (p.797). Once again, Woland’s appar- ent disapproval seems to be a deliberate provocation. Margar- ita, at least, pays it no heed, taking this as a sign of Woland’s tacit encouragement. She proceeds, therefore, to re-enact her earlier role, demanding that Pilate be released. And, as before, her demand elicits ah explanation by Woland regarding the limitations of his power: ‘ ““You do not need to ask on his behalf, Margarita, because he with whom he desires to con- verse has already asked for him.” At this Woland again turned to the Master and said: ‘‘Well then, now you can com- plete your novel with a single sentence!”’ ’ (p.797). The release of Pilate, like the release of Frieda before it, is to be under- stood, then, as part ofa higher scheme in which Woland plays a subordinate part. The Master is only too happy to supply the words which will ‘complete’ his novel. His cry, ‘Free! Free! He awaits you!’ echoes in the mountains, and Pilate prepares to ascend the moonlit path together with his faithful Banga. The insuffi- ciency of the Master’s novel is now both exposed and cor- rected. For all its unconventionality, the novel had continued that part of the Christian tradition which has insisted upon Pilate’s responsibility for the death of Jesus, an act for which

Enter the Hero. . . and the Heroine 257 he must stand condemned for all time. Whether Pilate’s suf- fering be the earthly torment of a troubled conscience, as it is depicted in the Master’s novel, or the supernatural horror of life on the mountain ledge, as it is embodied in the mythic transformation, the story is one of uncompromising retribu- tion. By the addition of the scene enacted jointly by the Mas- ter and Margarita, this ‘punishment’ plot is annulled at a single stroke, so that Pilate’s story can become a plot of redemp- tton and one which, by implication, bears the seal of Ieshua’s approval. Now, at last, the abiding enigma of Ieshua’s ‘ser- mon of peace’ has been revealed. The release of Pilate is a scene in which one of the central themes of The Master and Margarita is finally illuminated. This brief fable illustrates the need to supplant a morality based on retribution by a truly Christian ethic founded on the principle of mercy. As we have seen, this is a notion towards which Bul- gakov has been guiding his reader even from the very earliest scenes of the novel, but it is only now that the significance of those earlier passages can be fully appreciated. Woland’s mission has been achieved. To the Master and Margarita he has brought the power to fathom the workings of a higher des- tiny. It only remains for him to confer upon them their final ‘reward’. The Limits of Artistic Vision: Further Perspectives The previous section was concerned with the most obvious—and undeniably the most important—sense in which the Master’s novel may be said to be incomplete. There are, however, several other ways in which the problem of incompletion may be approached. The clues to these further levels of meaning are far more cryptic, and they present a more substantial challenge to interpretation, permitting an exploration of semantic possibilities, but denying the absolute certainty necessary for a fully confident statement. One set of clues to these further levels of meaning is con- tained in the instructions regarding the Master’s novel given, respectively, by Woland to the Master, and by the Master to Bezdomny. Woland’s instructions are conveyed during his interview with the Master in Chapter 24. Despite the Master’s unwillingness to discuss his novel, Woland makes the specific

258 Interpretation proposal that he continue his literary activities: ‘if you have exhausted the procurator, why not begin to depict that Aloisy of yours?’ (p.708). The Master’s reaction is predictably hos- tile, and the discussion goes no further. The reader is left, therefore, to ponder the significance of Woland’s remarks. Woland’s broad intention is quite clear; he is attempting to spur the Master on to further creative activity. Once again, then, the implication is that the Master’s novel is unfinished. But on this occasion Woland seems to be suggesting that it is incomplete in a different way from what we have already seen, and that it must be supplemented by the story of the Master’s own recent experiences. But why should he choose to make this point by referring to Aloisy Mogarych, rather than, say, to the literary critics or any of the others involved in the per- secution of the Master? Woland’s tactic would seem to be the same as that employed earlier during the testing of Margarita. We can be sure that this is no random choice. Aloisy Mogar- ych’s name ‘crops up’, just as the critic Latunsky’s had done during the conversation with Margarita, because Woland knows that this will be the severest challenge to the Master’s understanding. On the Master’s own admission, it was the treachery of Aloisy Mogarych that he had found the hardest to bear. Just to hear this man’s name is sufficient to revive all the bitterness and hatred stored up in his mind. Behind the Mas- ter’s smile, and his insistence that a novel about his betrayal would be neither publishable nor interesting, one detects a deep residuum of rancour which renders him incapable, for the time being, of taking Woland’s real meaning. This second aspect of incompletion, although quite unlike the first, is nevertheless closely bound up with it. The Mas- ter’s inability to write the ‘true’ story of Pilate (the one which ends with redemption, rather than eternal punishment) derives from the same source as his resistance to Woland’s oblique promptings. To use Nietzsche’s famous phrase, the Master is human, all too human. His novel about Pilate is marred by the fact that it has been mediated through a menta- lity in which the uncompromising categories of guilt and pun- ishment are dominant. As one critic has suggested, ‘the theme of cowardice looms so large in the Jerusalem chapters because the Master unwittingly reveals his own inclinations through

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 259 it.’*3 By the same token, the Master’s inability to rise to the challenge of telling his own story is the mark of an incapacity to transcend the outrage of personal injury so as to perceive his experience in another light. To be human, in The Master and Margarita, is to be afflicted with a blindness which will always thwart final illumination. It is only after his physical death, therefore, that the Master can truly come to understand what Woland has been trying to tell him. As in the Gnostic scheme, the end of physical exis- tence is experienced as a release from the constraints of the mundane sphere, as a passage to a state in which higher wis- dom may be achieved. That the Master has properly achieved this higher wisdom is suggested by what he says to Ivan Bez- domny before leaving this world for ever. By an ironic rever- sal, the Master now finds himself in the position that Woland had so recently occupied with regard to himself. In the person of Bezdomny he confronts a mortal man of inevitably inferior wisdom, to whom he can pass on his instruction only in a form so indirect that it cannot bring any real understanding. What is most interesting, however, is that (again like Woland before him) he chooses to embody this message in a cryptic remark about his ill-fated novel. At their meeting, Bezdomny tells the Master both that he has renounced his previous literary endeavour and that he now wishes to write ‘something else’. The latter disclosure is sufficient to convince the Master of Bezdomny’s suitability to receive encouragement: ‘Now that’s good ... good. Why don’t you write the continuation about him? Ivanushka’s eyes flashed. ‘But aren’t you going to?...’. Here he lowered his head, adding pensively, ‘Oh, yes... what a thing to ask.’ Ivanushka looked down at the floor with a frightened gaze. ‘Yes,’ said the Master, and to Ivanushka his voice seemed unfami- liar and deep, ‘I shan’t be writing about him any more. I shall be occupied with something else.’ (p.789) This exchange is as dense as it is suggestive. The new voice, ‘unfamiliar and deep’, with which the Master speaks immedi- 23 Margot K. Frank, “The Mystery of the Master’s Final Destination’, Canadian- American Slavic Studies, xv (Nos. 2-3) (1981), p.291.

260 Interpretation ately invokes the spirit of Woland, whose own voice is dis- tinguished by the same quality of deepness. But what is this voice saying? Leaving aside for the moment the Master’s anticipation of his own future creativity, let us concentrate on the implications of the first part of the dialogue. By instructing Bezdomny to write the ‘continuation about him’, the Master automatically admits that his novel is unfinished. That much, at least, is clear. Far less clear, however, is the precise referent of the personal pronoun ‘him’. Instinctively, perhaps, we might assume that the pronoun refers to Pilate. Certainly, it can only be to Pilate that the Master refers when he later maintains that he will ‘write about him no more’. Understood like this, therefore, the Master is urging Bezdomny to write a continuation about Pilate, although just what such a conti- nuation might involve will remain a mystery until we witness the mythic resolution of Pilate’s story contained in Chapter 32. Yet, in its immediate context, the pronoun ‘him’ has another possible referent—Woland—to whom the same pro- noun had been applied only a few lines earlier.** The ambi- guity, therefore, allows for precisely the same sort of double meaning implicit in what Woland had said to the Master. In both cases, it is suggested that the Master’s novel be con- tinued on two planes: by expanding the story of Pilate; and by the addition of new material relating to recent events in Mos- cow. And this means that the resultant novel, were it to be written, would be very similar to, if not identical with, the complete text of The Master and Margarita. The last comment leads directly to a third aspect of the problem of incompletion, which is raised by the bewildering matter of the novel’s final words. This is a subject which has often been discussed; indeed, it has inspired some of the most closely argued criticism of any devoted to The Master and Mar- gartta. In view of this, it will be helpful to begin simply by quoting the relevant sections of the text. (3) Chapter 32 ends with another variation on these words. As the Master enters his ‘eternal refuge’ we read: ‘Someone was releasing the Master into freedom, just as he himself had released the hero he had created. This hero had gone into the abyss, gone never to return, forgiven on the night prior to the Sunday, the son of the astrologer-king, the cruel fifth procura- tor of Judaea, the knight Pontius Pilate’ (Kto-to otpuskal na svo- bodu mastera, kak sam on tol'ko chto otpustil im sozdannogo geroya. The major difference is that the word ‘knight’ does not feature as predicted. Commenting on these divergences, one critic has recently concluded that the second passage is ‘not the real ending of the Master’s novel’.?° In other words, the slight disparity in the phraseology of these two passages draws attention to a gap between conception and execution. The novel that the Master writes does not end in quite the way that his original inspiration had dictated that it should. His novel is flawed. When we turn to passages 3 and 4, we enter far more dangerous territory, for the published versions of The Master and Margarita vary substantially at these very points. The Romany text cited here has the two passages diverge in one small, yet notable, respect: where Pilate’s name appears as ‘Pontiy Pilat’ in the third passage, it has the form ‘Pontiyskzy Pilat’ in the fourth. These textual difficulties place inevitable constraints upon interpretation. Confronted by divergent texts, and knowing the harrowing circumstances under which the Epilogue was composed and appended to the main body of the novel, we cannot be certain which, if any, of the available versions rep- resents Bulgakov’s own preferred redaction. Even if the Moskva text is excluded from consideration on the grounds of its general unreliability, the choice between the Romany and Possev versions will remain a matter of some controversy. The coincidence is striking, and all the more so in view of the earlier non-coincidence between passages 1 and 2. To put this in the terms of the earlier discussion, therefore, the entire novel up to and including Chapter 32 ends in the man- ner that the Master had originally imagined, and thus it is this larger novel which might be said to be the proper realization of his original creative inspiration. If the story of Pilate and Ieshua is the novel he managed to write, the thirty-two chapter novel of which it is a part is the work that he was ‘called upon’ to write. It is with the fourth passage that the choice between the Romany and Possev texts becomes crucial. If one follows Pos- sev, the second word-for-word repetition has to be accounted for, or else accepted as a meaningless (although perhaps delib- erate) redundancy. (It might be added here that the decision of the Moskva editors to exclude the third passage may well have been taken out of a desire to deal with this very prob- lem.) The Romany version of passage 4, however, adds a further dimension to the hermeneutic puzzle, which has been well defined by Milne: This textual detail [i.e. the wording of passage 4] indicates that the Epilogue is not part of the Master’s novel, which ends with ‘Forgive- ness and Eternal Refuge’. The ‘novel within the novel’ is suddenly revealed as occupying the same place as the ‘outer novel’ minus Epi- logue; the Epilogue reestablishes the separate identity of Bulgakov’s The Master and Margarita from the Master’s ‘novel about Pontius Pilate’. The two figures are not identical; one contains and forms a frame around the other.”® From this account it emerges that there are three ‘novels’ involved in The Master and Margarita, or at least in that version of it which appears in Romany.*9 The first is the Master’s novel about Pilate and Ieshua, which is an imperfect realization of his original conception. The second is the larger novel minus the Epilogue, which is the perfect realization of that concep- tion, but which lies beyond his powers to fulfil. The third is 28 Milne, The Master and Margarita, p.15. “2 On this point, see Fiene, ‘A Comparison . . . ’, p.353.

264 Interpretation the entire novel, the ending of which suggests that it exceeds even the original conception by the Master. THE PREDICAMENT OF THE ARTIST The three perspectives on the incompleteness of the Master’s novel contribute to a vision of the artist’s predicament that transcends the social and political level, revealing that Bul- gakov’s concern is ultimately metaphysical. The Master’s fail- ings are neither unique, nor personal. Nor are they the product of historical circumstance; they are an inevitable part of what it means to be merely human. For the novel that the Master is called upon to write, both by Woland and by his own original inspiration is, in real terms, quite unwritable. His inspiration moves him to achieve a part of the task (the novel about Pilate) and in such a form which suggests an uncons- _ cious realization that he should have done more. But this ’ knowledge only becomes conscious when he passes beyond the limits of this world. Constrained by the brute fact of his own mortality, the earthly artist is destined always to occupy the twilight zone between the ideal and the possible. This concep- tion is again decidedly Gnostic: even for the true artist this world is still a prison, Bulgakov’s great (and possibly unique) achievement in The Master and Margarita is that he manages to arouse both our awe at what lies beyond the mortal artist’s reach, and our joy at what can be achieved despite these limi- tations. The Master’s novel about the crucifixion is a monu- ment both to the truly miraculous potential of earthly art and to its inevitable limits. But the revelation that there are greater heights still to be scaled does not diminish the power and value of what has been achieved. CONCLUSION: A SYMBIOTIC RELATIONSHIP The story of the eponymous hero and heroine confers upon The Master and Margarita both its moral force and its philoso- phical depth. This is an impression which is not substantially impaired even on a first reading of the novel, when so many of the details are bound to be obscure. One critic has described

Enter the Hero... and the Heroine 265 their story as that of a modern Tristan and Isolde, a compari- son which may not be precise on points of detail, but which captures well its immediate mythic appeal.3° The mythic quality of The Master and Margarita derives most obviously from the truly magical transformation of the Master and Margarita themselves into vessels of higher understand- ing, or ‘pneumatics’, in whom the vital spark of potential knowledge is kindled into the ever-increasing glow of true wis- dom. The evidence of the Master’s ‘spark’ is, of course, his novel. In Margarita’s case it is her deep awareness (revealed most clearly in her prophetic dream) of a greater moral order in which she must play her part. Contact with Woland, there- fore, ensures that their past experiences are perceived in a new way entirely. The story of the Master and Margarita in this world had been one of frustration and failure. The Master, although possessed of rare artistic intuition, lacked the cour- age and the strength of will to ensure that the product of his inspiration would survive the onslaughts of philistinism. Mar- garita, although she displayed both fortitude and a maternal care for the Master, nevertheless failed him at the crucial moment; by delaying the final severance from her legal hus- band she unwittingly contributed to the defeat of the Master and the destruction of his novel. But once the Master and Margarita pass into the supernatural realm, their story is translated into a timeless vision of uninhibited achievement. Not only are the mistakes of the past cancelled out (the novel is restored from the ashes; the Master is returned from the cli- nic), but each begins to realize the potential which was thwarted by the conditions of their earthly existence. Margar- ita now displays fully her propensity for love and self-sacrifice. And the Master now sees his way clear to greater artistic achievement. Love and art, the two great forces in life, tragi- cally disunited in this world, achieve the perfect symbiosis in the supernatural realm. The earthly tragedy is now just a prel- ude to the extra-mundane comedy, and it no longer inspires sorrow or regret. The mythic power of the story of the Master and Margarita is also ensured by other means. Of particular note is the 3° Natov, p.536.

266 Interpretation extreme reductiveness of their love relationship. As at least one critic has pointed out, the story that emerges from the Master’s conversation with Bezdomny is quite devoid of any explicit reference to a sexual element in their liaison." In fact, their relationship seems to have its raison d’étre only in the pro- duction of the Master’s novel. This is implicit in the following passage, where the Master describes the period after the writ- ing of the novel: ‘Completely joyless days followed. The novel was written, there was nothing else to do, and we both spent our days sitting on the rug on the floor in front of the stove looking at the fire. In any case, we were now more often apart than before. She began going out for walks’ (p.560). Their earthly love, it would appear, had no other purpose than the furtherance of art. Of equal interest is the connection between the story of the Master and Margarita and the nineteenth-century Russian novelistic tradition. Many writers have indicated that Mar- garita belongs in the pantheon of great Russian heroines. Belza, for example, finds in her a synthesis of two famous Pushkin characters, a combination of the moral purity of Tatyana (Yevgeny Onegin) and the capacity for action of Masha (The Captain’s Daughter) .°* Others have suggested further that Margarita’s relationship with the Master might be set against the background of the traditional opposition of the strong woman and the superfluous man.%% But, as I have intimated above, the story of the Master and Margarita not only belongs to this archetypal pattern, it also provides a ‘solution’ to it. The Master is indeed the typical superfluous man, the outsider denied fulfilment both in his personal and his pro- fessional life. By rendering this plight both finite and rever- sible, Bulgakov therefore supplied a resolution to a dilemma which had haunted the Russian literary mind for at least a century. Ultimately, however, it is as a drama of mutual salvation 3" A. K. Beaujour, ‘The Uses of Witches in Fedin and Bulgakov’, Slavic Review, xxxili (1974), p.698.

Enter the Hero . . . and the Heroine 267 that Bulgakov’s love story achieves its immense appeal to the imagination. It is not simply that the Master and Margarita are reunited, but that their reunion is achieved by a process of reciprocal aid and enrichment. The Master and Margarita earn their final reward in different ways: Margarita through her capacity for spontaneous action; the Master through the power of his artistic insight. Yet neither would have been able to receive their reward without the other. The Master could not be retrieved from the clinic were it not for the intervention of Margarita. And, for her part, Margarita could not have been inspired to such an act were it not for the artistic ideal which is embodied, however imperfectly, in the Master.

BE WON Dep ARC) DY: THE GOETHE CONNECTION The connections between The Master and Margarita and Goethe’s Faust have long been the subject of intensive critical discussion. Of the many approaches adopted in interpretative studies of Bulgakov’s novel in the years immediately following its publication, none was the source of more fruitful and pro- vocative debate.’ Given the prominence of the Goethean epi- graph and the unmistakable correspondences between certain events and characters in the works of both authors, such an endeavour was clearly both natural and necessary. In the midst of the massive uncertainty generated by the novel, here was an approach which not only seemed to promise under- standing, but which also enjoyed the implicit sanction of the author himself. As one critic put it, by placing the epigraph from Faust at the beginning of his novel, Bulgakov ‘alleviated the problem for his: future commentators’.* Although this remark contains an obvious truth (the ‘Faustian’ element cer- tainly 7s important to an understanding of Bulgakov’s novel), it is likely to strike the latter-day student as an example of mis- placed optimism. The assumption that the ease with which the literary subtext is identified necessarily entails an ‘allevi- ation’ of the difficulties facing the reader is one which has failed to withstand the acid test. As we shall see, this subject has given rise to no less disagreement and dispute than many others. What is more, even on the basis of the discussion in Chapter 5, it could reasonably be claimed that the discovery of links between Bulgakov’s novel and Goethe’s Faust actually tends to create difficulties rather than eliminate them. But of " See, in particular, E. Stenbock-Fermor, ‘Bulgakov’s The Master and Margarita and Goethe’s Faust’, Slavic and East European Journal, xiii (1969), pp.309-25; Haber, op.cit. * Tatishchey, p.5.

Beyond Parody: The Goethe Connection 269 one thing there can be no doubt: The Master and Margarita immediately draws attention to itself as a self-consciously ‘Faustian’ novel. Let us first establish in a general way the nature and the extent of the Faustian allusions at work in the novel. Even a cursory inspection is sufficient to reveal both that they are most numerous and that they operate at many different levels. Most obvious, of course, are those already mentioned: the epi- graph, and the connection between Woland, the Master and Margarita and their ‘prototypes’ in Goethe. Certain import- ant episodes also have their counterparts in Faust: Chapter 1 (as we saw above) adheres to the contours of Goethe’s ‘Auer- bachs Keller’ scene; the Variety Theatre performance has much in common with the Emperor’s Court scenes at the beginning of Faust 2; Satan’s ‘Grand Ball’ has certain links with the first Walpurgisnacht episode. Some of the parallels are more local]: the self-igniting benzine which starts the fires that threaten several Moscow buildings in Part II of The Mas- ter and Margarita shares its magical property with the wine that is spilled at Auerbach’s cellar. Other demonological] elements may be traced to Goethe. The tradition of witches riding on sows (so delightfully reworked by Bulgakov in the story of Natasha’s nocturnal flight) recalls the following lines: ‘Die alte Baubo kommt allein,/ Sie reitet auf einem Muttersch- wein’ (Faust, lines 3962-3). Certain of Bulgakov’s images may also have their origin in the same source. The motif of roses has already been mentioned in another context.* It is equally possible that a far more important motif—the moonlight path—owes its genesis to Faust. At the very beginning of Goethe’s work, Faust apostrophizes the moon as follows: ‘Ach! Konnt ich doch auf Bergeshohn/ In deinem lieben Lichte gehn’ (Faust, lines 392-3). In brief, the points of contact between Bulgakov’s novel and Faust are as varied as they are numerous. It remains for the reader to discover the rationale governing this insistent allusi- % Yo be specific, the ‘Weitlaufiger Saal’ and “Lustgarten’ scenes from Act I of Faust 2 involve the production of false money and miraculous gifts which disappear. 4 See above, Chapter 4.

270 Interpretation veness, and to decide upon its potential as a hermeneutic lever with which to prise the novel open. THE CRITICAL PROBLEM In their discussions of the ‘Faustian’ dimension of The Master and Margarita, critics have engaged in two distinct exercises. The first is the discovery of the precise points of contact between the two works in the manner of the preceding section. Although this has not been without its small controversies,” it is a relatively uncomplicated matter. The second exercise, however, is altogether more complex. The nature of this endeavour has been described by Wolfgang Iser. Writing of Joyce’s Ulysses, Iser notes that ‘as [the reader] recognizes the implications of the allusions, he tries to equate them with the events now being set before him’.® The exploration of these ‘equations’, involves a series of decisions which turn on the same basic question: does the allusion point up a similarity or a difference between the two works in question? Thus, in the case of The Master and Margarita, critics have constantly asked themselves how far Woland resembles Mephistopheles, the Master Faust, and Margarita Gretchen. But this is not all. So numerous and pervasive are the allusions to Goethe in Bul- gakov’s novel that a question of a different order emerges: to what extent is The Master and Margarita to be considered a ‘Faustian’ novel? What is at issue here is not so much the indi- vidual characters and their respective fates, nor even the plots of the two works, but such larger abstractions as theme, philosophy and vision. Clearly, there is ample scope for dis- agreement at both levels of discussion. We shall see below that it is possible to argue that the Master and Margarita are both like and unlike their counterparts in Goethe. With regard to the second question, the potential for divergent opinion is even greater still. In the commentary which follows, I shall address two speci- ° See, for example, Beatie and Powell (‘Story and Symbol . . . ’, p.247), who take Stenbock-Fermor to task for identifying Korov’ev with Faust. ° Wolfgang Iser, The Implied Reader (Baltimore, 1974), p.228.

Beyond Parody: The Goethe Connection 271 fic problems. The first is of a logical order, and it is best explained by means of a practical example. Helen Muchnic was one of the first to deal with the Faust theme in any real detail. Like most others since, she performs both of the inter- pretative operations identified above, examining in turn the individual characters in the two works before comparing their broad philosophy. The critic argues, most persuasively, that Bulgakov’s hero, heroine, and ‘devil’ are really quite unlike those found in Goethe, and on this premiss she founds her interpretation of the novel’s overall design. The Master and Margarita, she concludes, ‘seems to be a version of Faust but is really a parody of it [ . . . ] the borrowings are only trappings for a work that is, on the whole, less solemn and more tragic than Goethe’s and very different in tone, meaning and concep- tion.’? What is of interest here is not the validity of the judge- ments contained in this particular account of the novel, but the manner in which the critic moves from the one level of dis- cussion to the other. Once it has been argued that Bulgakov’s characters differ markedly from those found in Goethe’s Faust, logic seems to demand that the novel as a whole must be iden- tified as being broadly parodic in purpose. But this is only a seeming logic; indeed, as I shall attempt to demonstrate below, it is quite possible to read The Master and Margarita as ‘parody’ at the first level without attributing a parodic thrust to the novel as a whole. To do this is also to make the case for Bul- gakov’s novel as one of the most complex and imaginative reworkings of the Faust theme since Goethe himself. My second concern is methodological. Critical discussion of the function of allusions in fiction has an inbuilt tendency to encourage an approach to the text which is both static and fragmentary. What this means in practice is that we are prompted to pose questions of the following type: to what extent is this character like that character, or is this scene like that scene, or is this speech like that speech? But such ques- tions inevitably ignore the rhetorical system of which the allusions are a part. The same is true even if we attend to more 7 Helen Muchnic, ‘Laughter in the Dark. Bulgakov’, Russian Writers (New York,1971), p.305; ‘Ihe Master and Margarita’, ibid., p.324.

272 Interpretation obviously ‘dynamic’ elements such as plot structure.® This is not to say that such questions cannot tell us a great deal about the work being studied. It may often be the case that they will reveal everything that needs to be seen. But The Master and Margarita (like Ulysses, Bely’s Petersburg and a great many other modern novels) demands an approach which will take careful account of the manner in which the motifs are intro- duced and developed in the course of the narrative. The allusions to Goethe’s Faust in The Master and Margarita have to be viewed, therefore, as an integral part of the rhetorical pro- cesses which plunge the reader into a disturbing and unstable world of constantly shifting perspectives. The model for such an investigation is provided by the dynamics of the novel’s ‘recognition’ plot. As we saw in Chapter 5, the Faust theme is first introduced in The Master and Margarita as part of the problem of identifying Woland and his purpose. After creating a powerful identification between his ‘devil’? and Mephistopheles, Bulgakov undermines that connection in two ways: he supplies Woland with attributes which sugges? that he has a less unambiguous family tree; and he situates him in a story which is decidedly ‘un-Faustian’ in shape. Not only does this ‘Faust story’ begin at the wrong place (in medias res as it were), there is no sign either of a Faust or a Gretchen. Even when the hero and heroine do make their belated appearance, neither plays a part bearing any obvious resemblance to those of their counterparts in Goethe. The Master makes no wager with any devil; Margarita is neither seduced nor betrayed in the manner of Gretchen. And in his subsequent dealings with the tragic lovers, Woland seems to serve a purpose quite different to that of Mephisto: not only does he evidently wish the hero and heroine no harm, he even works positively to ensure their salvation. In short, there seems to be a great deal of truth in Gasparov’s suggestion that the novel’s epigraph is a sort of practical joke designed to induce ‘Faustian’ expectations which are disappointed in the * See Beatic and Powell (‘Story and Symbol ...’, pp.224 f.), who attempt to demonstrate the parallel structure of The Master and Margarita and Faust by tracing scene by scene analogies.

Beyond Parody: The Goethe Connection 273 narrative proper.? We will return to this point later. But first it will be useful to explore further the connections between the hero and heroine in Bulgakov and Goethe. HERO AND HEROINE It is in a way curious. that, despite the points raised above, commentators have consistently stressed the importance of viewing Bulgakov’s hero and heroine against the context of Goethe. This is noteworthy because Bulgakov does not force the connection upon our attention in the way that he does with Woland. Although we know that the hero in one of the earlier versions of the novel was designated ‘Faust’, there seems little reason to dispute Chudakova’s suggestion that this was never intended seriously as his final name.'° When one looks at the published texts, it would certainly be most dif- ficult to indicate a point where it could definitely be stated that Bulgakov invites us to compare his hero or heroine with their counterparts in Faust. If we make the comparison, it is because of the overall pressure of the Goethean subtext; there is no question here of Bulgakov employing Faustian allusions to render problematical the identity of the Master or Margar- ita in the way he does with Woland. Amongst those critics who have undertaken a comparison of the hero and heroine in Bulgakov and Goethe there is a large degree of unanimity. Joan Delaney speaks for the major- ity when she writes that ‘as far as the portrayal of the hero and heroine is concerned [ .. . ] the Faust story is here honoured chiefly in the breach’.'’ The Master, to be sure, bears little resemblance to Faust. When first we encounter him within the confines of Stravinsky’s clinic he cuts a very sorry figure indeed. On this evidence one is tempted to agree with Eliza- beth Stenbock-Fermor, who says of the Master that he ‘can be considered the very image of the defeated intellectual artist’.'* But although the point about the Master’s present abject con- 9 Gasparov, p.242. '© Chudakova, “Ivorcheskaya istoriya . . . ’, p.237. "' Delaney, p.g6. '* Stenbock-Fermor, p.311.

274 Interpretation dition is well made, the same writer’s further comment that ‘we have no indication that there was ever in him much of the reckless, striving Faust’ seems to go too far, for it discounts entirely the Master’s singular achievement in writing his novel about Pilate. This is an achievement which fully deserves to be described in Faustian terms. The parallel with Faust, although far from complete, 1s nevertheless precise. The Master, like Faust before him, has given up a conventional occupation and academic learning in order to pursue his personal quest. In this gesture against their respective worlds, both characters obey a similar roman- tic urge to transcend the limitations imposed upon them by their environment. Yet we must beware of flattering the Mas- ter, for the comparison also brings out an obvious difference of scale. The Master’s urge to write his novel is only a pale reflection of Faust’s desire for experience and knowledge. Where Faust was moved by a desperation and a determi- nation which drove him to risk everything in a wager with the devil, the Master’s enterprise is altogether less dangerous. Had he not had the good fortune of winning the lottery money, one senses that he might never have displayed the will to break free. There is also an ironic reversal which works against the Master in much the same way. Where Faust’s adventure begins with his release from the confines of his book-lined study, the Master undertakes his ‘Faustian’ labour within the protective womb of a cosy basement apartment with similarly book-lined walls. Although the Faustian spirit lives on in the Master, it emits a very faint light. The comparison with Faust is, moreover, doubly demeaning for Bulgakov’s hero. From the story he tells Ivan Bezdomny it emerges that, in destroying his work and escaping to the asylum, he has succumbed in precisely the way that Faust never did. For, when faced with adversity, he had ceased to strive. In the past the Master could at least lay claim to being a rather tame Faust; in the novel’s present, however, it transpires that he is a failed Faust. But what about Margarita? For the Soviet critic Belza, at least, this question is simply answered. ‘From the Faust tra- dition’, he writes of Bulgakov’s heroine, ‘contrary to the opinion of many critics, especially foreign ones, the name

Beyond Parody: The Goethe Connection 275 alone is taken’.'? On the face of it, this statement (its gibe against Bulgakov’s non-Soviet commentators notwithstand- ing) appears to be unobjectionable. Margarita shares no obvious features with Gretchen either in her character or in her fate. In her case, unlike that of Goethe’s heroine, there is not even a suggestion of her being seduced by the Faustian hero. Nor can it be said that she is lured into a liaison by the temptation of wealth; on the contrary, she is quite prepared to give up a life of fe with her legal husband in order to become the Master’s ‘secret wife’. It cannot be claimed either that she is cruelly treated by her love in the way that Faust treated Gretchen. Probably the worst that could be said of the Master is that he underestimated the extent of Margarita’s love for him. Interestingly enough, if anyone has guilty feel- ings about the tragic outcome of their relationship, it is Mar- garita herself. Her constant regret is that she deserted her lover in what proved to be his hour of greatest need. But if Margarita is not much like Gretchen, it has been maintained many times (and this is presumably what Belza was complaining about) that she might be seen as a Faust figure. The basis for this suggestion is the link that has been perceived between Margarita’s dealings with Woland and the famous Faustian wager with the devil.'* On consideration, however, this parallel proves most imprecise, if indeed it can be rightly called a parallel at all. Several critics have pointed out that, even if this relationship is to be seen in terms of a ‘wager’ (which is debatable), it is a decidedly ‘un-Faustian’ wager. Margarita only too obviously does not enter into her agreement with the devil for the same reasons as Faust. Where Goethe’s hero had wagered his soul in return for the new experiences that Mephistopheles promised him, Margarita is prepared to expose herself to danger only because she wants the Master returned to her. This is the act of a desperate and remorseful woman; there is nothing ‘Faustian’ in it at all. Nor is this really a wager. Margarita never actually makes an explicit deal of any kind with Woland or his accomplices. When she meets Azazello, she agrees to follow his instructions '3 Belza, ‘K voprosu . . . ’, p.228. '4 See, especially, Haber, pp.393 f.

276 Interpretation only because he promises that she will learn something about the Master (p.643). Other than this, their agreement has no specific terms, a circumstance which, as we saw in the last chapter, is later exploited by Woland with most important consequences. The analogy between Margarita and Faust may also be challenged on different grounds, inasmuch as a more precise analogy can be found even within the pages of Goethe’s work. The test that Margarita undergoes in Part II of The Master and Margarita betrays a remarkable similarity to the story of Helen of Troy in the third act of Faust 2. In Goethe, Helen is brought before Menelaus for reasons which are not explained to her, and, even though she has every reason to fear for herself, she trusts in her fate. Like Margarita at Satan’s Ball, she is referred to during her subsequent ordeal as ‘Queen’, and (again like Bulgakov’s heroine) she shows immense courage for the sake of others. Helen is told during proceedings by Faust that she has the choice of punishing or showing mercy, which is again a theme of central importance to Margarita’s story. And finally the ‘Phorkyas’ who actually performs the testing of Helen turns out in the end to be none other than Mephistopheles in disguise. In this respect, at least, Woland lives up to the Mephistophelian tradition, as it is his job to supervise the testing of Margarita at his ball. Two points need to be stressed here. Those who identify Margarita’s actions with the behaviour of Faust not only draw an analogy which is demonstrably imprecise. They also dis- regard the immense mythic significance (and this is true of both Bulgakov and Goethe) of the distinction between the masculine and the feminine principles. If Margarita displays courage, it is courage of an order altogether different from the arrogant ‘masculine’ challenge of Faust; hers is the ‘feminine’ courage of Goethe’s Helen, a courage born of selflessness, love and mercy. The second point is that, despite the marked simi- larity between one part of Margarita’s story and the experi- ence of Helen, the ultimate destiny of Bulgakov’s heroine still demands to be measured against the example of Gretchen. This is because in the end Margarita, just like Gretchen before her, is enabled, through the power of her love, to secure the rescue of her erstwhile lover. In so doing, both heroines func-

Beyond Parody: The Goethe Connection 277 tion as agents of a supernatural scheme which allows for the salvation of the erring hero.'> SWITCHING PERSPECTIVES: BEYOND PARODY This last comment leads to the point where we must confront a seeming paradox which has dogged so much discussion of the Faustian element in The Master and Margarita. Margarita, it has been argued here (quite unoriginally), is not really like Gretchen in her character or in the details of her fictional experience, yet she zs like Goethe’s heroine when she saves the Master. This sounds like a contradiction, but on reflection it emerges that the two views may be accommodated within a single coherent reading of the novel. In the first place, it should be noted that the two conflicting statements involve different degrees of interpretative abstraction. When we talk of the differences between Margarita and Gretchen we are dealing with the concrete details of character and story. To borrow the terminology of transformational linguistics, we are attending here to the ‘surface structure’ of the narrative. The similarity between the two heroines, on the other hand, works at another level. Using the same linguistic terminology, the parallel between Margarita and Gretchen is perceived on the plane of ‘deep structure’; we have to probe beneath the surface dissimilarities between the two stories in order to discover the essential identity of the supernatural acts of salvation with which they end. There is also a second way in which the ‘contradiction’ proves illusory. To state the difficulty surrounding Margari- ta’s ‘Faustian’ nature as if it were a static opposition (as I did above) is to ignore the all-important dynamic element in the operation of the novel’s allusive machinery. Bulgakov does not ask us to perceive Margarita as being both like and unlike Gretchen at the same time. What requires explanation is the fact that a character who strikes us initially as a most un-Gret- '5 The striking similarity between the two works in this respect has often been noted. One of the first to do so was Pletnyov, ‘Zloizlodei . . . ’, p.7.

This observation leads us back once more to Woland, for it is he who plays the key part in Margarita’s metamorphosis. His function may, therefore, be redescribed in terms of the novel’s Faustian subtext: what Woland does in his dealings with Margarita is to serve as a catalyst, permitting her to realize her latent ‘Goethean’ potential. But it is not Margarita alone who benefits from Woland’s catalytic agency. The Master too finds that. contact with Woland results in the final discovery of his ‘Faustian’ self. In order to appreciate this better, we must turn to the details of the Mas- ter’s ‘reward’, for it is here that his ‘Faustian’ future is (albeit cryptically) revealed. Once more, we shall find that the explo- ration of the Faustian theme involves the reader in a journey beyond parody. THE MASTER’S‘REWARD Few passages in The Master and Margarita have elicited as much commentary as the words with which Matthew informs the assembled company in Chapter 29 of the Master’s fate: ‘He has not earned light, he has earned peace’ (p.776). The statement, although not fully explicit, invites certain assump- tions. In the reference to the ‘light’ there appears to be an implied denial of the reward promised in such religious texts as Revelation 20: 23—5, where the New Jerusalem is described as the city that ‘had no need of the sun’. Equally evident is the idea that the reward of ‘peace’ must be seen as much as a mark of the Master’s failure as of his achievement. ‘Peace’, most critics have assumed, is a lesser manifestation of grace than to be granted access to the light.'® Thus interpreted, Matthew’s words raise two questions. Why has the Master been found deserving only of the lesser reward? And what exactly is the condition of ‘peace’ to entail? To the first question several answers have been adduced, by far the most common being that the Master is excluded from '’ For an alternative interpretation, see Wright, ‘Mikhail Bulgakow’s developing World View’, pp.164 f.

After the announcement of the ‘reward’, Bul- gakov keeps us in considerable suspense. Only in Chapter 32 do the Master and Margarita finally reach journey’s end—the vine-covered building in an idyllic landscape which is to be the site of their new ‘peaceful’ existence. The importance of this moment is obvious, even on a first reading of the novel. This is, after all, the final event in the story proper and one which brings the narrative to its natural dénouement. The scene is prepared for not only by the narra- tive logic, but also by a series of earlier references in the novel which act as prefiguring devices. One of these has been men- tioned in another context: Margarita’s dream of the ‘small log building’, from which she had awakened at the beginning of Chapter 19 (p.634). There are also a number of references to vines which are interesting in the same way. During Satan’s Ball, for example, unidentified voices urge Margarita to drink the blood from Berlioz’s skull: ‘Do not fear, Queen. The blood has long soaked into the earth. And on the spot where it was spilt vines already grow’ (p.6g1). Earlier still, Gestas, driven to madness by the ordeal of his execution, had ‘sung quietly something about a vine’ (p.597). Nor should we forget the ‘curling vine’ in the shade of which the Griboyedov club mem- bers like to relax during the heat of the Moscow summer (p.474). With these preliminaries complete, we are now in a position to deal with the question of the Master’s ultimate fate. In the final text of the novel, the Master receives not one ‘reward’, but two, and in this opposition Bulgakov invites us to inspect two different conceptions of the all-important term ‘peace’. The Master is rewarded first in accordance with Margarita’s wishes. The lovers are reunited and returned to the book-lined basement apartment which had been the scene of their hap- piest moments. But the ‘peace’ that they enjoy there is a thor- oughly unsatisfactory affair. A deliberate act of withdrawal from the world, all it can offer is the sort of ‘unconditional repose’ (‘unbedingte Ruh’) against which Goethe repeatedly inveighs in Faust.3* This ‘peace’ can bring no joy, as it is char- acterized by an emptiness which renders new experience, either emotional or intellectual, quite impossible. All that remains is the oblivion of sleep, and the escape which Margar- ita discovers in re-reading the restored chapters of the Mas- ter’s novel. The ‘peace’ which Margarita secures for the Master, although a sign of her good intentions, is also a monument to her inferior wisdom. By removing the Master from Stra- vinsky’s clinic to the basement apartment, she merely demon- strates a truth of which the Master had been aware when he told Bezdomny, at their first meeting, that he had ‘nowhere to run off to’ (p.548). He has Woland himself explain to the Master and Margarita when they appear before him after their physical death: ‘Margarita Nikolayevna! As in the penultimate draft, pride of place in his vision of the future is reserved for the promise of Faustian cre- ation, made even more obvious now by the actual reference to Goethe’s hero by name. (It was Wagner, however, who created the homunculus in Goethe’s Faust.) But why then does Woland also evoke the possibility of mere passive recreation by talking of walks under the cherry trees and listening to

Beyond Parody: The Goethe Connection 287 romantic music? This ambiguity can be best understood, I think, if we are prepared to accept that even here Woland is testing his listeners. The real question at issue, therefore, is not so much the indeterminacy of Woland’s words as the particu- lar interpretation that the Master and Margarita choose to place upon them. Once again, this marks a division between the ‘masculine’ and the ‘feminine’ principles. The Master, as one might expect, responds only to Woland’s summons to new creative activity. We have already seen that he had alluded to some such endeavour during his final conversation with Bez- domny, to whom he had explained that he would no longer be working at his novel because he would be ‘occupied with something else’ (p.789). Margarita’s response to Woland’s ambiguous promise is the very opposite of the Master’s. For her, the vine-covered cottage offers nothing more than the prospect of idyllic rec- reation. The proof of her partial understanding is her descrip- tion of the final destination as it first comes into sight: ‘Listen to the soundlessness . .. Listen, and enjoy the silence you were never given in life. Look, up ahead stands your eternal home, which you have been given as a reward. The present reading of the Master’s ‘reward’ offers an alternative to those who have spoken of it either approvingly, as a sort of Arcadian dream, or else disparagingly, as a ‘senti- mental happy ending’.2? Common to both these opinions is the acceptance at face value of what I have taken to be ironic. It seems particularly appropriate that this irony should hinge on the reader’s appreciation of the Goethean sub-text. Yanovskaya has detected in the formula ‘not light, but peace’ a polemic with Goethe.%’ It is certainly true, as she suggests, that the Master’s fate differs markedly from Faust’s uncon- ditional access to heaven implied at the end of Goethe’s work. But ‘peace’ too is a crucial Goethean concept, which denotes the purely negative urge to be spared the anxiety which is the price of striving. It might also be suggested that the idyllic cot- tage of the conclusion contains an oblique allusion to the motif of the hut in Faust. During the ‘Wald und Hohle’ episode of Faust 1, for example, Goethe’s hero complains of his fate as a restless wanderer and thinks wistfully of Gretchen and her ‘little hut’ (line 3353). But Bulgakov invokes these Goethean motifs only to complicate their meaning, for the ‘peace’ to be enjoyed in ¢his ‘little hut’ is a healthy combination of striving and repose. Again, the relationship of the hero and heroine promises a perfect symbiosis. The ‘reward’ of the Master and Margarita commands attention, therefore, as a ‘Faustian’ puzzle which, once deci- phered, allows for the final redefinition of Woland’s myster- ious mission. Where his coming encouraged a false impression of his ‘Mephistophelian’ purpose, his departure from the novel enables a deeper understanding of his Goethean signifi- cance. Beyond Parody: The Goethe Connection 289 A‘FAUSTIAN NOVEL? The thrust of the above argument has been to suggest the important contribution made by the allusions to Goethe’s Faust to the playful rhetorical system of The Master and Margar- ita. As in so many other instances, the reader is obliged to per- form a disturbing double movement. From an initial position where Bulgakov’s purpose would appear to be broadly paro- dic, we progress to the point where the Goethean subtext is perceived quite differently as a key to the novel’s meaning. This movement ‘beyond parody’ parallels and augments the central ‘recognition’ plot, allowing us to identify and describe all the more clearly Woland’s catalytic effect upon the hero and heroine. It is difficult to find a precise critical vocabulary to convey this shift of perspective, although we might say that parody gives way to an ‘adaptive fantasy’. The latter term belongs to W. R. Irwin, who explains that in such works the author’s inventiveness, ‘however spectacular [ ... ] has its validation from the work that provided the original and con- tinuing impetus’.3® The point may again be stated in the ter- minology of transformational linguistics. Thus, we begin by perceiving the radical differences between the surface structure of the two works, discovering that the ‘Faust’ figure isn’t really like Faust, or the ‘Gretchen’ like Gretchen, and so on. But, in the end, we are permitted to understand that both stories may be transformations of a similar deep structure. This obser- vation leads automatically to the question which stands at the beginning of this section. To what extent can Goethe’s Faust be said to provide a model for The Master and Margarita? I shall address this question under four headings. Overall Cosmology The first (and deepest) level of similarity between The Mas- ter and Margarita and Goethe’s Faust lies in their overall cosmo- logy. Each work tells a tragic story of this world (the ‘kleine Welt’ in Goethe’s description) which finally becomes part of a larger universal scheme which permits that tragedy to be transcended. The sorrows and frustrations of earthly existence 38 Irwin, pp.153 f.

290 Interpretation are annulled once they are perceived as the prologue to the extra-mundane mystery which will be experienced by the pro- tagonists after the formal closure of the two works. Both works fit, therefore, within a conventional religious framework, according to which the ‘kleine Welt’ is understood as a lesser, transitional state which is experienced as a test of worthiness for the higher realm. Yet the relationship between the events of ‘this’ world and those of the higher realm is, in The Master and Margarita, no less than in Faust, a matter of no small difh- culty, for both authors challenge what we might call a naive apocalyptic explanation of the divine scheme and its oper- ation. The apocalyptic tradition, as represented by the myth of the Last Judgement, works with an uncompromising Old Testament notion of justice based on the ethical categories of vice and virtue—‘and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works’ (Revelation 20:12). In its crudest form, this mentality finds expression in the idea of the New Jerusalem as a reward for good deeds performed on this earth, and of Hell as the place where the evil are punished for their sins. Of the two works under consideration here, it is Faust which makes the greater assault on this conventional apocalyptic view. Much of Faust’s behaviour in the ‘kleine Welt’ is bound to evoke a feeling of antipathy in the audience. No matter how much we admire or identify with his restless striving, this feel- ing will inevitably be counterbalanced by the moral abhor- rence we must feel for the destruction of Gretchen and her family. Nor should it be forgotten that Faust’s initial quest was predicated upon his rebellion against God. The salvation of Faust was, as we know, Goethe’s major innovation in his treatment of a legend which had hitherto reinforced the con- ventional apocalyptic mentality to which we have referred. To strive is to err, the Lord says in the ‘Prolog im Himmel’, and, in the final reckoning, it is the striving, not the erring which has to be taken into account. To accept this involves the aban- donment of that ‘normal’ moral perspective which would grant salvation only to those who lead a ‘virtuous’ existence in the ‘kleine Welt’. The Master and Margarita does not challenge our everyday notions of right and wrong so radically. The Master is not

Beyond Parody: The Goethe Connection 291 implicated in any acts so heinous as those of Goethe’s Faust: he is to a large extent more sinned against than sinning. Hence, the commonly held view that his ultimate fate is only a fair reward for the suffering he endured at the hands of the literary establishment. In the words of Leatherbarrow, ‘Bul- gakov would seem to be suggesting that there exists an impar- tial, universal justice which eventually compensates for the injustices perpetrated by human law.’3? This judgement has its source in the feeling that most people probably experience on reading The Master and Margarita for the first time—a sense of rightness about the Master’s reward which is certainly very different from the profound ambivalence generated by the fate of Goethe’s hero. Nevertheless, Bulgakov’s novel resists the reading offered above in two ways. Firstly, it is made quite explicit in the text that the Master receives his ‘reward’ not as a ‘compensation’ for his unjust treatment by his contemporar- ies, but in recognition of his achievement in writing the novel. ‘He has read the Master’s composition,’ Matthew tells Woland when he brings the news of Ieshua’s decision, ‘and he asks you to take the Master with you and reward him with peace’ (p.776). Much as we might sympathize with the Master’s pre- dicament in the philistine world of Moscow literary politics, this has no direct bearing on his ‘reward’. There is nothing to suggest the working of any kind of ‘compensatory’ ethic. It is here that the second, and greater, difficulty arises. If the ground for the Master’s reward lies in the striving which produced the novel, it must be noted that this reward is granted even in the face of the Master’s withdrawal from the struggle when he meets with adversity. Our admiration for his achievement has to be weighed, therefore, against his failure of will. It is here that the basic similarity with Goethe’s Faust resides. Where Goethe tells us that to strive is to err, Bulgakov implies that to strive is to fail. In each case it is the striving which proves in the end to be the crucial thing. For both authors, therefore, even the most grave human failings do not automatically warrant the punishment demanded by the naive apocalyptic mind, for such failings are viewed as an inevitable consequence of life in an imperfect world. But the 39 Leatherbarrow, p.39.

292 Interpretation fact remains that Goethe’s vision is the more profoundly dis- turbing of the two. This is not only because Faust’s failings are more reprehensible than the Master’s, but also because his final reward is (unlike that of Bulgakov’s hero) unequivocally positive. At the end of Goethe’s work there is no suggestion that Faust has been granted anything other than accession to the light. His sins, it seems, are of no account at all when it comes to the final reckoning. Bulgakov, however, shrinks from the boldness of the Goethean resolution. As we have just seen, he has his hero receive a ‘reward’ which nevertheless appears to make an allowance for his failings: the Master has earned not light, but peace. The Role of the Devil Broadly speaking, the ‘devil’ plays a similar role in the cos- mological scheme of The Master and Margarita and Faust. Both authors adhere to an Old Testament conception which is neatly summed up in the words of Carus: ‘God needs the Devil for a servant and utilizes his malignity for the procrea- tion of good.’*° In Faust the devil’s part is spelled out in so many words in the ‘Prolog im Himmel’ and is alluded to later in the famous words of Mephistopheles which Bulgakov chose for the epigraph to his novel. Although Woland’s place in the divine plan 1 is never so explicity stated in The Master and Mar- garita, it is made plain that his powers, like those of Mephisto- pheles, are limited and subservient to a higher authority. On each occasion, the limitation concerns an act of mercy (the release from suffering of Frieda and Pilate; the granting of ‘peace’ to the Master), which Woland openly admits to lie outside his ‘jurisdiction’.*' But the deep similarity between Woland and Mephisto- pheles should not blind us to some most important differences. Mephistopheles plays his part in the divine scheme unwill- ingly and unwittingly. Woland, by contrast, seems much more 4° Carus, p.342. ** The limits to Woland’s powers were introduced at a relatively early stage in the novel’s composition. Where Mephistopheles employs every trick he knows to dis- tract Faust from striving, Woland’s task is the very opposite: to awaken the Master from the state of ‘unconditional repose’ into which he has fallen after the destruction of his manus- cript. And this is what leads to the feeling that Woland, for all his cynical posing with Margarita, is far less nihilistically inclined towards the mundane sphere than Goethe’s devil. Mephistopheles, as J. W. Smeed describes him in a useful thumbnail sketch, is ‘the adversary of all faith and optimism, the personification of mockery’.*? The Woland who promises to drink to ‘being’ from Berlioz’s skull at the end of the ball (p.68g) could hardly be further removed from the tempera- ment which finds its most memorable expression in the lines: ‘Ich bin der Geist, der stets verneint!’ (Faust, line 1340). But this is only to say what we have already discovered—that Woland is far less ‘devilish’ than Mephistopheles. In The Mas- ter and Margarita the ‘devil’ is assigned the role of messenger; this is perhaps Bulgakov’s most radical departure from the Goethean conception, the further implication of which will be considered in the very conclusion of this chapter. Man and Woman Apart for the salvation of the hero, Goethe’s principal inno- vation in his treatment of the Faust theme was to include within the framework of the original legend a love story. The fact that Bulgakov follows both precedents in The Master and Margarita is what makes it so distinctly “Goethean’ a work. (Compare the other great Faust novel of the twentieth cen- tury, Thomas Mann’s Doctor Faustus, which adopts neither of Goethe’s modifications.) And, as we saw in Chapter 7, Bulgakov excludes from the relationship between his hero and heroine the explicit sexual element which features so prominently in Goethe. Neverthe- less, the Russian author adheres in his novel to the same broad mythopoeic conception of the sexes as that which informs Goethe’s Faust. In both works the spirit of striving is invested in the hero, while it falls to the heroine to embody the merciful power of love. In each case also the potentially pro- ductive symbiosis of the ‘masculine’ and ‘feminine’ principles is rendered possible only beyond ‘this’ world. Good and Evil The connection between Goethe and Bulgakov with regard to the problem of theodicy has already been touched upon. The key to Bulgakov’s view of the matter in The Master and Margarita, most critics have agreed, is to be found in Woland’s words to Matthew in Chapter 29: ‘You utter your words as if you don’t acknowledge shadows, or evil either. But would you be so good as to consider this question: what would your good- ness do if evil did not exist, and what would the world look like if all shadows disappeared from it?’ (p.776). This objection to Matthew’s simplistic understanding of the working of a bene- volent providence can be traced to the passage at the begin- ning of Goethe’s ‘Prolog im Himmel’, where Gabriel describes earthly life as the constant alternation of day and night, a con- dition which is explicitly contrasted to the pure light of heaven (Faust, lines 251-4).** Commenting on this passage in Goethe, one critic has made an observation which holds equally for The Master and Margarita. The movement of night and day reminds us, she writes, that ‘the earth remains the unharmo- nious spot to which man is confined.’ Neither Bulgakov nor Goethe hold out any promise of reform for a world which is in this irretrievably fallen state. The ‘continuation of life’ promised to the hero and heroine at the end of Bulgakov’s novel is very much more concrete and physical than what is merely hinted at in Faust. Also, it is not so much the case that past good and evil are ‘accepted’ in this new realm of existence, but rather that they are annulled. Nevertheless, there is no mistaking the similarity of the overall providential scheme. No discussion of good and evil in Goethe and Bulgakov would be complete without some reference to what has remained one of the thorniest problems of all—Bulgakov’s choice of epigraph. The issue here is once again the connec- tion between Woland and Mephistopheles: can the latter’s description of himself as a ‘part of that power which wills for- ever evil yet works forever good’ be applied in any meaningful way to Bulgakov’s character? Most critics have answered this question in the negative.*” Although Woland does bring some evil into the world, this evil is largely incidental and incon- sequential and, for the most part, it does not result from his active participation in events. Even if one does hold Woland responsible for the behaviour of his entourage, Matthew’s later reference to him as the ‘spirit of evil’ (p.775) must still appear the grossest oversimplification. Matthew seems unaware of motive or scale: it is one thing to frighten a doctor by having a sparrow dance on his desk, and another thing altogether to create the sort of mayhem that Mephistopheles does. What weighs even more heavily against Matthew’s judgement, however, is Woland’s behaviour towards the hero and heroine.
