296 Interpretation But if the majority of Bulgakov’s commentators have been prepared to accept that the epigraph does not describe Woland, they have been much less willing to leave the matter there. Indeed, their determination to discern some other sort of relevance in this passage has resulted in some of the most inventive (although sometimes most confusing) interpret- ations. The most common line of argument has been to sug- gest that the epigraph should not be taken to refer to Woland at all. Thus, one critic writes that it ‘alludes to other devils— agents of the Soviet system who are indeed shown as doing good when they will evil’.4° In other words, it is not Woland, but such characters as Latunsky, Berlioz and the rest who unwittingly serve an ultimate good which les beyond their powers of understanding. Behind the obvious ideological appeal of such a reading lurks another, which is even more seductive; by transferring the Faustian reference from Woland to other characters in the novel, one is able to clear up what would otherwise have to remain the source of disturbing uncertainty. My criticism of the above interpretation of the epigraph (and of others that I have read) is that it does not so much explain its meaning as explain that meaning away. To shift the ostensible referent of Goethe’s lines is an arbitrary act which deprives the epigraph of its rhetorical force and seman- tic density: a challenging paradox is converted into a harmless puzzle which permits an easy ‘solution’. Boris Eykhenbaum puts his finger on the real problem in his well-known dis- cussion of Tolstoy’s epigraph to Anna Karenina. Taking issue with those critics who had attempted to translate the Tol- stoyan epigraph into a condensed statement of the novel’s meaning, he argued for a different approach, which would explore the rhetorical relationship between the epigraph and the novel which it precedes.*9 Following Eykhenbaum’s lead, the epigraph from Faust can be shown to serve several pur- poses. Its immediate function, as we have seen, is simply to trigger the all-important subtext, so that even as we embark on our reading of the novel we are set to wondering about its 48 Bolen, p.430. See also, Proffer, “The Master and Margarita’, p.4o1; Pope, p.21. Boris Eykhenbaum, Lev Tolstoy. Semidesyatyye gody (Leningrad, 1974), pp.168 f.

Beyond Parody: The Goethe Connection 297 possible connection with Goethe. Subsequently, the epigraph takes on further significance. On the one hand, the question with which it begins may be seen as an allusion to the main theme of the novel (Who is Woland?). On the other hand, it complicates that crucial issue by inviting a simple identifi- cation of Woland with Mephistopheles which cannot finally be sustained. If we wish to make the epigraph ‘mean’ any- thing more than this, it might be suggested that it captures a paradox which will set in train an interpretative exercise which leads to the very heart of the novel’s philosophy. To say that The Master and Margarita is a ‘Faustian’ novel does not necessarily mean that we need to make a final decision on the points of correspondence between the two works at all. What really matters is that the Goethean subtext is what brings the main issues of Bulgakov’s novel into the sharpest focus. THE LIMITS OF INTERPRETATION This is an appropriate moment to consider further the manner in which Bulgakov’s novel resists finite interpretation by reviewing some of the general matters raised in the preceding section. Let us take first the matter of the novel’s overall cos- mology. The above discussion, although precise as a broad description of the scheme at work in both Goethe and Bul- gakov, nevertheless runs the danger of making the ending of The Master and Margarita sound rather too cut and dried. In reality, the novel raises difficulties of an order which would be obvious to anyone with theological interests. These problems emerge when we attend closely to the implied connection between the outcome of the two main story lines. Taken by itself, the ‘reward’ of the Master involves no substantial chal- lenge to understanding. Bulgakov’s account of this particular operation is both full and explicit. The Master, we are led to believe, is rewarded by Woland in accordance with Ieshua’s wishes (see Matthew’s exchange with Woland—p.776). But the Master is not the only one to be rewarded in the novel; so too are Pilate and Matthew. And it is when we try to reconcile these various ‘rewards’ that the complications emerge. What is Matthew’s ‘reward’? His appearance in Chapter 29 as the bearer of the message from Ieshua seems to imply that

298 Interpretation he has been granted access to the light, an implication which is reinforced by the form of Woland’s later question to the for- mer disciple (‘Why don’t you take him with you into the light?’—p.776). But on what grounds, we might ask, has he achieved this lofty status? On the basis of our discussion in Chapter 6, it would be easy enough to argue for his exclusion from the light: why is it then that his faults do not weigh against him as the Master’s obviously do? And, if he has been taken into the light, why does Woland have to explain to him the insufficiencies of his understanding? In Matthew’s case, at least, accession to the light would seem not to be synonymous with enlightenment. The liberation of Pilate is a matter even more complex. As far as the story of Matthew is concerned, it is tempting to sug- gest that the uncertainty surrounding his destiny was the pro- duct of an oversight, and that Bulgakov may well have dealt with this problem had he been granted the opportunity to complete his revision of the novel. But this does not hold in the case of Pilate, for the drafts of The Master and Margarita show that Bulgakov had thought carefully about the connection between the procurator’s release and the Master’s ‘reward’. The variants of the novel, as we have seen, testify to the diffi- culties that this raised in the author’s mind. Where one vari- ant contains the instruction that the Master should follow Pilate, this solution was reversed completely in the published text, in which Woland tells the Master in so many words that he is not to follow the procurator (p.798). But if this final decision was clearly the product of some cal- culation, this does not change the fact that it leaves many vital questions open. Does the insistence that the Master is not to follow Pilate mean that the procurator has been admitted to the light? (Is this where the moonlight path leads?) If so, this would imply that Pilate’s act of cowardice is of a lesser order of significance than the Master’s failure, thereby reversing our more usual perception of the relative seriousness of their sins. Does the Master’s abandonment of his novel really place him below Pilate on the providential scale? But we do not have to read it this way. It could just as well be that Pilate’s ‘reward’ corresponds neither to ‘peace’ nor ‘light’ and that he is being judged, therefore, on entirely different criteria. (Note that,

Beyond Parody: The Goethe Connection 299 whereas in an earlier variant Pilate too had been granted ‘peace’, in the final text no name is attached to the procura- tor’s ‘reward’ other than the Master’s exultant cry, ‘Free! Free!’—p.797). Does Bulgakov perhaps wish to suggest by this change that the artist is subject to a different code from ordinary mortals? This interpretation might then be extended to encompass Woland?’s famous words at the ball: ‘To each will be given according to his faith’ (p.689). But, like all such ‘solutions’, this only brings other problems in its wake. As we have already seen, Woland’s dictum is itself hedged around with all manner of dangers. It is, of course, quite possible that the explanation is much simpler. As Yanovskaya has sug- gested, it could be that, for understandable reasons, Bulgakov baulked at a conclusion which would have granted an obviously autobiographical hero access to ‘heavenly light’.>° There are, however, more difficulties still. To return to the Master, is his ‘reward’ to be seen as a permanent state or as a transitional stage on the path to the light?>' Another range of imponderables is opened up if we ask how all these various ‘rewards’—in each of which Ieshua plays an important, though different, part—relate to the remarks made by Ieshua in his earthly incarnation about the coming ‘kingdom of truth’? Is that kingdom synonymous with the ‘light’, or are ‘light’ and ‘peace’ two different parts of that future kingdom? When one surveys what has been written about The Master and Margarita the most remarkable thing is that these ques- tions have been asked far less often than they should have been. Many critics have, in fact, claimed to have discovered in The Master and Margarita a metaphysical system which is reducible to a set of simple propositions. It is imperative, therefore, to emphasize just how great is the resistance of the text to exegesis at this point. As it stands, the novel is disturb- ingly open, ambiguous—perhaps even contradictory—once we begin to probe the operation of the providential order which it demonstrates. In this most fundamental sense, then, the ending of The Master and Margarita must be judged unread- able. Given the problems surrounding the novel’s composition, 5° Yanovskaya, p.313. 5! But even though it seems safe to assume that Bulgakov would have made further changes at this crucial point, it is far from certain that these would have resolved all (or even any) of the difficulties mentioned above. As it stands, The Master and Margarita concludes with a vision of grace which, because of its stubborn resistance to intellectual expla- nation, must inevitably remain a mystery beyond the grasp of mere reason. This is what makes it the most deeply religious of books. THEE PILOGUE: BETWEEN TWO WORLDS Bulgakov’s decision to conclude The Master and Margarita with an epilogue came late in the novel’s creative history. As we saw in Chapter 2, this final section was appended to the manuscript only in the spring of 1939, at the very time it was being read to a close circle of the writer’s friends.’ There could be more to this than mere coincidence. Bulgakov displayed a particular interest in the response of his first audience, and their reactions may well have inspired the inclusion of the new material, although we will probably never know for certain. But, whatever his reasons, there can be no doubt that by adding this final dozen or so pages, Bulgakov altered comple- tely the final impression conveyed by his novel. Anyone familiar with the works of Nikolay Gogol will experience a strong sense of déja vu on reading the Epilogue to The Master and Margarita. Gogol was, in fact, Bulgakov’s acknowledged favourite among Russian writers,” and it is in this final part of the novel that his indebtedness to the nine- teenth-century author is most evident. Of particular note is the unmistakable correspondence between the Epilogue and the conclusion of the two best-known ‘St. Petersburg Tales’-— ‘The Nose’ and ‘The Overcoat’. As in the Gogol stories, much of the narrative here is given over to the dissemination of gossip and speculation. The parallels even extend to points of detail: for example, the discovery of suspicious black cats in the wake of Woland’s disappearance is reminiscent of the repeated sightings of Akaky Akakiyevich’s ghost at the end of " Chudakova, ‘Arkhiv .. . ’, p.135. ? Popov noted that Bulgakov once said: ‘Of Russian writers I prefer Gogol; to my mind, there is no one to compare with him’ (ibid. 93). 3 On the subject of Bulgakov and Gogol, see: M. 304 Interpretation ‘The Overcoat’. But such local correspondences are of real importance only as symptoms of the profound narrative sub- versiveness which characterizes the works of both authors at this crucial juncture. Just like Gogol, Bulgakov chose to end his fiction with a deliberate anti-climax, retreating from the awesome realm of the supernatural into the comic inconse- quentiality of the familiar world. Rather than leave us to cel- ebrate the extra-mundane ‘comedy of victory’ (to borrow Milne’s felicitous phrase), Bulgakov ensures that we ponder the distance which separates that comedy from the grotesque reality of mundane existence. But, as was suggested in a different context earlier in this study, the disruptive impact of the Epilogue is ensured above all by the manner in which it reverses the apocalyptic expec- tations generated by the preceding narrative. The removal of the Master and Margarita from Moscow had been accompa- nied by numerous intimations that the Russian capital was doomed to imminent destruction. The apocalyptic associ- ations of this scene have been well described by Leatherbar- row: “The departure of Woland and his crew also contains a veiled reference to the trumpeting angels of the Apocalypse, for just as the trumpets bring down mountains, turn the sea to blood, sink ships and bring darkness over a third of the world, so do the farewell whistles of Korov’ev and Behemoth tear down trees, boil the river Moskva and ground the boats that sail upon it.’* Other critics have commented on the apocalyp- tic overtones of the fire which threatens to consume Moscow. Gasparov has suggested a possible connection with the ending of Dostoyevsky’s The Devils,> while Ericson has detected in the figures of Woland and his retinue an allusion to the four horse- men of the Apocalypse, an observation which leads him to conclude that the final part of Bulgakov’s novel is an ‘elabor- ate parody’ of the Revelation of St John.° Bulgakov’s intention may not always have been parodic, however. Chudakova reports that in an earlier redaction the fire of Moscow had been much more of a reality than in the final text. As the Mas- * Leatherbarrow, p.42. > Gasparovy, p.255. ® Ericson, p.36.

The Epilogue: Between Two Worlds 305 ter and Margarita flew high above the city, they witnessed horrific scenes of death and destruction.” But in the end the parodic impulse is to the fore: the pro- mised annihilation of Moscow, the modern ‘Harlot-City’, ON only to a busy night’s work for the emergency ser- vices. Not that this should come as any great surprise. Even as the flames leapt through the restaurant at the Griboyedov Club, we would have remembered Korov’ev’s earlier assur- ance that a new establishment will rise phoenix-like from the ashes of the old (p.778). The Epilogue merely confirms this prophecy. Moscow is not destroyed, and the lives of its inhabi- tants are not changed in any significant way. The sum effect of Woland’s sojourn is the destruction of four buildings, two deaths, three disappearances, and a temporary increase in the occupancy of the city’s psychiatric hospitals (p.801). In short, life returns to its normal course, and the people of Moscow, like Major Kovalyov at the end of “The Nose’, are enabled to forget about the recent intrusion of the supernatural into their world. The anti-apocalyptic element in the Epilogue has an important implication for the overall metaphysical scheme of The Master and Margarita. By means of the parodic reversal, Bulgakov reveals that his outlook is not eschatological; access to the higher realm is not contingent upon the end of this world. The denial of the temporal perspective is, however, less significant in itself than as an indirect challenge to the simple ethical conception which I have referred to as being naively apocalyptic. Bulgakov defies such a crude view of human des- tiny by placing the emphasis in this final section not on the notions of punishment and reward, but on the quintessentially Gnostic problem of understanding. During the account of the behaviour of the Russian population in the aftermath of Woland’s visit, we are constantly invited to laugh at their will- ingness to accept the ‘scientific’ explanations offered by the authorities, and hence at the inadequacy of a mentality which precludes even the possibility of any proper comprehension of the extra-mundane. 7 Chudakova, “I'vorcheskaya istoriya . . . ’, p.238. 8 In this connection, note Azazello’s earlier comparison of Moscow to Rome, the original ‘Harlot-City’ (p.775).

306 Interpretation The problem of understanding is also central to the depic- tion of Ivan Bezdomny in the passage which brings the Epilo- gue—and the entire novel—to a close. Bezdomny’s experience is similar to that of the majority of Moscow inhabitants, yet it is also different in one crucial respect. Although he too takes his place in the renewed normality of Moscow life, the return involves a major change in his life. On his release from Stra- vinsky’s clinic, he remains true to the promise he made to the Master. He does not resume his career as a poet; instead, when we meet up with him one spring evening several years after the main events of the novel, he is introduced as a ‘mem- ber of the Institute of History and Philosophy, Professor Ivan Nikolayevich Ponyryov’ (p.808). More importantly still, Bez- domny is further distinguished from his fellow-Muscovites by the fact that he has retained a dim memory of past events, a memory which returns to disturb him every spring full moon. Critics have differed markedly in their interpretation of these details, opinion being quite sharply polarized between an optimistic and a pessimistic tendency. The most extreme statement of the optimistic view belongs to Bolen, who writes: ‘Bezdomny, like the Master, becomes a student of philosophy. This is an indication that he will go beyond the discoveries of his teacher.’? Others, have been tempted to make even more speculative suggestions. Bagby surmises that the former poet ‘will continue the Master’s work’,'® and Pope looks still further into the future when he presumes that Bezdomny ‘will doubtless be taken unto Ieshua in the Kingdom of Light when he dies, just like that other reformed sinner, Matthew the Mevitese The parallel between the two ‘disciples’ is, however, open to a different construction. Altshuler has harnessed a similar observation to the less comforting argument that neither man proves adequate to the demands of his calling.'? This point is taken up by Gasparov, who comments that, just as Matthew’s ° Bolen, p.435. The Epilogue: Between Two Worlds 307 account of Ieshua is hopelessly defective, so Bezdomny will inevitably fail in the task with which he has been entrusted.'3 Haber puts the case somewhat differently, restating the pes- simistic position in political terms by reading the story of Bez- domny in the Epilogue as a metaphor of the predicament confronting all intellectuals in the Soviet Union. ‘In the per- son of Ivan Bezdomny,’ she writes, ‘Bulgakov seems to be sug- gesting that this Pilate-like double-life is bound to appear in the Soviet artist or intellectual who tries to live both in the world of his imagination and in the atheistic and oppressive everyday world.’ '# The optimistic arguments do not stand up well against these contrary opinions. As a further counterweight to Bolen’s sanguine view of Bezdomny’s future, it must be added that the former poet’s new activities as philosopher and historian do not necessarily bode well for him. To view this occupation as a pledge of his progress towards truth and the fulfilment of his duty as the Master’s ‘disciple’ is to ignore the serious con- straints imposed by party ideology on the practice of both disciplines, especially in Stalin’s Russia. If anything, Bez- domny’s new professional activities should perhaps be seen as a sign of his failure, or at least of his compromise with the forces of mundanity. The most serious weakness of the optimistic interpretations, however, is that they fail to take account of the irony with which Bezdomny is treated in the Epilogue. When Bulgakov tells us that ‘Ivan Nikolayevich is aware of everything, he knows and understands everything’ (p.808), we can be sure that he does so with his tongue in his cheek. For in the account which follows it is the limitations of his knowledge and under- standing which are stressed at every turn. We watch the for- mer poet, on the night of the full moon, as he is irresistibly drawn to an unknown apartment block where he listens to the incomprehensible ravings of a strange man who sits on the bench outside. The reader, of course, is privy to the very infor- mation that Bezdomny lacks: we know that the apartment block is Margarita’s, that the strange man is Nikolay Ivano- '3 Gasparov, p.209. '4 Haber, pp.407 f.

308 Interpretation vich, and that his peculiar mutterings relate to his experiences on the night of Satan’s Ball. But despite the emphasis on his earthly limitations, Bez- domny still displays signs of his higher calling. For all his new- found ‘worldliness’, he remains susceptible to the power of revelation. Returning home after his nocturnal peregrinations, the former poet has two dreams. The first is described as fol- lows: On the night of the full moon, the scholar is always awakened and driven to utter pitiful cries by the same thing. He secs an unnatural, noscless executioner jump up with a sort of grunting noise, and plunge a spear into the heart of Gestas, who is tied to the post, and has lost his reason. But what is terrifying is not so much the executioner as the unusual illumination in this dream, which comes from a cloud that boils, and tumbles down on to the earth, as happens only during world catastrophes. (pp.810—-11) Although obviously a traumatic recapitulation of the execution scene from his earlier dream in Chapter 16, this is a typically distorted nightmare vision, in which disparate details from the previous revelation combine to create a pic- ture of unrelieved horror. The ‘noseless executioner’ is almost certainly a dream image of Mark Krysoboy, whose facial disfi- gurement identifies him both as a victim and as an agent of extreme human cruelty. The ‘boiling’ cloud, on the other hand, reminds us of the violent thunderstorm which brought the execution to a hasty conclusion. Here too, the remem- brance of the earlier passage draws attention to the uncons- cious process which transforms past experience into present distress, so that the natural phenomenon becomes a symbol of apocalyptic catastrophe. As usual, Bezdomny awakes in terror from his nightmare, which is the signal for his wife to administer the injection which will relieve his suffering. As he sinks into a new sleep, his apocalyptic anxieties yield to a state of peace which is accompanied by a second dream: now he witnesses the meet- ing of Pilate and Ieshua on the moonlit path, and hears the latter swear to the procurator that the execution had never taken place. This is a consoling vision which nullifies the impact of the preceding nightmare by the simple denial of the

The Epilogue: Between Two Worlds 309 event which was its source. The resultant sense of liberation is marked by a reversal. The second dream, like the first, is char- acterized by a strange effect of lighting which brings it to a close: “he moonlit way boils up, a lunar river begins to gush from it, and to flow in all directions’ (p.811). The verb ‘boils up’ (vskipayet) recalls the awesome cloud which also ‘boils’ (Aipit) in the nightmare, yet this new image, despite its poten- tial connotation of destruction through inundation, is the source of aesthetic delight rather than existential anxiety.'> The juxtaposition of Bezdomny’s two dreams brings The Master and Margarita to a most appropriate conclusion, for it captures in microcosm the essence of Bulgakov’s metaphysical dualism. The evils of this world—suggested in the nightmare motifs of bondage, madness, and execution—are set against the sure promise of another realm of existence in which these evils will be forgotten. But this final section is more than a simple philosophical reprise. Its significance is extended con- siderably by the echoes within it of earlier key scenes in the novel. Most obvious in this respect is the connection between Bezdomny’s second vision and the dream which visited Pilate in Chapter 26. This is not just an example of partial overlap. Bezdomny’s double dream is, in effect, a total reenactment of the procurator’s earlier experience: both men are torn between the anxiety caused by the memory of the execution and the transcendence which comes with the assurance of the reversibility of that fateful event. But the former poet’s situ- ation reminds us not only of Pilate. As the exhausted Bez- domny sleeps, his faithful wife sits reading at his bedside. In so doing, she unwittingly emulates the behaviour of Margarita during her last night in Moscow with the Master. Because of this double allusiveness, the final scene acquires an extraordinary density, for Bezdomny’s dreams are thereby associated with the scenes in which the two main heroes of the novel—Pilate and the Master—experience the ‘anguish’ which is the fate of all those caught between the two worlds of existence. The connection between the three men is reinforced 'S Bulgakov’s first novel, The White Guard, also ends with the explicit contrast between two different types of dream. For details see my ‘Apocalypse or Revela- tion? ...

310 Interpretation by Bezdomny’s exclamation, ‘Gods, Gods!’ (p.809). Similar words had been uttered both by the Master and by Pilate at moments of stress; now they become a mark of the deep bond which exists between them as superior beings cast adrift in a hopelessly corrupt world.'° The conclusion of the novel therefore avoids the simple optimism that so many of the novel’s readers have fixed upon it. Like the earlier experiences of Pilate and the Master, Bez- domny’s dreams invoke the cruel logic of the Gnostic out- look—that those who are susceptible to extra-mundane awareness are inevitably burdened by a sense of despair at man’s earthly lot. Ericson makes this point well when he writes of the former poet: “Despite his intellectual rejection, some dim perception of the truth penetrates his soul. He occu- pies that twilight zone on the spectrum of faith, suspended between belief and disbelief. He is ““Homeless”’.’'7 The ambiguity of Bezdomny’s position is also to the fore in the brief vision which functions as a sort of postscript to his second dream. The explosion of moonlight gives way in the dreamer’s mind to a final encounter with the Master and Margarita. The meeting recapitulates the scene at the end of Chapter 30, where the hero and heroine had appeared to the former poet in his room at the asylum before flying off to their ‘eternal refuge’. Margarita plays an identical part in both scenes, even repeating word for word what she had told Bez- domny on that earlier occasion: ‘for you everything will be as it should be’ (pp.790, 811). In the final passage this consola- tion is enhanced by the addition of a sentence which has often been cited as a statement of the novel’s ‘message’: ‘Everything has ended, and everything ends’ (p.811). Yet here, as in the earlier scene, Margarita’s determination to ease Bezdomny’s distress has to be set against the Master’s purpose, which is quite different. The Epilogue: Between Two Worlds B11 lem of the Master’s novel, and its incompletion.'® As we saw in Chapter 7, the Master’s aim in returning to the asylum had been to alert Bezdomny to the need to write a ‘continuation’ of the novel with which he himself would no longer be occupied. Now, in this last encounter, he is assured that his follower has understood the full significance of what he has just dreamed. ‘So that’s how it ended: then?’ asks Bezdomny. ‘That’s how it ended, my disciple,’ is the Master’s reply (p.811). The exchange reveals that Bezdomny is fully apprised of the impli- cation of his dream for his calling as a ‘disciple’: he is now in possession of the wisdom which he has been instructed to pre- serve. Now, like the Master before him, he too could complete the novel about Pilate by transforming it into a story of redemption. But even as we marvel at this last example of the mysterious intuition vested in the chosen few, we are reminded of the double bind which afflicts all real artists in The Master and Margarita. For the circumstances under which this transcen- dent vision is transmitted ensure that it can never be commu- nicated to an audience in this world. The specific condition of Bezdomny’s return to health and consciousness the following morning is that he is deprived of the power of recollection: ‘His tortured memory grows quiet, and until the next full moon the professor will be troubled by no one. Neither by the noseless murderer of Gestas, nor by the cruel fifth procurator of Judaea, the knight Pontius Pilate’ (p.812). But this is not the only way in which the novel’s conclusion is unsettling. By drawing our attention once more to the status of The Master and Margarita as a literary conception which can never be com- municated, it raises the question of how it is that we could have come to be reading it at all. The novel leaves us to con- template the problem of its own provenance, and in so doing imparts an awareness of the unique privilege which has been granted to us: we have been permitted to read the ‘unwritable’ text. By leaving us to ponder this final paradox, Bulgakov con- fers upon his novel a sense of the profoundest mystery. CONCLUSION From the moment of his first arrival in Moscow to take up a writing career Bulgakov established a reputation as something of a maverick figure. As is so often the case with reputations, Bulgakov’s image owed more than a little to careful cultiva- tion on the part of the writer himself, and it was sometimes manifested in a rather unsubtle manner. Immediately upon joining the staff of the satirical weekly, Gudok, Bulgakov dis- tanced himself from his younger colleagues by the affectation of ‘aristocratic’ dress and mannerisms. At a time when prole- tarian caps and jackets were very much the order of the day amongst the new writing fraternity, Mikhail Afanas’evich sported well-tailored (if rather threadbare) suits, immacula- tely laundered linen, and—most outrageously of all—a mon- ocle, which has now become almost legendary.’ This ostentatious display of preference for pre-revolutionary sartor- ial elegance was a provocative gesture for which the writer paid dearly during the RAPP campaign against him. But it would be wrong to suggest that this was just a pose. It should be seen rather as a sign of a sincere concern to identify himself as a guardian of older cultural values. Ye. Sheremet’eva, who met Bulgakov towards the end of the 1920s, records him as insisting that he and she belonged to ‘different generations’. ‘Don’t forget,’ he wrote in a subsequent letter, ‘that you were born in the twentieth century, while I was born in the nine- teenth.” The above comments naturally give rise to the vexed issue of Bulgakov’s political stance. This is something which lies beyond my present concern; the reader interested in such mat- ters should consult the available biographical studies of the writer for guidance on this subject. Conclusion 313 address here is the place of The Master and Margarita in the Russian literary tradition. To what extent is Bulgakov’s final work to be considered a Soviet novel? In one sense, at least, this question is simply answered. It can easily be demonstrated how much The Master and Margar- ita is the product of the age in which it was written. We have already observed, for example, that Bulgakov’s satire is every- where rooted in the realia of post-revolutionary Russia, a practice which places him alongside such noteworthy contem- porary practitioners of the satirical art as Katayev, IIf and Petrov, Zoshchenko, and Mayakovsky. It has also been shown that Bulgakov’s treatment of the New Testament story occu- pies a special place in the religious debate of the 1920s. Add to this the prominent role of literary polemic in the novel, and it is not difficult to see how the case can be made for considering The Master and Margarita a ‘Soviet’ novel. But for all that, the heart of Bulgakov’s work lies elsewhere. In theme and manner, it announces its indebtedness to the art of the pre- revolutionary period, and in particular to the nineteenth- century tradition of the fantastic, as represented in the work of Gogol and Dostoyevsky. The marks of Gogol’s influence on The Master and Margarita are especially plain. Many of the novel’s supernatural motifs can be traced back to similar scenes in Gogol’s early ‘Ukrai- nian’ tales, which abound in all manner of diablery. It has often been noted, for example, that the scene of Rimsky’s terr- ible ordeal, from which he is saved only by the crowing of the cockerel, is a reprise of one of Gogol’s most memorable explo- rations of the supernatural, the story ‘Viy’.2 The idea of endowing some of his characters with names of the famous may have been suggested to Bulgakov by one of the ‘St Peters- burg Tales’, ‘Nevsky Avenue’, which features both a Schiller and a Hoffmann among its fictional personnel.* It was from the ‘St Petersburg Tales’ also, as I suggested in the last chapter, that Bulgakov learned much of the art of narrative 3M. The Dostoyevskian elements in The Master and Margarita are less pervasive than the Gogolian, yet they are no less import- ant. The connection between Bulgakov and Dostoyevsky is not so much a matter of style or narrative manner; it 1s to be encountered rather at the level of character and idea. There are, of course, certain obvious borrowings. We have already remarked that Korov’ev displays the same sartorial taste (or lack of it) as Ivan Karamazov’s devil. But this is only a super- ficial detail. It is in his portrait of leshua that Bulgakov’s real affinity with Dostoyevsky is most clearly in evidence.> The clash between Ieshua and Pilate in Chapter 2 is reminiscent in its spare dramatic form of the famous confrontation of Christ and the Grand Inquisitor in The Brothers Karamazov. In Bul- gakov’s novel, as in Ivan Karamazov’s fable, the two protago- nists are immediately identifiable as the representatives of two inimical principles, and their subsequent clash in both cases acquires the force of an existential parable. But this is not the only Dostoyevskian element in Ieshua’s portraiture. A combination of disarming idealism, gauche- ness, and utter helplessness, Bulgakov’s character also dis- plays his kinship with Dostoyevsky’s other well-known Christ figure, Prince Myshkin, the eponymous hero of The Idiot. It is of particular interest that Myshkin is portrayed more as the embodiment of the Christian principle than as its spokesman, for here too it might be suggested that Dostoyevsky left his mark on Bulgakov’s novel. Myshkin’s overt message is, like Ieshua’s, to be found only in the occasional aphoristic state- ment—‘beauty will save the world’, ‘humility is a terrible force’. The rest is to be inferred from his behaviour and his fate. But the most important connection between Bulgakov and Dostoyevsky may lie even deeper, in the metaphysical dualism which characterizes The Master and Margarita and (most especially among the latter’s works) The Brothers Kara- mazov. A recent detailed comparison of the two novels contains > Chudakova, ‘Opyt rekonstruktsii . . . ’, pp.103 f.

Conclusion 315 the suggestion that each is informed by the Kantian distinc- tion between phenomenon and noumenon.° The mention of Kant leads directly to the tradition with which Bulgakov’s novel most demands to be associated. For Kant was a key influence in the revolution of aesthetic, philo- sophical and religious ideas at the turn of the twentieth cen- tury which accompanied the rise of Russian Symbolism. Indeed, Gogol and Dostoyevsky too had a part in this intellec- tual ferment which was far from insignificant, insofar as they were instantly recognized by the major representatives of the new trend as their ‘precursors’. “The problem of Gogol,’ wrote Nikolay Berdyayev (himself an important figure in this cul- tural renaissance), ‘was present only to that religious-philoso- phical movement which took shape in our country at the beginning of the twentieth century.’’ Dostoyevsky was subject to a similar ‘rediscovery’. In books and articles by Bely, Bryu- sov, Vyacheslav Ivanov, and many others (including Ber- dyayev himself) the works of both great authors were reinterpreted so as to bring out their relation to the particular concerns of the new movement.® It was to this ‘Symbolist’ Gogol and Dostoyevsky that we should properly say that Bul- gakov was the heir. Bulgakov’s obligation to the intellectual heritage of Russian Symbolism is immense. The writer was in his impressionable teens when the movement enjoyed its heyday, and one can easily imagine the interest generated by its religious aspect in a household where the father was a professor of theology. Bul- gakov’s father apparently attended meetings of the Vladimir Solov’yov society (named after the religious philosopher acknowledged by such eminent Symbolists as Bely and Blok as their spiritual guide), to which he was accompanied by V. 316 Conclusion as a historian of Russian philosophy.? But the precise nature of Bulgakov’s acquaintance with the Symbolist movement seems destined to remain a mystery. Chudakova reports with regret that nothing has come to light regarding Bulgakov’s reading of Symbolist works, either literary or theoretical,’° and published sources yield precious little to shed light on his opinion of, or contact with, the ideas of that school. By the time he began his writing career Symbolism was already a spent force, having been succeeded by Acmeism, and—more noisily—by Futurism, as well as a host of the ephemeral groupings and re-groupings which make the literary history of the late tsarist and early Soviet period so interesting and con- fusing. It is possible that Bulgakov encountered some of the surviving members of the Symbolist school who remained in the Soviet Union. The Lenin Library has a copy of one of Bely’s books from Bulgakov’s personal collection which con- tains a handwritten dedication by the author, but there is no record of the two men having met.'' Although an uncompli- mentary reference to theosophy, apparently made in a conver- sation with Yermolinsky towards the end of the author’s life suggests a predictable scepticism about one of the more notorious excesses associated with the Symbolists,’* this really tells us nothing about his attitude towards a movement which has left an indelible imprint upon his last great masterpiece. Bulgakov’s twin interest in the themes of Christ and the devil will come as no surprise to the student of Russia’s ‘Silver Age’. The resurgence of religious thought witnessed an unpar- alleled interest in the founder of Christianity, and a veritable obsession with the black arts which was even more pro- nounced, if shorter-lived. Christian revisionism had received a strong, and much-publicized, impetus from the redoubtable figure of Lev Tolstoy, and now it became one of the most characteristic features of the age. 318 Conclusion Symbolism was the most overt manifestation of a dissatisfac- tion with philosophical materialism and scientific rationalism, an intellectual rebellion which had its roots in the work of Dostoyevsky and Solov’yov. The influence of these ideas was particularly profound after the abortive revolution of 1905, and its essence is captured in the words of Boris Pasternak, who was himself much attracted by Symbolist philosophy (he was talking in an interview many years later): During the short period of time that we live in this world we have to understand our attitude toward existence, our place in the universe. Otherwise, life is meaningless. This, as I understand it, means a rejection of the nineteenth-century materialistic world view, means a resurrection of religion—not in the sense of religious church dogma, but as an attitude to the universe.’® In the writings of the Symbolists, both philosophical and liter- ary, this conception of human existence was expressed in terms of a philosophical dualism, to which Russians often refer as dvoyemiriye. In the tradition of Plato and Kant, these writers postulated the existence of a second, higher reality (cf. Plato’s world of spirit, Kant’s noumenal world) situated beyond the everyday world of phenomena, which is only its reflection. The purpose of life, therefore, is to penetrate the ‘symbols’ of the phenomenal world, and expose the ‘real’ reality which lies beyond. The classic fictional statements of this type of thinking are Sologub’s The Petty Demon and Bely’s The Silver Dove. In these novels the everyday world is depicted either as a grotesque banality (Sologub), or as an unfathom- able nightmare (Bely). The result is in each case the same: the central character, lacking the wisdom which could provide deliverance, is sacrificed to the evil power which rules ‘this’ world. This metaphysical system carried with it important impli- cations both for the nature of art and for the role of the artist. Art was now defined as an act of ‘theurgy’; it was an essen- tially religious practice in which the artist was to function as a sort of priest, a mediator of the hidden truth about human existence. The question of the artist’s role was one which par- '© Cited in Leonid D. Rzhevsky, Solzhenitsyn. Creator and Heroic Deed, tr. Sonja Miller (Alabama, 1978), p.17.

Conclusion 319 ticularly occupied Andrey Bely. Writing of Bely’s early thea- trical interests, George Kalbouss has made a comment which could be applied to his entire endeavour, as well as to that of some of his fellow Symbolists. Kalbouss notes that Bely was especially drawn to the mystery, an art form which ‘through its symbolism, mythological imagery, and structure [.. . | would create a religious experience for its audience and reveal a world hidden within the ieal one’.'7 We are already in a position to see that The Master and Mar- garita is a quintessentially ‘Symbolist’ novel. The metaphysi- cal opposition of ‘two worlds’; the demonstration of the inadequacy of materialist philosophy; the purpose of art as the revelation of a hidden mystery—all of this speaks for Bulgak- ov’s indebtedness to the Symbolist tradition. But, for all that, the novel is perhaps best described as a post-Symbolist work. Bulgakov was, after all, writing long after the demise of Sym- bolism as an active movement on the Russian literary scene, and it would be foolish to suggest that he was working con- sciously within the framework of Symbolist philosophy or aes- thetics. Moreover, he harnesses these recognizably ‘Symbolist’ elements in his last novel to a vision which is unmistakably his own, and which actually counters the intense pessimism which characterizes so much Symbolist fic- tion. Taking The Petty Demon and The Silver Dove again as a par- adigm, we find that both novels offer a frightening picture of ‘this’ world, against which the ‘created legend’ of Lyudmila’s pagan eroticism (in Sologub), or the cryptic promise of trans- cendence by the astrologist Schmidt (in Bely) offer faint hope of improvement. So intensely did these writers experience the lowly condition of man’s everyday existence that their trans- cendent longings were almost inevitably translated into a vision of helplessness and frustration. The Master and Margarita is altogether more optimistic and affirmative. Although Bul- gakov too proceeds from the premiss that ‘this’ world is in an irreparably ‘fallen’ state, he makes this the source of laughter, not fear. As Nadine Natov puts it, he transforms ‘hostile, incongruous and frequently terrifying everyday realities '7 George Kaibouss, ‘Andrey Bely and the Modernist Movement in Russian Drama’, in Andrey Bely. A Critical Review, ed. Gerald Janacek (Lexington, Kentucky, 1978), p.147.-

320 Conclusion [ ... ] into a funny, carnivalesque fantasmagoria’.'" Thus he shifts the focus of his attention from the tragic implications of life in an inferior world to a celebration of man’s potential to ascend to the sort of higher condition to which the Symbolists aspired. Bulgakov’s singular achievement is that he manages this without trivializing the Symbolist dilemma or resorting to facile escapist solutions. I have often had occasion in these pages to refer to apoca- lyptic and Gnostic ideas. Both were traditions of thought which occupied a prominent place in the Symbolist tradition, and nowhere more so than in the work of Solov’yov. But although Bulgakov would certainly have been acquainted with Solov’yov’s ideas, which were widely discussed even out- side Symbolist circles, it seems likely that his influence upon Bulgakov’s intellectual development was mainly of a general, indirect kind. (This is not to say that a detailed examination of The Master and Margarita in the light of Solov'yov’s ideas might not yield interesting findings.) But there are others who may have exerted a more direct and specific influence on the direc- tion of Bulgakov’s thought. One is the the eighteenth-century Ukrainian thinker Grigory Skovoroda, whose philosophy, like Solov’yov’s, has a markedly Gnostic orientation. The case for Skovoroda’s influence on Bulgakov has been put most persua- sively in a recent Soviet article, which explores the broad afli- nity between the novel and Skovoroda’s metaphysical system, and also offers fascinating insights into such particular mat- ters as the role of Woland, the lunar motif, and the distinction between ‘peace’ and ‘light’.'9 It is also interesting to note that books which Bulgakov is known to have consulted during his work on The Master and Margarita often contain statements on apocalyptic and Gnostic ideas which bear directly upon crucial aspects of the novel’s conception. Renan’s discussion of the Kingdom of God in Chapter 17 of his Life of Jesus is a case in point. For the French writer, the apocalyptic predictions attributed to Jesus are the source of dissatisfaction, even embarrassment. This ‘false, cold, and impossible idea of an ostentatious advent’ he '® Natov, p.538. ‘9 Galinskaya, * “Master i Margarita” ...°, pp.111, 114.

Conclusion 325 declares to be quite out of keeping with the beautiful idealism expressed in the Sermon on the Mount, which, in his view, is where the ‘real’ Jesus is to be found.” A similar critique of apocalyptic thinking is present in the work of Robertson. Like Renan, he too was struck by the contradiction between apoca- lyptic statements about the Kingdom of God and the ideas contained in the Sermon on the Mount. But Robertson was not at all concerned by the problem of the authenticity of these sayings. His discussion of these key passages of the Gospels turns rather upon the distinction between the two different types of apocalyptic thinking that he discerns in them. The first, he says, is reflected in the promise of Heaven as the scene of future happiness, which he describes (not without sarcasm) as a ‘happy and lasting dwelling-place on high’.*’ This pro- mise Robertson finds in the Sermon on the Mount, which for him—in complete contrast to Renan—represents one of Christianity’s principal ‘opiates’, beguiling the oppressed with the hope of ‘the future state of reward’.*” In the idea of the Kingdom of God, on the other hand (particularly as it is con- veyed in Mark’s gospel) Robertson detects a different concep- tion of apocalypse, and one which turns on the importance of mystic revelation. In this conception, which Robertson expresses in recognizably Gnostic vocabulary, the Kingdom of God is a ‘mystery’, an item of knowledge which has to be passed on to the ‘unknowledgeable’ in the form not of sermons but of ‘cryptic parables’.”” These passages highlight issues which lie at the centre of The Master and Margarita. Renan’s determination to distinguish the retributive urge from the true essence of Christianity, and Robertson’s critique of naive apocalyptic expectations read like a commentary to Bulgakov’s novel. No less important is Robertson’s implicit recommendation of the cryptic parable as the proper vehicle for the expression of a transcendent truth. What better example of such a parable than The Master and Margarita itself? Consider also the following passage from ” Renan, p.162. *# John M. Robertson, Christianity and Mythology, 2nd edn. 322 Conclusion the work of Drews which rehearses ideas by now so familiar that it can stand without comment: Gnosticism also involves a completely dualistic philosophy in its opposition of God and the world, of spirit and matter, of soul and body, etc. [... ] It treats the ‘Gnosis’, the knowledge, the proper insight into the coherence of things as the necessary condition of redemption. The individual must know that his soul comes from God, that it is only temporarily confined in the prison of the body and that it is intended for something higher than to be lost here in the obscurity of ignorance, of evil and of sin; so that he is already freed from the trammels of the flesh, and finds a new life for himself. The God-Redeemer descended upon earth to impart this knowledge to mankind; and Gnosticism pledges itself on the basis of the ‘revela- tion’ received directly from God, to open to those who strive for the highest knowledge all the heights and depths of Heaven and earth.** A later passage in which the same author summarizes his objection to the gospel accounts of Jesus is equally arresting: The great idea, which Christianity brought to the consciousness of the men of the West and through which it conquered Judaism—the idea of the God-man—was utterly destroyed and the true content of this religion was obscured, hidden, and misrepresented in such dis- astrous fashion, that today it is no longer possible to assert its doc- trine of redemption without the sacrifice of the intellect.*> The Master and Margarita could almost have been written in support of Drews’s premiss and as a refutation of his conclu- sion. In his final novel, Bulgakov manages to retrieve this ‘great idea’ of Christianity, incorporating it into a mythic statement so powerful that it is indeed possible to ‘assert its doctrine of redemption’. As for the attendant ‘sacrifice of the intellect’, Bulgakov seems to invite the response that this is no real sacrifice at all. The passages from Renan, Robertson and Drews are per- haps best regarded as ingredients in the melting pot from which Bulgakov’s own ideas emerged. None of the works named represents a system of thought even remotely approxi- mating the artistic conception of Bulgakov’s last novel. For the rationalism of Drews and Robertson Bulgakov had only “t A. Drews, The Christ Myth, tr. C. Delisle Burns (London, 1911), pp.273 f¢. *5 Thid. 282.

Conclusion 309 contempt (witness the fate of Berlioz, their spokesman in The Master and Margarita), while Renan’s Life, although important as an influence on the treatment of the passion story, left no real mark on the philosophy of the novel as a whole. But there is one book which does appear to shed light on The Master and Margarita in this more fundamental sense. It is Nikolay Ber- dyayev’s The Meaning of the Creative Act, which was published in Moscow in 1916.?° It is not known whether Bulgakov ever read this book, but the points of concordance between the ideas which it contains and those expressed in the novel are sufficient to warrant a brief exposition of Berdyayev’s thesis. The Meaning of the Creative Act begins with a confession of what the author calls an ‘almost Manichean dualism’ (MCA, p.15). ‘Phe human being is in prison,’ Berdyayev proclaims in his typically aphoristic manner, ‘Prison is what I call this world’ (MCA, p.11). This ‘given world of necessity’, as he terms it in the same place, stands in marked contrast to God’s cosmos, which is the realm of the free human spirit. This dua- listic conception is not static, however, but profoundly histori- cal. Human history, as Berdyayev sees it, begins with the fall of man, which entailed the loss of the divine gift of freedom, and set in motion a process which will end with man’s return to original grace. The fall of man has been followed by two historical periods: the Old Testament era, the era of the ‘law’; and the New Testament era, the era of ‘redemption’. It is in this latter era that we are now living. The coming of Christ, which marks the division between these two eras, is, therefore, the most important event in the history of humanity. But, according to Berdyayev, this is an event which has not been properly understood; even worse, it has actually been misre- presented by the Church fathers and by later generations of churchmen, whom he criticizes for their ‘failure to reveal the anthropological truth of Christianity (MCA, p.85). This ‘anthropological truth’ resides, he claims, in the revelation that ‘through Christ every human person is a part not of the 20 N. Berdyayev, Smysl tworchestva. 324 Conclusion mortal world alone, but of the Divine as well’ (MCA, pp.78 f.). The coming of Christ, in other words, is a pledge for the future, and not merely a release from the past, and this is what Berdyayev believes not to have been fully appreciated. The true meaning of Christ will only be comprehended, in his view, when man becomes conscious of the ‘relationship between the mystery of creation and the mystery of redemp- tion’ (MCA, p.g3). For Christ has not only brought the pro- mise of redemption, he has also restored man’s creative freedom, and it is in this Christ-given ‘creativeness’ that we are to discover ‘the final revelation of the Holy Trinity—its anthropological revelation’ (MCA, p.110). The era of redemption has freed man for creation, and creation itself is the means to the final goal, which is an age of creation beyond the confines of ‘this’ world. The future age of creation is, however, a blessed state which is beyond mortal imagination, and quite different from the experience of creativity within ‘this’ world, which will always be felt more as a burden than as a benefit. Berdyayev explains: ‘In its essence, creativity is painful and tragic. The purpose of the creative impulse is the attainment of another life, another world, an ascent into being. But the result of a creative act is a book, a picture or a legal institution [ ... | Herein lies the painful contrast between the aims of creativity and the results of creating’ (MCA, p.119). Summarizing this same position towards the end of his life, he wrote: ‘Man’s creative act is doomed to fail within the conditions of this world.’?’ But the creative act, although inescapably tragic, remains the sole mark of conquest over the world, and the sacrifice of the artist in ‘this’ world must be understood as a promise of the future age—hence Berdyayev’s praise of the Russian Symbolists as the ‘sacrificial forerunners and heralds of the coming world- epoch of creativeness’ (MCA, p.241). Berdyayev’s metaphysical scheme is a creative fusion of eschatological and Gnostic ideas which bears an uncanny resemblance to the world-view implicit in The Master and Mar- *7 N. Berdyayev, Dream and Reality. An Essay in Autobiography, tr. Katherine Lampert (London, 1950), p.214.

Conclusion 325 garita. The drama of Woland’s coming to Moscow may readily be reformulated in terms of Berdyayev’s ‘three epochs of div- ine revelation’ (MCA, p.320). The figure who first appears to be the agent of retribution, and hence to represent the epoch of the ‘law’, proves in reality to be the ambassador who reveals the message of ‘redemption’ which is embodied in the person of Ieshua. As in Berdyayev, Bulgakov’s characters inhabit a world in which the true meaning of Christianity has yet to be revealed. And Woland’s final act may also be des- cribed in Berdyayevan terms as the release of the Master into the age of creation which is man’s ultimate destiny. As for Berdyayev’s idea of the creative act in ‘this’ world as one which is tragically doomed to failure, yet is the pledge of the future attainment of true creativity, it is hard to conceive that this could receive more faithful literary expression than in the story of the Master’s novel. ‘My predilection for the themes of eschatology did not inspire any special liking for the Book of Revelation, or any desire to indulge in interpretations and commentaries on it. If anything I recoiled at the apocalyptic literature from Enoch onwards, because of its odious elements of revenge and retri- butive justice and its tendency to establish a sharp division of humanity into the good and the wicked.’*® This is Berdyayev again, reviewing the conception of morality expounded in his later book The Destiny of Man. The same critique of naive apo- calyptic notions can be found in The Meaning of the Creative Act. Of greatest interest for the present discussion is the specific criticism in the earlier book of the ‘apocalyptic’ understanding of the coming reward, which is irretrievably ‘earthly’ in his opinion. ‘Even the Kingdom of Heaven,’ he complains, ‘is represented as eternal rest (MCA, p.279). Elsewhere he expresses his hope that such negative thinking will not ‘quench the Faustian desire for fulness of life’ (MCA, p.271). Resuming this theme towards the end of the book, he explains: ‘We cannot merely passively await the coming of Christ, we must be up to go toward Him. The sense of the apocalyptic will lead to a new religious life only ifit becomes actively crea- tive instead of passively expectant? (MCA, pp.335 f.). To 28 Thid. 291.

326 Conclusion indicate the connection between these statements and the con- clusion of The Master and Margarita would be to labour a point which should already be obvious. Also noteworthy are Ber- dyayev’s repeated references to the great demands placed upon the individual who exercises the gift of creative freedom. ‘For creativeness is needed great courage’, he says (MCA, p.107). He then goes on to warn against the danger of the art- ist being afflicted by the sin of cowardice: ‘he who coward-like refuses the terrible burden of the final freedom cannot be orientated towards the coming Christ’ (MCA, pp.107 f.). And what reader of The Master and Margarita could read the follow- ing passage without at least raising an eyebrow? Berdyayev is writing of repentance: ‘it should not lead to spiritual despair, for despair is the greatest sin’ (MCA, p.166). For both Berdyayev and Bulgakov it is the figure of Christ who stands at the centre of the human drama. Just as the cru- cifixion is the dividing line between Berdyayev’s two epochs in the history of man, so it is the story of Ieshua which marks out the elect in The Master and Margarita. ‘Man is reborn a new creature through the cosmic mystery of redemption. And man is reborn into the new Adam only if he has had an immanent experience of the Crucifixion’ (MCA, p.98). This is Berdyayev once more, but it could be Bulgakov’s novel that he is talking about. The two writers are also united in their belief that the story of Christ has been woefully misunderstood, even by those who have claimed to be Christ’s followers. ‘The authen- tic image of Christ,’ Berdyayev wrote later, ‘transcends the one disclosed in the Gospels which present its refraction in the dark glass of human limitations.’*9 The crucifixion is, there- fore, the ultimate challenge to human understanding, which, once accepted, contains the promise of further enlightenment. “The mystery of redemption,’ says Berdyayev, ‘conceals the mystery of creativeness’ (MCA, p.1o1). In the absence of corroborative evidence, the question of Berdyayev’s possible influence upon Bulgakov will have to remain open. The correspondences between The Meaning of the Creative Act and The Master and Margarita are quite remarkable, yet they may be purely accidental, a case of a philosopher and 9 Ibid. 300.

Conclusion 327 a novelist working independently towards a similar view of human destiny. But the broader matter of Bulgakov’s place in the aesthetic and philosophical tradition of the Silver Age can be in no doubt. This leads back to the point with which I began: Bulgakov’s sense that he was not just an outsider, but even something of an anachronism in Soviet literary life. The Master and Margarita substantiates that belief. Aithough the circumstances of its publication ensured that it became caught up in the post-Stalinist debate, it is as a spectacular belated flower of Russia’s Silver Age that it should command the attention of the literary historian. The novel’s continuing republication in the Soviet Union must, therefore, be judged one of the greatest signs of hope for the cultural life of that country. For The Master and Margarita provides a vital bridge to a cultural tradition which, until recently, had been almost entirely lost to the modern generation of Russians. It also offers a timely reminder that, even in a land where such values have not been officially encouraged, art retains the power to disturb and to amaze, to entertain and to puzzle, provoking us to think again about what it means to be human. What more could be asked of any novel?
